author: Equality Now
title: Consent does not depend on one’s level of intoxication: The Cornell University Case in review
content:
15th October 2026


Consent does not depend on one’s level of intoxication: The Cornell University Case in review


14 min read


News and Insights


End sexual violence


United States


The allegations presented in the

sexual violence case involving a Cornell University student

 describe egregious acts of sexual violence and profound violations of the human rights of the alleged survivor. The case returned to public attention two years after the alleged assault, when the accuser, known publicly as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit in 2026, bringing renewed scrutiny to the handling of her allegations and the evidence surrounding them while simultaneously raising serious concerns about whether criminal justice systems are fit to conduct thorough investigations, prosecutions, and adjudications of sexual violence cases. 


In November 2024,

a Cornell University student reported being sexually assaulted the month before by multiple men at a fraternity house

. According to her account and evidence subsequently reviewed by the University, she had consumed alcohol and drugs, including the dissociative drug ketamine, which left her severely incapacitated and unable to consent to sexual activity. She reported that multiple men entered the room at different points during the evening, and that several attempted to grope, kiss, or have sex with her despite her incapacitation. She also described gaps in her memory. During the alleged assault, one member of the fraternity shared messages on a group chat of more than 50 members, indicating that a woman was upstairs and available for sex, inviting others to join. Other members reportedly responded to and discussed the invitation in lieu of reporting the abuse. 


Cornell subsequently conducted a

Title IX investigation

, resulting in disciplinary sanctions against several students. The local District Attorney’s Office declined to investigate, and so no criminal charges were pursued at the time. The criminal investigation has now been reopened, with New York Attorney General Letitia James appointed as special prosecutor.


All criminal investigations must be assessed on the evidence, and anyone accused of a crime is entitled to due process. Yet, too often, criminal justice systems approach sexual violence cases through assumptions about force, resistance, credibility, or a survivor’s conduct and behaviour, rather than applying the same scrutiny to whether a person was able to freely consent to sexual activity.


A person who is unconscious or otherwise incapable of freely consenting cannot consent to sex. At the centre of this case, regardless of its eventual outcome, is a fundamental question: whether the one’s capacity to consent to sex was properly examined at all.  


Gaps in sexual violence law can harm survivors


Reporting sexual violence can require a survivor to recount deeply personal experiences to officials, investigators, police, prosecutors and lawyers, often while facing intense scrutiny of their choices, conduct, and credibility. In this case, the student has spent nearly two years navigating university, criminal and civil proceedings in pursuit of justice.


The reopening of a criminal case, particularly when the adequacy of a prior investigation of sexual violence allegations is under question,

has the potential to retraumatize survivors who will be forced to recount their experiences

 yet again. However, this case presents an important opportunity to examine how New York’s judicial system and the laws that govern it can become capable of delivering justice when survivors report sexual violence.  


In 19 US states, including New York, sexual assault laws distinguish between voluntary and involuntary intoxication

 in ways that can make prosecution for rape more difficult when a survivor voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs. In these states,

 the law fails to recognise that a person who has become incapable of consenting is incapable of consenting, regardless of how they reached that state.


Under New York’s Penal Law,

most sexual offences are defined by lack of consent based on either forcible compulsion or incapacity

, although certain offences, including rape in the third degree, also recognise when a person clearly expresses that they do not want s to engage in sexual activity, even in the absence of force or incapacity, as lack of consent. Circumstances including statutory rape where someone over 21 engages in sexual activity with someone under 17 …

author: Lisa Femia
title: Our Lawsuit Against the Trump Administration’s Social Media Surveillance Moves Forward. Here’s What the Court Said.
content:
No one should have to choose between speaking freely and protecting their immigration status. Yet that’s precisely the choice the Trump administration’s mass surveillance of online speech forces on noncitizens living in the U.S. 

  


Last fall, we

sued

 on behalf of three major labor unions to stop this surveillance program. And just this month, we won our first major ruling: A federal district court

denied

 the government’s motion to dismiss our lawsuit. This means the case can move forward—a win for free speech and a critical step in protecting our First Amendment rights online. We’ve already explained why this is a

big deal

 for our clients, so let's take a closer look at the court’s reasoning.

  


Our Lawsuit

 


 Since taking power, the Trump administration has used AI and other automated tools to

broadly surveil

 the social media and online speech of visa and green card holders, with the goal of identifying and punishing people who express views it opposes. The government is targeting a broad range of views, including

criticism of the


Trump administration

;

support for Palestine

 or

criticism of Israel

;

“rationalizing or making light of”

 Charlie Kirk’s murder; and anything nebulously

“hostile”

 to American culture,

founding principles

,

“traditional American views,”

 or

“our way of life.”

 

 


It has paired that surveillance with a public intimidation campaign. High-ranking officials have explicitly

threatened

 to punish noncitizens for their online speech, then followed through with a series of terrifying viewpoint-driven enforcement actions.

This has led to a significant chilling effect on speech, not just for noncitizens, but also for their families, coworkers, and friends.

 


In response, three major labor unions—the United Auto Workers (UAW), the Communications Workers of America (CWA), and the American Federation of Teachers (AFT)—

sued

 the Departments of State and Homeland Security alleging that this viewpoint-based surveillance program violates the First Amendment and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).  

The unions are represented by EFF, Muslim Advocates (MA), and the Media Freedom & Information Access Clinic (MFIA).

 


The government moved to dismiss our lawsuit, arguing first that federal immigration law prevents federal district courts from hearing the case, and second, that the unions don’t have “standing” to sue. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein of the Southern District of New York rejected both arguments and allowed the case to proceed. At this stage in the litigation, the court accepted all of the facts in our complaint as true and analyzed the law based on those facts. We will now prove these facts as the case proceeds.

 


Federal Immigration Law Doesn’t Block Our Lawsuit

 


 The government first argued that the court had no power to hear our case at all. It pointed to three provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) that restrict when federal courts can review immigration matters. The district court disagreed and rejected each provision in turn.

 


The first provision,

8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(9)

, is often called the “zipper clause.” It bars federal courts from hearing challenges that arise from efforts to deport someone, except through review of an individual’s final removal order. The government

claimed

 the zipper clause applies here because our lawsuit is really an effort to stop it from initiating adverse immigration actions.

 


 The district court wholly rejected this argument. Relying on the Second Circuit’s decision in

Ozturk v. Hyde

, it held that the zipper clause bars only challenges to a particular individual’s removal proceedings, not a lawsuit like ours that challenges the constitutionality of the surveillance program itself. That the surveillance program might affect someone’s immigration proceeding down the line doesn’t turn our lawsuit into a removal challenge.

 


 The court similarly rejected the government’s argument that

§ 1252(g)

 and

§ 1252(f)(1)

 prevent federal courts from hearing this case. Our suit, the court explained, “challenges the constitutionality of a government policy that is collateral to any active removal proceedings,” so § 1252(g) doesn’t apply. And § 1252(f)(1) only limits what kind of relief a court can give. So while the court may not be able to stop a particular person’s removal proceedings, it can still block “an unlawful surveillance program that suppresses free speech.”

author: bert
title: Antifaschist Gino stellt sich in Hannover
content:
Am heutigen Donnerstag, 15. Oktober 2026 stellte sich Gino um 18 Uhr selbstbestimmt in Hannover den deutschen Behörden, die ihn im Rahmen des sog. Budapest-Komplexes per Europäischem Haftbefehl gesucht hatten. Vorgeworfen wird dem Antifaschisten, Anfang 2023 an körperlichen Auseinandersetzungen mit Nazis in Budapest beteiligt gewesen zu sein. Gino, der in Italien aufgewachsen ist, lebte zuletzt in Frankreich, wo die Justiz 2025 seine Auslieferung an Ungarn abgelehnt hatte. Am 30. September 2026 hatte das Pariser Kassationsgericht jedoch einem deutschen Auslieferungsersuchen stattgegeben, woraufhin sich der Aktivist heute in Deutschland stellte. In Kürze soll Gino nach Karlsruhe verbracht werden, wo die Haftprüfung am Bundesgerichtshof stattfindet.

Die Verhaftung ist Teil des sog. Budapest-Komplexes, einer internationalen Kriminalisierungswelle gegen Antifaschist*innen, die hauptsächlich von Ungarn und Deutschland forciert wird. Auslöser sind mehrere Vorfälle am Rand des NS-verherrlichenden Großevents „Tag der Ehre“, des europaweit größten Nazi-Vernetzungstreffens, das jedes Jahr in Budapest stattfindet. Anfang Februar 2023 kam es dort zu körperlichen Auseinandersetzungen zwischen Antifaschist*innen und Nazis. Das nahmen die ungarischen Behörden zum Anlass für eine internationale Verfolgungsoffensive gegen die antifaschistische Bewegung, wobei die deutschen Repressionsorgane engagiert Schützenhilfe leisten. In Ungarn drohen bis zu 24 Jahre Haft unter folterähnlichen Bedingungen, doch auch in Deutschland laufen offen politische Gerichtsprozesse gegen Beschuldigte. Ein Höhepunkt der deutsch-ungarischen Komplizenschaft in diesem Repressionskomplex ist der Fall von Maja: Die non-binäre antifaschistische Person aus Jena wurde im Juni 2024 von den deutschen Behörden offen rechtswidrig an das queer- und trans*feindliche Ungarn ausgeliefert und sitzt seither dort unter unmenschlichen Bedingungen in Haft. In einem Schauprozess verhängte die ungarische Justiz am 30. September 2026 vor dem Berufungsgericht sieben Jahre Haft unter schwersten Bedingungen.

Zu den Beschuldigten zählt auch Gino, der in Mailand aufwuchs und später in Finnland lebte, aber einen albanischen Pass hat. Vor den Verfolgungen im Budapest-Komplex floh er nach Frankreich, wo die Justiz über das ungarische Auslieferungsersuchen per Europäischem Haftbefehl befinden musste. Im April 2025 lehnte das Pariser Berufungsgericht ab, Gino an Budapest zu überstellen. Dabei verwies es auf die katastrophale Menschenrechtslage, insbesondere die drohende Folter, und auf die fehlende Rechtsstaatlichkeit in Ungarn.

Im Rahmen der deutsch-ungarischen Zusammenarbeit bei dieser Verfolgungsoffensive verlangte daraufhin Deutschland mit einem eigenen Europäischen Haftbefehl Ginos Auslieferung. Zur Begründung verweist die Bundesanwaltschaft darauf, dass in Budapest auch zwei Nazis mit deutscher Staatsangehörigkeit verletzt worden seien. Deshalb wolle sie den Antifaschisten vor ein deutsches Gericht stellen – anhand der mehr als fragwürdigen Ermittlungsergebnisse der ungarischen Polizei.

Am 30. September 2026 hatte das Pariser Kassationsgericht dem deutschen Auslieferungsgesuch stattgegeben. Dabei ist die Verfolgung in Deutschland enorm, denn wegen der eigentlich banalen Körperverletzungsdelikte vor mehr als dreieinhalb Jahren drohen bis zu zehn Jahre Haft in einem politischen Prozess. Vollkommen ausgeblendet hatte die Pariser Justiz dabei zudem das hohe Risiko, dass die deutschen Behörden sich nur zum Handlanger Ungarns machen könnten, indem sie Gino an Budapest ausliefern und so das Pariser Urteil von 2025 umgehen.

„Ginos sofortige Verhaftung am heutigen Tag ist ein weiterer Höhepunkt in der deutschen Kriminalisierung von Antifaschist*innen im sog. Budapest-Komplex. Er hat sich freiwillig und selbstbestimmt den Behörden gestellt. Es gibt keinerlei Anlass, ihn in Untersuchungshaft zu nehmen!“, erklärte Hartmut Brückner vom Bundesvorstand der Roten Hilfe e. V. „Nun muss es in jedem Fall darum gehen, eine drohende Auslieferung an Ungarn zu verhindern. Die dortige Situation von Maja zeigt, dass auch unter Péter Magyar die unmenschliche Behandlung und Folter von Antifaschist*innen weitergeht und politische Schauprozesse an der Tagesordnung sind.“ Ergänzend bekräftigte er: „Wir stehen an der Seite von Gino und allen anderen verfolgten Antifaschist*innen und fordern die sofortige Freilassung. Wir sind alle Antifa!“

author: Daniel Hunter
title: How Vermont shut down ICE
content:
This article

How Vermont shut down ICE

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


After Operation Metro Surge, the Trump administration moved to rein in the Bovino-style spectacle with its made-for-TV arrests. In an attempt to avoid another public outcry, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has quietly settled into a new rhythm.


Arrests have still increased month after month, reaching

a record high

 of roughly 51,000 people taken into ICE custody in August. This is part of a new surge — carried out in hospitals, courthouses and airports — with an intent to stay off the nightly news. As

The


New York Times


reported

, this phase is “captured mostly by grainy security camera footage, through cracked blinds and from behind closed doors.” 


This phase is also backed by a dragnet of data. At airports, ICE has been

running name matches with TSA to detain people

 at check-in counters and gates. It has found a backdoor into the country’s license-plate cameras: Records show local and state police

ran more than 4,000 immigration-related searches

 on Flock’s camera network in a single year. (Yet another reason

Flock cameras should not exist

.)


Perhaps surprisingly, much of the tech infrastructure driving ICE’s new surge is headquartered in … Vermont. The town of Williston, outside Burlington, is home to both ICE’s

Law Enforcement Support Center

, which houses the agency’s national tip line, and ICE’s National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center, or NCATC, its social-media surveillance hub. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


As ICE tries a new approach, this new phase of resisting ICE requires moving to more offense — and the people of Vermont are offering us some clear lessons. 


Vermont resistance


Resistance started with the fight over flights. Early in Trump’s second term, activists

documented

 ICE moving detainees onto commercial flights out of Burlington’s airport — more than 450 people as of mid-July 2025, by their count. They showed up in airports as witnesses and disruptors, sometimes aided by empowered flight attendants. They forced an ICE retreat: organizers say

ICE hasn’t moved detainees through the airport in more than a year

.


More recently they’ve gone after the hard infrastructure. Sit-ins at the White Cap Business Park in Williston, where the NCATC facility is located, have led to arrests for allegedly blocking the entrance to the ICE offices, including

11 people in February and 13 in July.


After those arrests came some unusual twists, which speak volumes about the courage it takes to refuse unjust orders and to continue protesting in the face of repression.


Complicity and noncooperation


Responses to authoritarianism are as old as a time — many of the same dynamics from Vermont show up in the ancient story of Pharaoh and Moses.


Undeniably the most powerful person in his land, Pharaoh was the ultimate authoritarian. His big trick was taking beautiful work and turning it evil. Take the work of midwives, whose job is to usher life into the world — he turned that work into ugliness by ordering the Hebrew midwives to kill every newborn boy. 


But we all have a choice. And famously, several of the midwives refused. Their act of noncooperation with an unjust order is the reason Moses lived.


We are living through a moment when institution after institution is being turned toward evil. Some, like the Department of Justice, were already a mixed bag. But now it is being turned against the very logic of due process it claims to serve, as we’ve seen recently with the

criminal indictment of whistleblower Cassidy Hutchinson

. Other institutions, like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, are being perverted, with

great resistance from insiders

 who cling to the key values that these agencies were founded on.


Previous Coverage


The movement to defend the Minneapolis 15


In Vermont, the local prosecutor, Chittenden County State’s Attorney Sarah George, faced her own choice. When asked to

bring charges

 against the protesters who held the sit-ins, she repeatedly declined, citing limited resources. That makes sense: No one was harmed, and the protesters have a strong necessity defense — the argument that they were preventing an even greater harm. Every minute that ICE isn’t taking part in abducting people is good for the country.


Then came a bizarre turn of …

title: The Encampment Movement against Evictions and Gentrification : A Report from Madrid and Barcelona
content:
On September 23, 2026, Spanish authorities violently evicted Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, from her home in Madrid following her long judicial struggle with a real estate company named Urbagestión. She had lived there for 70 years, but could not afford the latest rent increases. In response, 10,000 people took the streets in protest that day. Three days later, a much larger demonstration established an encampment in the Puerta del Sol square, which had been the site of the

15-M movement

 in 2011, itself the trigger for the

Occupy

 movement in the United States.


Maricarmen Abascal passed away on October 7 as a consequence of the stress resulting from the eviction. Protesters have continued to occupy the squares in many cities across the Iberian Peninsula. A general strike has been called for November 11.


Here, our correspondents in Madrid and Barcelona offer a view from within the movement against evictions and gentrification that has spread across Spain and Catalunya.


Anti-fascists gather to defend the housing encampment in Madrid’s Plaza del Sol, 2026.


The housing movement in Spain has a long and complex history. For any period that we might choose as a point of departure, there always exists a prior precedent that could serve just as well—so where we begin depends on how we wish to make sense of what is happening today, how we wish to narrate this story that is still being written in the streets. What follows, then, is an attempt, however insufficient and incomplete, to tell this story, in hopes that you can learn or be inspired by something from it and, in this way, become part of this story and build upon it wherever you live.


We could perhaps begin with the

15-M movement

, which erupted a decade and a half ago as part of the sequence of uprisings that unfolded across the globe in 2011. Encampments spread across Spain much as they have today, full of people clamoring for “

real democracy

.”


Whereas elsewhere, repression often put these movements to an unresolved end, in Spain, this movement culminated with the formation of several far-left political parties, including Podemos, as well as strong municipalist movements in Madrid, Barcelona, and other cities. Today, these parties lie in ruins, while the municipalists have largely lost whatever power they once held. Ultimately, much like

Occupy Wall Street

 and the Arab Spring, the true legacy of this sequence remains ambiguous, contested, and open to interpretation. Perhaps the 15-M movement is not the beginning of the story we’re telling, but simply the ruins from which the current one is being told.


Riot police are covered in eggs and paint while attempting to evict a building in Barcelona, 2021.


The movement that is now swelling across Spain emerged as a result of strong and stable union-style organizations that operate apart from the official institutional structures that are otherwise so present and influential in political life here. These organizations were built to tackle the housing crisis using horizontal and grassroots power, while simultaneously driving widespread and popular mobilizations like those we are witnessing today. These unions are novel in that they don’t involve questions of work directly, but rather address the conditions in which we live. The movement’s most significant antecedents lie in the creation of organizations such as the PAH (Platform for People Affected by Mortgages), the first chapter of which was founded in Barcelona in 2009. Like the more recently created housing organizations, the PAH groups practice what we call “social unionism.”


The premise is simple: an individual problem like a person facing the threat of losing their home is transformed into a collective issue addressed through shared political action. A variety of union-style tactics soon began to emerge, leading to the halting of many imminent evictions.


A group of thirty or so people assembles in front of an apartment in the historic city center as the sun is rising. People cling to one another tightly, locked arm in arm, crowding in front of the door of the building’s entrance while several vans of riot police pull up and park nearby as scheduled. There’s an announcement from a police loudspeaker to the effect that people must disperse, but no one does. Eventually, the cops move in, struggling to pull each person away one by one, until finally everyone has been cleared. In the end, the eviction is successful, but it …

Every so often, I think about how they told us back in 2009 that a $15 minimum wage would make burger costs skyrocket & no-skill workers would be paid more than they’re worth, so they didn’t raise it.

But I guess the burger costs skyrocketing sounded …

pretty good

! so they killed Dollar Menu and put Value Menu in its place like “no it’s totally the same guy” and a single 2026 burger now costs the same as

four

2009 burgers, but a 2026 worker is still only worth $7.25.

a 2026 worker isn’t even worth 7.25 in 2009 dollars anymore. just to keep up with inflation, that minimum wage should have risen to 11.50 today. (thanks,

cpi inflation calculator

!) a $1 burger would only have risen to $1.59 by inflation

FUN FACT: it’s now been so long since the dems were able to raise the minimum wage that today’s minimum wage is now functionally lower than than at any point since

1949

. in fact, this is a chance to roll out my favorite radicalizing chart, the history of the minimum wage, adjusted for inflation:

This thing infuriates me almost beyond thinking. Look at it! American minimum workers haven’t had an actual raise since

1968

. We’ve been steadily losing ground for

58 years

. 2009 was the closest we’ve come, and even that only returned the wage to what it had been in 1983. Why is everything a catastrophe now? because a minimum wage worker in 2026 makes the exact same wage as one in 1939.

we haven’t had an actual raise since 1968, which was, not coincidentally, the only wage increase that happened after the passage of the civil rights act that made discrimination in wages illegal. the march on washington for jobs and freedom in 1963, the one where martin luther king jr gave the i have a dream speech, called for a $2/hour minimum wage. that would be the equivalent of $16.86 today. at the time of the march, that increase would have been a raise of about 60%. today it would be 132%. we’ve had so much stolen from us by the wealthy.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "Hyperscale": Paris Marx on Excess of Big Tech Data Empires & His Critique of Bernie Sanders' AI Bill
content:
We speak with tech journalist Paris Marx about his new book,

Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires

. In the book, Marx exposes the deceptive ways tech companies are taking resources from vulnerable communities in order to build massive AI data centers. “We have seen the tech companies that, back in 2019, 2020, wanted us to see them as climate leaders … completely throw their targets out the window in order to pursue generative AI and this data center buildout,” says Marx. He notes that after failing to connect to electrical grids in the locations where they were building data centers, some AI companies have pivoted to building “on-site gas plants,” further increasing dependency on fossil fuels.


Tech companies “want us to believe” that AI models are “starting to become so powerful that within 10 years they could decide that they want to wipe out humanity or a significant chunk of humanity,” says Marx. “That is a mix of science fiction and delusion … and it is also a very effective way to distract from the real harms that we’re seeing from these generative AI products.”

title: Flamingo-Revolution in Albanien gegen Jared Kushners Luxusresort im Schutzgebiet Vjosa-Narta betrifft längst mehr als Umweltschutz und Privatisierung
content:
Dossier


„

Eine Firma mit Verbindungen zum Schwiegersohn des US-Präsidenten will Hotelkomplexe in albanischen Schutzgebieten bauen. Der Regierungschef bestreitet eine Einigung. Bagger roden dennoch bereits Kiefernwald im Projektgebiet. Am Montag sind Tausende in Tirana, der Hauptstadt Albaniens, auf die Straße gegangen. Sie protestierten gegen ein Luxusresort-Projekt, das mit Jared Kushner, dem Schwiegersohn des früheren US-Präsidenten Donald Trump, in Verbindung steht. Das Investmentunternehmen Affinity Partners will küstennahe Feuchtgebiete in ein riesiges Ferienresort verwandeln. Das Projekt sieht Hotelkomplexe auf mehreren Hektar der geschützten Küstenzone Vjosa-Narta bei Zvernec und auf der unbewohnten Adriainsel Sazan vor

…“

Artikel von Anna Flori vom 02.06.2026 bei Euronews

 

 („Albanien: Tausende protestieren gegen Jared Kushners Luxusprojekt“) mit einem Video – siehe mehr Informationen:


„Die Zukunft gehört uns“: In Albanien schließen sich Studierendenproteste und Unterrichtsboykotte nun den 3. Tag der „Flamingo-Revolution“ an: Gegen Regierung und Polizeigewalt


Studentenproteste, Stunde um Stunde


„…

Schüler der Sekundarstufe in Korçë, Vlorë, Elbasan, Divjakë, Shkodër und Kamëz haben heute aus Protest den Unterricht boykottiert.

m dritten Tag der Proteste haben Tausende von Studenten und Schülern der Tiranaer Gymnasien die Straßen der Stadt gefüllt und den Rücktritt von Ministerpräsident Edi Rama gefordert. Der Protest, zu dem für 10:00 Uhr vor dem Parlament aufgerufen worden war, begann bereits früher, als die Abgeordneten den Plenarsaal verließen, nachdem die Plenarsitzung abgesagt worden war. In einem Interview erklärte Ministerpräsident Edi Rama, er werde nicht zurücktreten

…“ albanischer

LiveBlog der Redaktion von Citizens.al


 (Stand 15. Oktober 2026) mit Fotos und Videos (maschinenübersetzt)


Studentenprotest beginnt mit Boykott


„

Der heutige Morgen begann mit Protesten und einem Vorlesungsboykott an mehreren Universitäten und Gymnasien im ganzen Land als Zeichen des Widerstands gegen die Regierung.


Wie angekündigt haben die Studierenden der medizinischen Fakultät den Unterricht boykottiert und sind zu einem Marsch zum Bildungsministerium aufgebrochen, wo um 14 Uhr eine Protestkundgebung stattfinden soll.


Unter den Rufen „Rama ins Gefängnis“, „Berisha ins Gefängnis“ und „Die Zukunft gehört uns“ marschieren junge Menschen durch die Hauptstadt, und unterwegs haben sich ihnen weitere Studenten angeschlossen.


Dem Boykott haben sich auch Studierende der Polytechnischen Universität Tirana, der Wirtschaftsfakultät der „Alexander-Xhuvani“-Universität in Elbasan und der Universität für Rechtswissenschaften angeschlossen. Auch die Fakultät für Geschichte und Philologie sowie die Fakultät für Wirtschaftswissenschaften marschieren mit, nachdem sie den Unterricht boykottiert haben. Ebenso wurde der Unterricht am „Partizani“-Gymnasium in Tirana boykottiert.


Die heutige Demonstration findet einen Tag nach gewalttätigen Zusammenstößen zwischen Studenten und der Polizei in Tirana statt, die sich während der für den 13. Oktober vor dem Bildungsministerium einberufenen Demonstration ereigneten. Im Verlauf der Kundgebung kam es zu körperlichen Auseinandersetzungen, Stockangriffen und dem Einsatz eines Wasserwerfers, um die Menge zu zerstreuen. Demonstranten bewarfen das Gebäude mit Eiern, während die Polizei mindestens zehn Personen festnahm. Bei den Zusammenstößen wurden mehrere Menschen verletzt, und es gab Bilder von blutüberströmten Studenten

.“ albanischer

Bericht von Arbjona Çibuku vom 14. Oktober 2026 in Citizens


 (maschinenübersetzt) mit Fotos


Nationale und internationale Organisationen reagieren auf die Polizeigewalt bei der Demonstration.


„

Lokale und internationale Organisationen haben auf die Zusammenstöße während der seit drei Tagen andauernden Studentenproteste in Tirana reagiert. Sie haben Bedenken hinsichtlich des Einsatzes von Gewalt durch die Polizei und der Achtung des Versammlungsrechts geäußert und fordern ein Ende der Gewalt gegen Journalisten, die vor Ort berichten.


Das Albanische Helsinki-Komitee (AHC) äußerte sich besorgt über die Gewalt während der Proteste und forderte alle Parteien auf, Zurückhaltung zu üben, um eine weitere Eskalation der Lage zu vermeiden. author: Unknown
title: İstanbul: Selde can kaybı 4'e yükseldi, 5 kişi de kayıp
content:
İstanbul Valisi Davut Gül, 15 Ekim akşamüstü yaptığı açıklamada 3 kişinin yaşamını yitirdiğini, 5 kişi için kayıp başvurusu yapıldığını bildirdi. Gül'ün açıklamasının ardından Beykoz'da işçi Faik Şentürk'ün ölüm haberi geldi. 


Vali Gül, kurtarma ve sağlık çalışmalarına ilişkin şu bilgileri paylaştı: 


“7 hemşehrimiz tedavisi bittikten sonra taburcu oldu, 5 kişiyle ilgili kayıp başvurusu yapıldı. Arama çalışmaları devam ediyor.”


Gül, kentin normalleşmeye başladığını, hasar tespit çalışmalarının sürdüğünü ve zarar gören yurttaşlara ödemelerin en geç pazartesi günü başlatılacağını söyledi. 


84 yılın yağış rekoru kırıldı, 3 bin 50 kişi kurtarıldı


İçişleri Bakanı Mustafa Çiftçi, İstanbul'da yağışın bazı bölgelerde metrekareye

272 kilograma

 ulaştığını açıkladı. İstanbul Valisi Davut Gül ise kentin 1942'den bu yana kaydedilen en yoğun yağışla karşı karşıya kaldığını söyledi.


Vali Gül'ün akşam saatlerinde verdiği bilgiye göre selde mahsur kalan 3 bin 50 kişi kurtarıldı. Kurtarılmayı bekleyen kimse kalmadığını belirten Gül, kayıp başvurusu yapılan 5 kişinin aranmasına devam edildiğini bildirdi. 


İstanbul'da 16 Ekim Cuma günü de okullarda eğitime ara verilecek. Erdoğan, sağanağın devam edeceğine ilişkin tahminler nedeniyle yurttaşlardan resmi uyarıları izlemelerini istedi. 


838 sigortalı hasar ihbarı


Türkiye Sigorta Birliği (TSB), 15 Ekim itibarıyla İstanbul'da sel ve su baskınları nedeniyle sigorta şirketlerine 838 hasar ihbarı yapıldığını açıkladı. Bunların 776'sı yangın sigortası, 62'si kasko kapsamında kaydedildi.


TSB Başkanı Ahmet Yaşar, Bursa, Kocaeli ve Yalova'daki başvurularla birlikte toplam ihbar sayısının 897'ye ulaştığını belirterek şöyle dedi:


“Bunlar, henüz ilk bildirimler. Önümüzdeki günlerde yeni ihbarların gelmesi ve ekspertiz çalışmalarının ilerlemesiyle hasarın gerçek boyutu daha net ortaya çıkacaktır.”


İstanbul Valisi Davut Gül de hasar tespit çalışmalarının sürdüğünü, selden zarar gören yurttaşlara yapılacak ödemelerin mümkünse cuma öğleden sonra, en geç 19 Ekim Pazartesi başlayacağını bildirdi.


Barajlarda bir günde 7,16 puan doluluk artışı


İstanbul Su ve Kanalizasyon İdaresi'nin (İSKİ) 15 Ekim saat 09.14'te yayımladığı verilere göre, bir gün önce yüzde 38,06 olarak ölçülen kente su sağlayan barajlardaki ortalama doluluk oranı  yüzde 45,22'ye çıktı.


Elmalı Barajı yüzde 100 doluluğa ulaşırken, doluluk Istrancalar 'da yüzde 84,2, Alibey'de yüzde 68,13, Darlık'ta yüzde 67,74 ve Ömerli'de yüzde 62,17 seviyesine yükseldi.


Diğer barajlardaki doluluk oranları Terkos'ta yüzde 34,64, Büyükçekmece'de yüzde 29,02, Sazlıdere'de yüzde 27,47, Kazandere'de yüzde 8,28 ve Pabuçdere'de yüzde 3,41 olarak kaydedildi.


Yağış öncesinde Elmalı Barajı'nın doluluğu yüzde 77,79 olarak  ölçülmüştü.


Elmalı Barajı tamamen doldu: Taşkın tehlikesi var mı?


Elmalı Barajı'nın yüzde 100 dolması, barajın yıkılma veya denetimsiz taşma tehlikesi altında olduğu anlamına gelmez. Barajların olağan su tahliye sistemleri bulunuyor. Ancak güvenliğin değerlendirilmesi için doluluk oranının yanında baraja gelen su miktarı, dolusavak kapasitesi ve aşağı havzadaki akış koşullarının da bilinmesi gerekiyor.


(AEK)

title: У политзаключённого анархиста Никиты Уварова умерла тётя: поддержите его письмом!
content:
На днях в семье Никиты Уварова случилось горе — умерла Татьяна, сестра его мамы Анны. По сообщению группы поддержки, семьи были очень близки, Татьяна поддерживала Никиту и вместе с его мамой приезжала к нему на свидания. Никита уже знает о её смерти.

«Мы выражаем глубокие соболезнования Никите, Анне и всем родным и близким Татьяны, - пишет группа поддержки. - Переживать потерю близкого человека особенно тяжело в заключении, вдали от семьи. Сейчас Никита находится в одиночной камере СИЗО-1 Красноярска. При этом возможности общаться с родными у него практически нет: из-за того, что следствие сделало его маму свидетельницей по новому уголовному делу, им запрещены свидания и телефонные разговоры».

8 октября суд в очередной раз продлил Никите содержание под стражей ещё на два месяца. Напомним, он должен был выйти на свободу 19 марта, полностью отбыв 5-летний срок по «делу канских подростков», но незадолго до освобождения против него возбудили новое уголовное дело. В августе обвинение ужесточили — теперь ему вменяют сразу две статьи за один и тот же разговор с другим заключённым.

Адрес для писем: 660075, РФ, г. Красноярск, ул. Республики, 72, СИЗО-1, Уваров Никита Андреевич 2005 г. р. Отправить письмо можно через сервисы «Ф-письмо», «Зонателеком» и PrisonMail.Online (для зарубежных карт).

author: Gastbeitrag
title: Das Schweigen brechen – Wie eine Konferenz sexistischer Polizeigewalt den Kampf ansagt
content:
Am 18.10. findet in Berlin Kreuzberg eine Konferenz gegen sexualisierte Polizeigewalt statt. Die Organisator:innen sind vor allem politisch aktive Frauen aus unterschiedlichen Organisationen, wie ZORA oder der Prisoners Voice Platform (TSP). Wir haben mit ihnen über ihre konkreten Erfahrungen, das Programm der Konferenz und über die größeren Ziele gesprochen.


Interview: Osa Udushesheri


Könnt ihr euch einmal vorstellen und sagen, was euch dazu gebracht hat, die Konferenz gegen sexualisierte Polizeigewalt zu organisieren?


Erstmal lieben Dank für das Interview! Wir sind vor allem politisch aktive Frauen aus unterschiedlichen Organisationen wie ZORA und Prisoners Voice Platform (TSP – Tutsakların Sesi Platformu), aber wir werden in der Vorbereitung von vielen unterschiedlichen Genoss:innen und Organisationen begleitet, die schon in der Vergangenheit solche Konferenz z.B. in der Türkei gegen Vergewaltigung in Haft organisiert haben und im Kampf dagegen erfolgreich waren. Die Konferenz ist also ein Ergebnis vieler Genoss:innen, ein Ergebnis der Erfahrungen, die Frauen schon vor uns gesammelt haben.

Das hat uns aber vor allem dazu gebracht diese Konferenz zu planen: Auf Palästinademonstrationen in Berlin sehen wir auf fast jeder Aktion wie Frauen an die Brüste gefasst wird, wie Frauen der Hijab abgerissen wird, wie vor allem Polizisten ihre Macht gegenüber Frauen ausnutzen. Denken wir auch an die Aktionen des Rheinmetall-Entwaffnen-Camps. Auf der Großdemo 2025 wurden Aktivist:innen 12 Stunden im Kessel gehalten und die Polizei ging äußerst brutal gegen Frauen vor. Auch dieses Jahr bei den Blockadeaktionen des RME-Camps berichteten uns viele von Griffen in die Hose oder an die Brust, von sexistischen und abwertigen Kommentare und anderen Formen sexualisierter Polizeigewalt. Was besonders auffiel sind die Nacktdurchsuchungen die grundlos von Polizisten durchgeführt werden hier in Deutschland, es scheint fast so als solle das zur Normalität werden, in Fällen von Blockadeaktionen oder ähnlichem.


Vor allem nach den Veröffentlichungen im Dezember 2025 von Anna Liedtke zu der Vergewaltigung in israelischer Haft, kam es zu vielen weiteren Berichten der Flotilla-Aktivist:innen, die von sexualisierter Gewalt und Folter seitens der IDF berichtet haben. Auch während der People’s Caravan, die Anfang des Jahres nach Kobane reisen wollte, um von den Geschehnissen zu berichten folgten Veröffentlichungen zu körperlicher und sexualisierter Folter. Die Aktivistin der Föderation Klassenkämpferischer Organisationen Paula Maier machte im August dieses Jahres eine Veröffentlichung, bei der sie bekannt machte, dass sie bei der Jugenddelegation nach Bakur mit vielen anderen Aktivist:innen festgenommen wurde und dann in einer Einzelzelle von einem türkischen Beamten vergewaltigt wurde.

Das sind alles Fälle, die sich in den letzten Jahren gehäuft haben und zum Thema gemacht werden sollten. Wir sehen also wie unsere eigenen Körper als Waffe gegen uns selbst genutzt werden. Uns ist natürlich bewusst, dass überall da wo Frauen Widerstand leisten der Staat mit Repression antwortet. Obwohl das Thema jetzt aktuell ist, haben wir es als Frauenbewegung und linke Bewegung nicht geschafft, dass es Teil unserer Antirepressionsarbeit wird oder auch ein bewusster Kampf dagegen stattfindet.

Die Konferenz dient also als ein Ort, an dem wir als Bewegung zusammenkommen, uns austauschen über internationale Erfahrungen von Genoss:innen, über die Probleme, die wir aktuell haben und vor allem wie wir dagegen kämpfen können. Es soll für alle Menschen sein, die politisch interessiert sind, schon aktiv sind, Betroffene oder einfach jene, die was lernen möchten.


Was ist sexualisierte Polizeigewalt? Inwiefern spiegelt sexualisierte Gewalt die Strukturen der Polizei wider? Gibt es Unterschiede zu anderen Formen der Repression und der Polizeigewalt?


Die letzten Jahre haben uns deutlich gezeigt, dass die Polizeigewalt im Allgemeinen gegen alle, die gegen Krieg, Genozid, Ausbeutung und gegen dieses System kämpfen, sehr stark zugenommen hat. Der Staat hat vor allem auf eine starke Palästinabewegung mit brutaler Polizeigewalt und staatlicher Verfolgung geantwortet. Diese Repressionen, die wir in allen Bewegungen und Kämpfen erleben haben das Ziel durch Angst und Gewalt Einzelpersonen, aber auch ganze Kollektive von ihrem politischen Gedanken und Aktivismus abzubringen. Sexualisierte Polizeigewalt wurde bisher in Deutschland häufig auf eine Kontinuität der steigenden …

title: Îstixbarata Sûriyeyê ragihand ku wan Mihraç Ural zeft kiriye
content:
Ajansa nûçeyan a fermî ya Sûriyeyê SANAyê ragihand ku Mihraç Uralê ku li Sûriyeyê bi navê ‘Elî Kiyalî’ tê nasîn, dema hewl dida ji sînor bireve hat zeftkirin.


Dezgehên Sûriyeyê derbarê wê yekê de hûrgilî parve nekirin ku operasyon li ser kîjan xeta sînorî hat encamdan.


SANAyê destnîşan kir ku Mihraç Ural ji aliyê Servîsa Sîxuriyê ya Giştî ya Sûriyeyê ve hat zeftkirin ku ev jî “bi operasyoneke taybet ku di nav koordînasyona MİTê de hat encamdan”. Her weha fotografê Ural jî hate parve kirin.


المجرم علي كيالي، المعروف بـ"معراج أورال"، في قبضة جهاز الاستخبارات العامة، وذلك في عملية نوعية نُفذت بالتنسيق مع جهاز الاستخبارات التركي. #سانا https://t.co/DvgQn5ojMu


— الوكالة العربية السورية للأنباء - سانا (@Sana__gov)

October 15, 2026


Hat îdiakirin li nêzî Beyrûtê revandine


Di çapemeniya Libnanê de jî derbarê cihê ku Ural lê hatiye zeftkirin û awayê encamdana operasyona hatiye kirin de agahiyên cuda cih girtin.


Televizyona MTVyê ya ku navenda wê li Libnanê ye îdia kir ku Ural ji mala xwe ya li Mansuriyeyê ku li bakurê rojhilatê Beyrûtê girêdayî herêma Metnê ye, ji aliyê kesên nasnameya wan nediyar ve hatiye revandin û paşê ew birine Sûriyeyê.


MTVyê ragihand ku di dema serdegirtinê de hevjîn û kurê Ural hatine girêdan û Şaxa Îstixbaratê ya serbi Hêzên Ewlehiya Navxweyî ya Libnanê derbarê bûyerê de lêpirsîn daye destpêkirin.


Malbenda Çavdêriyê ya Mafên Mirovan a Sûriyeyê (SOHR) ku navenda wê li Londonê ye jî, li ser bingeha agahiyên ku ji çavkaniyên xwe wergirtine ragihand ku Ural piştî ku ji Nexweşxaneya Resulu’l-Azam a li Beyrûtê vegeriyaye, bi ser mala wî ya li Mansuriyeyê girtine û ew zeft kirine.


Malbendê ragihand ku kesên ku operasyon pêkanîne bi devoka Libnanê bi erebî axivîne, lê belê nasnameya wan hîn nehatiye diyarkirin.


Parvekirinên Balyozê Şamê Nuh Yilmazî


Balyozê Tirkiyeyê ê Şamê Nuh Yilmaz jî piştî nûçeyên girtina Ural, parvekirina xwe ya 4ê Cotmehê ji nû ve parve kir û nivîsî: “Elhamdulillah! Qehr û xezeba me li dijmin bibe malwêranî! eûzubillâh, eûzubillâh. xudâ ya şukr-i bihad!”


Yilmaz di 4ê Cotmehê de di parvekirina xwe de ragihandibû alîkarê Ural ê ku wekî Cemal Trablusi tê zanîn ji aliyê hêzên ewlehiyê yên Sûriyeyê ve hat zeftkirin û weha gotibû, “Gav bi Gav!!”.


Elhamdülillah! Kahrımız, gazabımız düşmana ziyân! eûzubillâh, eûzubillâh. hüdâ'ya şükr-i bihad!


— Nuh Yılmaz (@nuhyilmaz)

October 15, 2026


Banga SOHRê ya ji bo darizandina li Baniyasê


Dezgehên Sûriyeyê Mihraç Ural di nav berpirsiyarên komkujiyên ku di sala 2013an de li Baniyasê hatine kirin de nîşan didin.


Di gundê El-Beyda ê bajarê Tartusê ya Sûriyeyê û taxa Ras el-Nebe ya Baniyasê de, di 2-3ê Gulana 2013an de di êrişên ku ji aliyê hêzên girêdayî rêveberiya Esad ve hatin kirin de gelek sivîlan jiyana xwe ji dest dan.


Rêxistina Şopandinê a Mafên Mirovan (HRW) di Îlona 2013an de raporek weşandibû û li gorî wê raporê, hêzên hikûmetê û komên çekdar ên ku bi wan re, li du herêman herî kêm 248 kes kuştin.


Komîsyona Lêpirsîna Navneteweyî ya Serbixwe ya Sûriyeyê ya Neteweyên Yekbûyî jî di rapora xwe ya sala 2013an de cih da tespîtên ku nîşan didin hêzên hikûmetê û komên çekdar ên ku bi wan re ji komkujiyan berpirsiyar in.


Raporên HRW û Komîsyona Lêpirsînê ya NYyê derbarê berpirsiyariya takekesî ya Ural a di êrişan de li xwe nagire. Lêbelê Tora Mafên Mirovan a Sûriyeyê (SNHR), di rapora xwe ya Gulana 2013an de Ural di nav berpirsiyarên komkujiya Baniyasê de nîşan dide. Ural jî sûcdariyên ku beşdarî komkujiyê bûye red dike.


SOHRê jî di nûçeya xwe ya derbarê girtina Ural de, ji ber van sûcdariyan bang kir ku di pêşberî dadgeheke serbixwe û rayedar de, bi awayekî aşkera ji bo raya giştî û adil bê darizandin. SOHRê her wiha daxwaz kir ku heke mercên hiqûqî dest bide, darizandin li bila Baniyasa ku komkujî lê qewimîne bê kirin.


Derbarê Mihraç Uralî de


Mihraç Ural di sala 1956an de li Antakyayê ji dayik bûye û di nav rêveberên rêxistina THKP-C/Acilciler cih girt ku di salên 1970yî de dixebitî.


Di biryara bi hincet a 5ê Hezîrana 2026an a 9emîn Dadgeha Cezayê Giran a Enqereyê ya di derbarê Komkujiya Reyhanlıyê de îdiayek heye. Li gorî wê îdiayê, serokên THKP-C/Acilciler di sala 1976an de li Meletiyê hatin kuştin. Piştî vê bûyerê, rêveberiya rêxistinê kete destê Mihraç Ural.


Di biryarê de tê ragihandin ku Ural di sala 1979an de tevî Engin Erkiner ji girtîgehê reviyaye û di salên paşîn de xebatên rêxistinê birine Sûriyeyê.


Ural gelek salan li Sûriyeyê jiya. Xebatên wî yên bi taybetî li Lazqiyê û derdora wê û …

title: A Massa Carrara maxi-corteo: 15mila in piazza contro l’ondata di denunce, “si cerca di limitare il dissenso impedendo le manifestazioni”
content:
Almeno 15mila persone

 hanno sfilato per le strade di Massa Carrara nella giornata di mercoledì 15 ottobre, giorno in cui si sarebbe dovuta tenere la

prima udienza

 a carico dei manifestanti colpiti dall’andata repressiva contro il movimento per la Palestina.


Da Radio Onda d’Urto


Il governo Meloni, a botte di

decreti sicurezza

, ha cercato di mettere un freno alla straordinaria partecipazione alle proteste che hanno attraversato in particolare l’autunno 2025 in Italia. A Massa uno

spropositato numero di denunce

 – almeno 37 – sono state comminate contro altrettanti attivisti e attiviste massesi. La prima udienza a carico dei manifestanti, che si sarebbe dovuta tenere ieri, è slittata a marzo 2027:


Quella di ieri, afferma il segretario generale della Cgil di Massa Carrara

Nicola Del Vecchio ai microfoni di Radio Onda d’Urto

, “è stata una manifestazione non solo per esprimere solidarietà agli indagati, ma anche per denunciare quello che sta accadendo nel paese.

Si cerca di limitare il dissenso impedendo le manifestazioni

. Dobbiamo continuare ad indignarci di fronte alle ingiustizie esattamente come facemmo lo scorso ottobre”. Di fronte a un genocidio, dice dalla piazza, “non possiamo voltarci dall’altra parte”.


“Viviamo in un contesto gravissimo,

un contesto segnato dalle disuguaglianze che stanno sempre più aumentando

”, e “c’è una deriva bellicista che toglie risorse alla sanità, ai trasporti, alla scuola per buttarle via nelle armi. Se di fronte a tutto questo le persone vogliono dissentire, vogliono manifestare pacificamente come previsto dalla Costituzione, ecco i Decreti Sicurezza: questo è inaccettabile”, ha detto Rossano Rossi, segretario generale della Cgil Toscana, alla partenza del corteo nell’ambito della giornata di sciopero generale regionale indetta dal sindacato.


Ai sindacati, si sono uniti migliaia di giovani, studenti e studentesse, organizzazioni e singoli cittadini.

L’intervista a Nicola Del Vecchio, segretario generale della Cgil Massa Carrara.

Περιοχή: Γυναικείες φυλακές Κορυδαλλού (παιδική χαρά επί της Λαμπράκη)


Πέμπτη 15/10 στις 19.00 συγκέντρωση αλληλεγγύης στις φυλακές Κορυδαλλού


Την Τρίτη 13/10/2026 στις 10 το πρωί τα έγκλειστα συντρόφια Ελένη, Θύμιος και Κώστας καλέστηκαν και πάλι ενώπιον της ανακρίτριας. Το πλαίσιο γύρω από το οποίο θα κληθούν να απολογηθούν, είναι η αναβάθμιση και ο εμπλουτισμός του κατηγορητηρίου με το αρ. 187Α παρ. 1 περί ατομικών τρομοκρατικών πράξεων, καθώς και την επιπλέον κατηγορία για απόπειρα ανθρωποκτονίας κατά τον εμπρησμό του κτιρίου της Μαρφίν.


Η μεθόδευση αυτή μεταφέρει την αρμοδιότητα της δίκης εκτός ενός μικτού ορκωτού δικαστηρίου, σε ένα δικαστήριο, με επαγγελματίες δικαστές και με πολύ συγκεκριμένα χαρακτηριστικά.


Όλοι αυτοί, μαζί με όλο τον κρατικό μηχανισμό ανασύρουν για τρίτη φορά την υπόθεση παρουσιάζοντας την, αυτή τη φορά ως “δεμένη”, ενώ βασίζονται στην αποστολή ανώνυμων email και χωρίς να υπάρχει καμία ταυτοποίηση προσώπων. Είναι οι ίδιοι που ενώ μιλάνε για την αξία της ανθρώπινης ζωής, διαχρονικά μας ρίχνουν στον αγώνα της επιβίωσης, μας στερούν την ελευθερία και σκορπούν το θάνατο με εργατικά ατυχήματα, πνιγμούς μεταναστών και διαλυμένα τρένα. Τα κράτη είναι οι μόνοι δολοφόνοι.


Την Τρίτη, κόσμος του αγώνα ήμασταν στα δικαστήρια για να σταθούμε δίπλα στα συντρόφια μας. Να καταδείξουμε την επίθεση εν είδη ιδιωνύμου σε οποιοδήποτε αγωνίζεται, διαδηλώνει και αντιστέκεται εναντια στη λεηλασία των ζωών μας.


Να υπερασπιστούμε τους αγώνες του χθες, του σήμερα και του αύριο. Καμία κρατική μεθόδευση δεν θα σβήσει την κοινωνική ανταρσία της 5ης Μάη 2010.

author: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi
title: Reading List: Anooradha Iyer Siddiqi
content:
We are taught to think of a refugee camp as an object produced in an instant, only in response to an emergency — one brought on, perhaps, by those seeking refuge. We are taught that refugee environments are provisional and abject, moreover, to be naturalized as such within the African landscape —

as

 the African landscape. We are taught to misread migrant spaces as lacking history or architectural expression. To counter these misdirections,

Architecture of Migration: The Dadaab Refugee Camps and Humanitarian Settlement

 looks closely at the complex settlements, ecologies, domesticities, archives, and material aesthetics. In Ifo, Dagahaley, and Hagadera camps, established in 1991 by the Kenyan government and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees at Dadaab, Kenya, in lands shared with Somalia and Ethiopia, the book finds African, Muslim, and Afro-Asian aesthetic worlds and a historical repository of partition, sedentarization, and migration. Dadaab forms a material afterlife of events long unfolding, through colonial and postcolonial time and space, and in multiple registers, aesthetic as well as social.

My book is grounded in 14 years of feminist and critical collective practice and research (see

Cohabitations

,

Dadaab Commons

,

Feminist Architectural Histories of Migration

,

Insurgent Domesticities

, and

Settlement

). While researching in dozens of archives and libraries in Africa, Asia, and Europe, and interviewing hundreds of women practicing architecture and art, representing governments, cultural institutions, and nongovernmental agencies, or living life in refugee camps, I read many books! If the anticolonial thought in Frantz Fanon’s

Black Skin, White Masks

 and Walter Rodney’s

How Europe Underdeveloped Africa

 anchored my work, its everyday tugs and buoying came from feminists.

Ifo camp Chairlady Isnina Ali Rage. Photo by author, 2011.

My study of the handcrafted acacia camp environments and interviews with many of their builders — including Ifo Chairlady Isnina Ali Rage and shopowner Shamso Abdullahi Farah, and Dagahaley farmer Maganai Saddiq Hassan — gave shape to a consciousness rooted in the social and ecological worldmaking of African, Muslim, and Global South feminists. Let me begin with three. Sylvia Tamale not only insists on decolonizing master narratives that suppress multiplicity in

Decolonization and Afro-Feminism

, but through her years of activism in Uganda and beyond, plants the working and thinking of African feminists on the ground, in the natural environment. This perspective is hardly limited to African feminists, as Radha D’Souza demonstrates in the

Court for Intergenerational Climate Crimes

 — based on her book

What’s Wrong with Rights?: Social Movements, Law and Liberal Imaginations

 — which foregrounds the workhorse labor and the place of the indigo plant (Comrade Indigo) within majority-world feminist intellectual commitment; she dispenses with reductive “West versus Rest” critiques through the perspectives of European underground and Third World intellectuals in the co-edited

Decolonizing Knowledge: Looking Back, Moving Forward

 (

open access

). Further articulating the vitality of social difference to inform constructions of knowledge, Saba Mahmood argues that those constructions must assert against universalizing epistemes, secular as well as religious, in her foundational work on Cairo’s women,

Politics of Piety: The Islamic Revival and the Feminist Subject

.

Store and shelters designed and built by Shamso Abdullahi Farah, Ifo camp. Photo by author, 2011.

From there, global Black feminisms were my north star. Yvonne Adhiambo Owuor’s

Dust

 dwelt within the landscapes of Kenya’s Northeast, the erstwhile colonial “frontier” constituted of migratory lifeways and marabou storks; her habitations haunt my book’s histories of land, emergency territory, and sedentarized pastoralists.

Lose Your Mother: A Journey Along the Atlantic Slave Route

, Saidiya Hartman’s attempt to fill in the blank slate of the historical record and her own life, helped me think with the stories of enslaved children freed from Indian Ocean

dhows

, raised near Bombay, and resettled near Mombasa: the negotiation between rescuer and rescued in the East African abolitionist settlement of Freretown that forms Dadaab’s prehistory. My book stands on the shoulders of Mabel O. Wilson’s work on: (1) spatial agency, as rooted in the bodies of builders and the physical labor …

author: Shams Eddin Essam
title: Will Supply Ministry’s wheat intervention really rein in cost of unsubsidized bread?
content:
As the grain and bakery industries petition the government for permission to increase bread prices in order to protect their profits, the Supply Ministry has

announced

 it is injecting wheat onto the national commodity exchange to bring prices down and cut production costs.


The move came after calls for a government review of bread pricing guidelines in

August

 and

September

. Producers said they needed to increase consumer prices to compensate for rising production costs, particularly of flour.

Despite talks between ministry and industry representatives, the government has held the price caps and loaf weight specifications

steady

, announcing the supply release instead.


However, sources from the grain, milling and bakery industries who spoke to Mada Masr expressed doubt that the mechanism would meaningfully reduce production costs, indicating that the last time the ministry undertook a similar supply allocation in 2023, the move only fuelled profiteering on a secondary market that emerged in parallel to the commodity exchange.


The ministry has not said how much wheat it will offer via the commodity exchange, though ministry spokespeople

explained

 that the extra supply would be enough to bring costs down across the supply chain.


Speaking on condition of anonymity, two grain industry sources told Mada Masr that the imported wheat is expected to be available via the Egyptian Commodities Exchange either this week or next. Sales are to be capped at 500 tonnes per mill, and, as per the agreement with the ministry, two trading sessions would be held weekly, the sources said.


The CEO of the commodity exchange

told

 financial newspapers on Tuesday that trading had begun this week.


The ministry aims to sell wheat at LE16,500-LE16,700 per tonne. The sources said supplies will be available to all licensed mills, allowing more flour for bakeries that produce commercial bread, such as fino and “tourist” loaves.


However, the announced prices alone are not enough to convince mills to buy wheat through the exchange, said another grain industry chamber member.


A tonne of wheat currently costs LE16,800-LE17,200 on the open market, depending on quality.


But once the additional costs of participating in trading on the commodity exchange are factored in, the gap between the exchange price and the open market price narrows.


The source said that mills remain skeptical about the value of going to the exchange under its current system, given the registration and trading fees involved — costs they do not necessarily incur when purchasing directly from traders.


The source added that it would be difficult to assess whether the government’s price is competitive or not before learning more about the specifications and quality of the wheat being offered. When buying directly from private sector suppliers, mills can inspect a shipment before completing a purchase.


A mill owner said that there are questions beyond the immediate cost of the wheat: can the government ensure a steady supply of wheat through the commodity exchange to control costs and justify the cost of switching to the exchange?


Until the government’s mechanism proves capable of consistently meeting market demand, dealing with established suppliers is the more transparent option, he said. 


Global wheat prices have risen amid Russia’s escalating war on Ukraine, disrupting Black Sea shipping and ultimately pushing costs up in Egypt, the world’s largest wheat importer.


While the government says it has bought more domestically grown wheat, Egypt is still heavily reliant on wheat imports from both Russia and Ukraine. The cost pressures have become increasingly evident in Egypt’s domestic flour market over recent months. The price of a tonne of imported wheat stood at around LE12,500 in June, with a ton of unsubsidized flour at around LE17,000. Now, a ton of unsubsidized flour stands at around LE21,000.


Flour, in turn, accounts for between 60-70 percent of the production cost of commercial bread, according to an estimate from an anonymous General Bakeries Division source. This makes rising flour prices a direct strain on bakeries’ profit margins, particularly alongside

increases

 in other operating costs.


A bakeries division member told Mada Masr that resuming wheat sales through the exchange would not be an adequate solution to the gap between the production costs of unsubsidized bread and the prices set by the Supply Ministry. The …

author: Goktug Caliskan
title: Why China won’t build its own Wagner in Africa
content:
Attacks on Chinese workers in Mali are testing Beijing’s reliance on African security forces. Russia’s experience there gives China little reason to take on the fighting itself.


On 9 May, fighters from Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), al-Qaeda’s affiliate in the Sahel, stopped buses and trucks at Zambougou, in the Ségou region of Mali about 60 kilometres from Bamako, ordered the passengers out and burned at least 40 civilian vehicles. One passenger 

told Human Rights Watch

 that the fighters sent the travellers on towards the capital on foot, saying they had declared an embargo on Bamako. HRW found no Malian troops in the area.


On 12 May, the Chinese embassy in Bamako 

published a warning

 urging Chinese nationals to leave several mining districts, citing armed attacks and the government’s campaign against unlicensed mining. The incidents occurred in different parts of Mali, but both exposed the limits of state protection beyond Bamako. A 

second notice in July

 reported attacks on foreigners around Kenieba, Bougouni and Foulou. An embassy can tell its citizens to leave. It has far less to offer those who stay.


A 

BBC Monitoring review

 counted 38 Chinese citizens among the 89 foreigners abducted in high-profile cases across Africa in 2025, many of them working in the gold industry of south-western Mali. The figures cover foreign nationals and offer no comparable measure of the kidnappings experienced by Malians. Russia, meanwhile, has become directly involved in Mali’s military campaign, committing personnel to combat operations alongside Malian forces.


What fighting costs Russia


On 10 September, JNIM fighters overran the army camp at Dioura in central Mali. Military, security and local sources 

told AFP

 that at least 100 Malian soldiers and five members of Russia’s Africa Corps had been killed. The Malian authorities published no toll of their own. Bamako had already lost its defence minister, Sadio Camara, who was 

killed in an attack on his residence

 in Kati on 25 April.


Less than a month after Dioura, separatists announced what they called a temporary withdrawal from Kidal, and Malian forces backed by Russian fighters 

returned to the northern town

. The recapture was a significant political and military gain for Bamako, though JNIM’s attacks on civilian transport farther south remained a separate security challenge.


Wagner arrived in late 2021, as Mali’s relations with France broke down. When it announced its departure in June 2025, 

Africa Corps, which answers to Russia’s Defence Ministry, stayed on

, and Russian personnel remain part of the war. On 31 July, Human Rights Watch 

reported

 that Russian-controlled Africa Corps aircraft had struck Kyrnia, in the Mopti region, on 15 June. Eight civilians, including three children, were killed in what the organisation described as an apparently unlawful attack. Russia’s direct involvement has made its military reputation inseparable from the conduct of operations in Mali, including attacks that have harmed civilians.


Contractors outside the fighting


Chinese security companies have taken a much narrower role. When fighting trapped about 330 Chinese workers in Juba in July 2016, DeWe Security Service Group helped organise their evacuation despite having no armed personnel of its own. The company, founded by former officers of the People’s Liberation Army and the People’s Armed Police, hired armed South Sudanese as backup, told the workers to stay put and waited for Ugandan forces to secure the airport before the evacuation could begin, as 

Carnegie’s research on the episode

 records.


The pattern holds elsewhere. Chinese contractors assess threats and train guards, as DeWe has done for Kenya’s Chinese-financed Standard Gauge Railway, and rely on host-country police and soldiers to carry the weapons. These arrangements allow Chinese companies to organise protection while leaving combat operations to local forces. They also make effective oversight difficult when those forces commit abuses.


The Cité Chinoise in the outskirts of Bamako: one of the signs of China’s economic presence in Mali (Wikimedia Commons).


Control and cost


Beijing has its own reasons to keep armed force under tight political command. From 1 January 2018, 

the People’s Armed Police

 came under the command of the Communist Party’s Central Committee and the Central Military Commission and was no longer under the authority of the State Council …

author: Chief Nyamweya
title: Art & AI: The End of Creativity or A New Era of Artistic Expression?
content:
The conversation around Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the creative industries is often filled with hype and speculation. Is it a tool for liberation or a threat to livelihoods? Chief Nyamweya, co-founder of the Kenyan animation studio Pungulu Pa Productions, cuts through the noise by sharing his on-the-ground experience developing the African children’s series

Uli and Tata

. He explores the practical realities, ethical dilemmas, and unique opportunities AI presents for artists, particularly those from the Global South.


Q. As a creator, what has been your view of the interaction between art and state structures?


A. Our team was stopped at a police checkpoint during a research trip. The tension was high as we unpacked our gear. As an officer questioned me, I showed him my sketchbooks filled with dozens of drawings of camels that I had made during our trip. His demeanour changed completely and we ended up laughing together, in awe at the camel’s unique gait. Our driver was confused by the transformation. As we left, I told the officer to look for us on YouTube; my phone battery was dead, but thankfully, sketchbooks don’t need charging.


Q: As an animator creating content for African children, what was your initial, practical view of AI tools?


A: My approach was to see AI as a potential tool, not a magical solution. At our studio, Pungulu Pa, our mission is to create content that inspires African kids to love their land and culture – a direct response to the lack of quality, culturally relevant animation. We started with intensive, on-the-ground research, like travelling to Kakamega Forest to listen to stories and observe wildlife. So, when engaging with AI platforms like DALL-E or Midjourney, I evaluated them based on a simple question: are they a solution in search of a problem, or a genuine companion for a creative like me? The answer, I found, is complicated.


Q: Animation is a complex process. Where does AI fit into the “production pipeline”?


A: Animation isn’t just a software function; it’s a multi-stage “production pipeline” involving fundraising, research, screenwriting, storyboarding, voice acting, animation, and more. For our series

Uli and Tata

, primary research alone consumes 15 to 20 per cent of our budget because we are committed to archiving and accurately representing African cultures, avoiding the stereotypes you might find with a simple Google search.


In this context, AI’s potential is twofold. On one hand, giant Hollywood studios may use the “AI scare” to lay off workers. On the other hand, for a young industry like Kenya’s, where most studios are small and survive on corporate client gigs, AI tools could be a lever to close the gap with bigger players. As my friend and Art Director Shaddie has demonstrated, by building AI agents that mirror our pipeline, we have every incentive to grab any tool that might help. After all, how can you be disrupted when you’re not even at the feeding table yet?


Q: So, you experimented with AI. What was your hands-on experience like?


A: I decided to train as an AI storyboard agent. Storyboards are rough drawings that plan out an animation and are a major bottleneck in any pipeline. I thought it would be a perfect test because image quality isn’t the priority. However, I quickly hit a wall. I was spending more time training the AI – translating my thoughts into perfect text prompts – than if I had simply picked up a pencil and drawn the storyboards myself. This led me to a fundamental question: isn’t the whole point of freehand drawing to witness the unmediated mind of a human being?


Q: Beyond practical hurdles, what are the ethical concerns for artists?


A: The ethical issues are profound. First, there’s the issue of theft. AI companies are facing lawsuits because their models are trained on the work of artists without permission or compensation. The argument that “we are building the future” is vacuous. As technologist Dr Dwayne Munroe cautions, we risk projecting creativity onto what is essentially sophisticated statistical mimicry.


Furthermore, the “hidden costs” are alarming. The tech industry’s extractive logic treats artists as invisible, uncompensated data suppliers. Worse, we’ve learned that underpaid Kenyan workers are exposed to violent and traumatic content to “clean” AI training data for Western users. There’s also a deep cultural bias: these datasets overwhelmingly reflect Western aesthetics, threatening to further marginalise …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Morocco’s First Woman Prime Minister and the Terms of Freedom
content:
Something changes when a woman occupies an office men have treated as their natural inheritance. Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri’s

appointment

 on 29 September 2026 makes that change visible in Morocco. For women whose competence is routinely scrutinised, the pleasure is neither naïve nor trivial.


But the woman forming a government and the woman labouring in the fields, raising children without pay and denied an equal share of her inheritance encounter power differently. Representation changes who governs; emancipation changes what all women have the power to do. That distinction shifts our attention from PM Mansouri’s gender to the politics of the centre-right

 Party of Authenticity and Modernity (PAM

)

, which she leads. Will its programme redistribute the resources and rights on which women’s freedom depends?


The history beneath the headline


Calling women’s leadership foreign to Morocco requires forgetting its history. Historian Osire Glacier

documents

 women’s authority long before the contemporary premiership. Kenza al Awrabiya, the Amazigh mother of Idris II, helped secure the Idrisid dynasty, founded in the late eighth century in what is now Morocco. Zaynab al Nafzawiyya influenced eleventh-century Almoravid politics around Aghmat, near Marrakech. Sayyida al Hurra governed Tétouan, a city in northern Morocco, during the sixteenth century. Khnata bint Bakkar intervened in eighteenth-century dynastic politics.


Across the region,

Dihya

 is remembered as an Amazigh queen who led resistance to the Arab conquest in the Aurès, in present-day Algeria, during the late seventh century. Tuareg oral tradition remembers

Tin Hinan

 as a queen and founding ancestress of noble lineages in the Ahaggar, in present-day southern Algeria.


These histories expose how male authority is made to appear natural. Fatima Mernissi’s

The Forgotten Queens of Islam


challenges that selective memory. Colonialism also reorganised authority: French Protectorate administrators

reshaped

 customary courts around imperial priorities. What survives as tradition can carry the history of political intervention. 


Religious interpretation can give exclusion another claim to permanence. Islamist and other conservative opponents invoke this

hadith

 against women’s political authority:


«لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً»


Usually translated as saying that a people governed by a woman will not prosper, it becomes a prohibition irrespective of her competence. Asma Lamrabet, a

Moroccan Islamic feminist thinker

, questions turning a

narration linked

 to Persia’s dynastic succession into a universal ban. She reads it against the Qur’anic Queen of Sheba, whose judgement demonstrates capable leadership. Her argument contests male authority’s claim to divine necessity.


PAM’s promises and its record


Women have long contested how authority is distributed within the family. Fatima Sadiqi

documents

the Union de l’Action Féminine’s 1992 million-signature campaign to reform the Moudawana, Morocco’s family code. The 2004 reform abolished wives’ duty of obedience but retained unequal inheritance and exceptions to the marriage age of eighteen. Proposals announced in December 2024 left fundamental equality demands unresolved. In October 2025, more than sixty civil society organisations and public figures

joined to call for comprehensive reform

. Rights in Morocco have advanced through organised demands, not the gender of an officeholder.


PAM, a centre-right party founded in 2008,

advocates

 social modernisation and positions itself against the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD). It entered government in 2021 alongside the National Rally of Independents and conservative nationalist Istiqlal. Opposition to Islamist conservatism, however, does not itself entail reforming the laws and economic conditions that subordinate women.


PAM’s

2026 programme

 promises improved widow pensions, childcare, safe transport, a women’s enterprise fund and labour inspection. The commitments leave inheritance equality, abortion reform and decriminalisation of consensual same sex relations unaddressed. Mansouri called for

banning child marriage

 without exceptions in 2024, yet PAM’s electoral programme

omits that commitment

. Employment can support independence, but a wage does not cancel criminalisation or unequal property rights. The programme leaves those constraints intact.


Even PAM’s narrow promise to increase …

author: WoMin
title: Press Release | Women’s Climate Assembly strengthens Pan African solidarity, women-led resistance and the struggle for a just future
content:
“

Empowering women is a radical way to transform the world!

” –

Ivorian activist


The fourth regional

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA), held in Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 5–8 October 2026, concluded with a powerful reaffirmation of African women’s determination to defend their lands, territories, livelihoods and communities, and to demand climate justice and reparations.


Under the theme, “

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations!

”, the Assembly convened over 75 women community leaders, activists, feminist organisations, civil society groups and allies from twelve countries including Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Guinea-Conakry, Liberia, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Senegal and Zambia.


The gathering provided a vital space for women on the frontlines of the climate crisis, extractive industries, land dispossession and environmental destruction to share their experiences, strengthen relationships across borders and build collective strategies for change.


As the Assembly closed, one message rang clear: African women are not merely bearing the costs of the climate crisis. They are leading the struggle for solutions, defending their communities and shaping the future they want.


“

There’s an adage in my village that women cannot build a nation. The Women’s Climate Assembly has proved that women build nations. We counter this adage with the unity and solidarity of African women!”

 –

DRC activist-participant


Turning shared struggles into collective power


From communities confronting oil and gas expansion and destructive mining to women defending forests, seeds, water sources and ancestral lands, participants brought forward the lived realities of communities too often excluded from decisions about their territories and futures.


Through collective reflection, popular education and movement-building, women connected struggles that may take place in different countries but are rooted in common systems of exploitation, inequality and environmental destruction.


Designed by women activists and members of the WCA Steering Committee, the thematic teach-ins explored a range of political concepts, questions and practices, including:


The erosion of farmers’ seeds

: A challenge for building resilient and sustainable food systems. What solutions are there for preserving our seed heritage?  


Nature Commons

: The defence of the Congo Basin’s forests.


Counting the Costs of Mal/Bad Development and Demanding reparations

: The case of the African Development Bank campaign.


Fighting some of the false solutions to the climate crisis

: Gas extraction, enclosure of our forests and lands for carbon trading, green conservation and more.


Building democratic, accountable, ‘loving’ leadership

: Why are these principles so important to feminist leadership? What else do we feel is critical to leading as feminists?


Lessons on organising and movement building

: Growing National/sub-regional grassroots movements.


Building knowledge from what we know

: Building feminist popular knowledge as the basis for Building Women’s Power. How can we go about doing this locally in our communities and beyond that.


The WCA celebrated the knowledge, resistance and organising power of rural, Indigenous, peasant and working-class women. The

Each One, Teach One

 sessions embodied this spirit of knowledge-sharing, collective learning and liberation. On Day Two, participants exchanged practical skills, crafts and tools, sharing techniques for making baobab candies, producing eco-briquettes from cassava and creating seed bricks to cultivate and protect Indigenous seeds. Weaving, cloth-dyeing, beadwork and other practices also featured, affirming the value of knowledge held, practised and passed down through generations of women.


The gathering reaffirmed the importance of strengthening a Pan African ecofeminist movement that recognises the connections between the climate crisis, extractivism, gender injustice, food insecurity and the loss of community control over natural resources.


It also reinforced a fundamental principle: communities must have the power to determine their own futures, including the right to say NO to destructive development projects that threaten their lands, livelihoods and ways of life.


Climate justice means reparations, not empty promises

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Memorial service held for victims of the Strand mass shooting
content:
In the early hours of Sunday morning, 27 September, gunmen opened fire on patrons at a shisanyama in Lwandle, near Cape Town, killing ten people. “Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities. Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained. Lwandle police have opened murder and attempted murder cases,” said the police. The community believes the mass shooting is related to the extortion racket that is ravaging Cape Town townships.


One of the victims, Khululekani Ndlovu, will be laid to rest this weekend. The nine other people killed will be buried next weekend in the Eastern Cape. The Nomzamo Community Hall in Strand, south east of Cape Town, was packed with mourners and members of political parties for the memorial service.


Speaking to

Elitsha

, the chairperson of the police board in South Africa, Francina Lukas, said that extortion and business rivalry and lack of opportunities for young people are some of the factors contributing to high crime rates in the townships of Cape Town. She said that the lack of trust the community has in the police contributes to high crime rate.


“The police need to do much more than what they are doing in terms of compliance to make sure that businesses in the township comply with their licenses and bylaws. But the issue of trust is still a burning issue in our communities. So we need to overcome that issue to see that trust in the police is restored,” she said.


Families of the Strand 10


Speaking on behalf of the Sikweza family who lost their daughter, Avuyile, her uncle, Luyanda Macokeni, said she had plans to return to school next year. The 20-year-old passed her matric in 2024. She applied to continue her education next year and had just received responses from two universities offering her a place to study. She was expected to make a choice between the two. “Avuyile is supposed to the one burying us as elders but we are the ones burying her. It’s not God’s will that we are here today, it is because of someone’s will,” he said.


Siyathemba Jilaji was one of the victims who died on his way to the hospital, according to his friend. “He said he was going to change in the car so when the shooting began, I thought he was still in the car. A bullet grazed me under my arm. After the shooting, I went to the car to check for him. But, I didn’t know that he was amongst the bodies that were lying next to the entrance that I ran past,” she said.


Sivenathi Manxiwa’s father, Lubabalo Ndamane, said that he is not going to forgive the person who murdered his son. “I also don’t want to know who they are. Even if they can be arrested, I would not go to court. I leave everything to God and God will deal with him. I want to know what drove him to shoot at the young people who were out enjoying themselves,” he said.


The 10 people who died during the mass shooting in Strand last weekend
