Photo from Facebook

.


The police said that the investigation into the mass murder is still ongoing.

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: Eliel Peterson
title: Death as liberation
content:
Death as liberation is hardly a comfortable political proposition to digest. In a world where Black death is often the common condition, there is a well-established insistence on our living. So what do we make of two of Africa’s greatest filmmakers, Ousmane Sembène and Souleymane Cissé, whose earliest cinematic visions, expressed through their respective debut features

Black Girl

 (1966) and

Den Muso

 (1975), center on the suffering, alienation, and eventual deaths of Black women?

Sembène’s

Black Girl

 is preoccupied with racial violence and the economic exploitation that continues to structure relations between Senegal and France. The film follows Diouana, a young Senegalese woman who accepts employment with a white French family and travels to Antibes believing she is embarking on a new life. While Cissé’s

Den Muso

, turns inward, examining interpersonal violence and the ways patriarchal power consumes family life and communities, weakening the broader social fabric of a nation. The film follows Tenin, a mute young woman who becomes pregnant after being raped, exposing the brutal underbelly of the patriarchal violence imposed upon her. Despite the differences in their circumstances, both films position death as a troubling possibility of liberation for their central characters.

Tenin (Dounamba Dany Coulibaly) in a still from Souleymane Cissé’s

Den Muso

 (1975).

The history of Black resistance has not solely been confined to the preservation of life. From enslaved Africans who leapt from ships during the Middle Passage, to those who faced death in the fight against their oppression,

It is true

 that to rather die than to endure is not a popular or digestible form of liberation. Although these acts are not equivalent, nor do they carry the same weight as the deaths of these fictional characters, Sembène and Cissé, raise an uncomfortable question: what does life mean for a person stripped of agency, recognition, and self-determination?

For Diouana and Tenin, freedom remains out of reach because of the structures governing their everyday lives that continually deny these women full humanity: Tenin’s father and her rapist, Diouana’s white employers. This sustained stripping of humanity produces what I would argue is already a death, albeit a social one, that precedes their physical endings. Sembène and Cissé challenge audiences by asking what is living for the dehumanized. Diouana travels to France only to find her livelihood replaced by isolation and unpaid, alienated labor, while Tenin’s body becomes a site upon which familial and communal shame, punishment, and control are dumped. Death, therefore, is at the core of both films from the outset, existing not only as a shocking culminating event, but as a condition of violence. By the end of each film, Sembène and Cissé are not arguing over whether death is a worthy or noble choice for self-liberation; rather, they position the act of self-annihilation as the only remaining form of control available to their characters, and as an indictment of a society in which death is the only option. 

It is understandable to recoil at the self-inflicted violence that ultimately claims both Diouana and Tenin. One might ask why their rage is not directed solely towards those who harmed them. Why does Tenin’s retaliation extend beyond her rapist? Why doesn’t Diouana exact revenge on her employers and flee France? These questions linger because death feels like an unsatisfying conclusion, one that denies us, as audiences, the catharsis of resistance. We want these women to fight back and survive. We want their suffering to lead somewhere other than death. Yet perhaps the more daunting question is not why these women die, but whether we find their deaths more difficult to accept than the suffering that precedes them. What is ultimately more uncomfortable to confront: their deaths, or the conditions that made life itself unbearable?

Neither film offers an uncomplicated answer. To read Diouana’s and Tenin’s deaths as acts of liberation is not to suggest that their deaths resolve the violence they endure, or that self-annihilation is freedom in any complete sense. Their deaths do not dismantle the structures that dehumanized them. What death offers these women, perhaps then, is not freedom but a final assertion of agency within those systems. This is what makes their endings so devastating: the possibility of control emerges only when the possibility of living on their …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Ehsan Salah
title: Sudan, Egypt to pursue joint border security, as public tensions flare after deadly mine bombing
content:
In the aftermath of the bombing of a mine in the

Halayeb Triangle

 that left scores of Sudanese miners dead, Egypt and Sudan are discussing a new security framework along the countries’ shared eastern border.

 


That framework would provide for joint coordination to pursue what both sides regard as security risks arising from organized crime, Sudanese and Egyptian officials

told

 Mada Masr.


The push toward closer coordination comes amid public outcry in Sudan and diplomatic concern in international quarters over the killing of scores of artisanal miners in the disputed

Halayeb Triangle

 on Saturday.

 


That public outcry was accentuated on Monday when a gunman killed two Egyptians in a main market in southern Khartoum in what Sudanese security officials involved in the investigations told Mada Masr was a retaliatory attack.


The shooting took place at around 2 pm near the

Export Development Bank in the Local Market

, a security source in

Khartoum State police

 told Mada Masr.

 Three Egyptians were targeted in the market’s commercial area.

Two died at the scene, while the third was taken to the

Omdurman Medical Corps Hospital

for treatment.


Ali al-Laouta, a vegetable seller at the market, witnessed Monday’s shooting.

He told Mada Masr that he noticed a man wearing a

military uniform bearing the badge of the joint force of military-allied armed movements buying some items in the market.

 


He then suddenly pointed his weapon at the three Egyptians shopping nearby, opened fire and fled the scene, Laouta adds.


Police patrols and security units responded to the scene and tracked down the suspect, a source in the Khartoum police’s criminal investigations department told Mada Masr. The suspect initially resisted arrest, opening fire on security forces, but officers eventually subdued him, seized the weapon used in the attack and took him into custody, the source said.


One member of the arrest unit was shot in the leg during the exchange of fire, a security officer involved in the operation said. The injured officer was hospitalized and is in stable condition, he added.


The suspect is a member of the “support forces” — a wide range of armed formations that fight alongside the Sudanese military in the current war — a source informed of the preliminary investigation told Mada Masr.


Sudan’s military-led government adopted a wartime policy that put the joint force, its main battlefield ally, in charge of protecting state institutions and supporting security operations in cities under military control. That has left the alliance with a heavy presence in urban areas.

But a

string

 of violent incidents involving joint force members in recent months has stoked public concerns and prompted authorities to review the policy and seek to curb the allied group’s urban presence.


The source informed of the preliminary investigation told Mada Masr that the suspect was subjected to intensive questioning about his military affiliation and how he had obtained the weapon used in the attack.


The interrogating officer told Mada Masr that, in his initial statement, the suspect said he had shot the Egyptian men in retaliation for his brother’s death in Saturday’s strikes.


The shooting comes amid a wave of polarization in Sudanese public opinion following the deadly airstrike near the Sudanese-Egyptian border that killed scores of Sudanese people.


The shooting adds more complexity to an already charged public sphere.


Sudanese lawyer Oweis Salah Eddin al-Iraqi urged authorities to disclose the facts related to the miners’ deaths directly to the public, saying the case had become a matter of public concern and that any mishandling could provoke backlash.


Many in the public and political arena are viewing the shooting in the context of wider accountability for the miners’ deaths.


Viewing the market shooting in isolation from the attack on the miners would offer an incomplete assessment of the situation, said Adel Ibrahim Hamad, the head of

Sudan’s Ashigga Party.


The party was re-established by former members of the Democratic Unionist Party, drawing inspiration from an earlier party of the same name that called for union with Egypt.

 The revived party focuses on national issues, paying particular attention to Sudanese-Egyptian relations.


Discussion of Monday’s shooting, Hamad argued, must begin with the original incident, saying Egypt’s response was disproportionate to the violation, “if any.” …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: US Reportedly Considering Dropping “Mother of All Bombs” on Iran
content:
The US has only ever dropped a MOAB once before — on Afghanistan in 2017.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

The Pentagon has reportedly drawn up plans to attack Iran with the “Mother of All Bombs” (MOAB), the largest conventional weapon ever developed by weight, after being ordered by President Donald Trump to develop strike plans for targets that include “a lot of energy infrastructure.”

Energy infrastructure is largely considered to be civilian in nature and thus protected under international law.

The GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb, or MOAB, is the U.S.’s largest non-nuclear bomb. It is designed to explode a few feet before hitting the ground, creating a massive blast and shooting out plumes of fire, destroying everything within a 0.6 mile radius and causing damage within one mile. It is not an effective weapon against targets like Iran’s highly fortified nuclear infrastructure, experts said, because it does not penetrate deep below ground.

Legal experts have previously raised concerns about disproportionate harm to civilians in the U.S.’s use of 2,000-pound bombs on Iran. The MOAB, by contrast, weighs 21,000 pounds, and has a much larger blast radius.

The MOAB options were first reported by CNN and confirmed by CBS. The MOAB was first tested in 2003, as the George W. Bush administration developed its strategy of “shock and awe” in Iraq; as CNN notes, at the time, the Pentagon said it hoped that the mere existence of the MOAB was enough to cause “psychological” damage to the enemy.

The bomb has only been used once before in combat, by Trump. In 2017, the U.S. dropped a MOAB east of Kabul, in Nangarhar, Afghanistan, a province with a population of 1.5 million people. The Pentagon claimed that more than 94 ISIS members were killed in the attack. No civilian deaths were reported; some reports said that the area had long been evacuated. But some local reports suggested that civilians were harmed, and critics afterward noted that the U.S. had previously never considered using the bomb in Iraq because of civilian damage concerns. It caused a mushroom cloud visible from 20 miles away.

.@USFOR_A releases GBU-43 #MOAB strike video against #ISIS-K cave complex, #Nangarhar, #Afghanistan #DefeatDaeshhttps://t.co/MuhU7JXuNn pic.twitter.com/qBqptpuzbE

It is unclear what the timing of such an attack on Iran would be. Trump has said that he won’t relaunch strikes against Iran before the midterms, but reports have also said that his administration has drawn up plans to do just that. CNN said advisers privately wonder if Trump’s pledges are definitive.

CNN additionally found that the Trump administration and military planners have spent recent weeks looking for “an off-ramp that gives Trump a ‘symbolic’ win — at minimum — he can try to sell to the American people without preventing a potential diplomatic breakthrough, starting with an agreement to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.” This includes plans that could amount to strikes for a “fireworks show,” after which Trump would declare victory.

“The Trump administration’s threats to commit war crimes in Iran cannot be normalized,” said Ryan Costello, policy director for the National Iranian American Council, in response to the MOAB report. “President Trump acts on many of his threats, necessitating more urgent action to bring this illegal war of choice to a definitive end.”

The Trump administration has already been under fire for killing civilians in Iran, with several attacks having been described as war crimes by UN experts. This includes the February 28 strike on an elementary school in Minab, Iran, which killed 160 people, including 123 children.

Pentagon officials said in May that their report on the Minab attack, which is the single worst strike on civilians by the U.S. in the 21st century, was nearing conclusion. But Bloomberg reported on Thursday that the Pentagon is planning to withhold the report at least until after the midterm elections next month, and potentially even longer.

The attempt to withhold information about the U.S.’s conduct in the deeply unpopular war has incensed critics.

Defense Secretary Pete “Hegseth eliminated staff who prevent civilian casualties, called the rules of engagement safeguarding civilians ‘stupid,’ & now he’s covering up the report on the Minab school strike that killed over 120 children,” said Sen. Chris …

author: Local Journalism Initiative
title: Nunavut community’s hunters opposed to Grays Bay Road and Port could get answers by Oct. 23
content:
Inuit-owned West Kitikmeot Resources Corporation is aiming to answer 70 questions from the Kugluktuk Angoniatit Association by Oct. 23, hoping to clear another hurdle in the

Grays Bay Road and Port project

 approval process.


The project, proposed by West Kitikmeot Resources Corporation, would connect a deep-sea Arctic port to Canada’s highway system for the first time.


That would allow for critical minerals like copper and zinc to be mined in Nunavut on an industrial scale.


But the Kugluktuk Angoniatit Association, representing hunters and trappers, contends that the port and road project threatens caribou herds in the area.


The road would run through the migration route of the Dolphin and Union caribou herd, which is already listed as endangered by the Government of the Northwest Territories.


In June, the Kugluktuk Angoniatit Association submitted 70 questions to the Nunavut Impact Review Board regarding environmental impacts of the project.


The following month, the harvesters group and World Wildlife Fund Canada released a 13-minute video opposing the project.


In the video, Kugluktuk Angoniatit Association manager Amanda Dumond said that West Kitikmeot Resources Corporation was ignoring the harvesters’ concerns.


West Kitikmeot Resources Corporation has met with the group five times since 2023, including a site visit and fishing trip last summer, according to the company’s CEO Brendan Bell..


“Our discussions with their board members, staff and advisors have been constructive and helpful,” Bell said.


Grays Bay Road and Port

 would connect the highway system in the Northwest Territories through areas with critical minerals deposits and end at between Kuglukuk and Cambridge Bay, where a port would allow those minerals to be shipped to markets abroad.


Inuit perspectives have been integrated into the project, according to Bell, and he said he’s disappointed that the hunters aren’t satisfied.


Kugluktuk Angoniatit Association did not respond to a request for comment.


Two Kugluktuk hunters told Nunavut News they see benefits and drawbacks of the proposed road and port.


Nigel Allukpik is a former Kugluktuk Angoniatit Association board member and was featured in the video from July. He said there used to be so many caribou they would come through Kugluktuk.


“It started to slow down after the exploration camps come around early 2020s,” Allukpik said, “exploration for possible mining, for zinc and copper.”


Harmonic vibrations underground are disturbing the migration patterns of the caribou, according to Allukpik, who added that he’s been hunting since he could walk.


These days, he said he’s lucky to see five or six caribou on his hunting trips when he used to see about double that.


Despite believing that development is already affecting caribou herds, Allukpik also sees the potential benefits of the road and port project.


“It is much more needed because then you feel some sort of connection to the rest of Canada, and with people wanting to start business that could be for their kids and their grandkids. Whereas hunting-wise, it’s like our great, great, great grandparents hunted there, and it’s still there for us today,” Allukpik said.


The Grays Bay proposal could provide much-needed defence infrastructure for Nunavut, Allukpik noted, which he counts as an important aspect.


Kevin Ongahak, also from Kuglutuk, was taught to hunt caribou by his father when he was four-years-old.


There’s been a significant decline in caribou near the Grays Bay area, Ongahak said, but he’s also noticed a rebound in numbers over the past two years.


He cited two reasons why he thinks the population of Dolphin and Union caribou herd has declined.


“One thing was over-harvest. I know of multiple occasions people over-harvesting, like harvesting way too many,” Ongahak said.


Read More: 


All major projects announced by feds will affect Indigenous communities 


Climate change was also a factor, as the Dolphin and Union herd migrates across sea ice in the winter.


“That ice forming a lot later, and the caribou trying to stick to their old migration patterns coming across the ocean — they’ll definitely run into thin ice. I’m pretty certain whole herds probably drowned from that,” Ongahak said.


He also sees the potential benefits to the Grays Bay initiative, particularly from shipping goods up north by road, despite believing that hunting in the area will suffer.

author: Daron Letts
title: Taloyoak’s new Pangniq High School unveiled with public ceremony
content:
Metalshop students at Taloyoak’s new $90-million Pangniq High School crafted the qulliq that will be lit at an unveiling ceremony set for Friday.


The school overlooks the community from atop a raised plot of ground next to the airport.


Its stature in the landscape is mirrored by its name —  pangniq, an Inuktitut term for the most prominent bull in a caribou herd. Students helped choose that name as part of a contest last year.


“The school is outstanding — state of the art,” said first-year principal Rodney Drover Wednesday in a phone interview.


The school’s 16 staff members and 200 students from grades 7 to 12 began their fall semester in the 3,300-square-metre facility for the first time since

construction

, which was completed on schedule, began in 2023.


It’s the fifth school completed by Iqaluit-based general contractor Pilitak Enterprises Ltd., Winnipeg-based Accutech Engineering Inc., and Parkin Architects, which has offices in Ontario and B.C.


The building blends traditional learning with technology that includes smartboards, microphone systems, and screens in every classroom, Drover said.


“There’s not much that we don’t have,” he said, adding that the

 science lab is “what you would expect to find in a university.”


There’s also a culinary training facility and processing room, in which elders can lead students through lessons in skinning and breaking down country food.


Early in the semester, students used the brand-new stoves to cook muskox recipes. On Wednesday, they prepared seal dishes to serve at Friday’s public event.


The shop, overseen by instructor Bill Akerly, is equipped for carpentry, electrical, welding and other trades.


The building is designed to accommodate more than 400 students.


Friday’s ceremony includes two bands, accordian jigs, throatsinging and drumdancing.


The gymnasium at Taloyoak’s new Pangniq High School is set up in anticipation of Friday’s public unveiling, which Premier John Main is expected to attend. (Photo courtesy of Rodney Drover)


Those on Friday’s guest list, which will include Nunavut Premier John Main and other MLAs, will be greeted by the natural light that floods into the foyer through large banks of north- and east-facing windows.


Guests will be led on a private tour before doors open to the public at 2 p.m. A community feast is scheduled to follow at 3:30 p.m.


“[The school is] a wonderful gift to the community and, more importantly, the students,” Drover said.

author: Valerie Anne
title: ‘The Body’ Is a Sapphic, Ritual-Gone-Wrong Teen Horror Show Coming to Netflix
content:
Do you ever feel like a show was made just for you using all your favorite media keywords? That’s how I felt when I first heard about Netflix’s The Body. I saw Catholic school, dancers, ritual-gone-wrong, horror and I was beyond sold.

And in case those words and phrases didn’t make it obvious: The story is also sapphic. Writer and creator Quinn Shephard (who acted in movies like The Miseducation of Cameron Post and wrote/directed episodes of Under the Bridge) started writing the show the year she came out. She says: “It’s satirizing some of the trauma of growing up queer and repressed and the confusion around that.”

A lot of the main cast of girls are relative newcomers on the scene (aka they don’t have Wikipedia “personal life” pages yet) so I’m not sure who among them are queer, but the show WILL feature lesbian reality star Gabby Windey in a recurring role as a coach. Also, almost all of the episodes have women listed as writers.

The show looks freaky and weird in all the best ways, and I can’t wait. I hope it’s just as fun as shows like Yellowjackets and even Mike Flanagan’s Carrie. May the teens-getting-into-supernatural-mischief genre never die.

The series drops next month and you can watch the full official trailer right now!

author: David S. D'Amato
title: Jalan Libertarian Menuju Egalitarianisme
content:
Oleh:

David S. D’Amato

. Teks aslinya berjudul “

The Libertarian Road to Egalitarianism

”. Diterjemahkan ke Bahasa Indonesia oleh Taratsa.


Sebuah studi terbaru dari

National Bureau of Economic Research

 yang dilakukan Emmanuel Saez dan Gabriel Zucman

 menemukan bahwa “

0,1% keluarga [di Amerika Serikat] yang berada di puncak distribusi kekayaan kini memiliki bagian kekayaan yang kira-kira sama dengan 90% keluarga yang berada di bagian terbawah.

” Lebih jauh, studi tersebut menunjukkan bahwa “pemulihan” ekonomi yang terus kita dengar ternyata belum sampai kepada kelas menengah. Hanya mereka yang berada di puncak piramida ekonomi yang benar-benar menikmati manfaatnya.


Ketika sebagian kecil penduduk menimbun begitu banyak kekayaan negara, para pakar kebijakan dan akademisi sibuk mencari pihak yang harus disalahkan sekaligus menawarkan berbagai solusi. Seperti yang bisa diduga, pasar bebas kemudian menjadi sasaran kritik sebagai sumber semakin lebarnya ketimpangan kekayaan dan pendapatan. Sebagai pendukung deregulasi dan pasar bebas, kaum libertarian sering dituduh hidup dalam dunia fantasi dan menutup mata terhadap persoalan ketimpangan.


Kami, kaum libertarian, sebenarnya ikut memperburuk keadaan. Ketika persoalan ini tak terhindarkan muncul, terlalu banyak dari kami justru terlihat gelisah dan bersikap defensif dengan bersikeras bahwa ketimpangan

sama sekali bukan

 masalah, bahwa yang seharusnya kita lihat adalah standar hidup atau ukuran lainnya. “Kapitalisme sangat baik bagi orang miskin—sumpah!” Kaum libertarian harus menerima kenyataan yang pahit bahwa ketimpangan memang merupakan persoalan yang sangat besar.


Namun, kita tidak perlu memandang ketimpangan sebagai titik lemah dalam argumen kita mengenai kebebasan ekonomi, atau sebagai persoalan yang tidak mungkin kita menangkan. Hubungan ekonomi yang ada saat ini bukanlah hasil dari kebebasan pertukaran maupun kepemilikan pribadi yang sah. Justru kaum libertarian berada pada posisi yang kuat dalam persoalan ketimpangan. Kebebasan dan kesetaraan pada kenyataannya saling melengkapi dan memperkuat satu sama lain; yang pertama secara alamiah menghasilkan yang kedua.


Kaum anarkis individualis seperti Lysander Spooner berpendapat bahwa “ekstrem dalam kekayaan maupun kemiskinan” merupakan hasil dari “legislasi positif”, yakni ketika hukum-hukum arbitrer menggantikan hukum alam dan “menciptakan monopoli serta privilese”. Dalam kapitalisme, menurut Spooner, pemilik modal memperoleh kekuasaan khusus dalam perekonomian—kekuasaan yang tidak ada hubungannya dengan kebebasan sederhana untuk memproduksi, bertukar, dan berkompetisi. Jika dilihat secara menyeluruh, intervensi negara pada akhirnya menguntungkan orang-orang kaya dan mereka yang memiliki koneksi politik, yakni elite ekonomi yang mempunyai akses khusus kepada mereka yang membuat dan menjalankan aturan yang harus kita semua patuhi.


Intervensi-intervensi tersebut memang tidak selalu sempurna, dan sistem kapitalisme monopoli di negara ini tentu dilapisi dengan berbagai kebijakan yang secara formal dimaksudkan untuk melindungi pekerja, konsumen, dan masyarakat miskin. Namun, tidak satu pun kebijakan tersebut mengubah tujuan mendasar intervensi negara: merampas hak para pemilik yang sah dan menempatkan massa masyarakat dalam posisi bergantung pada para pemberi kerja. Singkatnya, tujuan historis negara adalah perang kelas yang permanen, yakni penggunaan kekuasaan negara untuk melindungi sebuah kelas bangsawan sosial-ekonomi.


Karena itu, kaum kiri sebenarnya cukup tepat dalam persoalan ketimpangan, meskipun mereka cenderung keliru dalam memahami kebebasan, hak-hak individual, dan pasar. Kaum anarkis pasar menghendaki

keduanya

, kebebasan dan kesetaraan, dengan memperjuangkan masyarakat tanpa negara yang menjadikan kesetaraan dalam kebebasan dan otoritas sebagai hukum tertingginya.


Persaingan yang benar-benar terbuka merupakan kekuatan yang membubarkan sekaligus menyebarkan konsentrasi kekuasaan. Kaum libertarian seharusnya berhenti mencari-cari alasan untuk membenarkan ketimpangan yang luar biasa besar saat ini, seolah-olah kita sampai pada kondisi ini melalui

laissez-faire

 dan kedaulatan individu.


Seluruh hasil publikasi didanai sepenuhnya oleh donasi. Jika kalian menyukai karya-karya kami, kalian dapat berkontribusi dengan berdonasi. Temukan petunjuk tentang cara melakukannya di halaman Dukung C4SS:

https://c4ss.org/dukung-c4ss.

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Tablets Make Communication Easier Behind Bars – But Deaf People Are Left Behind
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


Tablet computers have revolutionized communication inside prisons for hearing prisoners. Prison systems from across the country — including in

New York

,

California

, and

Illinois

 — have

distributed tens of thousands

 of tablets to incarcerated people, which they can use to call home, watch movies, message loved ones, or attend virtual classes (although they are often

charged predatory fees

 for accessing these benefits). As of 2022,

25 state prison systems

 had tablet distribution programs, according to the Electronic Privacy Information Center. 


But as the rollout of such tablets continues, many deaf incarcerated people have been left behind. 


Disability justice organization HEARD points out that

it’s

unknown

 how many deaf people are incarcerated in U.S. prisons, but a

2015 report

 by the Bureau of Labor Statistics estimated that 6.2 percent of incarcerated people in

state

 and

federal

 prisons have a hearing disability, which would equal about 71,000 people.


Daniel Valenzuela, who is deaf, is incarcerated at Danville Correctional Center in Illinois. Last year, the Illinois Department of Corrections (IDOC)

distributed tablets

 to all incarcerated people. But IDOC blocks videophone capabilities, preventing Valenzuela from communicating in his primary language, American Sign Language (ASL).  


In September, Valenzuela sued the IDOC director for violating the Americans with Disabilities Act.


“I have six kids, four grandkids, and one of my sons is in the military. I cherish and love my family so much,” said Valenzuela in a

press release

 announcing the lawsuit. “I just want to tell them happy birthday and I am so grieved when I can’t call because I don’t want them to think I forgot.”


There are at least three other deaf individuals at Danville who primarily use ASL to communicate, according to the

complaint

 filed by Disability Rights Advocates, Equip for Equality, and the law firm Much Shelist. 


“Across the Illinois Department of Corrections, people can use tablets to communicate with their loved ones, which has been a game changer in removing restrictions on communication,” Valenzuela’s attorney, Rachel Weisberg, the directing attorney at Disability Rights Advocates, told

Truthout

. “But for Mr. Valenzuela and other deaf people who use American Sign Language, that same access simply isn’t available.” 


IDOC did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication.


Last year, in addition to distributing tablets to incarcerated people, IDOC

announced

 it would provide every incarcerated person with 775 free domestic phone call minutes per month. In a press release,

IDOC said

 that these initiatives, working in tandem, “enhance family connections and increase access to technology that supports rehabilitation.” 


But deaf prisoners are excluded from accessing these critical programs. 


Unlike hearing prisoners who can use their tablets to make calls from their cells, Valenzuela must get a guard’s permission to walk to another building to use the one videophone that’s available to him. In at least one instance, Valenzuela had to go out in the pouring rain to use the videophone, according to the complaint. 


“When prison officials don’t communicate with deaf/disabled people in ways they can understand, they may be written up for being ‘non-compliant.'”


The videophone is often unavailable because the unit itself breaks down, the prison is on lockdown, or a guard denies his request, according to the complaint. Last year, Valenzuela was unable to speak with his family during the holidays because the phone was not working for 54 straight days, from November 2025 to January 2026. However, if the tablets malfunction, there are several backup phones that incarcerated hearing people can use, the complaint says.


“We’re asking for equal access, as that’s what the law requires,” said Weisberg. “Equal access is not static — it must reflect the benefits currently offered to others and account for the needs of people with disabilities as technology and communication systems evolve.”


These issues are not limited to Illinois. Advocates say incarcerated deaf people have to contend with discriminatory communication practices in prisons throughout the country.


“In prisons where we’ve seen scores of deaf/disabled people, there may only be 2 videophones,” Kah Mendoza, the communications coordinator for

HEARD

, told …

author: Jeremy Appel, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Indigenous rights at forefront of anti-AI data centre rally in ‘Edmonton’
content:
Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation speaks at an Oct. 3 rally against data centres outside the ‘Alberta’ legislature building in amiskwacîwâskahikan (Edmonton).

Photo by Jeremy Appel


This story was originally published in

Alberta Native News

 on Oct. 6,

and appears here with permission and style edits

,

with added context from the author’s

earlier article

 from May 14

.


More than 100 people gathered outside the Legislative Assembly building in amiskwacîwâskahikan (Edmonton) on Oct. 3 to protest the provincial and federal governments’ permissive approach towards building artificial intelligence data centres.  


Elder Taz Bouchier opened the rally with a land acknowledgement before tying the proposed 7.5-gigawatt Wonder Valley data centre near Grande Prairie’s potential water usage to the oil industry’s plans to release treated tailings fluids into the Athabasca watershed. 


“When did people lose sight of how valuable water is to living? When money came into play. That’s all these data centers are about,” said Bouchier. 


Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation is challenging the province’s decision to award a water license of 24-million cubic metres to the Municipal District of Greenview for Wonder Valley without consulting the Treaty 8 First Nation, which relies on the Smoky River for its water. 


At the protest, Chief Sheldon Sunshine outlined a series of “very basic questions” he has for data centre proponents, including whether existing rules are sufficient “for the size and scale of what is being proposed” and whether there are sufficient water protections.


READ MORE:


AI data centers are booming. Indigenous People want help protecting their lands and knowledge


“What happens to our communities when these projects operate for decades?” Sunshine asked. “What happens to the land? What happens to the water? What happens to the wildlife? What happens to the air quality? What happens when multiple projects are operating in the same region? And perhaps most importantly, where is the assessment of the cumulative impacts?


“We can’t look at every project at one time and pretend the others don’t exist. We have to look at the whole picture.”


As first

reported

 by online news outlet

Canada’s National Observer

, Environment Alberta has exempted Wonder Valley from an environmental assessment. 


“Why are governments creating pathways to accelerate these developments before the public has confidence that the rules are strong enough? Why is the push happening so fast? What concessions are being made to attract these projects? Who negotiated those concessions?” asked Chief Sunshine. 


“Those are reasonable questions. Asking them does not make us anti-development. It makes us responsible.” 


He emphasized that he understands the government’s “economic strategy behind these projects,” in terms of attempting to create a new market for the province’s substantial natural gas resources. 


“But economic development cannot come at any cost,” said Sunshine. “You cannot build a new economy by putting the foundation of that economy on water that communities depend on, land that cannot be replaced, or an electrical system that people already rely on.


“You cannot call something responsible development simply because it creates jobs. Responsible development means understanding the consequences before you build.”


Edmonton-Strathcona NDP MP Heather McPherson opened her remarks by “acknowledging that Indigenous people in this country are on the front lines of this fight, and on the front lines of so many fights that we are being asked to fight as citizens right now,” referring to First Nations’

opposition

 to the province’s separatist movement. 


“We all owe Indigenous people in this province a debt of gratitude,” she added, “for being on the front line, protecting our sovereignty, protecting our climate, protecting our water and our land.”


READ MORE:


After court win, First Nations denounce ‘Alberta’ premier’s separation referendum plan


McPherson called it greatly “frustrating” that data centres are being fast-tracked while crucial community needs are being unmet. 


“We can’t build the homes that people need in this community, but we can build a data centre,” she said. “We can’t build clean water facilities for people in this country, but we can build a data center.


“The priority here for this government is to make billionaires wealthy at the expense of every single one of us here.”

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: JAWS Reception Celebrates Legacy of Women in Journalism
content:
The Journalism and Women Symposium (JAWS) celebrated the legacy of women journalists at a reception on October 2 hosted at the Ms. office. The gathering brought together journalists, longtime JAWS members, and feminist advocates to recognize the women who helped shape media and discuss the importance of preserving their work for future generations.

The reception highlighted the connections between JAWS, Ms. and the Feminist Majority Foundation (FMF), publisher of Ms. magazine. Kathy Bonk, a longtime feminist advocate and leader, recalled how Ms. founder Gloria Steinem reached out to ask FMF to keep the magazine alive. With the support of Ellie Smeal, Katherine Spillar, Peg Yorkin, and others, FMF committed to sustaining Ms. feminist journalism.

Bonk also reflected on the role of feminist journalism in advancing the women’s movement, arguing that the journalists who documented the movement helped make its progress possible. Bonk shared, “It’s no longer just news coverage. It’s looking for an impact. It’s looking at how we change people’s lives.”

A central focus of the reception was JAWS’ Legacy Fund and its efforts to preserve the history of women in journalism. Pam Morland, a former JAWS president and longtime journalist, described donating decades of professional and personal materials to archive her materials going back to 1985.

Morland encouraged fellow journalists to preserve their own work rather than discard it, explaining that materials that may seem unremarkable today can become valuable historical records. The archives offer researchers an opportunity to explore the experiences and contributions of women journalists and document the development of organizations such as JAWS.

The reception highlighted the importance of preserving women’s experiences in journalism, particularly as the profession continues to confront challenges. JAWS is helping ensure the future generations can study their work and understand the history of feminist media.

As Ms. approaches its 55th anniversary in December, marking 25 years with the Feminist Majority Foundation as publisher, the gathering celebrated the relationships, reporting and feminist organizing that have sustained the magazine and the broader movement. Speakers closed by celebrating Ms., Gloria Steinem, and the community of women journalists whose work continues to shape feminist media.

author: Admin101
title: ATX Solidarity Network is Fighting Wage Theft, La Migra, and Apathy
content:
AK, a founding member of ATX Solidarity Network, discusses their experience organizing immigrant workers to confront wage theft and other issues in right-to-work Texas.


Increased ICE enforcement has raised fears about fighting back, turning many to seek services in a field dominated by


nonprofits. In this interview we explore the tensions organizing for direct action amid these conditions.


Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN): We understand that you all in Austin, Texas have begun to build a solidarity network. What is that? How is it structured?


AK:

 A solidarity network is basically made up of workers and tenants from all over the city (or, in some cases, parts of a city) who have or may have issues with their bosses and landlords. Instead of organizing with our immediate coworkers or neighbors, we are individuals from different workplaces and living in different areas of town who fight for each other where we are at. Solidarity networks are meant to fill the void where workplace unions and tenant unions don’t exist. Since Texas is a “right to work” state, capital strategically undermines workers from building fighting organizations like unions. Solidarity networks are flexible enough to meet one or a few workers at one workplace or tenants at a complex, and temporarily bypass the immediate need for longstanding organizations.  


When you meet someone with a workplace or tenant issue, the whole solidarity network takes on the demands of the case, with those with the grievance–the issue(s) they want to fight around that directly affects them–being core organizers of their own campaign. We use direct action tactics, which means we don’t go through the courts or ask the cops or nonprofits to take care of the situation for us; we rely on just us to get the demand met by putting pressure on the boss or landlord until it becomes so unbearable they have no choice but to give in.


Like most solidarity networks there is a small group of core organizers who respond to the day- to-day needs of the organization. The people with the demands must be a part of this group. Then, there is a larger membership which is involved in many of the functions of the organization, but not all of its functions. They may pass out flyers with us, make phone calls, or research campaign targets, for example. Then there is a much larger network of people who will come out to actions when called on.


BRRN: Walk us through how you started it. Why this kind of organization, and what kinds of fights do you take on?


AK:

 Our specific solidarity network wanted to take on wage theft campaigns as our main, but not exclusive, area of struggle. We began working with another organization here that works in immigrant communities around stopping deportations. They were getting a lot of calls about wage theft, and helped us start the solidarity network to meet this need. Most of our initial calls came directly from them, and our first campaign came out of one of these calls. We also understand that the immigrant community, especially here in Texas, is very vulnerable to wage theft, and they often feel they do not have a lot of options for getting back stolen wages. We want to change that! Eventually, we want to create a citywide network of people who can respond to wage theft grievances, and other workplace and housing issues. We want to make bosses and landlords scared to even think about messing with us! 


In ATX, we have a small and unorganized left with a larger activist scene. A solidarity network is one form of organization that can work well under these conditions because you really only need a handful of core organizers and access to lots of people to show up to actions. We also see this form of organization being one in which committed leftists can develop relationships with other members of the working class. We see a lot of the left in ATX being very insular and removed from other everyday people. We feel it is important to be organizing in working-class communities since it is us as a class that are capable of transforming society. 


We also want to help normalize direct action tactics to push our collective ability to struggle even further. Ultimately, we would like to see more working-class organizations in our neighborhoods, workplaces, schools, and more. The solidarity network isn’t meant to be

the form

 of organization for widespread worker rebellion, but it is one form of organization that can respond to specific conditions that …

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Trump Cancels Livestream of Firing Squad Execution After Fierce Backlash
content:
Polling released before the announcement found only 18 percent of Americans support the livestreaming idea.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump has cancelled a plan to livestream the firing squad execution of former soldier Nidal Malik Hasan after widespread backlash from the public, politicians, military members, and faith leaders.

Trump made the announcement on Truth Social.

“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device,” he said. Studies have repeatedly found no evidence that the death penalty acts as a deterrent to crime.

“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump added. “That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. They deserve to witness JUSTICE!”

On Thursday, shortly before Trump announced his decision, polling by The Washington Post, ABC News, and Ipsos found that the idea of livestreaming an execution is extremely unpopular among the public. According to the poll, 80 percent of Americans say they oppose it, while only 18 percent said they are in support. The idea is even overwhelmingly unpopular among the respondents who said they overall support the firing squad execution of Hasan, with 69 percent opposition to and 30 percent approval of the livestream among that group.

The only group that saw majority support of the livestream was among MAGA Republican men, among whom 57 percent backed the idea.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who often speaks of violence as a virtue, initially announced the livestream last week during an interview with far right commentator Jack Posobiec.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it. That it’s public. Because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said.

But the idea was faced with immediate opposition, and in recent days, Trump had reportedly been gathering opinions from allies as to whether he should make the killing publicly watchable.

After Hegseth’s announcement, both Democrats and Republicans in Congress condemned the livestream idea. Vice President J.D. Vance, perhaps seeing the backlash, said that he would not personally watch it. The military’s archbishop put out a statement disapproving of the idea, saying that it would harm the reputation of the U.S. military.

Many other religious leaders condemned the idea. Pope Leo put out a statement, meanwhile, calling for the abolition of the death penalty altogether.

“The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” said the pope. “The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.”

Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) introduced a bill on Thursday that seeks to ban the public broadcasting of any military executions.

The Trump administration has reveled in imagery of state-perpetrated violence. Pentagon officials have repeatedly published footage of its deadly strikes on boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean, which have been likened to snuff films. His administration has gone produced propaganda videos with video game footage spliced between clips of alleged war crimes, making light of killing.

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your …

author: Isabela Dias
title: Eduardo Bolsonaro vive noite de celebridade na festa da extrema direita nos EUA
content:
Na noite de quarta-feira (14), empresários conservadores, influenciadores digitais e autoridades do governo dos Estados Unidos se reuniram no Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium, na capital Washington, D.C., para a festa de gala da Hispanic Heritage, organizado pela plataforma financeira Latino Wall Street.


O homenageado do evento foi Javier Milei, presidente da Argentina. Seu principal aliado no Brasil, Eduardo Bolsonaro, foi um dos convidados de honra.  


Na entrada, convidados trajados com roupas brilhantes e smokings cercaram Eduardo para tirar selfies e apertos de mão. Muitos perguntavam sobre o pai, Jair Bolsonaro, que cumpre em casa a pena de 27 anos de prisão por tentativa de golpe de Estado. Outros demonstravam entusiasmo com a liderança do irmão Flávio Bolsonaro no primeiro turno da

disputa presidencial

 contra o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. 


Eduardo conversou com veículos de comunicação identificados com o movimento MAGA (“Make America Great Again”, um dos slogans de Donald Trump), como a ex-boxeadora Cara Castronuova, uma das

correspondentes da Casa Branca

 alinhadas ao governo. Ele também

posou

 ao lado de Javier Negre, comunicador espanhol apelidado de “Rei Midas da viralidade”. Negre é sócio de Fernando Cerimedo, marqueteiro argentino de extrema direita,

detido

 em agosto na Bolívia, acusado de envolvimento em ataque a tiros contra a ex-companheira.    


Em determinado momento, na entrada do evento, uma mulher que parecia ser uma das convidadas segurou o braço de Eduardo e ambos olharam para baixo, compenetrados. Eles rezavam pelo Brasil. Quem também tietava Eduardo Bolsonaro era a autointitulada diplomata espiritual, consultora de direitos humanos e empresária gaúcha

Luciana Pananos

, que mora nos EUA. 


Do lado de dentro, iniciada a cerimônia, os oradores no palco falavam sobre acabar com a criminalidade e derrotar o socialismo na América Latina. Na plateia, os convidados, que pagaram entre US$ 3 mil e US$ 10 mil para participar do evento, saboreavam almôndegas de wagyu (carne bovina de origem japonesa), pato defumado com amoras, abacate recheado grelhado e filé-mignon bovino defumado. 


“Vamos expulsar o ditador comunista do Brasil”, bradou o homenageado da noite, Javier Milei, após

abraçar

 calorosamente Eduardo, que deu chutes no ar como se estivesse expulsando Lula do posto. O presidente da Argentina disse ainda que os conservadores “não podem ceder um centímetro em nossa reconquista do hemisfério”. 


“Um discurso inspirador”


Após a fala de Milei, Eduardo discursou. Ele ponderou que o resultado da eleição ainda não estava definido. Mas o tom era abertamente comemorativo. “Quando confirmarmos a vitória do meu irmão, o senador Flávio Bolsonaro, como presidente do Brasil, vamos entrar em uma nova era, que eu chamo de Era de Ouro da América Latina!”


O deputado cassado adotava um dos slogans de Donald Trump, que costuma dizer que o país vive uma nova “era de ouro” sob sua batuta. “Temos tudo para ser iguais aos Estados Unidos”, completou Eduardo.


Durante o discurso, ele também louvou outros presidentes de extrema direita na América Latina, como Nayib Bukele, de El Salvador, e o colombiano Abelardo de la Espriella.


“Amamos todos aqueles que dificultam a vida dos criminosos”, declarou, acrescentando que “pela primeira vez veremos todos os países [da América Latina] combatendo o narcoterrorismo”. O público aprovou e aplaudiu entusiasmado. Um empresário do setor imobiliário que atua em Honduras disse à reportagem que considerou o discurso “inspirador” e que o Brasil deveria adotar o “modelo Bukele”. 


Flávio e Eduardo já

visitaram

 o CECOT, o megacomplexo penitenciário para onde o governo Trump enviou imigrantes que, segundo

relatos

, foram torturados. Se a vitória de Flávio Bolsonaro se concretizar, o Brasil pode integrar a coalizão

Escudo das Américas

, formada por 19 países da região e liderada pelos EUA.  


“O melhor ainda está por vir”, declarou Eduardo Bolsonaro, prometendo libertar o Brasil, começando por seu pai.


Mais que entusiasta da candidatura do irmão à Presidência, Eduardo é um dos nomes mais

cotados

 para se tornar o próximo ministro das Relações Exteriores do Brasil em um eventual governo de Flávio. Desde que se mudou para os EUA, no início de 2025, o filho 03 de Bolsonaro perdeu o mandato de deputado federal por faltar a mais de 80% das sessões e também foi despojado do

emprego

 como investigador da Polícia Federal por abandono de posto.

title: Cómplices: quiénes son los diputados peronistas y de otros bloques que salvaron a Milei y al DNU 70/23
content:
Este jueves finalmente no hubo quórum para tratar en Diputados el DNU 70/23, así como tampoco emergencia en dispacidad y endeudamiento. Conocé uno por uno quiénes fueron los diputados que resultaron claves para impedir esta sesión.

 Por La Izquierda Diario.


Cuando el reloj marcó las 14:30 hs, quedó claro que este jueves no habría quórum para tratar el DNU 70/23, emergencia en discapacidad y endeudamiento familiar. El decreto, en particular, fue una herramienta fundacional de La Libertad Avanza que avanzó con desregulaciones a favor del mercado en múltiples áreas y favorece desde hace casi 3 años al lloby inmobiliario, de las prepagas, farmaceúticas y otros, afectando gravemente la vida de las mayorías populares.


En ese horario se llegó apenas a 121 presentes. Faltaron apenas 8 para el quórum. Los faltazos que ayudaron al gobierno de Milei y al poder económico fueron transversales y comprometieron a varios gobernadores del PJ, de los ex Juntos por el Cambio y hasta integrantes de Unión por la Patria.


Uno por uno, los responsables claves de no haber dado quórum fueron los 3 tucumanos del PJ de Osvaldo Jaldo (Medina, Noguera y Fernández), 1 de Salta de Gustavo Sáenz (Vega), 1 de Córdoba de Llaryora (Torres) , 2 jujeños de la UCR de Sadir (Rizzotti y Zigarán), 1 misionero de Passalaqcua (Vancsik), 2 santafesinos que respoden a Pullaro (Scaglia y Núñez). Además hubo 2 ausencias de Unión por la Patria: Neder de Santiago del Estero y Tita de Tierra del Fuego. En el caso de Santiago del Estero, hay más sospechas porque su gobernador Zamora ha dado colaboración a Milei en otras oportunidades. También jugaron a favor del gobierno de Milei los diputados del gobernador de Chubut Torres del PRO (Avila) y la de Neuquén de Rolando Figueroa (Maureira).


Diputados. Hubo 121 sentados. Faltaron 8 para el quórum de gobernadores de Tucumán (3), Salta (1), Jujuy (2), Misiones (1), Córdoba (1), Santa Fe (2), Chubut (1), Neuquén (1). Y 2 de Unión por la Patria (de Santiago Del Estero y Tierra del Fuego) https://t.co/uetPVGD3vs

author: Maríangeles Guerrero
title: "Creemos en la potencia política de los feminismos para sembrar semillas de esperanza"
content:
Por Mariángeles Guerrero


Desde Córdoba


De todas las provincias, del campo y de la ciudad, llegan mujeres, lesbianas, travestis, trans. Viajan hace 40 años para encontrarse. Para compartir con otras lo que viven cotidianamente en sus territorios, para aprender de otras experiencias, para contar las propias. Este año, el

39° Encuentro Plurinacional de Mujeres, Lesbianas, Travestis, Trans, Bisexuales, Intersexuales y No Binaries

 se realizó el fin de semana pasado en Córdoba capital. Los temas a debatir se organizaron por ejes. En el Eje Soberanía, la soberanía alimentaria tuvo su propio taller. Carina Vallejo, de la Unión de Trabajadoras y Trabajadores de la Tierra (UTT) de Santiago del Estero rescata “la fuerza de poner en común nuestras realidades y darte cuenta de que no estás sola”.


Y añade: ”Poder encontrarnos, escucharnos y ver que las problemáticas del agua, la tierra y el modelo de producción nos atraviesan a todas por igual en distintos puntos del país nos fortalece muchísimo. Nos permite

salir del aislamiento del interior

 y llevar nuestras voces comunitarias a debates colectivos y asambleas de mujeres”.


Dhanna Moyano es travesti, productora caprina en Luján de Cuyo (Mendoza), integrante del Movimiento Nacional Campesino Indígena-Somos Tierra (MNCI-ST) y representante de Argentina en la Coordinadora Latinoamericana de Organizaciones del Campo (CLOC) - Vía Campesina. Fue una de las participantes del Encuentro y señala que la masividad que tuvo es una muestra del enojo que hay hacia el Gobierno. “

Hemos tenido travesticidios, femicidios, ventas de nuestras tierras

. Hoy estamos defendiendo la soberanía alimentaria porque es preocupante para nuestros cuerpos y cuerpas en todo el país. Este 15 de octubre tenemos que salir a defender que no nos vendan las tierras, porque venderlas es despojar a las familias campesinas, a las comunidades indígenas y al colectivo de la diversidad que está retomando ese camino”, denuncia.


Y agrega: “Nos abrazamos, lloramos, porque estamos mal en todo el país pero también estamos dando una gran lucha por un país soberano, libre y con igualdad de derechos para todos y para todas”.


Subraya que las diversidades sexuales son parte de la lucha campesina porque es un proyecto de vida concreto para ellas. “El Estado dice que las travestis nos morimos entre los 35 y 40 años por la calidad de vida que llevamos. Volver al campo implica que esa calidad de vida aumenta, porque es una vida más sana, más saludable”, explica.


Ante el desmantelamiento de las políticas para la agricultura familiar y las políticas de género,

la presencia de la realidad campesina en los debates feministas se vuelve urgente

. En este Encuentro, por primera vez la UTT, el MNCI-ST y el Movimiento Nacional Campesino Indígena marcharon en una misma columna, representando a las organizaciones campesinas.


Carolina Llorens, del MNCI-ST y del Movimiento Campesino de Córdoba (MCC) remarca “la potencia política que tenemos los feminismos de articular luchas ante un horizonte tan fragmentado y sembrar semillas de esperanza y de organización”. Y apunta que ese es el rol que tienen los feminismos campesinos, indígenas y populares. Y que los encuentros son un espacio potenciador de esa presencia política, del protagonismo de las mujeres y las diversidades.


Graciela Salto vive a 60 kilómetros de la localidad de Quimilí (departamento Moreno, al este de Santiago del Estero). Es la primera vez que participa de un Encuentro. “Aquí se dice la verdad, uno no viene con invento, dice lo que conoce. En la vida del campo es muy importante la tierra. Y si la defendemos, es para algo bueno, para algo sano. Es para la familia, para nuestros abuelos, para nuestros hijos”, valora.


Salto participó del Encuentro con la bandera del MNCI en la espalda, junto a su hija y otras compañeras que viajaron con ella. Cuenta que el mensaje que fue a compartir con compañeras de otras provincias es lo que sucede en su territorio: las fumigaciones con agrotóxicos y los desalojos. “No podemos criar animales porque te los envenenan, no podemos poner una fruta o una verdura por el tema del veneno. Y si nos desalojan, ¿adónde vamos a ir? No queremos irnos, somos nacidos y criados en el campo”.


Al encuentro llevó su bandera y la realidad del lugar donde vive. Y vuelve a su casa, dice, “con muchos recuerdos de todo lo que se habló y de las compañeras que conocí”.

author: Administrador
title: Europa Zapatisra ¡¡Por el derecho a una Educación Autónoma. Alto a las agresiones  a las comunidades zapatistas!!
content:
¡¡Por el derecho a una Educación Autónoma. Alto a las agresiones a las comunidades zapatistas!!

Desde la Europa Insumisa denunciamos los ataques, hostigamientos, multas y encarcelamiento de varias personas bases de apoyo zapatista, en el Ejido La Culebra, perteneciente al Caracol 9, Nuevo Jerusalén, situado en el municipio oficial de Ocosingo.

Estos ataques se deben a que los compañeros y compañeras bases de apoyo, no llevan a sus hijos a las escuelas oficiales, sino a sus escuelas autónomas. Y es la existencia de estas escuelas lo que quieren hacer desaparecer los malos gobiernos, como paso previo a erradicar la autonomía zapatista, y con ella, a los zapatistas mismos. Y mientras, las autoridades oficiales quieren adherir sus escuelas oficiales al programa llamado “La Escuela es Nuestra”, que, promovido por la 4T, entrega un subsidio a las escuelas cuya cuantía depende, entre otras cosas, del número de alumnos inscritos; así, el maestro de la escuela oficial de La Culebra, junto con el comisariado ejidal y su suplente, pretenden aumentar el número de niños de su escuela, presionando, multando y encarcelando a quienes se resisten a que sus hijos reciban la mala educación que se da en las escuelas de la 4T.

Para ello, los oficialistas, no dudan en multar y encarcelar a los compañeros y compañeras bases de apoyo, por los “delitos” de no inscribir a sus hijos a la escuela oficial y por denunciar estos hechos ante sus autoridades autónomas. En este contexto, un compañero tuvo que soportar un encarcelamiento de 68 horas, otros dos, 48 y 24 horas de cárcel respectivamente, y tres más, 12 horas cada uno de ellos. Las multas que les han puesto van de 150 a 8.000 pesos, sumando un total de 48.450 pesos.

Las autoridades zapatistas denuncian, una vez más, la guerra del mal gobierno contra su autonomía, la cual se sigue dando en varios frentes; en el Ejido La Culebra es la educación, pero en otras comunidades se expresa en negar el derecho al agua, en despojarlos de sus tierras ancestrales, en negarles el derecho a la salud y su derecho a ejercer su modos y costumbres.

Desde cada uno de nuestros territorios, denunciamos estos hechos, denunciamos las manipulaciones y falsedades de las autoridades oficiales de la Cuarta Transformación y sus aliados, y les decimos que ya va siendo hora de que entiendan que la Autonomía Zapatista va a salir adelante, que los Zapatistas NO están solos y que tienen el derecho de sus niños y niñas reciban la educación autónoma que se imparte en sus escuelas, con seguridad, aprendiendo en su propia lengua a relacionarse con la naturaleza y a pensar por sí mismos y no ser adiestrados para que de adultos sean títeres del mal gobierno.

¡Exigimos respeto a la Autonomía Zapatista y a su sistema educativo!! ¡Exigimos la anulación total e inmediata de las multas a las Bases de Apoyo Zapatistas! ¡Exigimos un alto a todo tipo de agresiones a las Comunidades Zapatistas! ¡Exigimos el respeto a usos y costumbres de los pueblos originarios!

author: Rizomatica
title: 83,000 hectáreas, 400 familias y 150 actores colectivos consolidan inclusión y participación relevante: Destacan al espacio costero (ECMPO) Mañihueico-Huinay
content:
La microserie «Zonas de Resguardo» estrenó su tercer capítulo sobre el ECMPO Mañihueico-Huinay, el espacio costero más extenso del sur de Chile, con 83.000 hectáreas, 400 familias y 150 convenios de uso. Por su parte, el geógrafo Álvaro Montaña destaca que la ley permite incluir a múltiples usuarios y genera un nuevo equilibrio de poder.


La ECMPO más grande del sur de Chile


El Espacio Costero Marino de Pueblos Originarios (ECMPO) Mañihueico-Huinay, en Hualaihué, es el más extenso del sur de Chile: 83.833 hectáreas de mar, 16 años de tramitación, decenas de organizaciones incluidas y 9.368 personas viviendo en su entorno. La Ley 20.249 permite que comunidades indígenas administren un espacio costero y que otras organizaciones locales participen como usuarios del mar, según establece el artículo 11. Pesca, choritos, algas, mariscos y turismo forman parte de la economía y la vida de Hualaihué, y la pregunta que surge es qué significa esto para el futuro del mar en Chile.


La inclusión como cambio de paradigma


Consultado al geógrafo Álvaro Montaña, quien desde Chiloé ha apoyado técnicamente algunos procesos de Espacios Costeros

, señala: «El artículo 11 de la ley que crea los espacios marinos costeros de pueblos originarios establece algo que es inédito en las figuras de administración territorial de la playa y el mar de Chile. Permite la inclusión. Si bien esta ley surge por una demanda de las comunidades indígenas y solo puede ser invocada por ellas, en la administración de los espacios marinos, las comunidades indígenas pueden integrar a otros usuarios. Juntas de vecinos, comités productivos, escuelas, centros de investigación, personas naturales, empresas, ya una serie de actores que se vinculan al uso y al manejo de los recursos del mar».


Montaña agrega que esto «sin duda genera un nuevo equilibrio de poder en la administración territorial de la playa y el mar porque transfiere poder a las comunidades locales, quienes hacen la gobernanza, toman las decisiones sobre el uso de sus espacios comunes». Y sostiene: «Este es, a mi juicio, uno de los aportes principales de la ley de los espacios costeros marinos de pueblos originarios porque permite esta inclusión de usuarios. Y a mi juicio, el espacio costero de Mañihueico-Huinay es un ejemplo, un modelo en el sur de Chile de cómo la ley de espacios costeros integra y da cabida a orilleros, pescadores, buzos, armadores y una serie de organizaciones sociales, culturales, ambientales y productivas que conviven a orillas del mar».


Vivir en una isla: la voz de Yohana Coñuecar


En el marco del tercer capítulo de la microserie

«

Zonas de Resguardo

«

, Yohana Coñuecar Llancapani,

destacada dirigenta, relata su experiencia: «Es algo que es muy difícil de explicar, pero muy fácil de sentir. Que esa relación con el mar en ningún rato se corta. Está ahí, constante, latiendo como la sangre, como del corazón». Yohana vive en la isla Llanchid, en la comunidad AdMapu kaLafken, en el espacio territorial de los Coñuecar Llancapani. «Vivir en una isla es único, así que los desafíos que implica vivir acá sean siempre constantes», dice.


«Nosotros dependemos del mar», afirma. «El hecho de vivir en una isla implica que tu única conexión con el mundo exterior es a través de la navegación. El hecho de que se pueda bajar a mariscar cuando quieras comer una cazuela de marisco, un curanto, no sé. Vas al mar, no vas al mercado, aquí vas al mar directo a buscar los recursos. Y además porque toda la gente de acá sabe dónde están los recursos. Dónde están las almejas, dónde están las chorras, dónde ir a buscar choritos, dónde ir a buscar piures, qué sé yo. Entonces hay un conocer constante de la gente de la isla sobre nuestro propio espacio».


Sobre el ECMPO, detalla: «El espacio costero Mañihueico-Huinay es un espacio costero de 83.833 hectáreas. Y como es un espacio costero como de fiordos, es el espacio costero más grande otorgado en el sur de Chile». Y agrega: «Este espacio costero reconoce a 150 actores, algunos individuales y otros más en organizaciones. Así que tiene una inclusión importante de pensamiento local. El uso de la habitabilidad habla en el fondo de un uso histórico de vivir cerca del mar. Que implica no solamente tener la casa cerca del mar, sino que es tener la casa y todos los elementos necesarios para vivir. Y eso que hoy día esté acreditado y puesto como un derecho, no nos habla solamente de un derecho presente, también habla de un derecho futuro».

author: Publicación Abierta
title: 12 de octubre: la conquista remata ahora la vida
content:
12 DE OCTUBRE: LA CONQUISTA REMATA AHORA LA VIDA


Por Rafael Bautista S.


La colonización ahora se propone


aniquilar al mundo entero, pues si no todos somos iguales,


la rebelión de las víctimas es el pecado


que hay que escarmentar,


porque dice Occidente: “toda la culpa la tienen las víctimas.


El verdugo es siempre inocente”.


Para los fines de la conquista, fue preciso, necesario y estratégico cercenar las memorias y ceremonias antiguas de los indios, porque en esos residuos de resistencia se reproducía su modo de vivir. La inversión religiosa la describe muy ben Guaman Poma de Ayala cuando señala que “les quitaron su ley antigua y les pusieron temor y culpa donde antes había justicia”. Para arrebatarles y despojarles de humanidad, no bastaba con reducirlos a la miseria sino acabar con su memoria y sus costumbres, con su historia y su cultura.


Pero lo que las armas habían pretendido terminar, sólo logró su aplazamiento, pues la memoria comenzó a renacer, una y otra vez que la amenaza del exterminio prendía sus terruños, pero también su rebeldía. Las armas jamás pudieron doblegar el espíritu de liberación que atravesó, hasta el día de hoy, todas las formas que adquirió la dominación, el despojo y el robo de su tierra sagrada.


Hoy la liberación se expresa como

restauración

. El “progresismo” no entiende que el progreso es un mito, que la alternativa ya no es aferrarse al tren del progreso sino ponerle un freno y proponerse, con mayor denuedo, despertar y

conservar

 los valores que la tradición de nuestros pueblos nos ha legado, frente al desastre y el desmoronamiento de los valores moderno-occidentales. Pero

restaurar

 no es volver sino

recrear

,

actualizar

 lo que hemos perdido: una existencia más digna, libre y justa, re-ligada a lo natural y espiritual, a la simpleza que significa vivir en plenitud; lejos del dinamismo, ritmo y la inclemencia del tiempo inhumano del capital y el mercado (una vida válida para todos, donde ya no gobierne la ambición de unos cuantos).


En el siglo XV, el Abya Yala estaba atravesando una época de esplendor civilizatorio, superior, en muchos casos, a la Cristiandad latino-occidental (porque Europa recién se estaba reconociendo como nueva entidad ontológica y geopolítica). En realidad, en 1492,

quien se descubre no es América sino Europa

 y lo hace no a partir del “encuentro” con el otro sino negando su humanidad, para afirmarse como superioridad absoluta, una vez que ha diezmado la capacidad de resistencia de los pueblos dominados. El Abya Yala no fue reducida civilizatoriamente por vivir en el atraso histórico, en la barbarie (que es una pura leyenda negra que está siendo desmentida, cada día, por los nuevos hallazgos y argumentos antropológicos, arqueológicos, demográficos, tecnológicos, etc., etc.).


No nos vencieron por astucia, inteligencia o superioridad sino por una incompatibilidad radical. La

cultura de la vida

 (en todas sus expresiones) respeta los límites éticos que manifiesta la idea del bien. Una cultura de muerte, basada en la culpa infinita, el sacrificio, la aniquilación del

humanismo del otro hombre

, no admite límite alguno. Como en la actualidad, cuando el Imperio y Occidente, en su decadencia, desatan la política del odio, desatan un poder sin límites. Salah ad-Dîn o Saladino lo expresaba así, refriéndose a los cruzados cristianos: es casi inhumano luchar contra ejércitos tan hambrientos de sangre y muerte. Si el monje Bernardo de Claraval estimulaba a los cruzados con el perdón de los pecados y el paraíso eterno, por cada moro que se aniquile, se comprende la crueldad que despierta el odio al “infiel”. Como hoy en Gaza, el Imperio y Europa jamás abandonaron esa brutalidad sin coordenadas morales. Los pueblos expulsados a ser periferia del “primer mundo”, fuera de las fronteras del

humanismo liberal-moderno excluyente y selectivo

, aun cargan con la interrogante: ¿cómo puede ser posible vivir en un mundo sin respeto por la vida?


Occidente nunca fue superior. Su moralidad los retrata en la figura de aquél que afirma que “lo único que puede detenerme es

Mi propia moral

,

Mi propio pensamiento

.

No necesito

 del derecho internacional”, Trump dixit. Occidente es el nicho de la tradición imperial, que siempre debe retornar, como dice Dostoievsky, al lugar del crimen. Es su condena y, por eso mismo, debe acallar a los vencidos, para dejar de escuchar el clamor de los muertos que deja su progreso y desarrollo.

author: La Zarzamora
title: DESPEDIR A JUAN…
content:
Esta mañana nuestro compañero Juan Aliste Vega ha partido de su cuerpo, cuerpo que el poder mantuvo en encierro los últimos 16 años, cuerpo que practicó el conflicto y lo materializó en acciones armadas, que acompañó su vida en el álgido recorrido de ser él. Fue en el hospital penitenciario de Santiago, donde en compañia y calma, se fugó definitivamente.

Aún no podemos confirmar donde ni como será su despedida, ló que sí sabemos es que serán muchas, en muchos territorios, en las calles, en los puentes, en las jaulas, en avenidas y carreteras.

Juan Aliste es y será reivindicado, pese a los esfuerzos incansables de la prensa del enemigo y de sus múltiples intentos de desprestigiarlo, nosotrxs sus compañerxs sabemos que en este momento estamos despidiendo a un guerrero de gran envergadura. Pese a sus miserables conjunciones de palabras, el mundo sabe quien es Juan y en todos los territorios se levantará fuego en su memoria.

Que desesperanza deben sentir los poderosos, al saber que amamos pese a estar en guerra, que nuestra historia es escrita por nosotrxs, pese a sus asquerosos relatos oficiales, tan indignos como ellos mismos.

Hoy es un día de nuestra propia historia, hoy parte el guerrero combatiente que se alzó en armas contra la dictadura y la pestilente democracia de burgueses y traidores, el que no se dejó abatir, el que atacó y acertó, el que siguió compartiendo conocimientos y enseñanzas pese al encierro, el que enviaba notas y saludos, el que hacía llegar sus palabras a actividades y espacios.

Cada vez es más difícil despedir, esto no es una noticia, ni tampoco un comunicado, es nuestro adiós a un hermano…

A nosotrxs ahora nos quedará volver a mirarnos, tensionar el encierro de nuestrxs compañerxs, cuestionarnos y autocriticarnos, dejar de hacernos tolerantes al encarcelamiento, dejar de normalizar la sociedad carcelaria y hacer. Arduo camino nos dejas.

Juan que tu fuga sea eterna querido compañero.

Ternura y ataque frontal por ti y por todxs nuestrxs muertxs.

author: Comunizar
title: Revista Crítica Anticapitalista 6 – La Comuna, la clase y la lucha de clases
content:
PRESENTACION


¿Qué relación existe entre la Comuna como forma política de la emancipación social y la clase, entendida ésta no como categoría positivizada y sociológica, sino en su carácter dual y contradictorio? ¿Es la Comuna una manera de entender la clase y la lucha de clases en clave no identitaria, no positivizada? ¿La oposición entre Comuna y clase es algo derivado de una concepción anti-dialéctica de la lucha de clases? En ese campo ¿a qué dialéctica nos referimos? ¿A la dialéctica hegeliana orientada a la síntesis estatal como forma política de la identidad? ¿A la dialéctica negativa que la cuestiona? ¿La lucha de clases, entendida en clave dialéctica no-identitaria, permite entender la Comuna como proceso contradictorio de disolución de la clase? ¿Implica esto un desafío a nuestro concepto de proletariado y a la idea de revolución calcada en el canon leninista?


CONTENIDO
