title: A misoginia de diálogos de Vorcaro e CEO que expôs atrizes: “Mulher não pode fazer isso”
content:
Com a boca vermelha e a pele totalmente pintada de verde, Deborah Secco adentrou o Baile da Vogue de 2024, no Copacabana Palace, alternando entre sorrisos fartos e carão carregado nos olhares sensuais, um combo recorrente que já virou tradição no evento, no qual é convidada de destaque. A atriz encarnava um ser extraterrestre de roupas curtas, brancas, com direito a um bebê alien a tiracolo, no estilo carnavalesco típico da celebração, uma das grandes apostas publicitárias da Vogue Brasil e da Editora Globo nas semanas que antecedem o Carnaval.


Mas enquanto posava para os fotógrafos de dezenas de publicações e curtia a festa com sua tradicional animação, Deborah, que dividia o espaço com a nata executiva do Grupo Globo, estava desavisada do julgamento de alguns dos presentes mais relevantes do evento.

“Eu só olhava pra bunda dela rs”. As palavras são do então diretor-geral de mídias impressas e rádios da Editora Globo, Frederick Kachar, para o dono do Banco Master, Daniel Vorcaro, horas depois. “Mas tava muito feia kkk”, rebateu o banqueiro. “Concordo que a fantasia era broxante”, completou Kachar.

 “Tá doido, mulher não pode fazer isso”, disparou Vorcaro.


Os diálogos fazem parte de um conjunto de mensagens interceptadas pela Polícia Federal (PF), entre outubro de 2023 e julho de 2025, cujo vazamento ganhou força nesta semana e levou à demissão do executivo de mídia nesta quinta-feira (15). Em nota, o Grupo Globo não menciona o conteúdo misógino das mensagens como um dos motivos da demissão, mas sim a preservação da independência editorial da Editora Globo.


Nota na íntegra


Grupo Globo comunica desligamento de Frederic Kachar e reforça independência editorial de seus veículos.


O Grupo Globo comunicou hoje o desligamento do diretor-geral de Mídia Impressa e Rádio, Frederic Kachar. O conteúdo das conversas privadas mantidas com Daniel Vorcaro entre outubro de 2023 e julho de 2025, às quais a empresa teve acesso ontem, revela uma relação inadequada do executivo com um anunciante.


A Editora Globo reforça seu compromisso com a ética e a transparência e reafirma a absoluta independência editorial do jornalismo de seus veículos, premissa essencial de sua atuação. O protagonismo da cobertura crítica, isenta e independente que tem feito do caso Master é a demonstração concreta do compromisso inegociável de seus veículos com os Princípios Editoriais do Grupo Globo.


A empresa reconhece os 29 anos de dedicação de Kachar ao desenvolvimento de seus negócios de mídia e informa que o nome de seu substituto à frente da Editora Globo e do Sistema Globo de Rádio será divulgado em breve.


Comunicação Globo

Rio de Janeiro, 15 de outubro de 2026

Mais informações:

https://imprensa.globo.com/


Além de comentários objetificando atrizes ligadas ao próprio Grupo Globo, o conteúdo revela comentários machistas e convites mútuos para festas com mulheres, discrição “sem celular” e encontros descritos como idas à “Ucrânia”.


Um baile de machismo


“Muita mulher pro crime e só gay. Elas tavam dando em cima mesmo acompanhado”, foi assim que Fred Kachar descreveu o ambiente do evento da revista até então sob sua responsabilidade. E completou: “Me fodi. Minha ex foi e marcou em cima”. A ex em questão é a atriz Monique Alfradique, que também chegou a se envolver com Daniel Vorcaro meses depois. “No final não teve jeito. Marcação cerrada”, escreveu ainda. Alfradique não quis se pronunciar sobre os conteúdos das mensagens até a publicação desta reportagem.


“Deborah secco tava pra jogo”, escreveu Kachar. O executivo da Globo ainda relata que a atriz seria madrinha do camarote do Grupo no Carnaval do Rio de Janeiro e teria dito querer “curtir solteira” nos festejos. “Relação aberta. Preciso de uma dessas”

, escreveu Kachar. “Todos nós”, respondeu Vorcaro.


A assessoria de Déborah Secco repudiou a associação indevida do nome da atriz a comentários de teor machista, desrespeitoso e irresponsável, disse que a atriz não conhece Daniel Vorcaro e que sua relação com Fred Kachar sempre foi estritamente profissional. “Tiveram encontros em trabalhos, onde foram fotografados, sem qualquer vínculo entre eles”. A equipe da atriz também destacou que os comentários que se tornaram públicos diz respeito a um evento “onde ambas estavam trabalhando”.

title: Kurdish Conference: The Kurdish question must be placed at the center of EU relations
content:
A session titled “The European Union, Turkey and the Kurds: Between Strategic Partnership and Democratic Expectations” was held as part of a Kurdish conference at the European Parliament.


The session was moderated by Hişyar Özsoy, a former member of parliament for the HDP (Peoples’ Democratic Party).


Speakers at the session included Li Andersson, a Finnish Member of the European Parliament and member of The Left group; Pernando Barrena, a Spanish MEP from The Left group; Vladimir Prebilič, a Slovenian representative from the Greens/European Free Alliance; Raziye Öztürk of the Asrın Law Office; and Eleonora Scala, a member of the International Bar Association’s Human Rights Institute from the United Kingdom.


The full conference can be watched here 


https://left.eu/events/20th-international-conference-the-european-union-turkey-the-middle-east-and-the-kurds/

left.eu


Li Andersson, in her remarks, drew particular attention to the European Union’s silence and inaction in the face of authoritarian regimes, stressing that resolving the Kurdish issue must be placed at the center of EU–Turkey relations.


Eleonora Scala shared several observations on behalf of the Independent Legal Mission for the Peace Process in Turkey, of which she is a member.


The mission was established under the auspices of the European Association of Lawyers for Democracy and World Human Rights (ELDH) and the Association for Democracy and International Law (MAD).


Raziye Öztürk of the Asrın Law Office said, “We are going through a process of historic importance,” adding: “We are at a stage where we are discussing whether it is possible to bring an end to a conflict that has continued for many years and to resolve the Kurdish question through democratic and political means. Yet, despite this major change, unfortunately, we still have to talk about the right to hope and, in connection with it, Europe’s policy towards Turkey and the Kurds.


This is because, as I will explain shortly with concrete examples, it is almost impossible to say that Europe has made any changes to its approach towards the Kurds.”

title: No, not the Generation: Political Mobilisation and Changing Grammar of Protest in India
content:
Both academic and non-academic spheres are recurrently using terms like “Gen-Z protest,” “Gen Z’s political anger,” “Gen Z pressure,” “Gen-Z consciousness,” and “Gen Z politics” to describe the follow-up events. US public broadcaster NPR, despite accentuating the statistics of joblessness and inequality across South Asia as latent sources of unrest, concludes its argument by portraying “Gen Z” as an active political force. I feel some edginess with how a demographic detail is so readily treated as an explanation, when it is, at best, merely a description. Young people marching in large numbers, staging sit-ins, occupying public spaces, and facing tear gas are not new phenomena of 2026. These have long been a persistent feature of political activism in India. For instance, Bhagat Singh’s Naujawan Bharat Sabha (1926) had already demonstrated the political mobilization of youth nearly a century before.

Protests against exam-leaks are not new to India. We witnessed similar protests regarding the NEET exam in 2024. However, in 2026 the movement evolved into a mass youth mobilization, garnering national and international attention. It was driver not solely due to the examination scandal, but its collision with an unrelated event. Chief Justice Suryakant likened unemployed youth who turned to media and RTI activism to ‘cockroaches,’. Later he clarified that his remarks were intended merely for those who had entered professions such as the Bar through fake degrees, and not youth in general (Bar & Bench, 2026). Nonetheless, this clarification remained ineffective and within 24 hours a satirical social media account named ‘cockroach Janta Party’ (CJP) was created, open to anyone. This account gained 15000 followers within 24 hours, and over 19 million Instagram followers within a week. The NEET exam-leak and subsequent students-suicides provided impetus, leading tens of thousands of protestors to march towards Parliament Street under the overarching leadership of CJP and veteran Sonam Wangchuk, and ended with the resignation of a union minister.

The protesters were widely framed as a representation of a globally lucid generational style that is exasperated with institutional reverence, smooth in satire, and native to the platforms on which the movement lived. The movement has been routinely presented as a ‘Gen Z phenomena,’ that includes humour, memes, slang, and digital presence as its principal vocabulary. Gen Z has become a dominant frame, or popularised as one. Here, the concern is not whether the specific age-group people participated in the protest, but why this frame has become the media’s preferred explanation of it? Generational categorisation, such as Gen Z, Gen Alpha, Millennial, is neither an analytical lens nor an ideology in itself. A generation is just a demographic category that may have diverse socio-political orientations (Kumar, 2026); different structure[s] of power they may have confronted; and navigated varied trajectories of struggle. This essay raises the question of whether a demographic category is an appropriate explanation of a political mobilisation.

Instagram posts, memes, sarcastic placards, or even irreverent slogans are forms of political expression that should not be mistaken for an account of the politics. Labelling it as ‘Gen Z protest’ can highlight the prominent demographic cohort of protestors. But it does not shed light on the concerns, grievances, institutional failures, leadership, or political orientations that catalyzed these protests. The essay argues that while the youth presence in the protests is not new, the available grammar has shifter in the key dimensions: (a) the mode of communication through which issues, objectives and planned actions are circulated; (b) the mode of mobilisation through which sympathisers are turned into participants; and (c) the mode of campaigning through which a protest sustains public attention and pushes its demands. It is not the generational essence, but rather a recurring structural feature of youth combined with the accessibility of modern media, that explains the difference between the 2026 movement and its predecessors.

Theoretical framework: Beyond the birth-year bracket

A widespread discourse about ‘Gen Z’ typically considers a generation as a straightforward demographic fact demarcated by shared birth years, commonly dated 1997 to 2012. It is presumed to share a psychology, a politics, and a communication style as a consequence of …

title: প্রেম ভালবাসা ও সম্প্রীতির বার্তা ছড়াতে কলকাতার গান্ধী ভবন থেকে শান্তিনিকেতন পদযাত্রা
content:
গত ২ রা অক্টোবর মহাত্মা গান্ধীর জন্মদিনকে কেন্দ্র করে সর্বসেবা সংঘের নেতৃত্বে কলকাতার গান্ধী ভবন থেকে বোলপুর শান্তিনিকেতন অব্দি সর্ব সেবা সংঘের নেতৃত্বে এক পদযাত্রার আয়োজন করা হয়েছে। এই পদযাত্রার প্রধান উদ্দেশ্য মানুষের মধ্যে প্রেম ভালবাসা ও সম্প্রীতির বার্তা ছড়ানো। প্রায় ২৫৫ কিলোমিটার পথ পায়ে হেঁটে তারা আগামী ১৬ই অক্টোবর বোলপুরে পৌঁছবেন। এই যাত্রাপথে বিভিন্ন সময় বিভিন্ন মানুষজন এই কাফিলার সাথে যুক্ত হয়েছেন। ঠিক তেমনই আমরা কয়েকজন, যাদবপুর বিশ্ববিদ্যালয়ের কিছু ছাত্র-ছাত্রী, এই পদযাত্রায় ওনাদের সাথে যোগ দিই ১০ই অক্টোবর রাত্রিবেলা। পরের দিন ১১ তারিখে বর্ধমান থেকে আমরা সবাই তালিতের উদ্দেশ্যে রওনা হই। সেই সম্মন্ধে অভিজ্ঞতা ও এই উদ্যোগের পেছনের যারা প্রধান কারিগর তাদের সাথে কিছু কথাবার্তার অভিজ্ঞতা নিয়ে এই প্রতিবেদন লেখা হয়েছে।


 


সর্ব


সেবা


সংঘের


নেতৃত্বে


হওয়া


পদযাত্রা


সম্পর্কে


প্রতিবেদন


 


“आग लगी इस वृक्ष को, जलने लगे सब पात,


तुम क्यों जलो पंखेरुओं, पंख तुम्हारे साथ।


फल फूल खाये इस वृक्ष के, भीत भरे हैं पात,


उड़ना हमारा धरम नहीं, जलना वृक्ष के साथ।”


~ संत कबीर


 


খবরটা পেয়েছিলাম চাঁপাডাঙ্গা থাকতেই। শুনে যেমন অবাক হয়েছিলাম, তেমনই একটা অদম্য জেদ অনুভব করেছিলাম এই উদ্যোগে। কী উদ্যোগ? হাঁটার উদ্যোগ। যে উদ্যোগে বিশ্ব বিখ্যাত হয়ে উঠেছিলেন হিউয়েন সাঙের মতো পর্যটকেরা, তৈরি হয়েছে ভারতের বিশ্ব ইতিহাসের পাতা; আবার এই সেই হাঁটা, যার দৃঢ়চেতা জেদ, সাহস জুগিয়েছে লাখো লাখো ভারতবাসীর বুকে অস্ত্রের সামনে নিরস্ত্র হয়ে বুক চিতিয়ে দাঁড়ানোর। হাঁটার ঐতিহ্য বহুকালের, একটু বিচার করলে দেখা যায়, মানুষের সম্পূর্ণ ইতিহাস আসলে হেঁটে চলার ইতিহাস। কখনও এক ভূখণ্ড থেকে অন্য ভূখণ্ড; আবার কখনও মননের জটিল স্তর বেয়ে মনুষ্যত্বের চরম সীমাগুলোতে। এই বিবিধ ভারতবর্ষ ও তার ব্যতিক্রম নয়। সম্পূর্ণ ভারতের রাজনৈতিক ভৌগোলিক চরিত্র পাল্টে গিয়েছিল একজন ব্যক্তির হাঁটার ডাকে! লাখে লাখে মানুষ সেদিন হাঁটতে শুরু করেছিল শুধুমাত্র তাদের সম্বলটুকুকে বাঁচানোর তাগিদেই নয়, বরং নিজেদের অধিকারটা বুঝে নিতে। অত্যাচারের শিকল ভাঙতে সেই হাঁটার প্রয়োজন ছিল। জগদ্দল পাথরের মতো চেপে বসা ঔপনিবেশিকতা বুকের শ্বাস আটকে দিলে মানুষ হাঁটতে চেয়েছিল, শিরদাঁড়া উঁচু করে। আইন নামে প্রহসনকে ঠেকাতে তাই আজও মানুষ রাস্তায় নেমেছে, হাঁটতে শুরু করেছে। হিংসা, ভেদাভেদের বিপরীতে ভালোবাসা, সৌহার্দ্য আর বিভিন্নতার বাণী নিয়ে ২ রা অক্টোবর মহাত্মা গান্ধীর জন্মদিনকে কেন্দ্র করে কিছু মানুষ রবীন্দ্রনাথ ঠাকুরের পদধূলিমন্ডিত এই বাংলার শান্তিনিকেতন অবধি হেঁটে যাওয়ার উদ্যোগ নেন। এই উদ্যোগের পিছনে মূলত রয়েছেন গান্ধীবাদী সংগঠন সর্ব সেবা সংঘ, সঙ্গে যোগ দিয়েছেন বেশ কিছু গণতান্ত্রিক সংগঠন ও সচেতন নাগরিকবৃন্দ। ২ রা অক্টোবর কলকাতার গান্ধী ভবন, অর্থাৎ সেই ঐতিহাসিক হায়দরি মঞ্জিল থেকে শুরু হয় ভালোবাসা ও শান্তির বার্তা নিয়ে এই পদযাত্রা। ১৫ ই অক্টোবর সে যাত্রা পৌঁছাবে শান্তিনিকেতনে। প্রায় কুড়িটি রাজ্যের প্রতিনিধিরা এই পথে পা মেলাচ্ছেন, অর্থাৎ হাঁটার এই ডাক আর শুধু বাংলার নয়, ছড়িয়ে পড়েছে ভারতের নানা প্রান্তে।


 


ইতিহাস ঘাঁটলেই বোঝা যাবে, জায়গাটা বেছে নেওয়াও কোনো আকস্মিকতা নয়। ১৯৪৭ সালের ১৫ ই আগস্ট, যখন সারা দেশ স্বাধীনতার উৎসবে মেতেছিল, তখন কলকাতার ভয়াবহ দাঙ্গার আগুন নেভাতে মহাত্মা গান্ধী এই হায়দরি মঞ্জিলেই অনশনে বসেছিলেন। আবার ১৯০৫ সালে ব্রিটিশ সরকার সামাজিক বিভাজনের উদ্দেশ্যে বঙ্গভঙ্গ করলে তার জবাবে কবিগুরু রবীন্দ্রনাথ ১৬ ই অক্টোবর রাখিবন্ধনের ডাক দিয়েছিলেন, পারস্পরিক ভ্রাতৃত্ব অটুট রাখার জন্য। এই দুটো তারিখই ইতিহাসে খোদাই হয়ে আছে, আর এই দুইয়ের মধ্যে দিয়েই আমরা ডাক দিতে পারি সম্প্রীতি ও ঐক্যের বার্তা। সেই দুই প্রান্তকে জুড়ে দেওয়ার চেষ্টাই যেন এই পদযাত্রা, হায়দরি মঞ্জিল বা গান্ধী ভবন থেকে শান্তিনিকেতন পর্যন্ত। সংগঠকদের মতে, প্রতিটি যুগের নিজস্ব কিছু চ্যালেঞ্জ থাকে এবং সমকালীন প্রজন্ম সেগুলোকে নিজস্ব পদ্ধতিতে মোকাবিলা করে। চ্যালেঞ্জের রূপ বদলায়, কিন্তু মানবসমাজের বিকাশের ইতিহাসে এমন কখনও ঘটেনি যে চ্যালেঞ্জ একেবারেই থাকবে না। আজও নানা সংকট আমাদের সামনে। বিশ্বজুড়ে যুদ্ধ আর পরিবেশগত বিপর্যয় মানবজাতিকে নতুন কোনো পথের সন্ধানে ঠেলে দিচ্ছে। নেপালের ধ্বংসাত্মক বন্যা তারই সাক্ষী, যা মানুষের হাতে পরিবেশ ও প্রতিবেশ-ব্যবস্থায় নির্বিচার হস্তক্ষেপের পরিণতি। যুদ্ধ বরাবরই সম্পদ দখল নেওয়ার একটা পন্থা ছিল। আজ তা সম্পূর্ণ অস্ত্র-বাণিজ্যের এক কৌশলগত কর্মসূচিতে পরিণত হয়েছে। তাই তাঁরা স্বপ্ন দেখেন যুদ্ধ ও অস্ত্রমুক্ত এক পৃথিবীর, আর অঙ্গীকার করেন প্রকৃতির সঙ্গে সামঞ্জস্য ও সহযোগিতার পথে হাঁটার। আবার আমাদের ঘরের ভিতরের চ্যালেঞ্জও কম নয়। ভারতের সংবিধান সংসদীয় গণতন্ত্রের পাশাপাশি আইনের শাসন এবং আইনের চোখে নাগরিকদের সমতার নীতি প্রতিষ্ঠা করেছে। অথচ বর্তমান পরিস্থিতির বিচারে অত্যন্ত দুঃখের সঙ্গে দেখা যাচ্ছে, যাঁরা ধর্মনিরপেক্ষ সংবিধান ও সমানাধিকারের আদর্শ রক্ষার নামে শপথ নিয়ে দেশ ও রাজ্যের ক্ষমতায় অধিষ্ঠিত হয়েছেন, তাঁরাই ক্রমাগত ধর্ম ও জাতপাতের ভিত্তিতে ঘৃণা ও বিদ্বেষের সাম্প্রদায়িক রাজনীতি করে চলেছেন। এই রাজনীতি আসলে সংবিধানের প্রতি অপমানই শুধু নয়, এতো রক্তদান ও …

author: Aizel Tugalon
title: Progressive solons file bill, resolutions on academic freedom
content:
Photo by John Andrei Rarang, The Staple

Progressive lawmakers under the Makabayan bloc filed House Bill No. 11678, or the Academic Freedom Act on Monday, October 12, a bill seeking to defend academic freedom.

The bill came after recent attacks on academic freedom, such as the suspension of four University of Santo Tomas (UST) student activists for protesting against a campus exhibit by the Philippine Air Force (PAF) and the red-tagging of students and faculty members of the University of the Philippines Rural High School (UPRHS).

In her statement, Kabataan Partylist Rep. Renee Co condemned attempts to silence students who have been at the forefront of the fight for social justice and against corruption, especially since the onset of the flood control scandal.

“Discipline offices and military propaganda must not be used to silence students who are simply asking questions about and wanting to stop state abuse,” the statement read.

The bill, which adopts the 2024 UN Draft Principles for Implementing the Right to Academic Freedom and the 2026 Special Rapporteur Report on Youth Activism, seeks to impose imprisonment and fines on violations of academic freedom, such as militarization of campuses, infiltrating student organizations, filing disciplinary punishments against students who engage in peaceful political dissent, and enacting threats and violence against members of the academic community,

Furthermore, the three lawmakers also filed House Resolution No. 1541condemning the red-tagging perpetrated by former National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC) spokespersons Lorraine Badoy and Antonio Parlade and other actors related to NTF-ELCAC against students and faculty members of UPRHS and the UP Los Baños (UPLB) College of Arts and Sciences (CAS) Department of Humanities.

These attacks came after UPRHS’ commemoration of the UP Day of Remembrance during the 54th anniversary of the declaration of Martial Law on September 21.

Read: Badoy red tags UP Rural High School teacher, community

The resolution also cited the red-tagging of a Facebook page misusing the name of UPLB Perspective against campus journalists, student leaders, and administrative officials of UPLB.

Read: UPLB decries systematic red-tagging of constituents

Additionally, the Makabayan bloc filed House Resolution No. 1540, which condemns the profiling, surveillance, and intimidation of officers of the Philippine National Police (PNP) against members of the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT)-Region V Union in Camarines Sur.

In line with the Supreme Court’s ruling on red-tagging as a threat to life, liberty, and security, the resolutions call for an investigation of the said cases and the crafting of legislative measures to defend students’ rights and academic freedom. (AMU, RVO)

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Social media ban may exclude children instead of protecting them, advocates warn
content:
Child rights advocates have warned that a proposed social media ban could restrict children’s access to information, education, expression, and participation without addressing the perpetrators and platforms responsible for online abuse.


The warning followed the Senate’s approval of Senate Bill No. 2424, or the proposed Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act, on third and final reading on October 8.


The Senate approved the measure by a vote of 16-1, with no abstentions, advancing a proposal sponsored by Sen. Robinhood Padilla that would restrict minors’ access to digital services classified as high-risk.


Salinlahi Alliance for Children’s Concerns argued that the government must protect children from online exploitation, grooming, bullying, and other forms of digital harm without treating their access to digital spaces as the problem.


“Banning children from social media does not make the internet safe. It impedes children’s right to participation while the perpetrators remain,” said Teacher Elle Buntag, Salinlahi secretary general.


The group warned that restricting children’s access would not, by itself, establish whether platforms would respond more effectively to abuse or whether authorities would investigate and prosecute offenders more consistently.


Instead, Salinlahi called on the government to strengthen investigations into online sexual abuse and exploitation, require platforms to detect and remove abusive content, improve reporting and rescue mechanisms, and provide survivors with psychosocial and legal support.


“If the government’s answer to online abuse is simply to remove children from the platform, then we are asking children to bear the burden of a problem created by perpetrators and enabled by weak systems,” Buntag said.


The group maintained that children have rights to information, expression, education, participation, and connection in digital spaces, and urged the government to protect these rights while making online environments safer.


“The state must not confuse restricting children’s access with protecting children. Protection means making the digital spaces they inhabit safe and holding those who exploit them accountable,” Salinlahi said.


Different approaches


The debate over the Senate measure centers partly on whether an under-18 restriction offers a proportionate response to online harm or whether lawmakers should adopt age-specific safeguards.


Sen. Risa Hontiveros, the sole senator who voted against the measure, argued for a more targeted approach that would allow older adolescents to use social media with adequate safety measures.


Hontiveros had proposed restricting access for children under 13 while allowing those aged 13 to 18 to use social media if platforms provided adequate safeguards.


The Child Rights Network Philippines’ explainer questioned the basis for setting the minimum age at 18, and urged lawmakers to examine the evidence behind a blanket restriction before limiting children’s digital rights.


Sen. Win Gatchalian, a co-author and co-sponsor of the Senate measure, argued that aligning the age threshold with the legal definition of a child under existing laws would make enforcement more consistent and easier for authorities, according to the network’s explainer.


Padilla, meanwhile, said lawmakers could amend the measure after assessing its effects, and cited other countries’ experiences with restrictions and subsequent policy reviews, the explainer said.


The Child Rights Network challenged the idea that ease of enforcement should determine the age threshold, arguing that lawmakers must also consider the measure’s effects on children’s rights and daily lives.


The debate therefore goes beyond whether authorities can enforce an age restriction and asks whether the restriction would protect children effectively without imposing unnecessary limits on their participation.


Beyond entertainment


Child rights advocates said children use social media for more than entertainment, including research, learning, creative work, communication, and maintaining relationships.


The Child Rights Network noted that children also use digital platforms to connect with friends and peers and to communicate with parents working overseas.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Delivery Workers Criticize Plans by Grab to Acquire Foodpanda
content:
DELIVERY WORKERS from the National Delivery Workers’ Union demonstrated outside the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) earlier this month against plans by Grab to acquire Foodpanda. Specifically, delivery workers have criticized that the acquisition of Foodpanda by Grab would create monopoly conditions that would be detrimental to workers’ rights.

Taiwan’s food delivery landscape is already a duopoly between Foodpanda and Uber. Uber holds 13% of shares in Grab. Likewise, previously Uber sought to acquire Foodpanda in a deal that was blocked by the Fair Trade Commission. As such, Uber is accused of potentially seeking to acquire Foodpanda through a different means.

At the time, the National Food Delivery Workers’ Union called for the FTC to investigate the impact of the deal on workers’ and consumers’ rights, as well as the impact of what a monopoly would be. Namely, Uber Eats and Foodpanda were already criticized in the past as unilaterally raising costs for workers and prices for consumers, and the former’s acquisition of the latter may make this problem more severe.

Nevertheless, one notes that Grab has also been criticized over potential links to China. Consequently, members of the National Delivery Workers’ Union were joined by the Economic Democracy Union and DPP politicians such as Wang Shih-chien and Kao Chia-yu. Grab was singled out for past cooperation with Huawei on mapping apps, as well as operating an R&D center in Beijing, and the acquisition of a Chinese robotics company in the past.

Grab has mostly framed itself as a Southeast Asian company. Indeed, Grab is the leading food delivery and ridesharing company in Southeast Asia. Grab has also asserted that it will store data in Taiwan and Singapore, rather than China. Nevertheless, concerns have been raised about Chinese laws that require cooperation with state security services, as well as investment in Grab by Chinese ridesharing app Didi.

The Fair Trade Commission has been criticized for opening the door to Grab entering the Taiwanese market without sufficient due diligence, then. It is to be seen what actions that the Fair Trade Commission takes in the face of public pressure, especially with both pan-Green groups opposed to Grab’s entrance into the Taiwanese market on national security grounds, and delivery drivers themselves concerned about the potential impact on labor rights.

author: Kodao Productions
title: One Man’s Trash is Another’s Declining Catch: Julugan Fish Market’s Growing Worries
content:
Text and photos by

Jasmin Julia Rusios


TANZA, Cavite — At dawn, murmur start to break a market’s relative silence a moment back. As fisherfolk unload their catch and display them on the glistening floor wet with seawater, buyers lean in on their ears to whisper their bid on tubs brimming with fish. As more are unloaded and other bidders join in. The hum become din, waking a fish port from a trance as the sun rises.


Fish, crabs, shrimp, squid, shellfish and other marine products are sold and bought at Julungan Fish by whispering. The bidder who whispers the highest amount wins. Fishers and fishmongers call it

bulungan

.


Bidders check the catch before starting the ‘bulungan.’ (Photo by Jasmin Julia Rusios/Kodao)


This unique bidding style had symbolized the town’s rich fishing and trading culture. It has sustained the community through decades, contributing to the people’s livelihood and food supply even beyond its borders.


But whispers are tinged with a worried buzz nowadays, anxious at a creeping problem that increasingly ebbs and flows with the fisherfolk’s daily lives.


The bidding starts. (Photo by Jasmin Julia Rusios/Kodao)


Steady decline


Sexagenarian Romeo Cerillo’s life had been mostly the Manila Bay. He had been fishing since the age of 18, until a heart ailment forced him to hang up his paddle. But his beloved boat is still being used his nephew, allowing him to still be a part of his community’s daily commune with the sea.


Romeo witnessed fishing’s steady decline, a once steady livelihood that provided stable income for many families in their community. “Fishing was still good around 2010 and 2011. But since 2012, the catch has started becoming very poor,” he sighed.


He said the decline is the result of several factors, including overfishing and the resulting depletion of fish stocks in nearby waters. But another problem has become impossible to turn a blind eye to, he lamented.


“Sometimes, what we catch isn’t fish anymore. It’s garbage,” Romeo said.


A fisher unloads the preview night’s catch, ready for the ‘bulungan’ to start. (Photo by Jasmin Julia Rusios/Kodao)


Growing concern


The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) said marine litter threatens coastal ecosystems by damaging habitats, entangling marine animals, and being mistaken for food by fish and other aquatic species. Plastic pollution also contributes to the degradation of breeding and nursery grounds, reducing fish populations that sustain coastal communities.


Duke University’s Nicholas Institute for Environmental Policy Solutions reported the Philippines is the third-ranking contributor to plastic pollution in the world, producing between 2.7 and 5.5 million tons of plastic waste annually. About 20% of this leaks into the environment, including the sea.


The study says the country’s heavy use of single-use plastics – notably sachets for cooking condiments to toiletries – only worsen year after year. Leakage from open landfills and inefficient garbage collection at the municipal level dump plastics into rivers and open waters.


Plastics litter the beach that once only had shells. (Photo by Jasmin Julia Rusios/Kodao)


For Romeo, this problem translates directly into economic hardship. The cost of going to sea often exceeds the value of the catch, especially with increased expenses such as fuel as the wars in West Asia rage.


“One fishing trip costs around ₱1,500 for fuel and food,” Romeo explained. “Sometimes, we only earn ₱1,000 from our reduced catch. We can’t even pay the crew. We end up losing money,” he revealed. Earning ₱500 in an entire week has become something to be grateful for, he added.


But Romeo’s crew continues to sail his boat because fishing remains the only livelihood many of them know. “We have no choice,” he said. “This is our livelihood. Even if we lose money, we still have to go out to sea.”


Fighting an Endless Tide of Waste


Last May, declared Month of the Ocean, the DENR collaborated with Cavite local government units, including Tanza, in simultaneous coastal cleanup drives. More than 7,500 kilograms of waste were collected from coastal municipalities, with more than half of it classified as residual waste: plastics, cigarette butts, diapers, and other kinds of waste.

author: chuang
title: “Every War Is a World War”: Interview with a Member of Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine
content:
The following is an interview with friends from Taiwan who have formed the umbrella coalition Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP). The interview includes an overview of the rifts in the Taiwanese left, and the frustration of TWAFP organizers carving out their place amid divisions between pro-unification and independence, or pro- and anti-American positions, in the contentious and highly polarized politics on the island.


The organizer recounts their efforts to confront Taiwan’s growing ties with Israel and direct support for the genocide in Palestine. They speak with sadness that, even as Taiwan is now the fourth-largest supplier of arms to Israel, surpassing mainland China, most Taiwanese care little for the distant genocide and the struggle in Palestine seems far away. And yet, TWAFP has led successful demonstrations, pulled together a broad coalition of disparate groups in support of Palestine, and conducted research to expose Taiwan’s complicity in the ongoing genocide.


Be sure to read their

report


from 2025, outlining specific pathways of material component support for Israel, including radar, armor, and an array of military hardware.


See also a recent

piece

 submitted to us, outlining Taiwan’s deepening ties with Israel under the DPP government.


–

Chuang


Q: To begin, let’s just set the stage. Over the last few years, the Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP) has helped to organize the largest mobilizations against the genocide in Palestine seen in Taiwan. Can you tell us a little about how TWAFP formed and maybe review some of the protests it has organized?


A:

Taiwan Alliance for a Free Palestine (TWAFP)

 was founded in April of 2024. Prior to this, Taiwan had already seen several groups doing Palestine advocacy work arise spontaneously, including Palestine Action Front, Taiwan Palestine Solidarity Network, and Parallel Government. As its name suggests, TWAFP is an “Alliance” that brings together groups that were already involved in initiatives related to Palestine. In addition to the three groups already mentioned, the alliance also includes a migrant worker organization, the

Taiwan International Workers’ Association (TIWA)

; the human rights organization, Taiwan Association for Human Rights; the cultural collective, Taiwan Rave & Punk Solidarity Front for Palestine; the gender issues group, Queer Margins; and the Christian group, Taiwan Olive Branch Peace Collective. From 2024 to today, we have organized one petitioning campaign, issued two open letters, held one candlelight vigil, hosted one book club meeting, staged five protest actions, held three press conferences, and organized three marches. In the future, we plan to engage in a number of other activities, many of which may be smaller in scale.


Q: TWAFP also did some very interesting research on material links between Taiwan and Israel. We can link to the report here, but can you briefly go over the main findings, and maybe go over any new information that you’ve found since that report was released? For example, have there been more details since then?

      


A: In September of 2025, we released our report,

Taiwanese Companies’ Complicity in Israel’s Ongoing Genocide

, which identified specific manufacturers assisting Israel in the production of military weapons, including via the production of components. For example: Gloria Material Technology Corp (GMTC) supplies superalloys and high-grade steel produced through electroslag remelting, while ADLINK Technology supplies embedded computing systems and industrial-grade computers. In another case, Transcom marketed its vertically integrated capabilities—spanning chip design to module production—to enter the Israeli defense supply chain and is now a key, long-term supplier of components for the EL/M-2084 multi-mission radar, which is a core element of the Israeli “Iron Dome” air defense system designed by Israeli defense company Elta.


Since the primary purpose of this report was to provide accurate information that could be used by media outlets and other organizations, who would ideally follow up with their own reporting and investigation, we were relatively restrained in our writing approach and did not engage in much interpretation or extrapolation. title: Announcing Asian Labour School Oct-Nov 2026 Semester
content:
Dear friends,


We are back with an amazing list of new and returning courses for the Asian Labour School. If you are interested in

acquiring democratic facilitation skills, navigating conflicts and taking collective care, working cooperatively, strengthening a union core or leading your own radical walking tours

, please check out the course information below and study with Asian Labour School.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Chie Matsumoto


We all have attended meetings where decisions were made by only a few members, most outspoken ones or someone at the top. We may have once thought, “Why am I even here?” and left without saying a word. Democracy starts in the smallest conversations, dialogues and meetings by raking in most diverse opinions and ideas, piecing them together to create something new and meaningful to all participants.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Facilitators: Emi Do and Matt Noyes


Worker cooperatives are enterprises that are owned and governed by workers. When all of our working experiences have been in profit-maximizing enterprises, or in workplaces that are structured hierarchically, it is no wonder that we can encounter challenges when attempting to work together cooperatively. In this course we will explore the challenges and tensions when there are no bosses to hate!


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Facilitator: Nash Tysmans


Movements are built through relationships. Yet the pressures of organizing (urgency, conflict, exhaustion, political disagreement, and unequal power) can strain those relationships and undermine our collective capacity. How can we build movements that are both effective in challenging injustice and caring in how we work together?


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Sithar Chhim


In order to win any campaign at workplace, unions need to be strong enough to pressure the company. Building a strong and representative committee is the only way to win over the bosses who have well organized structure at workplace compare to workers.


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)


Facilitator: Kevin Lin


Have you ever thought about leading your own radical walking tour to share with friends the significance of places and histories in your city? Leading and participating in a radical walking tour is not only educational but fun and always memorable. A walking tour provides a concrete sense of places, people, and histories. This course will walk you through the conceptualisation, research and logistics of a radical walking tour, and hear ideas and experiences from other participants across Asia.


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)

author: Unknown
title: Resistance against geothermal project in Varto: Court schedules site inspection for November
content:
Resistance against a planned geothermal power plant in the village of Xwarik in the Varto district of Muş province continues. For 165 days, local residents have maintained a protest vigil against the project proposed by the US-based company IGNIS H2 Energy. As the protests continue, the Administrative Court in Bingöl has set a new date for a court-ordered expert inspection of the project site.


Local residents filed a lawsuit against the power plant project on April 9, requesting a suspension of its implementation. On July 21, the court ordered an on-site inspection and the preparation of an expert report. After objections were raised to the inspection initially scheduled for October 8 over the need for a suitably qualified geophysicist, the inspection was postponed to November 2. The project site in the neighboring district of Karlıova is also scheduled to be examined on the same day.


DBP joins protest vigil


The protest vigil, initiated by the Youth Council of the Varto Ecology Platform, is being supported by different groups on a rotating basis. On the 164th day of protests, the local branch of the Democratic Regions Party (DBP) took over the vigil. A banner displayed by the protesters reads: “The people of Varto do not want a geothermal power plant. Hands off our water and our land.”


Aziz Oral, co-chair of the DBP district branch in Varto, welcomed the upcoming court inspection and reaffirmed his party’s support for the resistance. He said the ongoing destruction of nature was the result of policies pursued for years at the expense of ecological livelihoods.


“For us, ecology is not an issue that can be postponed. It concerns not only the future but also the present. When nature is damaged, it affects every aspect of our lives,” Oral stated.


“The struggle against the power plant project is therefore not merely a local issue. It also concerns people who have moved from Varto to major cities. We do not see the ecological struggle as separate from the struggle for life,” Oral said, announcing that the DBP would continue to actively participate in the protests. Meanwhile, the protest vigil in Xwarik continues, with supporters visiting in solidarity.

author: Jim McIlroy
title: ‘Wall of Tears’ memorialises Gaza’s lost children
content:
The Wall of Tears exhibition, memorialising the 18,500 children officially recorded as killed by Israeli forces over two years in Gaza from October 7, 2023, opened at the Pitt Street Uniting Church, in Sydney, on October 9.

The exhibition is supported by Amnesty International Australia (AIA) and Palestinian Christians in Australia. The 15-metre-long artwork is on loan from Perth Doctors Medical Aid for Palestine and is open to the public until October 28.

The Wall of Tears lists the names of children killed in Gaza between October 7, 2023, and July 19, 2025, alongside photographs and stories.

Barbara Gorman, convenor of AIA's Pennant Hills Action Group, told Green Left that the exhibition “confronts us with the human reality behind the devastating number of children killed in Gaza. Every name on this Wall represents a child, a life, a family and a future.

“We hope that by bringing the Wall to Sydney, people will take the time to see those names, reflect on the scale of this loss and remember the children behind the numbers.”

Created by United States artist Phil Buehler, the Wall was first displayed in Brooklyn, New York, in January. A replica was later brought to Australia and has been displayed in Western Australia and on the lawns of Parliament House in Canberra.

“If you approach from a distance, it looks almost like an abstract painting and that draws people in to see, what is that?” Buehler explained. “Then you’ll see they are names of the children killed in Gaza since October 7 and there are thousands of them...

“You see these faces full of joy and hope, snapshots from graduations and birthday parties and family gatherings and knowing that these kids’ lives were just cut short.

“I hope that might lead people to think about how they might help, even if it’s just, tak[ing] a photo of the mural and pass[ing] it along on their social media or to their friends.”

Guest speakers at the moving Sydney launch included international human rights lawyer Chris Sidoti; Dr Saira Hussain, four-time volunteer doctor in Gaza; and Suzan Wahhab, president of Palestinian Christians in Australia. Other speakers included representatives of Muslim, Christian, Jewish and Hindu faiths.

Sidoti told the audience, which numbered more than 100: "The Wall of Tears is about hope, not just tears. In singling out a list of individual children who were killed in Gaza, the Wall shows the true identity of these children, not just names."

Importantly, said Sidoti, the Wall lists children who have died directly from Israeli military attacks, not those who died of starvation and disease, or whose bodies have not been recovered so far.

Dr Hussain said: "Many more Palestinians in Gaza will die unless the Israeli attacks are stopped. This exhibition is part of the essential movement to end the Israeli genocide in Palestine.”

[Visit the Amnesty Internation Pennant Hills Action Group's website for opening hours.]

author: April Holcombe
title: Chinese youth in a very shit time of their lives
content:
Certain quarters of the internet are filling with content lauding contemporary China as an advanced, anti-imperialist, even socialist society. Its unrivalled high-speed rail network and its continued use of Communist jargon have encouraged some disillusioned Western youth to declare themselves in “a very Chinese time of my life”.

State-of-the-art infrastructure and Communist iconography have obvious appeal to a section of people living in decaying, imperialist and increasingly far-right-controlled Western capitalism. But there is a big difference between Instagram China, a Potemkin country showcased by influencers at the invitation of the tourism bureau and marketed to disillusioned Western youth, and the real China, a nuclear superpower ruled by bureaucrat-businessmen.  

Young Chinese people on social media—students, workers and the unemployed—use a very different kind of language than influencers do. Theirs is the language of alienation, exploitation and oppression in a society every bit as capitalist as our own.

“Involution”: an obscure word for a common problem

Ever heard of “involution”? Me neither. This obscure academic term, translated into Chinese (内卷

neijuan

), has entered common parlance among young people trapped in the country’s hypercompetitive economy. Literally meaning “inwardly curling”, anthropologists repurposed the term to describe activities that increase in complexity but lead nowhere. Chinese youth decided it captured their social predicament: instructed to work ever harder to stay ahead of their peers, they end up doing much more without being any better off.

Neijuan

describes many things: the gruelling hours at Big Tech companies; the notoriously competitive university entrance examinations; the apps pushing food delivery workers to ride ever faster; and the impossible social media-influenced beauty standards. The second character is now used as a standalone verb, meaning “to work or try too hard”.

Many young people who reject the

neijuan

 rat race opt instead to “lie flat” (躺平

tang ping

), a vibe somewhere between “quiet quitting” and “bedrotting”. The Ministry of State Security finds it deeply disturbing that anyone would want to lie flat, claiming in a Douyin (like TikTok) video that “an unnamed overseas organisation heavily funds ‘lying flat’ influencers, mass producing short videos promoting ‘anti-involution equals anti-exploitation’”.

Successive surveys show scepticism and pessimism rising sharply. In 2014, 62 percent of 10,000 respondents agreed that “effort is always rewarded in our country”; only 28 percent agreed a decade later. One-fifth blamed “the unfair economic system” for poverty in 2014; more than one-third did a decade later. Two-thirds agreed their families’ lives would improve from 2014-19, but less than half thought so for 2023-28.

“Graduation means unemployment”

University degrees once guaranteed well-paid government or tech jobs, providing the Communist Party’s dictatorship with a large, stable base of middle-class support. But now, often, “graduation means unemployment” (毕业即失业

biye ji shiye

). The gradual slowdown in economic growth has intensified competition for entry-level positions (more than 600 people, for example, applied for one basic Beijing office job in November 2025). Stable employment has given way to job flux. “I have family members who, since the early 2000s, never lost their jobs”, labour researcher Kevin Lin told

Red Flag

. “Last year, my cousin was laid off for the first time. Then he struggled to find another job, got laid off again, and is on to his third job.”

Unemployment is roughly twice the official figure of 5.2 percent, according to estimates by economist Li Daokui. “There are roughly 24 million long-term discouraged unemployed people, which is highly unfavourable for social stability”, the Tsinghua University academic told the China Macroeconomic Forum in July. The youth unemployment rate, officially hitting 17.9 percent that same month, has not included students since it soared past 25 percent in 2024, and hides a vast pool of underemployed youth working as little as one hour per week.

For the first time, the Communist Party’s most recent five-year plan includes no job-creation target. On the other hand, the government has a very clear target of 70 percent AI adoption across key industries by next year, inciting fears of layoffs among many IT workers. “I still can’t shake the feeling that I’m getting closer to being …

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: Climate and Capitalism
title: Super El Niño a ‘postcard from the future’
content:
Climate and Capitalism editor Ian Angus presented the following excerpts from a “frightening” forecast from the University of Chicago’s Climate Impact Lab, posted on September 23. The original report was written by Michael Greenstone, Tamma Carleton, Genevieve Maricle and Emily Grover-Kopec.

Scientists project that global land temperatures will be 1.2⁰C above normal in the coming months, due in large part to the current “Super El Niño” that began in June and is expected to last through the Northern Hemisphere spring.

These anomalously warm conditions will resemble the higher temperatures that climate change is projected to deliver 20 years in the future and will lead to 44% more extremely hot days than we would expect in a normal year. El Niño is effectively pushing us into the future — exposing us to temperatures that won’t be the norm for another two decades — before we have time to adapt and protect ourselves.

As a result, we project that 451,000 lives will be lost due to heat the first nine months (June–February) of El Niño, compared to a normal year. This is about 65 times larger than the 6800 people believed to be dead or missing from the recent Nepal flash flood. In just the next 6 months, this includes 239,000 ± 11,000 deaths across the globe.

With current forecasts suggesting El Niño will remain in place through March–May 2027, we expect all of these numbers to grow even higher, particularly as impacts such as higher-than-average temperatures and heat-related deaths will linger into June and July.

Regions that are projected to see the largest increase in heat-related deaths over the next six months are spread across the Global South.

The most impacted countries across the Sahel are forecasted to see an additional 66,800 heat deaths from September–February compared to a normal year, with nearly half of those lives being lost in Nigeria (31,400). Elsewhere in the region, Sudan will face 17,500 additional heat deaths; Niger will face 10,000 and Chad 8000.

In South East Asia, the extra heat is projected to cause an additional 19,400 deaths in the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia, and 19,300 deaths in Indonesia. Other highly impacted regions over the next six months include India (15,800) and Brazil (13,300).

Our analysis shows that the timing of deaths will vary considerably between countries over the next six months. Those countries projected to see the largest number of excess heat-related deaths in the latter half of our forecast period — allowing more time to act — include Nigeria and Indonesia, which will face 15,400 and 10,400 more heat deaths than normal between December and February, respectively, and Brazil and India, which we project to see 8000 and 7400 additional heat-related deaths, respectively, over that three-month period.

Looking beyond the current 6-month forecast window — which runs through February 2027 — we anticipate that key areas in the northern hemisphere, such as India and Pakistan, will see heat-related deaths continue to rise into their summer.

We will provide updated, interactive forecasts pinpointing where heat-related deaths are likely to be concentrated and shift over time, giving decision-makers what they need to target interventions in real time through this period.

The anomalously warm temperatures that most of the globe will see during this El Niño event are a “postcard from the future”: while they feel anomalous now, they will become normal just a few decades into the future.

Mortality projections for the near term provide a signal of where we are headed if new adaptation investments do not materialise. The difference with climate change is that there is more time to undertake adaptations to save lives.

[Abridged from Climate and Capitalism. Read the full report, including impact maps at impactlab.org.]

author: Priya T.
title: Eugene Debs—the socialist who won a million votes
content:
Eugene Debs was the most popular and beloved socialist leader in United States history. Famed for exceptional speechmaking, the Socialist Party of America raised $20,000 to buy a train for Debs’ inaugural run for president in 1906. The “Red Special” carried Debs across the country to hundreds of meetings, from the union halls of mining towns to a mass gathering of more than 10,000 workers at New York’s Madison Square Garden. 

A lifetime of struggle, and the lessons born from bitter defeats, transformed Debs from a trade unionist and Democrat to a socialist committed to building a working-class party. 

Debs was born in 1855 in the small town of Terre Haute in Indiana. At fourteen, he started working on the railroads. Railways were central to the industrial expansion going on in the United States at the time, connecting major cities and transporting commodities between them. Capitalists employed gangster violence against unions, keeping working conditions dangerous and wages pitiful. Ray Ginger, in his famous 1949 biography of Debs, writes that in his fifth year on the railways, a friend and workmate of Debs fell under a train and died. Worried he’d meet the same all-too-common fate, Debs returned to Terre Haute shortly afterwards. 

While working at a grocery store, Debs took an administrative role at a trade union, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers. Initially, his attitudes were relatively conservative. He supported the system of craft unionism that dominated the United States, where workers were organised by trade. Railway engineers, firefighters, drivers and conductors might all be in different unions, working on the same train. Debs also viewed strikes as messy actions of last resort, writing in 1880 that while the Brotherhood sympathised with the “deluded and miserable wretches” who engaged in strikes, they believed in “a different way of settling difficulties between employer and employee. We believe in arbitration”. 

Over time, Debs became fed up with craft unionism and turned against it. The various brotherhoods did not support each other. Scabbing during strikes was common, as brotherhoods wanted to advance their own section’s interests, even at the expense of other workers. Debs encountered sectionalism as a barrier to organising the engineers. He began to believe that if unions remained divided, working conditions on the railways would never improve.

Although it caused considerable internal strife, Debs tried to amalgamate the brotherhoods to form a larger union covering the entire industry and all the trades within it. This industrial unionism approach was widespread among socialists at the time. Debs was particularly inspired by the Western Federation of Miners and its leader, “Big” Bill Haywood. 

In 1893, Debs helped form the American Railway Union as an industrial union. It was exceedingly popular, with thousands of workers joining in the weeks following its establishment, many of them young and previously unorganised. The overwhelming enthusiasm for the ARU seemed to vindicate the approach of industrial unionism. 

But as president of the ARU, Debs’ politics were contradictory. In 1894, he argued that if workers achieved vast industrial organisation, striking “would be remanded to the chamber relic of the past. An era of good will and peace would dawn”. This perspective was simultaneously militant and limited. Debs advocated working-class unity, but believed that class interests could be reconciled.

The 1894 Pullman dispute, later known as the “Debs Rebellion”, changed everything. Workers at the Pullman Factory, outside Chicago, were impoverished. The company owned all the town’s housing. After years of work, many were indebted to their employer because of extortionate rents. A proposed wage cut pushed ARU members to launch a wildcat strike, which expanded into a national boycott of all Pullman goods. The dispute was seminal; at its height, more than 100,000 workers stopped work to respect the boycott, and rail transportation came to a standstill in much of the country. 

In response, Chicago’s mayor and President Grover Cleveland, both Democrats, intervened, issuing an injunction against ARU leaders speaking about the dispute and sending in federal troops to break up the strikes. The broader labour movement, including the conservative American Federation of Labor, had refused to support the ARU and scabbed extensively. Without the necessary solidarity, the strike was isolated and ended in …

title: From CPAC to NatCon to BACPAC : Trumpism Down Under
content:

author: Jacob Andrewartha
title: Merri-bek council workers strike over below-inflation pay offer
content:
Merri-bek City Council depot workers took strike action for 24 hours over October 14–15 in response to management’s below-inflation pay rise offer, after several months of negotiations. Hume Council workers also came to add their support.

The group of eight councils’ management offered a pay rise of 2.75%, from January 1 next year, with back pay to when the agreement expired in July. It was rejected by the Australian Services Union (ASU).

Merri-bek workers gathered outside Coburg Town Hall to hear from several speakers, including Merri-Bek Socialist Alliance Councillor Sue Bolton, who said it was a “disgrace”.

“Some of the lowest paid workers are the home care workers. We need to council bosses to pay up and abide by all their own slogans about ‘fairness’ and ‘social inclusion’.”

ASU members from eight metropolitan councils, including Merri-bek, Melbourne, Yarra and Darebin began the campaign in April.

The ASU is demanding a 22% pay rise over four years, including 10% in the first year to make up for a decline in real wages due to inflation since 2021.

author: Connor Knight
title: When Australian socialists dared to dream
content:
In the years after World War One, the Australian socialist movement reached its peak influence. Socialists led big strikes, gave speeches to crowds of tens of thousands and oversaw a flourishing radical press. Thousands of workers believed socialism was possible. But until now, few historians have given this generation of Australian socialists the acknowledgement they deserve. 

Duncan Hart has been a prominent socialist in Brisbane for nearly two decades.

His new book

,

From Revolutionary Hopes to Shattered Dreams: The Socialist Movement in Australia:1918-1925,

 brings this momentous period of Australian socialism to life—its revolutionary promise, the fierce debates that animated it and its eventual decline. He spoke to

Red Flag

’s Connor Knight in Brisbane about the book. 

What inspired you to write this book? 

I was inspired at first by reading some of the history on the period that did already exist. I started to get the sense that it was a much more significant period than it has been given credit for. I was inspired by reading about the people in the movement—they were genuine socialists who wanted to overthrow capitalism, not supporters of dictatorships or advocates of gradual reform. 

Your book covers the period directly after World War One. How did the war affect life in Australia, and how did it contribute to the growth of the socialist and workers’ movements?

The war leads to a huge polarisation in Australian society. Around 300,000 Australians go to the war; half of those are casualties and 60,000 are killed—it’s a horrific conflict. At home, the Labor government tries to implement conscription through two referendums. 

Though the Labor Prime Minister Billy Hughes is confident he will win, the unions, in many cases led by the socialists, launch a campaign which ends in conscription being rejected. In this process, you see multiple general strikes, including the 1917 New South Wales Great Strike involving around 100,000 workers. This leads to a split in the Labor Party, which expels the leaders who had pushed for conscription. So, a big space is opened up for the left to influence the party. 

You argue in the book that this radicalisation peaked in 1919. What happened in 1919, and what prevented a revolutionary situation from developing? 

It’s still an open question whether there could have been a revolution in Australia in 1919. Based on where things were at, probably not, but there’s certainly a huge strike wave and political polarisation. 

The strike wave involves around 15 percent of the working class across the year. The most significant strike is led by seamen, which paralyses other industries and leads to food shortages in northern Queensland and Western Australia. The leader of the strike wanted it to spark a general strike.

As well, hundreds of thousands of soldiers are returning from the war. The government is very concerned about this, as some soldiers had been radicalised by their experiences in the war and were open to socialist arguments. 

Unfortunately, the revolutionaries were not interested in relating to the soldiers. Instead, the right-wing Returned Services League steps in, and the Labor Party on the other side organises soldiers into a loyal voter base. This defuses some of the revolutionary potential. 

You argue that the socialist movement in this period is best understood as a radical

current

within the broader workers’ movement. 

Yes, it’s a very diffuse current, and so the main way it has been looked at is through studying the individual organisations. For example, there are books on the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW), the Victorian Socialist Party, as well as various studies of the Labor Party. But there wasn’t anything written that looked at the broader movement and investigated their shared framework and political outlook across the competing tendencies. 

What were some of the features of this shared political framework? 

The main argument I make is that they shared a conception which separated industrial and political action, which I call the “industrial-political framework”. There’s also shared practices. They looked to the working class as the agents of change and promoted working-class self-education. They are very focused on the union movement as well as propaganda in public spaces like the Domain [in Sydney], Botanic Park in Adelaide or Yarra Bank in Melbourne. 

You go on to show how the Russian Revolution forced socialists in Australia to …

author: @ndy
title: Yeah Nah Pasaran #300 w Emma Hagberg on ‘Comrades, Not Friends’ & The Revolutionary Front : October 8, 2026
content:
This week on Yeah Nah Pasaran! we talk to Emma Hagberg. Emma is the author of Comrades, Not Friends: The Revolutionary Front, Antifascism, and Class Struggle (PM Press/Working Class History, 2026), translated by Gabriel Kuhn and with a preface by Tomas Rothaus (both of whom have been previous guests of the show).

According to Hagberg, RF had ‘a strong collective identity, the view of fascists as class traitors, and the critique of an autonomous left that often had no place for working-class people’; Comrades was originally published in Swedish as 18.6 – Kamrater, Inte Vänner (B.E.L Publishing, 2024) and is also available in a German translation.

The Revolutionary Front (RF), 2001–2015, was the most militant organization on the left in recent Swedish history. Staunchly working class, the first generation of RF members engaged in numerous street battles with Swedish fascists. When the fascists retreated from the streets, RF attacked them in their homes. The police cracked down on the organization in 2013, raiding the apartments of several alleged members at the crack of dawn. The courts handed out prison sentences of up to six and a half years. Two years later, the organization folded.

See also : Presentation on the book about Revolutionära Fronten (Revolutionary Front) (April 13, 2025).

author: Ayda Issa
title: Ayda Issa: ‘People power can undo the colonialists’ maps’
content:
Ayda Issa, from the Tasmanian Palestine Advocacy Network, and a Palestinian-Australian, gave the following speech to the Lutruwita protest on October 11 to mark three years of genocide in Gaza.

Having recently returned from Lebanon, I was invited to share my reflections from the trip.

As we observe three years of accelerated genocide in Gaza, these insights feel more urgent than ever, offering a necessary testament to a deeply interconnected region.

In a gallery in Beirut, I found so-called Australia.

I went to Marfa’ Gallery to see As I Weep, an exhibition by Lamia Joreige, a Palestinian-Lebanese artist. There, in the middle of the gallery, was a replica of a mosaic from Gaza.

The Shellal Mosaic is 1500 years old. It was the floor of a church a few kilometres from Gaza City. In 1917, after the Battle of Beersheba, Australian soldiers found it while digging defensive positions near Shellal along the Wadi Ghazzeh. They glued its tiny stones onto linen canvas, lifted it from the ground and shipped it to Australia.

Since 1940, it has been set into a wall at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra. The mosaic that once decorated a holy site is now permanently displayed as a war trophy.

Joreige asks: If the mosaic were returned, who would it go back to? The villages around Shellal were destroyed in 1948 by Zionist militia and the people who lived there were expelled.

How do you return something to a land that has itself been stolen?

I had to travel to Lebanon to learn that a piece of my homeland is sitting in this country’s capital. Gaza’s mosaic is kept safe in Canberra, while Gaza itself is being turned to rubble.

Australia is not a bystander to what is happening in West Asia and it never has been.

The same Australian soldiers who took the mosaic were fighting to help Britain take Palestine. Joreige spent years reading their diaries and the work she built from them was shown at the Biennale of Sydney this year.

That victory handed Britain the power to draw lines across the region; lines that would tear families apart for the next hundred years.

In 1947, Australia helped steer the United Nations plan that carved up Palestine. Today, Australian-made parts go into the fighter jets bombing Gaza and Lebanon, while Australia continues to support Israel with impunity.

Australia will deny its complicity and responsibility, because it was built the same way: on the genocide of Aboriginal people and the theft of Aboriginal land, which this nation still refuses to fully reckon with. Terra nullius, the myth of an empty land waiting to be settled, is the very same colonial narrative used to justify the erasure and colonisation of Palestine.

This always was, and always will be, Aboriginal land. Sovereignty was never ceded.

Joreige’s exhibition is called As I Weep. For over a year, she found herself unable to cry. She watched the genocide in Gaza and the destruction of Southern Lebanon every day, speechless and powerless, yet she could not shed a tear.

Then she went to the archives in London to research the history of this violence, tracking the legacy of the Paris Peace Conference, the Zionist meetings and the Palestinian petitions that were ignored. She eventually unrolled the original Sykes–Picot map, in which Britain and France first carved up this region between them. Without warning, she cried. Her tears fell onto the paper, smudging the lines and blurring the borders that started it all.

What I kept coming back to in Lebanon was this concept of borders. Colonial lines, drawn with arrogant indifference, that divided communities and shaped what came after: both occupation and resistance.

Our friend Hanan lives in a refugee camp in Beirut. She was born in Lebanon, but her family is originally from the Hula Valley.

Before 1923, the Hula Valley and the hills of Southern Lebanon were one world. Farmers grazed their animals across neighbouring valleys. They sold their crops in the next town over. Roads ran from Tyre to Acre, from Bint Jbeil to Safad; these villages functioned as one economic unit.

Then, in 1923, Britain and France drew a line through the middle of it.

The Hula Valley went to Palestine. Nobody asked the people who lived there, who shared a life of farming, trade and community, whether this was okay. Hanan’s family ended up on the Palestinian side. That line made her northern Palestinian.

Hanan’s family was expelled, pushed north across that same line into Southern Lebanon. Their villages were …

author: Gabby Soltura
title: University workers on strike in Brisbane
content:
National Tertiary Education Union members from Brisbane’s three major universities rallied in Queens Gardens on 8 October during a simultaneous

half-day strike

. After walking out at 11am, staff from the University of Queensland, Queensland University of Technology and Griffith University gathered in the city, chanting, “Chop from the top”! and “Union power”!

The popularity of the “chop from the top” slogan shouldn’t surprise anyone; QUT and UQ vice-chancellors

Margaret Shiel

 and

Deborah Terry

 both took home whopping $1.2 million salaries in 2025. Across the street from the rally stood a symbol of the bosses’ greed: Brisbane’s Treasury Building, which

Griffith recently bought for $67 million

, despite not having enough office space for staff. While vice-chancellors live in luxury and splurge on real estate, the workers who make our universities run are being offered crumbs.

UQ management’s most recent wage offer is

15.5 percent over 4 years

, or 3.9 percent per year, lower than current and projected inflation. Matthew Campbell, UQ branch vice-president and national councillor, told the rally that this offer would drive workers into rental stress. Management at

QUT

 and

Griffith

 have so far refused to present a pay offer.

Along with wage increases, the workers want secure jobs and sustainable working conditions.

Around 60 percent

 of workers in the industry are on casual or fixed-term contracts. “Permanent jobs for permanent work”, read one of the signs at the rally, and “Working conditions are student learning conditions” was a popular phrase among staff.

A report by the NTEU

 found that most Australian university tutorials are now two to three times larger than what academics say is optimal. It’s no wonder

engagement is declining

, as students are squeezed into overcrowded tutorials with overworked teachers who can’t cater to each student.

Workers’ declining wages reflect universities’ increasing corporatisation. Izzy, a teaching associate from UQ, told

Red Flag

:

“If you look around the world, you see the exact same thing happening in every education sector ... class sizes ballooning, workloads ballooning, forced restructuring, stripping out courses and degrees ... It’s not just one little policy here and there, it’s a systemic issue.”

Paul, a worker at UQ, spoke to

Red Flag

 about the significance of the strike involving workers from several universities: “We’ve got a hell of a long way to go ... but I really want to have a win in these struggles so that they can hopefully inspire other sections of the trade union movement to do the same thing”.

title: Gök yarılırken cepheye sürülür gibi: İstanbul’un altında kalanlar
content:
Valilik “zorunlu olmadıkça dışarı çıkmayın” dedi. Fabrikada, tersanede, sokakta, hastanede çalışanlar için o zorunluluğu yine patronlar belirledi.

19 yaşındaki Mazlum Gürbüz, 29 Eylül'de Eyüpsultan Kemerburgaz'daki bir şantiyede yağmur hafifler hafiflemez tabela montajı için sahaya geri çağrıldı. Elindeki metal çıta yüksek gerilim hattına değdi, bir haftalık yaşam mücadelesinin ardından 5 Ekim'de hayatını kaybetti. Çocukluk arkadaşı Levent Çelik, o gün neden işi bırakamadıklarını şöyle anlatmıştı: “İşten çıkarılma korkusuyla mecbur kaldık, çalıştık.”

Aradan iki hafta geçmeden İstanbul ve çevresi çok daha büyük bir sağanakla boğuştu. Valilik okulları tatil etti, kamuda yalnızca belli gruplara idari izin verdi, motokuryeleri trafikten çekti ve halka “zorunlu olmadıkça dışarı çıkmayın” çağrısı yaptı. Özel sektörde çalışan milyonlar için ise tek bir düzenleme çıkmadı.

Kocaeli Başiskele'de Hayat Kimya ve Özka Lastik fabrikalarını su bastı, işçi servisleri tekerlek hizasına kadar suya gömüldü. Arslanbey OSB'de işçiler fabrikaya suların içinden geçerek ulaştı. Ford Otosan'da su basan bölümlerde işçiler sırılsıklam çalıştı. Tuzla ve Yalova tersanelerinde üretim bir an bile aksamadı, vinçlerin yalnızca “kontrollü” kullanılması istendi.

Bunlar ulaşabildiklerimiz. Ulaşamadığımız nice işyerinde de afet koşullarında bile kâr hesabı işçinin canının önüne kondu. Bu koşullarda çalıştırılan her işçi, kapıda bekleyen yeni bir Mazlum Gürbüz demek.

PTT'de taşeron olarak çalışan üç çocuk babası bir dağıtımcı, paketleri sokak sokak yürüyerek dağıtıyor. Çarşamba 165 paketle çıktı, ancak 135'ini teslim edebildi. Dün yine sokaktaydı: “Valilik 'zorunlu olmadıkça çıkmayın' demiş ama bize kimse 'bugün çalışmayın' demedi. Bu sabah da 130 paketle çıktım, bu en az 15 kilometre yol demek. Bizim gibi insanlar için zorunluluk bu.”

Dağıtımcıları yağmurda sokağa iten prim sistemi. 60 paketin üzerine çıkınca prim devreye giriyor: “Üstüne bir 60 daha koyarsam bir yevmiye daha almış gibi oluyorum. Böyle çalışmasam yetiremem. Böyle de yetmiyor gerçi.” Yetmediği için PTT'den sonra Maslak'ta servis şoförlüğü yapıyor, dün eve ancak 23.30'da girebildi: “İnsan işi değil ama başka yolu yok. PTT'den aldığım para ancak çocukların okuluna, beslenmesine gidiyor. Kirayı, faturayı kim ödeyecek?”

Uber Eats'te çalışan bir kurye, sabah birkaç paket teslim edip eve dönmüş ama çalışmayı sürdüren arkadaşlarına kızamıyor: “Hepimiz borçla yaşıyoruz. Ben çalışmadım çünkü bir dayanağım var. Dayanağı olmayan adam mecbur çalışacak, hem de bu havada daha çok çalışacak.” Sokakta kurye azalınca kişi başına düşen paket artıyor, sağanak birçok kurye için bir “fırsata” dönüşüyor. Boynuna kadar suya gömülmüş kurye görüntüsü için şunları söylüyor: “O insanı zincirle sürüsen suya sokamazsın. Ama bizi kendilerine köle ettiler, sıcak evimizden kendi ayağımızla çıkıp suyun içine giriyoruz.”

Motokurye yasağı ise sabit ücreti olmayan kurye için gelirsiz gün demek: “Millet ne yiyecek diye düşünmek yasağı koyanların görevi değil mi? Bunu ücretli izne dönüştürmek çok mu zor? Şirket paketini düşünüyor, devlet gelişigüzel yasak koyuyor, kurye ne yapacak? Beni düşünmediğin yasak önlem değil.”

Bakırköy Belediyesi'nin süpürge işçileri yağmurun bıraktıklarını temizlemek için sahaya sürüldü. Daha önce de haberlerimize konu olan soyunma kulübeleri artık kullanılamaz durumda: “Sivil kıyafetlerimizi koyacak yerimiz bile yok. Dün mesai bitiminde üstümü değiştirmeye girdiğimde kıyafetlerimi su içinde buldum. Herkes evine kaçmanın yolunu ararken kenti temizleyen işçilere reva gördükleri soyunma yeri bu mu?” İşçiler insani dinlenme alanı talebini yılın başında, sözleşme sürecinde dile getirmişti: “Kulak arkası ettiler. Şimdi damı akan, çamur içindeki kulübelerde üstümüzü değiştiriyoruz.”

Park bahçeler ve fen işleri müdürlüğündeki işçi sayısı ise eski başkan Kerimoğlu döneminde 95'ken işten çıkarmalar ve emekliliklerle 35'e düşmüş. Bir işçi anlatıyor: “Dün koca Bakırköy'ün felaketini 5 işçi 24 saat çalışarak toparlamaya çalıştı. 20'nin üzerinde ağaç devrilmiş, onlarca evi, dükkânı su basmış. Hepsine yetişmeye çalışıyoruz.”
