author: Radikal Perspektif
title: Örtüşen Ordular
content:
Yazan: Benjamin Tucker


Çeviren: Gorthim


Çevirilen Asıl Metin


PDF Linki


Son zamanlarda “Twentieth Century” dergisi tanımlama konusunda epey çaba sarf ediyor. Oysa tanımlama çok titiz bir iştir ve bana öyle geliyor ki, “Twentieth Century” dergisinin yazı işleri bürosunda bu iş her zaman gereken özenle yapılmıyor.


Örneğin şuna bir bakın: Bir sosyalist, “her sektörün, ilgili tüm tarafların karşılıklı yararı için, devletin cebir kullanması yoluyla koordine edilmesi gerektiğine inanan kişidir.”


Ünlü yazarların, yukarıdakinden esasen hiçbir farkı olmayan sosyalizm tanımları ortaya koydukları doğrudur — bunlardan biri de General Walker’dır. Ancak bu köşelerde, General Walker’ın hem sosyalizm hem de anarşizm hakkında konuşurken tamamen yolunu kaybetmiş olduğu ayrıntılı bir şekilde kanıtlanmıştır. Aslında bu tanım temelden hatalıdır ve yalnızca devlet sosyalizmini doğru bir şekilde tanımlamaktadır.


Başka bir alanda buna benzer bir tanım şöyle olabilir: Din, İsa’nın Mesih olduğuna dair inançtır. Bunun Hristiyan dininin doğru bir tanımı olduğunu varsaysak bile, dinin kendisi için bir tanım olarak açıkça yanlıştır. Hristiyanlığın bu bölgede diğer tüm din biçimlerini gölgede bırakmış olması, ona dini fikrin tekelini elinde tutma hakkı vermez. Benzer şekilde, son on ya da yirmi yıl içinde devlet sosyalizminin diğer sosyalizm biçimlerini gölgede bırakmış olması da ona sosyalist fikrin tekelini elinde tutma hakkı vermez.


Sosyalizm, kendi başına ne özgürlük ne de otorite anlamına gelir. Kelimenin kendisi, uyumlu bir ilişkiden başka bir şey ifade etmez. Aslında, o kadar geniş bir terimdir ki, tanımlanması zordur. Bu konuda kesinlikle özel bir otoriteye ya da yetkinliğe sahip olduğumu iddia etmiyorum. Sadece şunu savunuyorum: Sosyalizm kelimesi, yıllardır genel kullanım ve mutabakatla çeşitli düşünce ve görüş okullarına genel bir terim olarak uygulandığı için, onu tanımlamaya çalışanlar tüm bu okulların ortak unsurunu aramak ve onu bununla özdeşleştirmek zorundadırlar; bu kelimeyi herhangi bir okulun kendine özgü doğasını temsil edecek şekilde kullanmaya hakları yoktur. “Twentieth Century” dergisinin tanımı bu sınamayı hiçbir şekilde geçemez.


Belki de bunu karşılayan bir tanım şudur: Sosyalizm, ilerlemenin esas olarak insanın çevresine etki etmesinden ziyade, çevrenin insan üzerinde etki etmesiyle sağlanacağına dair inançtır.


Bunun çok genel olduğu gerekçesiyle eleştirileceğini tahmin ediyorum ve bu eleştiriyi kabul etmeye meyilliyim. Bu tanım, açıkça “sosyalist” olarak adlandırılmaya hak kazanan herkesi kapsıyor, ancak muhtemelen böyle bir unvanı olmayan herkesi dışlamıyor.


Tanımı biraz daraltalım: Sosyalizm, ilerlemenin bir sonraki önemli adımının, servet sahiplerinin haraç almaya zorlayacak antisosyal bir güç elde etmelerini sağlayan her türlü ayrıcalığın ortadan kaldırılmasını da içerecek şekilde, insanın çevresinde ekonomik nitelikte bir değişim olması gerektiği inancıdır.


Bu tanımın daha da iyileştirilebileceğinden hiç şüphem yok ve bu yöndeki öneriler ilgi çekici olacaktır; ancak bu, en azından mevcut tefecilik temelli ekonomik sisteme karşı her türlü protesto biçimini kapsama yönünde bir girişimdir. Kendimi her zaman büyük Sosyalist hareketin bir üyesi olarak görmüşümdür ve sırf Karl Marx’ın takipçisi olmadığım için General Walker, Bay Pentecost ya da başka herhangi biri tarafından bu hareketin dışında bırakılmaya ya da tanımlanmaya itiraz ediyorum.


Şimdi, “Twentieth Century” dergisinin bir başka tanımını ele alalım: Anarşizmin tanımı. Bu tanımın yer aldığı makalenin sayısını bilmiyorum ve tam olarak alıntı yapamıyorum. Ancak bu tanım, işbirliğine olan inancı kesinlikle anarşizmin temel bir unsuru olarak gösteriyordu. Bu, sosyalizmin tanımı kadar hatalıdır. İşbirliği, anarşizmin temel bir unsuru değildir; tıpkı cebirin sosyalizmin temel bir unsuru olmadığı gibi. Anarşistlerin çoğunluğunun işbirliğine inanması, onları anarşist yapan şey değildir; tıpkı sosyalistlerin çoğunluğunun cebre inanmasının onları sosyalist yapan şey olmaması gibi. Sosyalizm ne özgürlüğün yanındadır ne de karşısındadır; anarşizm özgürlüğün yanındadır ve başka hiçbir şeyin ne yanındadır ne de karşısındadır. Anarşi, işbirliğinin anasıdır — evet, tıpkı özgürlüğün düzenin anası olması gibi; ancak tanım olarak özgürlük düzen değildir, anarşizm de işbirliği değildir.


Anarşizmi, eşit özgürlük ilkesiyle bağdaşan en yüksek düzeyde özgürlüğe olan inanç olarak tanımlıyorum; ya da başka bir deyişle, başkalarına saldırma özgürlüğü hariç her …

author: Trojka
title: Nasze ulice, Wasze granice – Relacja Toruńskiej Grupy Anarchistycznej
content:
To może tylko nasze wrażenie. Jednak wierzymy, że nie urodziłyśmy się po to, żeby zagrać w „życie”, bo wiemy, że ta plansza nie powinna tak wyglądać. I nie będziemy pionkami. Ani systemu, ani politycznych szachrajek. Nie będziemy narzędziem w cudzej manipulacji.


Wczoraj szłyśmy i szliśmy wszystkie i wszyscy właśnie z tą myślą.


Było po toruńsku. Z lekką obsuwą. Ale jak mawiają nasi lokalni bardowie: „Wy macie zegarki, ale my mamy czas”.


Początek był mocny. Huraganowy. I, niestety, dość przewidywalny. Bo przecież wiemy, jak często w takich sytuacjach działa policja. Nasze demo było legalnie zgłoszone, a mimo to prawo do spokojnego przejścia po mieście najwyraźniej komuś przeszkadzało.


Prawicowa kontrmanifestacja jeszcze przed rozpoczęciem naszego wydarzenia ustawiła się z nazistowskim banerem i zaczęła wykrzykiwać swoje hasła. Akustycznie było nawet ciekawie — kilkanaście głosów w trakcie mutacji tworzyło coś na kształt bardzo osobliwego chóru słowików. Tyle że zgodnie z ustalonymi prawnie zasadami kontrmanifestujący powinni znajdować się co najmniej 100 metrów od nas.


Nie znaleźliśmy szczególnego powodu, żeby udawać, że tego nie widzimy. Zbieraninę cherlawych weszpolaczków przed utratą baneru uratowała policja. Po odbiciu naszych przyjaciół z rąk policji wyruszyliśmy w drogę.


Ważną drogę. Przez Bydgoskie Przedmieście.


To najbardziej zaludniona dzielnica miasta, określana jako zdegradowana. Miejsce, którego mieszkańcy mierzą się z wykluczeniem wynikającym z sytuacji ekonomicznej, problemów uzależnieniowych i systemowej opresji.


Szłyśmy i szliśmy wolno. Te drugie dema chodzą szybko. Po żołniersku.


My szliśmy inaczej. Z hasłami anarchistycznymi. O pomocy wzajemnej, szacunku, równości. O tym, że razem można próbować wyjść z obłędu, który systemowo oczekuje od nas nienawiści jako dowodu wspólnoty kulturowej.


W marszu rytm wystukiwała nam niezawodna samba. Rytmy oporu rozbrzmiewały nadając rytm naszym krokom.


Był też soundsystemowy rower prowadzony przez wybitną, specjalistyczną ekipę, która serwowała RAP. Prawdziwy – antyfaszystowski, antyrasistowski. Bo taki jest rap z założenia.


Mówiłyśmy i mówiliśmy o mechanizmach ludobójstw, o kapitalistycznej opresji, o przemocy władzy i systemu. Dawałyśmy głos osobom, które doświadczyły rasizmu i ksenofobii. Apelowałyśmy o wyobraźnię.


Bo bez wyobraźni bardzo łatwo jest zaakceptować świat, w którym cudze cierpienie staje się czymś odległym. Statystyką. Nagłówkiem. Problemem „kogoś innego”. A przecież każda przemoc zaczyna się od odebrania komuś człowieczeństwa.


Po drodze zatrzymałyśmy się również przed byłym domem Nestora Machno. Nie zabawił u nas długo – musiał uciekać. Pozostali za to jego towarzysze, zmarli na emigracji, których mogiły stoją na cmentarzu przy ulicy Grudziądzkiej. Cmentarzu obok którego przechodziła nasza demonstracja.


W pewnym momencie okazało się, że policja nie zamierza pozwolić nam dojść do zaplanowanego punktu zakończenia demonstracji. Trasa została więc zmieniona.


I wiecie co?


Wyszło nam to na plus.


Żałujemy tylko, że wcześniej tego nie rozkminiłyśmy.


Nowa trasa prowadziła obok dwóch dworców. Widzieliśmy ludzi w drodze. Ludzi z bagażami, plecakami, torbami. Ludzi zmierzających gdzieś — pewnie do „nieopodal”, może dalej, może tylko na kilka przystanków.


Ale każda osoba, która choć raz taszczyła bagaż przez dworzec, rozumie, czym jest trud drogi.


A czym jest droga bez konkretnego celu?


Drogą w niewiadomą?


O tym też mówiłyśmy.


O ludziach, którzy są w drodze nie dlatego, że wybrali przygodę, ale dlatego, że zostali do tej drogi zmuszeni. O przekraczaniu granic. O tym, że granice są tworzone przez ludzi i przez ludzi mogą zostać przekroczone.


Nasze ulice.


Wasze granice.


Zakończyłyśmy demonstrację na dworcu Toruń Miasto. Zgromadzenie zostało nienachalnie zamknięte, a my skierowałyśmy się na słuchanie antyfaszystowskiego rapu.


Oczywiście policja zdążyła jeszcze coś pomylić, jak zwykle. Tym razem pomylili człowieka z kimś innym. Padła wersja, że miał zrywać flagi kontrmanifestacji — tej, której w ogóle nie powinno być tak blisko nas.


Tyle że to nawet nie był on. Ale my znamy ten rodzaj przemocy – znamy policyjne prowokacje. Znamy tę specyficzną mieszankę rozluźnienia politycznego i etycznego, która pozwala pomylić człowieka, wydarzenie, odpowiedzialność i fakty, a potem zachowywać się tak, jakby nic się nie stało.


Ponownie udało nam się zabrać z rąk pałkarzy potencjalną ofiarę całej sytuacji. Ponownie się …

author: Unknown
title: Gary Dean Jaworski - Pitirim A. Sorokin’s Sociological Anarchism
content:
Author

: Gary Dean Jaworski

Title

: Pitirim A. Sorokin’s Sociological Anarchism

Date

: 1993

Notes

: Paper presented at the 62

nd

 Annual Meeting of the Eastern Sociological Society, Arlington, Virginia, April 1992. The author gratefully acknowledges the advice of Robert K. Merton, Lewis A. Coser and two anonymous reviewers for this journal.

Source

:

journals.sagepub.com

.

History of the Human Sciences

, 1993, Vol. 6 No. 3 © 1993 SAGE (London, Newbury Park and New Delhi) pp. 61–77.

doi: 095269519300600304


Introduction


 Pitirim A. Sorokin (1889–1968) was a Russian emigre, an internationally renowned sociologist, the first chairman of the Department of Sociology at Harvard University, a president of the American Sociological Association, among many other honors, and a gadfly to the discipline of sociology (Sorokin, 1950a, 1963a, 1963b). Robin M. Williams, Jr (1980 : 103), a former student of Sorokin’s at Harvard, called his teacher a sui generis thinker and a man who thinks otherwise. He was a thinker who, as Nietzsche might have said, was ‘out of season’ with the discipline with which he identified.


 Sorokin was a lone scholar during the ascendancy of team research (cf. Merton, 1959), a pessimist during a period of postwar optimism, an antipositivist during the reign of positivism, an internationalist during the rise of American sociological hegemony, an advocate of cyclical theories of change while the contrasting view of liberal progressivism prevailed, and a grand theorist during a period of skepticism and hostility toward such theories.


 But times change. At present, when there is a renewed appreciation for grand theory (e.g. Skinner, 1985), when there is a return to cyclical theories of change (e.g. Kennedy, 1987), when there is a renewed interest in altruism (Piliavin and Chamg, 1990), and when, with the evident conclusion of the cold war and collapse of state communism, there is a revived interest in global harmony (see Goldfarb, 1989), the time is ripe for a re-examination of Sorokin’s work. The challenge of this undertaking has been accepted by scholars both here and abroad. Not only is a Russian scholar writing Sorokin’s comprehensive intellectual biography,

[1]

 but in the United States Barry Johnston (1986, 1987, 1991) continues his efforts to elucidate Sorokin’s life and work.


 The present essay contributes in a modest way to this re-examination. It does not provide an analysis of Sorokin’s work in its entirety, which, given the extensiveness of his output, would be a monumental task (e.g. Cowell, 1952). Rather, the present study investigates an important but neglected strain in Sorokin’s oeuvre, the anarchistic dimension of his work. With few exceptions, such as Tiryakian’s (1968) encyclopedia article on Sorokin, most studies fail to mention Sorokin’s links to the anarchist tradition. Yet, my recent survey of Sorokin’s published writings and unpublished correspondence demonstrates the centrality of this tradition to his works.

[2]

 A re-examination of his writings along these lines is long overdue.


 In what follows I first establish the pertinence of this line of thought to an understanding of Sorokin’s work and, second, explore the ethical project of Sorokin’s writings and reveal its roots in ethical anarchism. In the conclusion, I draw implications for future Sorokin studies and for contemporary theorizing.


Sorokin as ‘Conservative, Christian Anarchist’


 Pitirim Alexandrovich Sorokin was born in a rural village in the north of Russia in 1889. The beauty of the terrain, its pristine rivers and lakes, vast forests and flowery meadows, provided an aesthetic counterpoint to the simple but harsh conditions of life. Sorokin’s mother died when he was about 3 years old, and his father, an itinerant artisan, and a loving man when he was sober, became depressed and violent during his occasional alcoholic binges. Leaving home to escape their father’s domination and wrath, Pitirim Alexandrovich and his older brother moved from village to village while earning their living in their father’s trade, as gilders of religious icons and other cult objects (Sorokin, 1963b: 4–7).


 Sorokin’s background in the village communities of northern Russia at the turn of the century provided fertile ground for developing sensibilities favorable to the anarchist tradition in at least two respects. First, the Russian anarchist literature, such as the writings of Peter Kropotkin, was consistent …

author: ROAPE
title: Fanon’s continuing presence and revolutionary Sudan
content:
Each generation must out of relative obscurity discover its mission, fulfil it, or betray it.


– Frantz Fanon,

The Wretched of the Earth

, 1968


I do not come with timeless truths … Every human problem must be considered from the standpoint of time.


– Frantz Fanon,

Black Skin, White Masks

, 2008


 


Introduction


Fanon was very aware of his time. And yet one hundred years after his birth, he remains strangely present, as if we are repeating the same history, the long durée of the unfinished anticolonial revolutions (see Gibson 2021). Published in 1961, Fanon’s last book,

The Wretched of the Earth

, is a product of his experience and reflections on Africa’s anticolonial struggle, including its first crisis in the Congo in 1961. Written as an intervention and addressing the readers as comrades, Fanon introduces the colonised challenge to the colonial world not as a rational confrontation of points of view, ‘but the untidy affirmation of an original idea propounded as an absolute’ (Fanon 1968, 41). Aware that colonialism carved up the continent into colonial fiefdoms, Fanon recognised that while the social struggle takes on a national form, it would inevitably degenerate into the regional, ethnic and racial lines often promulgated by colonial rule

if

 it did not put into practice a ‘minimum humanist’ programme (Fanon 1968, 163).


Challenging the imperial countries who speak of humanism but kill human beings wherever they find them, Fanon ends the book returning to the question of rehumanising the world, ‘For Europe, for ourselves, and for humanity, comrades, we must turn over a new leaf, we must work out new concepts, and try to set afoot a new [hu]man’ (Fanon 1968, 316). This was his idea of African liberation. Yet, on the hundredth anniversary of Fanon’s birth, not only has Africa become proportionately poorer and more unequal over the past 30 years but the post-independence ‘wa-Benz’, the newly embourgeoisified African ruling elites or simply ‘new whites’ (Nzongola-Ntalaja 2012, 40) – the ‘little greedy caste … with the mind of a huckster, only too glad to accept the dividends that the former colonial power hands out to it’ (Fanon 1968, 175) – keep reappearing.


While often dismissed as an advocate of violence rather than a thinker of African liberation, what is often elided in discussions of Fanon’s thought is the connection between the necessity of violence against settler colonies and Fanon’s criticisms of the military and the need for demilitarisation. This article focuses on what an engagement with Fanon’s thought could offer Sudanese revolutionaries. Understanding such an engagement dialectically, Fanon emphasised the importance of subjectivity in the ‘situation’ (and what Fanon also called the ‘lie of the situation’ (see Fanon 2018, 525)), which takes on a specific perspective because the Sudanese revolution involved millions of people in a non-violent revolution against military rule. It is this movement for life and liberation that must not be forgotten in the face of the reality of a counter-revolutionary military civil war that has led to daily human catastrophe for the Sudanese people.


While the Sudanese revolution began as a rejection of military rule, regional and world powers, including the United Nations (UN), have played a significant role in supporting the so-called civilian partnership of the Transitional Military Council, established in 2019, and have continued to support the armed forces following the 2021 military coup. The repeated failure of ‘international diplomacy’, notes Muzan Alneel (2023a), ‘is mainly due to the counter-revolutionary doctrine that animates its participants’.

1


The first section of this article discusses Fanon’s idea of demilitarisation and decolonisation. The second section, on the Sudanese revolution, discusses the importance, and legacies, of the resistance committees, while the final section returns to Fanon’s idea of revolutionary humanism in the praxis of anticolonial organisations.


National military or African solidarity through a corps of volunteers?


Fanon’s idea of an African legion was proposed in his speech delivered in December 1958 at the First All-African People’s Conference in Accra, Ghana. In an article in the Algerian National Liberation Front’s

El Moudjahid

, Fanon explained that the principle adopted in Accra was a ‘concrete response of the African peoples to the will to colonial domination of the Europeans to create a corps …

author: infolibre
title: Συγκεντρώσεις αλληλεγγύης στον παλαιστινιακό λαό, την Τετάρτη 7/10
content:
Την Τρίτη 7/10 συμπληρώνονται τρία χρόνια απο την έναρξη της αιματηρής γενοκτονίας του παλαιστινιακού λαού από το κράτος – δολοφόνο Ισραήλ και τη συμμαχία του με τις  ΗΠΑ και το ΝΑΤΟ. Πάνω απο 75.000 νεκρούς παλαιστίνιους των οποίων το 1/3 αποτελούν παιδιά μετράει η γενοκτονία η οποία 3 χρόνια μετά βρίσκεται ακόμα σε εξέλιξη και το Ισραήλ και οι ΗΠΑ συνεχίζουν την προσπάθεια καθολικής επίθεσης στις χώρες της Μέσης Ανατολής. Την ίδια μέρα, σωματεία, οργανώσεις και συλλογικότητες καλούν σε συγκεντρώσεις αλληλεγγύης στον παλαιστινιακό λαό, σε διάφορα σημεία της χώρας, διαδηλώνοντας ενάντια στην γενοκτονία και κατοχή της Γάζας από το κράτος – δολοφόνο Ισραήλ αλλά και στη πιστή συμμετοχή του ελληνικού κράτους σε αυτήν.


Καλέσματα:


Αθήνα, στις 18.00, στο Πάρκο Ελευθερίας


Θεσσαλονίκη, στις 19.00, στο Άγαλμα Βενιζέλου


Καρδίτσα, στις 19.00, στη κεντρική πλατεία


Ηράκλειο, στις 19.00, στη πλατέια Λιονταριών


Αθήνα:


Πρωτοβουλία Αλληλεγγύης στον Παλαιστινιακό Λαό Εργατικών Σωματείων και Συλλογικοτήτων –

Ένωση Παλαιστινίων Εργαζομένων Ελλάδας


Τρία χρόνια από την εισβολή στη Γάζα – Καμία συνενοχή | 7/10, 6μμ, πάρκο Ελευθερίας


Καμία σιωπή. Αλληλεγγύη στον Παλαιστινιακό λαό


Όλοι/όλες στη συγκέντρωση την Τετάρτη 7 Οκτώβρη 2026, ώρα 6μμ., στο πάρκο Ελευθερίας και στην πορεία προς τις Πρεσβείες ΗΠΑ και Ισραήλ


Η

Πρωτοβουλία Αλληλεγγύης στον Παλαιστινιακό Λαό Εργατικών Σωματείων και Συλλογικοτήτων

 καλεί τους εργαζόμενους, τους συνταξιούχους, τη νεολαία και τα συνδικάτα σε μαζική κινητοποίηση την Τετάρτη 7 Οκτώβρη 2026, με αφορμή τη συμπλήρωση τριών χρόνων από την έναρξη της εισβολής στη Γάζα του κράτους-δολοφόνου του Ισραήλ. Διαδηλώνουμε για να απαιτήσουμε τον άμεσο τερματισμό της γενοκτονίας του παλαιστινιακού λαού, το τέλος της κατοχής και την πλήρη απεμπλοκή της Ελλάδας από το σφαγείο στη Μέση Ανατολή.


Τρία χρόνια μετά την 7η Οκτώβρη 2023, ο Παλαιστινιακός λαός βρίσκεται αντιμέτωπος με μια άνευ προηγουμένου συστηματική προσπάθεια εξόντωσης και εθνοκάθαρσης. Τα επίσημα στοιχεία του Γραφείου Συντονισμού Ανθρωπιστικών Υποθέσεων του ΟΗΕ (OCHA) αποτυπώνουν το μέγεθος της φρίκης: πάνω από

74.900 νεκροί

 Παλαιστίνιοι -στη συντριπτική τους πλειονότητα γυναίκες και παιδιά- και περισσότεροι από

174.000 τραυματίες

, ενώ χιλιάδες παραμένουν θαμμένοι κάτω από τα συντρίμμια.


Στη

Γάζα

, το κράτος του Ισραήλ έχει ισοπεδώσει σχεδόν το σύνολο των ζωτικών υποδομών: νοσοκομεία, σχολεία, δίκτυα ηλεκτροδότησης, σταθμοί αφαλάτωσης και αντλιοστάσια νερού έχουν καταστραφεί ολοσχερώς. Ο πληθυσμός στερείται ακόμη και το πιο βασικό ανθρώπινο δικαίωμα, την πρόσβαση σε πόσιμο νερό και τροφή, αντιμετωπίζοντας έναν τεχνητά επιβεβλημένο λιμό και την εξάπλωση επιδημιών.


Την ίδια στιγμή, το σιωνιστικό κράτος κλιμακώνει τον πόλεμο και στην κατεχόμενη

Δυτική Όχθη

. Με πάνω από 1.000 νεκρούς, καθημερινές πολύνεκρες στρατιωτικές επιδρομές σε καταυλισμούς προσφύγων (Τζενίν, Τουλκάρμ), αθρόες κατεδαφίσεις σπιτιών, βίαιους εκτοπισμούς ολόκληρων κοινοτήτων και πάνω από 1.600 καταγεγραμμένες επιθέσεις φασιστών εποίκων με την κάλυψη του ισραηλινού στρατού, επιχειρείται η de facto προσάρτηση των παλαιστινιακών εδαφών.


Αυτό το διαρκές έγκλημα δεν θα μπορούσε να συντελεστεί χωρίς την ενεργή στήριξη, χρηματοδότηση και τον εξοπλισμό του Ισραήλ από τους ιμπεριαλιστές. Οι

ΗΠΑ

, το

ΝΑΤΟ

 και η

Ευρωπαϊκή Ένωση

 δεν κάνουν απλώς «πλάτες» στο κράτος- δολοφόνο, αλλά αποτελούν συνενόχους πρώτης γραμμής.


Με αμύθητα πακέτα στρατιωτικής βοήθειας, διαρκή αποστολή οπλικών συστημάτων και διπλωματική ασυλία, η Ουάσιγκτον και οι Βρυξέλλες νομιμοποιούν την εθνοκάθαρση στο όνομα της δήθεν «αυτοάμυνας» του Ισραήλ, εξυπηρετώντας τα δικά τους γεωστρατηγικά και οικονομικά συμφέροντα στη Μέση Ανατολή.


Η γενοκτονία του Παλαιστινιακού λαού έχει και τη σφραγίδα όπως έχει και τη σφραγίδα της

Ελληνικής Κυβέρνησης

, που προχωρά σε περαιτέρω εμβάθυνση της στρατιωτικής συνεργασίας με το κράτος-δολοφόνο του Ισραήλ, επιβεβαιώνοντας το ρόλο της ως τοπικού τοποτηρητή των αμερικανονατοϊκών σχεδιασμών. Στα τέλη του Αυγούστου, μάλιστα, η

κυβέρνηση Μητσοτάκη

 υπέγραψε στο Τελ Αβίβ την απαράδεκτη διακρατική συμφωνία για την «

Ασπίδα του Αχιλλέα

», με προϋπολογισμό άνω των

3 δισ.

 ευρώ (που σε βάθος χρόνου αναμένεται να φτάσουν τα

5 δισ.

 ευρώ), με τη γιγαντιαία συμμετοχή ισραηλινών αμυντικών εταιρειών.


Για την

author: Antisystemic
title: Εξέγερση και αντι-εξέγερση στη Γαλλία
content:
Εξέγερση και αντι-εξέγερση στη Γαλλία


“Η βία αυτή δεν είναι σήμερα αστήρικτη, ασήμαντη, παραβατική. Λέγει ουσιαστικά πράγματα για τη ζωή των πληθυσμών των προαστίων και άρα για ολόκληρη την κοινωνία […] Η βία αυτή είναι υγιής, γιατί εναντιώνεται στη διατήρηση της αδικίας και του κοινωνικού χάους […]”.


Michel Ganozzi, La violence d’une partie de la jenuesse des banlieues est legitime, necessaire et saine


Οι λαϊκές εξεγέρσεις στη Γαλλία τα τελευταία χρόνια τείνουν να μετατραπούν σε μόνιμο γνώρισμα της πολιτικής και κοινωνικής πραγματικότητας. Ο κύκλος της βίας εξαπλώνεται και έλκει σταδιακά όλο και περισσότερα ταξικά υποκείμενα στη συγκρουσιακή ακολουθία του. Κάποιοι σχολίασαν ειρωνικά ότι τα “μπάχαλα” έχουν γίνει το νέο εθνικό σπόρ των “Γάλλων”. Προσπαθούν έτσι να απαξιώσουν τη σημασία των γεγονότων και να εμφυσήσουν την ιδέα μιας, αντεστραμμένης έστω, εθνικής ομοψυχίας. Την ιδέα της ύπαρξης μιας “εθνικής” τάσης, εκεί που στην πραγματικότητα υπάρχει μονάχα σύγκρουση, αντίφαση και φυγόκεντρες δυνάμεις που παλεύουν να αποκτήσουν την αυτονομία τους απ’ το κέντρο της κρατικής εξουσίας. Εκεί δηλαδή όπου υπάρχει μόνο η σταδιακή αποσύνθεση αυτού που αποκαλούμε “έθνος” ως ζώσας κοινωνικής πραγματικότητας.


Άλλοι επιχειρούν να στρέψουν επιδέξια την μία μερίδα των εξεγερμένων ενάντια στην άλλη, καλλιεργώντας το μίσος και τον ταξικό ρατσισμό, που αποτελεί τον κύριο μηχανισμό ιδεολογικής κυριαρχίας του νεοφιλελευθερισμού στις καπιταλιστικές μητροπόλεις. Αυτό για παράδειγμα είναι το περιεχόμενο της στρατηγικής “εθνικής σωτηρίας” που συνιστά την αιχμή του δόρατος της εκλογικής προπαγάνδας της Μαρίν Λεπέν. Η κινητοποίηση της λευκής μάζας των δυσαρεστημένων μικροαστών της ενδοχώρας, οι οποίοι πριν κάποια χρόνια συσπειρώθηκαν στις μεγαλειώδεις αντικυβερνητικές διαδηλώσεις των Κίτρινων Γιλέκων, ως αντίβαρο στις εξεγερσιακές διαθέσεις του προλεταριάτου των πόλεων, καθώς και του πολυεθνικού λούμπεν προλεταριάτου των προαστίων. Αν κάποιο συμπέρασμα προκύπτει αβίαστα από αυτή τη συνεχή κοινωνική αναταραχή στη Γαλλία, είναι η έκδηλη αδυναμία του  νεοφιλελεύθερου κράτους να οικοδομήσει ένα ταξικό μπλοκ που θα του εξασφαλίσει την απαραίτητη κοινωνική αποδοχή και θα εγγυηθεί την μακροημέρευση της κυριαρχίας του.


Το πρόβλημα βέβαια με αυτόν τον επαναλαμβανόμενο κύκλο εξέγερσης και αντιεξέγερσης είναι η αδυναμία που επιδεικνύουν εξίσου οι επιμέρους ανταρσίες κι εκστρατείες κοινωνικής ανυπακοής που συγκροτούνται αυθόρμητα από-τα-κάτω, να συμμαχήσουν σε ένα ενιαίο κίνημα και να καταφέρουν το οριστικό χτύπημα στη νεοφιλελεύθερη χούντα του Μακρόν που παραπαίει. Μπαίνουμε εδώ στον πειρασμό να θυμηθούμε τον ιστορικό Eric Hobsbawm που κάποτε είχε γράψει ότι κατά την πρώτη εποχή της κυριαρχίας της, στα χρόνια που ήταν ακόμη σε εξέλιξη η βιομηχανική επανάσταση, η αστική τάξη είχε μάθει να ζει με τα περιοδικά ξεσπάσματα αγανάκτησης των προλετάριων. Είχε μάθει να τα θεωρεί ως ένα αναγκαίο κακό, όπου όμως “δεν δικακυβευόταν τίποτε […] πέρα από κάποια περιουσιακά στοιχεία που μια πλούσια χώρα μπορούσε κάλλιστα να τα αντικαταστήσει”.i Με άλλα λόγια, οι αστοί έδειχναν μια ανοχή σε αυτές τις παροδικές εξεγερσιακές εκρήξεις των φτωχών, διότι είχαν καταλάβει ότι αυτό ήταν τίμημα που έπρεπε να καταβάλλουν για να εξαγνίσουν την κυριαρχία τους.


Παρ’ όλα αυτά, η απελπισία των ελίτ στη Γαλλία έχει φτάσει σε τέτοιο σημείο ώστε επιστράτευσαν το παραμύθι των “πρακτόρων της Μόσχας” που δήθεν υποδαυλίζουν τις κοινωνικές ταραχές σε ολόκληρη τη χώρα.ii Εδώ τα διδάγματα από το υπερσυντηρητικό εργαστήρι της εμπόλεμης Ουκρανίας είναι κάτι παραπάνω από πολύτιμα. Λίγο μετά τη λαϊκή εξέγερση που ανέβασε στην εξουσία την ακροδεξιά χούντα του Μαϊντάν, ο τότε πρωθυπουργός Γιάτσενιουκ αποκάλεσε τους ανθρώπους που διαμαρτύρονταν στους δρόμους για την απότομη αύξηση στις τιμές του πετρελαίου θέρμανσης και τις περικοπές στις δαπάνες για την υγεία και την παιδεία, “πράκτορες των Ρώσων” και πέμπτη φάλαγγα που ενεργούσε καθ’ υπόδειξη του εχθρού, δηλαδή της Ρωσίας.iii Να λοιπόν που η ρωσοφοβική προπαγάνδα για το μαύρο χέρι του “Μόσκοβου” είναι σαν τη διαφήμιση της κοκα-κόλα. Πάει με όλα. Παρά την προφανή γελοιότητα της, η θεωρία του “ξένου δάκτυλου” που απεργάζεται στο παρασκήνιο την αποσταθεροποίηση των ευρωπαϊκών κοινωνιών είναι το τελευταίο καταφύγιο των ευρωπαϊκών πολιτικών και οικονομικών ελίτ που έχουν απωλέσει τα κοινωνικά στηρίγματα τους και βυθίζονται σε μια κρίση νομιμοποίησης της εξουσίας τους. Είναι επίσης ένα τρόπος για να τεθούν εκτός του “υγιούς” κορμού της …

author: Unknown
title: Adam Gary Lewis - Cultures of Anarchist Anti-Colonialism
content:
Author

: Adam Gary Lewis

Title

: Cultures of Anarchist Anti-Colonialism

Subtitle

: Considering Anarchist Prefigurative Possibilities for the Future

Date

: 2026

Notes

: *A text edited for the workshop “Cultures of Anarchist Anti-Colonialism” at the 2026 Hamilton Anarchist Bookfair. **Note: This zine is a heftily edited version of chapters, ideas, and discussions that appear in the 2026 PhD dissertation. I have aimed to condense this work, and dispense with some of the excess academic referencing, language and theory. This is not to suggest that these elements cannot be useful to anarchists, but in the spirit of generating wider forms of discussion I present this initial edited version. The interviews referenced here come from my conversations with 17 anarchists in Southern Ontario, that span a range of cities, communities, and scenes, and encompass a range of complex social identities. In particular, I highlight the words and perspectives of Indigenous participants. Pseudonyms were used to help to maintain some aspect of anonymity. I hope these ideas further some of the ongoing and important conversations on anarchism and anti-colonial politics both here in Southern Ontario, but also further afield as well. My heartfelt and ongoing thanks to all who participated and supported this project over many years, and all the anarchist crews in Southern Ontario. Of course for those with more academic and theory oriented desires I invite you to check out the full dissertation work as well: Adam Gary Lewis. 2026. Cultures of Resistance, Cultures of Potential: Anarchist Value-Practices, Settler Colonialism, and Indigenous Resurgence. PhD Dissertation. York University.

Source

: Retrieved on October 4, 2026 from https://anarchistnews.org/content/cultures-anarchist-anti-colonialism


Someday, somewhere, today’s empires are tomorrow’s ashes.


—Propagandhi


 Commitments to resist settler colonialism and articulate affinities with Indigenous struggles carry potentials for greater forms of anti-colonial politics within anarchism. Such commitments are important points of resistance and action within anarchism, but they are often limited, and require greater expansion in both theory and practice in order to actually generate disruptive forms of anarchist anti-colonialism.


 Anarchists have long named settler colonialism as a key form of oppression and domination that needs to be opposed, alongside more standard anarchist oppositions like the state and capitalism. This is most readily visible in intro to anarchism books, zines, and discussions. Opposition to colonialism is nestled alongside the wide range of opposition to all forms of oppression and domination that characterizes contemporary anarchist politics. In many of these accounts, and especially those that are more theoretical in nature, there is little discussion as to what this sort of anti-colonial opposition might look like. There may be vague nods to support for Indigenous resurgence, or wider histories of complicity with international forms of anti-imperialist struggle, but rarely is there more detailed discussion of how committed form of anti-colonial politics might be enacted in here and now –in specific places at specific times– and with direct reference to the histories and flows of struggle that might disrupt anarchism for the better.


 This results in a tendency to leave colonialism among a wider laundry list of things to be opposed, and lacking in greater qualification and consideration of what this means as practical forms of politics. How, then, are anarchists actually seeking to practically, materially, and intentionally oppose settler colonialism, and support Indigenous resistance and resurgence? This zine attempts to shed light on some of the everyday ways that anarchists in Southern Ontario are engaging this work, and how they are thinking about the relationship between anarchism and anti-colonial politics.


 I consider how spirituality, history, relationships to land and place, and prefigurative imaginations for the future interact with anarchist anti-colonialism. I begin with spirituality as a tension that is perhaps even less discussed amongst anarchists, but which intersects directly with Indigenous resurgence politics, given the centrality of Indigenous cosmologies, grounded normativities, and relationships to land. The limited anarchist approach to spirituality is a stumbling block for anarchist affinities with Indigenous struggles, as well …

author: Kévin Drif
title: The North African family French critics couldn’t see
content:
Since her 2016 debut feature

Raw

, the French auteur Julia Ducournau’s films have been a staple of the body horror genre. Her movies reflect an unapologetic approach to exploring physical transformation and the “monstrous feminine,” an idea coined by feminist film scholar Barbara Creed to underscore the significance of gender and sexuality in the construction of monstrosity. In Ducournau’s films, female characters strive for emancipation from social and familial norms through cannibalism or transhumanism. Yet while

Raw

 and her sophomore feature

Titane

 (2021) center white protagonists,

Alpha

 (2025), her third film, foregrounds the complex dynamic of a family of North African descent, marking a significant departure for the auteur. Curiously, this demographic difference has been almost entirely absent from discussions of the film.

Set between the 1980s and 1990s,

Alpha

 follows its 13-year-old eponymous character; her mother, who is a doctor; and her uncle Amin as they confront a mysterious virus that transforms bodies into blue-veined marmoreal statues that eventually turn to dust. Critics have understandably focused on the epidemic narrative, the stigma attached to the infected, and its evocation of the AIDS crisis, but in doing so, they have overlooked another dimension of the story:

Alpha

 is one of the few contemporary French films to place a family of North African origin at the center of a national trauma.

Ducournau hardly conceals the central family’s roots. She casts actors of Algerian, Moroccan, and Iranian descent and the characters move between French and dialectal Arabic. In one scene that features the most cinematic French postcolonial locality — the

banlieue

 —

Alpha

 joins her extended family to share a couscous meal for an Eid celebration. The problem here is not simply that reviewers omitted demographic details but that their silence in effect reproduces a broader tendency and difficulty within French cultural discourse to see race, acknowledge colonial history, and address postcolonial belonging even when it permeates the screen.

Approaching

Alpha

 through a postcolonial lens opens more interpretative possibilities. Consider the body itself, a central concern of Ducournau’s cinema:

Alpha

’s makeshift tattoo, which symbolically binds her to Amin, evokes traditions of Amazigh inking while also drawing attention to the postcolonial body as a site of inscription, memory, and belonging. The gesture turns the body into a site where cultural memory can persist without being explicitly articulated;

Alpha

’s body becomes a postcolonial archive — a place where histories and affiliations that remain largely unspoken can nonetheless be inscribed, carried, and transmitted. Furthermore, the film’s concern with body regulation recalls the colonial politics of visibility explored by Frantz Fanon in his writings on French Algeria, where the control of bodies, especially female bodies through the practice of unveiling, functioned as a mechanism of domination.

Alpha

’s epidemic narrative also takes on new meanings when viewed through the history of North African migration. The AIDS crisis in France disproportionally affected marginalized communities. According to

a 1999 study

 led by the French Institut de veille sanitaire, or Institute of Health Surveillance, between 1978 and 1998, immigrant populations accounted for 14 percent of AIDS cases in France, when they only represented 6 percent of the adult population at the time. Drug users of North African origin infected through contaminated needles, much like Amin, represented the main mode of contamination for heterosexual men and accounted for 45 percent of North African immigrant cases. Still, they remain largely absent from narratives of the epidemic. This omission and silence of the infected is the result of the religious taboo attached to the disease and the larger structural disinterest in these populations. Ducournau’s attention to Amin gestures towards histories that have largely escaped commemoration.

Alpha

’s imagery of suffocation, disease, and social abandonment invites reflection of the lives and afterlives of colonial violence beyond France. The calcification of infected bodies recalls forms of historical petrification through which colonial atrocities are rendered distant, abstract, and invisible within French national memory. author: Alfredo Seguel
title: Masiva marcha anticolonial de PPOO en Chile denuncia genocidio, militarización y más de 100 presos políticos mapuche
content:
Una multitudinaria marcha anticolonial se realizó este 12 de octubre en el cerro Welén, Santiago, convocada por la resistencia mapuche urbana y organizaciones sociales. Denunciaron el genocidio europeo, la militarización del Wallmapu, la persecución judicial y los más de 100 presos políticos mapuche en el presente. También en otras localidades se realizaron manifestaciones con alta asistencia.


A 534 años de la invasión europea: pueblos originarios y organizaciones sociales desbordan el centro de Santiago en la marcha del 12 de octubre


Una masiva y concurrida marcha anticolonial se realizó este lunes 12 de octubre a las 10:00 horas en el cerro Huelén (Santa Lucía), en Santiago, convocada por diversas organizaciones de pueblos originarios y agrupaciones sociales chilenas. La concentración, que reunió a cientos de personas, tuvo como fin “expresar las fuerzas de la resistencia y autonomía” en una fecha que, según señaló la convocatoria, “evoca la brutalidad, saqueo y genocidio europeo sobre la población preexistente del Abya Yala”. El llamado fue efectuado por la resistencia mapuche urbana en Santiago, en momentos en que desde el Wallmapu se convoca a manifestarse de manera unitaria por las diversas comunidades al sur del río Biobío.


La jornada, que se desarrolló con alta participación y diversos actos culturales, tuvo un fuerte componente de denuncia. Los organizadores señalaron que “son más de 100 los prisioneros políticos mapuche”, mientras se encuentran procesados los comuneros de los emblemáticos casos Lautaro y Grollmus, “entre cuyos aspectos en común comparten la utilización fraudulenta de testigos protegidos en su contra por parte de las fiscalías”. Según los convocantes, “el Ministerio Público chileno, sin pruebas concretas ni evidencias contundentes, pretende encarcelar por más de mil años a los comuneros involucrados a discreción en las causas mencionadas, con el fin de castigar de forma racista y ejemplar, a jóvenes comprometidos con la recuperación de tierras, con los derechos de su gente y con la cosmovisión mapuche”.


La marcha también abordó el contexto de militarización del territorio ancestral. Los convocantes recordaron que “desde el gobierno chileno anterior las zonas de resistencia indígena están bajo el estado de excepción, la militarización del territorio originario y la doctrina de seguridad interior del Estado”. Sin embargo, advirtieron que “el daño en todos los planos contra niños y ancianos para beneficio de las industrias extractivistas y el latifundio colonial, sólo ha multiplicado las voluntades de lucha mapuche y unido sus fuerzas”.


La convocatoria, que se extendió durante toda la mañana y parte de la tarde, incluyó cantos, danzas y diversas intervenciones, reafirmando la demanda de autonomía y recuperación de tierras. La movilización se replicó en distintos puntos del país y en el extranjero, en una jornada que los pueblos originarios conmemoran como un día de resistencia.

author: Unknown
title: Manifestation DECOLONIZE « solidarité avec les Autochtones des Amériques »
content:
Dans le cadre de la Journée internationale de solidarité avec les Autochtones des Amériques, le 12 octobre et des célébrations des 30 ans du Congrès National Indigène au Mexique (

CNI

)


Du Chiapas à la Kanaky, de Palestine à Abya Yala / Turtle Island ...


Venez participer à la manifestation déclarée ce lundi 12 octobre à 18h Place d'Iena à Paris


Le 12 octobre 1492, Christophe Colomb «

 

découvrait

 

» soit disant, un nouveau continent sur la carte du monde :

l'Amérique pour les colons

, désormais nommé

Abya Yala

 par les

peuples originaires

.


Aujourd'hui, les institutions célèbrent la «

 

rencontre

 

» entre deux mondes et la multiculturalité qui en résulte. Une commémoration

qui passe sous silence l'extermination, l'exploitation, le racisme, les viols et les multiples formes de violence

 qui ont permis la

colonisation

 et la

domination européenne

. Une manière aussi pour les nations «

 

souveraines

 

» de dissimuler que les violations des droits à la terre et à la culture des peuples originaires sont toujours d'actualité sous leurs gouvernements.


1492

 est sans aucun doute une

référence incontournable

 de

l'histoire de la colonisation

 et des États modernes qui célèbrent la «

 

Découverte

 

». Pour le mouvement indigène d'Abya Yala, la date du

12 octobre

 est le

symbole

 d'une

lutte continentale pour le droit à l'existence et à la dignité des peuples originaires.

 Mais il ne s'agit pas seulement d'une opposition symbolique entre calendriers et mémoire, entre celle d'en haut et celles d'en bas :

la lutte pour la dignité des peuples, la défense des territoires et la résistance aux guerres impérialistes, coloniales et capitalistes

 sont encore, partout, d'actualité.


Ces dernières décennies, du Chiapas à la Kanaky, la

prédation coloniale

 et la

voracité capitaliste

 propagent la guerre par la destruction des territoires et le

dépeuplement généralisé des populations «

 

indésirables

 

»

. L'éco-génocide en Palestine depuis 2023 en est un témoignage poignant.


Aux quatre coins du monde, on observe

l'avancée terrifiante de la fascisation, du culte identitaire d'une nation

 ou d'une civilisation fantasmée,

la militarisation des États

 et la

répression des contestations sociales et des soulèvements populaires

. En France, le processus de fascisation de la société est favorisé par le

désespoir lié à la crise structurelle violente

 qui affecte les conditions d'existence d'une partie considérable de la population et un arsenal politique et médiatico-juridique particulièrement offensif. Sur les continents américain et européen,

le fascisme se banalise dangereusement

 pendant que des partis politiques d'extrême droite s'installent durablement, par les urnes, dans les centres impériaux de la modernité capitaliste.

Le ravage écologique et la brutalité systémique obscurcissent l'horizon d'un lendemain meilleur

 à mesure que les crises s'amplifient.


Face à ces constats inquiétants, le temps n'est pas à la résignation. Au contraire, c'est le moment

de prolonger les rencontres

 et d'

approfondir les complicités

, de respecter ce qui nous distingue et d'écouter ce qui nous lie pour apprendre ensemble de celles et ceux qui,

 en bas et à gauche, combattent les guerres «

 

intérieures

 

» et coloniales, les replis identitaire, l'écocide terrestre et les génocides en-cours.

 Le temps présent est celui de l'apprentissage et de l'approfondissement de l'organisation, à l'aune de la

résistance séculaire des peuples originaires d'Abya Yala, de la lutte contre

ICE

 à Minneapolis ou du sumud palestinien.


C'est pourquoi,

à l'occasion des 534 ans de la résistance des peuples originaires d'Abya Yala

, plusieurs collectifs et syndicats vous invitent à rejoindre

Lundi 12 octobre à 18h00 à la manifestation pour la journée internationale de la résistance indigène

. Nous marcherons

de Iéna jusqu'à la place du Trocadéro

 pour affirmer, jusqu'au coeur de l'Europe, notre solidarité avec les peuples originaires d'Abya Yala dans leur lutte permanente pour la vie, une vie digne et bonne pour toutes et tous et contre le capitalisme, la colonisation et le patriarcat.


Que la rencontre soit celle des résistances qui partagent un horizon d'émancipation en commun,


Nous vous attendons nombreux.ses

 

!

Comité de Solidarité avec les Peuples du Chiapas en Lutte -

CSPCL


Comité de Solidarité Internationale avec les Autochtones des Amériques - …

 ήταν μια πράξη αντιαποικιακής και αντιιμπεριαλιστικής αντίστασης. Μια συνέχεια της αντίστασης που χρονολογείται από τη στιγμή της ίδρυσης του κράτους του “Ισραήλ” το 1948, αλλά και ακόμη νωρίτερα, κατά τη διάρκεια της βρετανικής αποικιακής κατοχής. Ήταν ένας λαός και ένα κίνημα που ξεσηκώθηκαν ενάντια στην κατοχή. Η ημέρα αυτή θα συνεχίσει να τιμάται ως τέτοια για τις επόμενες γενιές, ακόμη και αν οι σιωνιστές και οι ιμπεριαλιστές προσπαθήσουν με κάθε μέσο να ελέγξουν και να αλλάξουν το αφήγημα. Η Γάζα έχει ισοπεδωθεί από τους βομβαρδισμούς και, παρόλο που γίνεται λόγος για κατάπαυση του πυρός, συνεχίζουν να βομβαρδίζουν και να πυροβολούν αδιακρίτως. Ο Λίβανος και η Συρία τελούν υπό κατοχή και δέχονται συνεχείς επιθέσεις από τη σιωνιστική οντότητα. Οι κυβερνήσεις αυτών των περιοχών καταστέλλουν την αντίσταση και την εναντίωση στη Δύση και το “Ισραήλ” στα εδάφη τους, ενεργώντας ως εντολοδόχοι των ΗΠΑ. Όλα αυτά συμβαίνουν ενώ το “Ισραήλ” καταλαμβάνει όλο και περισσότερα εδάφη, αποσταθεροποιώντας περαιτέρω την περιοχή.

content:
Ein Jahr später. Wir alle sind wieder zurück und wir lassen uns weder von der Staatsgewalt, noch von der medialen und parlamentarischen Hetze gegen die kämpferische Palästina-Demo vom letzten Jahr einschüchtern!


Wenn wir uns die Strasse nehmen wollen, dann nehmen wir sie uns! Weil der Genozid in Gaza noch immer anhält, die Schweiz noch immer imperialistische Komplizin ist und weil der Widerstand gegen Imperialismus, Genozid und gegen ihren Krieg weiterhin als extremistisch geframed und kriminalisert wird.


Die antiimperialistische und antikapitalistische Velodemo startete beim Eigerplatz. Um 15:00 fuhren wir los und widersetzten uns der grossen Polizeipräsenz. Wir nahmen uns die Strassen und den Kreisel beim Eigerplatz und schon von Anfang an solidarisierten sich auch Menschen in Autos mit den Inhalten der Demo! Daraufhin fuhren wir auf die US-Botschaft zu, welche symbolisch für Trump und die US-imperialistische Tyrannei im Allgemeinen steht. Wenig überraschend wurden die umliegenden Strassen bereits von Robocops und Kastenwägen abgeriegelt. Wir führten unsere Smash-US-Imperialism Aktion deswegen mitten auf dem Bubenbergplatz durch.


Wir blockierten mit unseren Velos alle Strassen dieser grossen Kreuzung, und fesselten eine lebensgrosse Trump Figur an eine Säule.


Schliesslich luden wir Demonstrierende wie Passant*innen ein, Trump mit gefüllten Robidogsäckli, zu bewerfen bis er noch beschissener aussah als sonst schon!


Etwas später hörten wir eine Rede eines kurdischen Genossens, der für die kurdische Befreiung gekämpft hat.


Dabei sprach er über die PKK, welche den Aufbau des demokratischen Sozialismus und den 50-jährigen antiimperialistischen Kampf massgeblich vorangetrieben hat. Zudem betonte er die Wichtigkeit der Frauenbewegung, die eine führende Rolle im Kampf und beim Aufbau des demokratischen Sozialismus eingenommen hat. Die Frauenrevolution in Rojava und die Aufstände von Rojhilat unter der Parole Jin-Jiyan-Azadî (Frau-Leben-Freiheit) spielten eine Schlüsselrolle bei der weltweiten Verbreitung des kurdischen Frauenkampfes für Freiheit.

Unser Genosse ruft antikapitalistische, anarchistische und progressive Genoss*innen in der Schweiz auf, nicht den Frieden der Herrschenden zu unterstützen, sondern den sozialen Frieden in Kurdistan, den das kurdische Volk von unten aufbauen wird.


JIN JIYAN AZADî

author: ROAPE
title: African Labour and Liberation
content:
African Labour and Liberation

 brings together the experiences of workers, trade unions and labour movements across the continent to ask what they can tell us about work, power and liberation today. We assembled this collection because of the surprisingly few recent accounts of the emergence of a class politics on the continent. Labour is central to understanding the present political economy of Africa.  More than 90 percent of Africa’s 500 million workers work in informal and precarious jobs in a labour force that will grow rapidly in the next three decades.


The social and political mobilization of workers in multifarious contexts across the continent is imperative to improving their socio-economic conditions. It is necessary to situate Africa’s workers at the centre. This collection starts from the premise that labour struggles are essential to improving the conditions of work and stamping out poverty and inequality that the confronts most African workers today and form the basis for building new forms of collective power.


This heterodox collec­tion finds six primary patterns prevalent in the struggle for the working class liberation in the post-independence era.


1. Most governments in Africa are comprador-bureaucratic regimes beholden to foreign capital and imperialists’ interests to protect and maintain unequal exchange of trade and the attenuation of demands by the masses for national control over natural resources and production. Comprador-bureaucratic regimes remain loyal to their post-colonial powers and pay fleeting attention to national sustainability, the rights of women, natu­ral ecology, and the ever-growing needs of the masses for health care, education, housing, infrastructure, water, and electricity.


Government legislation to defend popular interests that have been enacted by national assemblies are rarely fully implemented and are likely to be opposed by international banks and lenders, predominantly from the West through structural adjustment programs that undermine evanescent attempts to ameliorate the most significant challenges.


2. Diverse workers’ movements form to resist t the comprador-bureaucratic political economies which formed in the colonial era which most often extract surplus value from workers and natural resources from the continent  through what  Arghiri Emmanuel  identified as

unequal exchange of trade

, and despoiling, and plundering African nations. Control is maintained by local elites attached to state power who are beneficiaries of rentier capitalism. These national elites have welcomed Western powers to establish military bases osten­sibly to establish peace and order.


In most instances, the emergence of violence and disorder were generated by Western military intervention. However, as Samir Amin shows, workers and peasants drive the enduring imperative for the formation of national projects for popular sovereignty, which are often imperfect and challenged by imperialists seeking to maintain the unequal exchange of trade.


3. African states are ruled by comprador state-centric bureaucratic elites who maintain rentier capitalism as the primary source of revenue rather than investing in productive technology. The historical pattern is opposition to the redistribution of wealth and income to the masses.


This process, in which bureaucratic elements seek to transform themselves – sometimes successful sometimes not, but nearly always drawing links to imperial­ism and thereby fusing the bureaucratic and comprador elements – can be seen nearly everywhere. Unquestionably, compliant and often corrupt political elites provide the patina of legitimacy for all practical purposes, for the expansion of inequality.


4. In Africa, racial justice must include an anti-imperialist per­spective which acknowledges the legacy of European colonialism and the protracted nature of imperialism which sustains racial subordina­tion. Markedly, South Africa, a semi-peripheral mineral-rich state, did not redistribute wealth and property with the end of political apartheid and the development of a superficially democratic state. Black South Africans, composing over 80 percent of the country’s 65 million popu­lation, remain marginalized through the 1994 accords, which did not include a redistribution of wealth and resources – causing higher levels of poverty and inequality and impeding the working class from improv­ing its living standards.

author: Brasil 247
title: Celso Amorim Warns of U.S. Interference in Second Round Elections
content:
Ambassador Celso Amorim, special adviser to the presidency on international affairs, warned of the risk that the United States could interfere in Brazil’s election process. He said the October 25 presidential runoff carries consequences that reach far beyond Brazil’s borders. In an interview with Tutaméia on Friday, the former foreign and defense minister discussed pressure from the Trump administration on Latin America, the challenges facing Brazilian sovereignty, and the importance of the country’s technological and military independence.

Amorim said Brazil holds a strategic position in the global balance of power, and that the country’s political decisions have ripple effects across the Global South and relations between major powers.

“What happens in Brazil will have an influence on the global balance itself,” he said.

The diplomat stressed that Brazilian sovereignty depends on maintaining diverse international relationships and avoiding dependence on any single power.

“In the complex world we live in today, sovereignty doesn’t mean isolation. It means having relationships with more than one country. It means diversifying your relationships. It means not depending on a single power in any sense, economically, socioculturally, or even militarily in terms of defense,” he said.

Amorim Calls Out Washington’s Pressure on Brazil

Asked about possible attempts by the Trump administration to interfere in Brazil’s election, Amorim said he believes the influence of certain U.S. political sectors on Brazil’s political landscape is real.

He said this interference doesn’t need to target voting mechanisms directly. It can take the form of diplomatic, economic and political pressure, along with support for Brazilian ideological movements.

The presidential adviser cited the tariffs imposed by the United States, diplomatic restrictions, and initiatives from sectors of the American far right as examples of actions that, in his view, go beyond the limits of a balanced bilateral relationship.

Amorim also referred to reports of attempts to send American representatives to Brazil to inspect the electoral system, calling the idea absurd.

In the diplomat’s assessment, strategic U.S. documents reveal an intention to reassert American dominance over the Western Hemisphere. He said these initiatives need to be analyzed together, not as isolated incidents.

Diplomat Sees Risk of Unprecedented Submission to the United States

Discussing the Bolsonaro family’s international positions, Amorim said that unrestricted access to Brazil’s strategic information by the United States would represent a profound break from the country’s diplomatic tradition.

The former foreign minister compared the current situation to U.S. interference in the 1964 military coup, recalling the role played by then Ambassador Lincoln Gordon and U.S. plans to provide military support to the coup plotters.

Amorim noted that even during the military dictatorship, Brazil at times took positions independent of Washington, including on nuclear policy, maritime issues, and recognizing Angola’s independence.

For Amorim, control over natural resources and strategic technologies sits at the center of today’s international disputes. He cited critical minerals and artificial intelligence as areas where Brazil needs to preserve its own decision making power.

He argued that sovereignty isn’t an abstract concept, but something directly tied to economic development and the population’s quality of life. As an example, he pointed to the creation of Petrobras and the importance of Brazil having its own oil production capacity, especially during periods of international instability.

China and Strategic Autonomy Take Center Stage

Amorim also discussed the growing rivalry between the United States and China and what it means for Brazil.

He said competition between major powers can create opportunities for countries that maintain autonomy in choosing their trade and technology partners. The diplomat noted that the expansion of economic ties between Brazil and China stems partly from China’s ability to offer competitive trade and investment terms.

He argued that Brazil should maintain relationships with multiple partners, without subordinating its decisions to the interests of either Washington or Beijing.

author: M. Reza Behnam
title: The Imperial Pen: Geopolitical Vandalism in West Asia
content:
For centuries, the lands stretching from the Levant to the Persian Gulf have been subjected to a strange form of conceptual alchemy. Driven by Western Orientalist scholarship, colonial cartography and modern geopolitical agendas, the dynamic, pluralistic mosaic of West Asia has been systematically reduced to a monolithic caricature, defined by violence, archaic fundamentalism, and in need of rescue.

These mutations are more than mere scholarly failures; they represent a destructive erasure of history. By denying complex societies their natural path toward modernity and stripping them of historical agency, these misrepresentations serve to validate existing systems of oppression.

To truly understand contemporary Arab West Asia, one must recognize that its political boundaries and power dynamics are essentially an imperialist artifact; and that it remains shackled to a modern version of the colonial 1916 Sykes-Picot ghost: artificial borders drawn by foreign pens, hyper-economies addicted to petrodollars, governance models built and local rulers chosen to appease external patrons and crush internal dissent.

British and French colonialists, Mark Sykes and Francois Georges Picot, engineered the systemic underdevelopment of West Asia, through calculated geopolitical vandalism. By secretly carving up Ottoman lands into European spheres of influence during World War I, with total disregard for demographic, tribal and economic realities, they deliberately trapped millions within artificial borders designed explicitly to facilitate trade routes and resource extraction at the expense of organic state-building and stability.

To maintain control and to serve the industrial demands of London and Paris, these external brigands thwarted local independence, weaponized sectarian and religious divisions, and essentially reduced entire societies into fractured resource-milked protectorates.

The Sykes-Picot Agreement and sibling treaties did more than redraw a map, they locked the region into ongoing instability. Imperial powers carved out unnatural states and installed local satraps—chronically fragile in legitimacy—willing to repress their own populations to stay in power and to carry out the bidding of their colonial overlords. This has left a consequential foundational legacy that the region’s people are forced to navigate today.

Even the conventional designation “Middle East” is a colonial byproduct; not born of indigenous geography. The imperialist term originated within the British India Office in the 1850s and gained public attention in 1902 when American naval strategist, Alfred Thayer Mahan, used it to describe the area around the Persian Gulf as a middle zone between the Near East and the Far East.

The Eurocentric label became official terminology during World War II after the British Armed Forces set up their Middle East Command in Cairo. In the 1950s, the United States integrated the term into official foreign policy, transforming a strategic naval calculation into a commonly accepted and used geopolitical descriptor.

Beyond the physical lines on a map, the legacy of imperialism endures in how borders drawn more than a century ago are understood and interpreted today.

When violence erupts in these states, Western discourse routinely defaults to essentialist tropes. They attribute the instability to “ancient ethnic, tribal or religious animosities” or an “inherent inability to govern,” rather than looking at the real roots of the conflicts.

Such oversimplified stereotypes are convenient fiction that absolve colonial powers of their historical responsibility. They conceal the ways in which modern authoritarian regimes, sectarian conflicts, religious factions and state collapses were systematically engineered, armed and manipulated by foreign powers seeking resource dominance and geopolitical control.

In his foundational critique of Orientalism, Palestinian-American scholar, Edward Said, demonstrated how Western academia, literature and media manufactured a false binary, framing the West as rational, logical and progressive, while painting the East as emotional, static and despotic.

In this construction, the people of West Asia are rarely permitted complexity as historical actors pursuing their own liberation, economic self-determination or social reform. Instead, they are filtered through reductionist archetypes; such as:

content:
by Paul Cudenec, who reads the article

The corrupt cabal which

runs the modern world

 [1] seems to enjoy giving inappropriate, in fact inverted, names to the manufactured events through which it advances its vile agenda.


Thus the

nightmarish bloodbath

Great

 War [2] and a century later the

techno-totalitarian heist

 it tried to pull off on the basis of a fake pandemic was called The

Great

 Reset. [3]


This was doubly the case in 1688 with England’s

Glorious Revolution

, since this was neither a revolution nor a glorious moment for the people of that country – it was rather an invasion and full seizure of power by the network whose contemporary form I term

ZIM

, the zio-imperialist mafia. [4]


This entity, which

Mees Baaijen

 calls Glafia (global mafia), [5] had originally been based in Venice, then moved to Holland and, at the end of the 17th century, switched to London to use England as the springboard for the commercial, financial and industrial imperialism that we today call globalism.


This was the second assault on the country by such characters, who had also formed the financial wing of the Norman invasion and occupation starting from 1066, as I explained in ‘

How England was “colonised”

‘. [6]


Researcher Will Keyte (

pictured

video

TheRealMagnaCarta1215

 channel, which is part of an in-depth series on the misnamed Glorious Revolution. [7]


He says of the mid to late 1600s: “It’s a fascinating and dangerous period of change, all of it, and not the kind of change that ultimately resulted in benefit for the people. The depth of the skullduggery is just unimaginable”.


He begins with Oliver Cromwell, who led the parliamentary side in the English Civil War from 1642 to 1651, and whose victory resulted in the beheading of the Stuart king Charles I and Cromwell installing himself as Lord Protector of the Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1653 until his death in 1658.


Keyte notes that Cromwell received “massive financial backing from Amsterdam and rich individual financiers” – I have

previously highlighted

 his particularly close connections to Rabbi Menasseh Ben Israel. [8]


That article focuses on the Invisible College, the precursor of the Royal Society, created in 1660, and Keyte mentions that latter body as being part of the new network rising to prominence in London at the time.


“Essentially, the undercurrent, or the sort of strain of influence, was certainly a banking one, mixed with early pre-formal masonry”.


He explains that the masonic guilds had originally been literally made up of stonemasons, but that changed and others were allowed entry. “This allowed merchants, lawyers, scientists, academics, to come into that organisation and be members – and they could network independently of the authorities of the Church and the Crown”.


“Cromwell had allowed these changes during the interregnum in relation to the influence of wealthy bankers in the City – he’d sort of promoted their influence.


“But when the Crown was restored in 1660, when Charles II came to the throne, he was not able to reset those changes… So you’ve got this heavy influence of these rich money people. These wealthy players remained the dominant influence in the City”.


Keyte says that the 1666

Great

 Fire of London (

there’s that adjective again!

) “hit at perhaps the most vulnerable point, economically, and many have asked in history ‘was that a false flag event?’ Many people have said that it is”.


“What’s interesting about that is the timing, because you’ve just had the Plague of London as well [‘The

Great

according to

 [9], I see!]. I don’t know whether that was a false flag as well… You’ve got everything coming together at the same time. You’ve got forces at work – because it didn’t work in the interregnum, they couldn’t get rid of the old constitution of England, they couldn’t quite do it…

title: 1976 – 1991: Das Albartus-Papier der Revolutionären Zellen
content:
Die Jahre 1976 und 1991 markieren zwei deutliche Abstürze in der Geschichte der radikalen Linken in der BRD. Bezeichnenderweise kam Ende 1991 das Albartus-Papier der Revolutionären Zellen auf 1976 zu sprechen: die Flugzeugentführung von Entebbe. Anlässlich des 50. Jahrestags haben wir in der aktuellen Wildcat einen langen Artikel, der diese Verbindungen aufzudröseln versucht: »Entebbe und die Folgen«. Hier eine Kürzestfassung plus update:


Im Juni und Juli 1976 herrschte in Europa eine Hitzewelle. Die Temperaturen in Deutschland stiegen wochenlang regelmäßig über 30 Grad auf Spitzenwerte bis 36 und 37 Grad.


Politisch endete vor 50 Jahren das »rote Jahrzehnt«: 24. März 1976 Militärputsch in Argentinien. Am 9. Mai 1976 starb Ulrike Meinhof. Anfang Juni brach auf dem »Pfingstkongress« ein breiter Teil der radikalen Linken mit der Militanz und machte sich auf in die Institutionen. Am 10. Juli begann die Chemiekatastrophe in Seveso. Im August das Massaker von Tel al-Zaatar. Am 6. Oktober der Militärputsch in Thailand.


Auch kulturell war 1976 schlimm: ABBA »Dancing Queen«, Jürgen Drews »Ein Bett im Kornfeld«, Boney M. »Daddy Cool«. Kurz danach kamen dann die BeeGees »Stayin’ Alive« – der Sound zum Deutschen Herbst!


Für die deutschen Maoisten der diversen K-Gruppen lag 1976 zwischen dem Besuch von Franz Josef Strauß bei Mao (Januar 1975) einerseits, dem Krieg Vietnams gegen Kambodscha und den »Reformen« von Deng Xiao Ping (beides im Dezember 1978) andererseits. Die meisten fielen vom Glauben ab, viele von ihnen gründeten die Grüne Partei, andere später die Antideutschen. Diese eroberten nach 1991 die Hegemonie in der radikalen Linken.


Die Flugzeugentführung nach Entebbe…


Seit Anfang 1976 eskalierte der libanesische Bürgerkrieg. Nach monatelanger Belagerung stürmten Falangisten am 12. August das Lager von Tel al-Zaatar und töteten Tausende palästinensische Flüchtlinge.


Im Zusammenhang damit entführte ein deutsch-palästinensisches Kommando aus RZ und PFLP-EO am 27. Juni 1976 ein Flugzeug nach Entebbe und forderte die Freilassung von politischen Gefangenen. In der Nacht zum 4. Juli befreiten israelische Spezialkräfte die meisten der Geiseln. Das wird von gewissen Kreisen bis heute als das beste Kommandounternehmen aller Zeiten bejubelt (etwa: »Mit der Geiselbefreiung von Entebbe zeigte Israel vor 50 Jahren, wie man den Terror bekämpft« Nius 2. Juli 2026). Benjamin Netanjahu, dessen älterer Bruder bei der Befreiungsaktion starb, hat seine gesamte politische Karriere auf »Entebbe« und den »Kampf gegen den Terrorismus« aufgebaut.


»Die Aktion von Entebbe wurde rasch zu einem Vorwand für verschiedene Akteure, die bislang mit dem Milieu der radikalen Linken verbunden waren, sich von Internationalismus und Antiimperialismus ganz zu lösen.« (Gerhard Hanloser: »Desaster mit Nachspiel«)


Wegweisend war der Anti-Repressionskongress des Sozialistischen Büros Anfang Juni (»Pfingstkongress«). Am Abschlusstag hatte der spätere Außenminister Joschka Fischer vor 20.000 Besuchern in der berühmten Römerberg-Rede mit seiner militanten Vergangenheit gebrochen. Später hat er – die Dinge chronologisch auf den Kopf stellend – auf seinem Weg ins Außenministerium immer mal wieder betont, »Entebbe« sei das Ereignis gewesen, das ihn vom Saulus zum Paulus gemacht habe. Dabei lieferte es nur nachträglich den Vorwand.


»Entebbe« ist bis heute wirkmächtig. Das sah man an den Dutzenden von Artikeln und mehreren Büchern, die zum 50. Jahrestag erschienen. Das sah man aber auch daran, dass im März 2023 Mitglieder der Entebbe-Spezialeinheit eine der schärfsten Kritiken an Benjamin Netanjahu in einem offenen Brief formulierten. Netanjahu opfere den Staat Israel und das israelische Volk für seine eigenen Interessen, diffamiere Demonstranten gegen die Justizreform als Anarchisten und alle, die ihn nicht unterstützen, als Terroristen; er hetze Israelis gegeneinander auf.


… und die beginnende Institutionalisierung der radikalen Linken


1976 hätte auch anders ausgehen können. Im Juli hatten Chemiearbeiter in Seveso gestreikt, um die Katastrophe überhaupt öffentlich zu machen – aber sie hatten nicht mehr die Macht wie Jahre zuvor, die Wirtschaftspolitik des Landes neu zu orientieren. Die massenhaften Schüler- und Studentenproteste in Soweto seit Juni waren größtenteils selbst organisiert und schienen politisch endlich eine Alternative zum ANC zu eröffnen. Aber die Bullen schlugen die Bewegung brutal nieder; sie töteten mehr als 500 der …

Anti-Imperialism and National Liberation

“Each generation must out of relative obscurity discover its mission, fulfill it, or betray it … As for we who have decided to break the back of colonialism, our historic mission is to sanction all revolts, all desperate actions”

Anti-Zionism has entered the phase of sabotage. Lobbying governments to sanction Israel has been replaced with breaking drones and dismantling factories; boycotts traded for slashed truck airlines and arson; rallies and peace marches superseded with red paint and shattered office windows. It is a medium of tactics signaling a shift in the repertoire of collective action undertaken against Zionist Imperialism. This form of resistance did not emerge out of Al Aqsa Flood – but it too signals a new terrain upon which Palestine will be fought. It deserves an uncompromising theory of struggle.

The time has arrived for us to create something new. The mainstream Palestine Solidarity Movement has demonstrated its inability to effectively counter the growing international Zio-fascist alliance. It continues to rely on outmoded, outdated and counterinsurgent formulas of struggle while putting considerable effort into restricting, internally-policing, ignoring and countering the most dynamic, effective and generative aspects of Anti-Zionism that have emerged over the past six years.

In both theory and practice, the Palestine Solidarity Movement has been co-opted by self-aggrandizing opportunists, NGO/Academic careerists and racist paternalists,[1] committed to an understanding of social struggle that has no room in its conceptual landscape from which to comprehend what has been happening in front of it. Inside its performative rallies, on the edges of its peaceful pickets and fake boat blockades, circulated anonymously on social media: militant Anti-Zionist resistance.

Interpersonal opportunism, peace policing and activist influencers only explain a part of the problems many of us have experienced since October 7th 2023. Individuals, spokespeople and careerists are provided platforms by the rest of us in a movement that remains confined to theories, ideas, strategies and weapons of struggle which we must now finally discard. author: Rodrigo Acuña
title: Cubans See Hope in Reforms But Worry Over How the US May Thwart Them
content:
Residents of Havana discuss the obstacles facing the revival of the Cuban economy amid the US fuel blockade.

Residents of Havana discuss the obstacles facing the revival of the Cuban economy amid the US fuel blockade.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Last month, Cuban Prime Minister Manuel Marrero Cruz declared that 158 new economic and social measures, out of an original package of 176 approved in July by the Cuba’s National Assembly, were being implemented and backed by 197 legal decrees. The measures include allowing private business to import medicines and other goods, loosening restrictions on private tourism, and authorising privately owned banks — under Central Bank supervision — on a regulatory basis equivalent to state banks. Adding to these measures, the National Assembly for the first time permitted foreign capital to invest directly in Cuban private businesses instead of having to operate exclusively through state-controlled structures. Private companies also will no longer be restricted to a maximum of 100 employees.

According to Daniel Torralbas, a London-based Cuban economist, the National Assembly’s new measures are “the most profound economic reform programme … since the 1959 revolution.” Headed by Fidel Castro, the government in Havana between the mid and late 1960s nationalized a vast array of U.S.-owned businesses that controlled major shares in key industries such as public utilities, mining, railways and infrastructure, and land and agriculture.

Mauricio Alonso, a 68-year-old former nuclear engineer who lives in Havana and now runs an Airbnb rental, is embracing the government’s new economic measures.

“On a personal level this is going to benefit me,” says Alonso, “because it’s going to allow, for example, me — since I’m self-employed — to partner with foreigners, to team up, to be part of a larger organization, and to carry out actions with my lodging business, and so on.” Working with travel agencies, in Alonso’s view, will now be made easier with the lifting of restrictions. “If I qualify, if I get accredited as such,” says Alonso, “I can carry out the work of a tour guide without any kind of problem.”

During the 1980s, Alonso worked at the Central Electronuclear de Juraguá, near the city of Cienfuegos, which was being built with the aid of the Soviet Union to become Cuba’s first nuclear power station. Alonso says that, “when the Soviet Union collapsed in late 1991, work on the plant came to a halt in 1992.” Although Alonso continued working in the nuclear sector until 1995, he “realized that the project couldn’t go on — due in part to [the] intense pressure from the U.S. government.” At that point, he decided to “switch to the private sector and start renting out rooms” after inheriting a large apartment from his mother.

Had Cuba’s nuclear power station become operational, it is doubtful the island would be facing its current energy crisis.

Despite a small recovery between 2021 and 2022, after Cuba’s GDP in 2020 contracted by 10.9 percent as COVID-19 effectively shut down international tourism, the island’s economic crisis has been worsened by the Trump administration’s fuel embargo. When U.S. President Donald Trump began to take action against Venezuela’s oil shipments to Cuba in 2025, which approximated 26,500 barrels per day, Cubans saw a serious reduction of fuel on the island. On January 29, the Trump administration formalized the oil sanctions on Cuba by signing Executive Order 14380, which did not simply add another sanction on the island, but instead, created a mechanism to penalize third countries that supply oil to Cuba. Should a country provide crude oil or petroleum products, then the United States government can impose further tariffs on that country’s goods entering the U.S.

For Amalia Díaz Pérez, a 21-years old recent graduate in philosophy from the University of Havana, the Trump administration’s oil embargo disrupted her final year of study. Speaking to Truthout, she said:

The total blockade of fuel imports — with only one ship arriving in nine months — caused public transportation to disappear and reduced daily electricity availability to a minimum. Consequently, my study conditions and most of my daily recreational activities were affected. Compounding this situation, household chores became increasingly difficult due to the strain of the nationwide fuel shortage placed on water and …
