title: Flávio Bolsonaro y Lula van a segunda vuelta en Brasil
content:
Con casi el 100% de las mesas escrutadas, Flávio Bolsonaro se impone con el 47,05% de los votos y suma en total 56.082.216 votos. Este resultado no le alcanza para ganar la presidencias, por lo que se disputará una segunda vuelta con el actual presidente Lula Da Silva que consiguió 45,14% de los votos, que equivalen a 53.799.870. Las elecciones se dan en un contexto de extrema polarización, incertidumbre e injerencia del imperialismo yanqui. El resultado de las elecciones brasileñas tiene un especial peso en la balanza de las fuerzas políticas en Latino América. Tanto por el tamaño de la economía de Brasil como por la polarización entre el actual presidente Lula y el hijo de Bolsonaro subordinado al alineamiento del continente a Trump, el Escudo de las Américas y su doctrina de seguridad Donroe.

Por La Izquierda Diario.


Distintos analistas sostienen que el voto indeciso fue el que sorprendió en esta primera vuelta al volcarse a favor de Flavio Bolsonaro, que quedó dos puntos arriba de Lula. Este resultado refleja lo que las encuestas captaron días antes, una mejora de Bolsonaro quien capitalizó el voto útil de otras fuerzas conservadoras.


La presión del imperialismo parece haber surtido efecto como en la Argentina en las elecciones intermedias de 2027. Allí con el respaldo de dinero y la amenaza de retirar el apoyo y hundir las finanzas del Estado, de la mano del Secretario del Tesoro yanqui Scott Bessent. En Brasil, la amenaza se materializó con el cierre de consulados y la embajada por una supuesta cuestión de seguridad que la Policía Federal investigó y descartó. Además, está el antecedente de Venezuela y todas las acciones de presión con aranceles, y otras presiones diplomáticas sobre el gobierno de Lula.


Por otro lado, en todos estos años de gobierno petista no se cambió la estructura de la nación dependiente del imperialismo, así como tampoco se resolvieron las diferencias sociales, el racismo ni la concentración de tierras en manos de los latifundistas. Los salarios bajos y las familias endeudadas demuestran eso. No es solo el grave tema de las apuestas on line, son los ingresos de las familias, cada vez peores.


Cronología de este domingo 4 de octubre


22:41


«Brasil quiere un cambio»


Después del triunfo en primera vuelta, el candidato opositor Flávio Bolsonaro habló desde su bunker en Brasilia y aseguró que «Brasil quiere un cambio», sin hacer mención a la fallida presidencia de su padre.


También afirmó que este resultado muestra el fin del PT (Partido dos Trabalhadores) y dijo estar muy contento con los resultados regionales.


22:25


Un resultado inesperado


A poco de conocerse los resultados oficiales, Lula habló dió un discurso diciendo que el resultado lo había sorprendido y hasta aseguró que había confiado en que ganaba en primera vuelta.


Pensando en el próximo round, le dijo a sus seguidores que en la segunda vuelta «mostraremos la verdadera foto de Brasil.» También afirmó que su campaña se centrará en convencer a todos los que se ausentaron de las urnas de la importancia de ir a votar.


22:01


Segunda vuelta confirmada


Con casi el 100% de las mesas escrutadas, Flavio Bolsonaro se impone con el 47,05% de los votos y suma en total 56.082.216 votos. Este resultado no le alcanza para ganar la presidencia, por lo que se disputará una segunda vuelta con el actual presidente Lula Da Silva que consiguió 45,14% de los votos, que equivalen a 53.799.870.


Muy lejos se ubica el tercer candidato, Augusto Cury, con algo menos del 3%. Cury adelantó que no apoyará a ningún candidato en la segunda vuelta.


20:30


El Partido Liberal acumula gobernadores


Según resultados proyectados, los candidatos del partido de Bolsonaro fueron electos en Rio Grande do Sul, Rondonia, Roraima y Santa Catarina, donde reelige. Además, disputa en una segunda vuelta los estados de Paraná y Rio de Janeiro, donde actualmente gobierna, para un posible total de 6 estados.


San Pablo, el distrito electoral con mas peso y centro económico más importante del país, queda en manos del mismo gobernador de la ultraderecha, Tarcísio de Freitas, que no es del partido del Bolsonaro PL, sino de otro de la derecha, República. content:
Gegen Ihre Repression


Am Sonntag, 11.10.2026, geht es wieder auf die Strasse. Und es hängt ein dunkler Schatten über dem Tag. Das war zu erwarten und wir möchten uns dazu nun positionieren. Klar ist, wir werden auf die Strasse gehen, denn die Berner Shitshow des letzten Jahres lassen wir so nicht stehen.


Zunächst eine erneute Einordung der aktuellen Lage


Die Schweiz ist eine Mörderin. Zum einen bietet sie ein ruhiges Hinterland für andere Mörder*innen wie UBS, Palantir, Glencore, Syngenta, die Weltbank oder Valcambi. Andererseits bringt sie als Teil des US-imperialen Blocks seit hunderten von Jahren unsere Geschwister auf der ganzen Welt um. Auch wenn gerade alle Augen dem seltsam faszinierenden Spektal der Trump-Administration zuschauen, fallen weiterhin echte Bomben, werden weiterhin echte Menschen verdrängt, sterben weiterhin echte Kinder. Kurz: die Lage hat sich nicht verbessert, sie ist nur nicht mehr so interessant für die bürgerliche Presse. Für uns heisst das nur, dass alle bereits bestehenden Analysen zu Krieg und Genozid weiterhin anzuwenden sind. Sie zu wiederholen, sparen wir uns an dieser Stelle. Wer es noch nicht kapiert hat, wird für den Moment wohl selbst dahinter kommen müssen (gäu Alec).


Zur Demo


Wir wissen, viele Menschen sind verunsichert und trauen sich aufgrund der Repression nicht mehr, an diesem Tag ihre Wut auf die Strassen zu tragen. Schöne neue Demokratie. Genau diese Menschen wollen wir mit diesem Communiqué ansprechen.


Wir nehmen an, ihr wollt euch grundsätzlich auch nicht von der Repression unterkriegen lassen. Aber das von Medien, Politik und Bullen kreirte Klima macht einfach keine Lust die "Demokratie" zu leben. Wir verstehen das und haben eine Antwort: Eine kreative Anti-Kessel-Demo. Ein Konzept, um am 11. Oktober auf die Strasse zu gehen und trotz Repression ein Ereignis zu schaffen, das uns im Widerstand gegen unseren mörderischen Staat und im Kampf für eine andere Welt zusammenbringt und unsere Banden stärkt. Um nichts über die aktuellen Entwicklungen zur Anti-Kessel-Demo zu verpassen und am Tag selbst optimal vorbereitet zu sein, ist es wichtig, dass du dem Demoticker beitrittst. Die Links dazu findest du unten im Beitrag.


Zur Frage der Bewilligung


Wir leisten Widerstand gegen den Schweizer Staat und lassen unser Handeln darum nicht von ihm bewilligen. Was wäre das auch für eine witzlose Logik.


Für die Repression ist die Bewilligung immer der erste Angriffspunkt. Und angegriffen wird, wenn es der Polizei beliebt. Oder was war das bitte am Smash WEF dieses Jahr? Einer bereits aufgelösten Demo in den Rücken prügeln?


Zum prophezeiten "Aufstand"


Die Herrschenden dominieren die Medien - wir sagen, sie kontrollieren den Diskurs - indem sie selektiv berichten und unsere Inhalte verschweigen. Diese Kontrolle des Diskurses erlaubt es dem Staat der Öffentlichkeit zu vermitteln, unser Widerstand sei nicht legitim, verwirrt, sinnfrei oder sonst irgendwie falsch. Und unser Aufruf vorallem eine Ansage zur totalen Eskalation. Das wurde einwandfrei klar aus den bereits veröffentlichten Beiträgen, siehe NZZ, BZ, Blick. Die Demo ist zur Projektionsfläche für alle möglichen Ängste und Unzufriedenheiten der Bürgerlichen geworden. Das ist bei linken Demonstrationen nicht ungewöhnlich, doch gerade der 11. Oktober 2025 wird immerwieder als Referenzpunkt verwendet, um die Verschärfung staatlicher Repression und Überwachung zu rechfertigen. Um verfassungswidrige Repression gegen uns zu legitimieren und unsere Inhalte unsichtbar zu machen. Der Staatsapparat will uns verunmöglichen, das "Recht" auf Protest auszuleben und zeigt damit im Endeffekt, was Rechte für diese "rechtsbasierte Ordnung" bedeuten - nichts.


Zum vergangenen "Aufstand"


Lassen wir letztes Jahr nochmal Revue passieren. Es waren locker 10 000 Menschen auf der Strasse. Es war friedlich, bis die Demo mehr wollte, als nur eine Platzkundgebung auf dem Bundesplatz. Zu laufen war legitimes Anliegen. Die Reaktion darauf unverhältnismässig. Die Eskalation danach verhältnissmässig. author: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs
title: Dene leaders declare homelessness a crisis, call for greater control over housing and major projects
content:
Dene leaders have declared homelessness a crisis affecting every Dene First Nation and also called for stronger wildlife protections and greater control over economic development in Denendeh.


These resolutions, among several others, were passed at the 56th Dene National Assembly, held at Kátł’odeeche First Nation earlier this month. Leaders discussed housing, wildlife conservation, major projects and the need for Dene governments to have greater influence over decisions affecting their lands and communities.


The assembly opened in a good way with traditional drumming and prayers and traditional foods, including moose meat that was harvested by Irene Graham, a hunter and head of the guardianship program at Kátł’odeeche First Nation.


“It’s food sovereignty, it’s cultural resilience, it’s all those and it’s our Dene way of life,” Graham said.


Graham also described the protocol of harvesting on the land.


“We give an offering of tobacco. It’s a contract that we have with animals that we respect them and it brings you luck, you have a safe journey while you’re out harvesting on the land,” she said.


Dene leaders call for caribou conservation


Honouring and protecting wildlife was a major theme at the assembly, where delegates discussed how development has already affected traditional harvesting and wildlife habitat.


Gwich’in leader Chief Robert Charlie-Tetlichi of the Inuvik Native Band described efforts to balance economic development with environmental protection in the Mackenzie Delta region during the creation of the Dempster Highway.


“We put a good corridor in place. We tried to get people to hunt the traditional way, which is walking and hunting on the path of the caribou,” Charlie-Tetlichi said.


Fred Sangris, an Elder, hunter and chief with Yellowknives Dene First Nation, warned that the Bathurst caribou herd is facing a serious crisis.


“The most important animal that our ancestors defended and kept around was caribou,” Sangris said. “Today, there’s a crisis with caribou, and no one’s protecting them.”


Sangris referenced numbers

APTN News

 has reported in the past, whereby the Bathurst herd has declined from about 500,000 animals in 1985 to fewer than 4,000 today. He pointed to several possible contributing factors, including overharvesting, development, climate change and disease.


The assembly passed a resolution supporting Yellowknives Dene First Nation’s efforts to establish a conservation area to protect the Bathurst herd while it is in Chief Drygeese Territory.


The proposed area would be established under Dene law and knowledge and led by the Yellowknives Dene.


Sangris also called for hunter education programs and protected areas to help the herd recover.


A resolution passed at the assembly calls for federal projects serving both defence and community needs deliver lasting benefits for Dene communities. Photo: Charlotte Morritt-Jacobs/APTN.


Dene leaders seek greater benefits from major projects


Delegates also called for major projects, including the proposed Mackenzie Valley Highway and Arctic Economic and Security Corridor, to be designed, built, owned and operated with Dene participation.


The assembly’s economic development resolution calls for cooperation among Dene regions, governments, businesses and communities to pursue long-term benefits while protecting Dene rights, lands, waters, wildlife and culture.


Jeffrey Rosnawski, a Yellowknives Dene First Nation delegate, raised concerns that First Nations could miss procurement opportunities because of communication and capacity barriers, including in discussions involving the Department of National Defence.


“We have expressed the importance of increasing benefits to the Indigenous people in the north,” Rosnawski said. “And we have expressed that we wanted those efforts tracked diligently to ensure these benefits are being thought of and established with Indigenous peoples from the north.”


The resolution calls for work with federal departments and infrastructure programs so projects serving both defence and community needs deliver lasting benefits for Dene communities. It identifies opportunities including employment, training, procurement, business partnerships and Indigenous equity ownership.


It also says participation must be led by the Dene themselves, with each First Nation retaining authority over its own lands and decisions.

title: NSW Socialists launch campaign with a bang!
content:
“Our message is clear: the working class isn’t going to take this shit lying down anymore”, roared Ryan Chapman, NSW Socialists candidate for the seat of Wollongong, at the launch of the party’s 2027 state election campaign.

The 300-strong crowd burst out in applause. The venue, Ashfield Town Hall, was packed to capacity.

The speakers, three of the party’s six lower-house candidates, reflected Australia’s modern, multicultural working class. The first speaker, Alma Torlakovic, candidate for the Western Sydney seat of Granville, spoke movingly of her childhood in war-torn Bosnia and Croatia. Shovan Bhattarai, candidate for the inner-west seat of Newtown, humorously described the multicultural lunchtimes at her Western Sydney primary school. Chapman spoke of growing up working class on the South Coast and joining the navy as his only option.

The housing crisis was a recurring theme. Chapman spoke about the campaign to defend the Bellambi housing estate north of Wollongong. Labor MP for the area and state planning minister Paul Scully wants to knock down the estate because it is on prized beachfront property. After detailing the eye-watering average rent rises in the inner-west, Bhattarai explained the party’s housing policy of slashing rents by 35 percent, implementing a rent freeze and building 150,000 new public housing units.

Housing is a clear example of how the NSW Labor government screws over workers to protect the profits of the rich. Labor is happy to take workers’ votes, but once in government, the party, in Torlakovic’s words, “treat Western Sydney like garbage”. The crowd was full of boos and cries of “shame” at any mention of federal or state Labor politicians.

“We are the party for the millions of people who make this city run”, declared Bhattarai. This unashamed emphasis on class politics is a refreshing antidote to a mainstream politics filled with either middle-of-the-road progressivism or vitriolic far-right bile.

After the speeches, people stuck around for food, drinks and campaign strategising. New volunteers met the campaign managers in their electorates, and people signed up for the numerous party activities planned for the coming weeks. The launch kicked off a frenetic fortnight of activity. Party activists hope this will help firmly establish the party among prospective voters and meet more people who will join the movement.

While we may not be backed by billionaires or the mainstream media, the socialist movement has always been fuelled by endless enthusiasm and dedication combined with a radical vision of a better world. If you want to be a part of that, get involved with the campaign today.

author: Javier Moreno Zacarés
title: Fifteen Years Later
content:
Fifteen years after the indignados occupied the Puerta del Sol, Madrid’s central plaza is once again the locus of a mass movement that has brought Spain to a political impasse. How are we back here again? The immediate trigger was the eviction of an elderly tenant. Maricarmen Abascal, who had occupied her rent-capped apartment in central Madrid since 1956, was expelled from her home on 23 September after the investment fund Urbagestión acquired the property and exploited a legal loophole to quintuple her rent. Maricarmen’s age and vulnerability – the 87-year-old was removed on a hospital bed and has since died – made it a particularly egregious breach of the moral economy. The case struck a nerve, prompting a political storm; the government has now announced a snap election. As protests spread nationwide, the encampment at Puerta del Sol consolidated under the leadership of the Sindicato de Inquilinas, Madrid’s tenant union. Media outlets are reporting on the motions passed at the open-air general assembly. One decision has been of particular public interest: a general strike for the right to housing, announced for 11 November, a few weeks before the election.

The political elite faces a reckoning. At the outset of the current parliamentary term in 2023, the progressive coalition headed by Sánchez’s centre-left Socialist Party (PSOE) placed housing at the top of the agenda. The promises were ambitious: the provision of mass social housing, the imposition of rent controls, the reassertion of the public interest against rentier logics. Yet these commitments yielded little. This was partly due to the obstruction of the right, both in parliament and in the regional governments under its control. But a share of the blame lies in the ambivalence of the Socialist Party itself, whose ministers have repeatedly expressed discomfort with what they regard as excessive regulation of housing. The junior coalition partner Sumar, a nebulous alliance of progressive parties, has proven feeble in holding the Socialists to account. They are now also a target of the protests, who charge the entire governing alliance of complicity with the rentiers. Amid the fury in the streets, Sumar’s cabinet members hastened to pressure the Socialist housing minister, Isabel Rodríguez – herself a landlord who owns multiple properties – to approve emergency measures to block evictions and institute permanent rolling contracts, both key demands of the tenant unions. Last Friday, both measures were struck down in parliament, to the anger of the masses gathered outside.

That a recalcitrant right-wing opposition – comprising the conservative People’s Party (PP) and the far-right Vox – would block the measures was entirely predictable. What was less so was that the deciding vote would be cast by an ally of the government: the centre-right Junts, party of the Catalan-nationalist bourgeoisie. The vote revealed a peculiarity of the Spanish conjuncture. Though the right-wing bloc is the largest in parliament, it is divided along nationalist lines, fractures the government has exploited – drawing support from the Catalan right to keep the Spanish unionist right out of power. It was always an unstable arrangement, premised on nation trumping class. On the housing question, the plurinational right voted in alignment with its shared interests (Junts has the largest proportion of landlords in parliament).

The Spanish right now enjoys a comfortable lead in the polls, which point to a PP–Vox coalition if elections were held tomorrow. But the wind is blowing in an uncomfortable direction for them. Over the past week, public opinion has swung massively in favour of regulating house prices, even among a slim majority of right-wing voters. In a matter of days, the protests have shifted the national conversation away from the right’s preferred talking points of crime and migration, overwriting a summer of hysteria around the border crisis in Ceuta. They have also deflected attention from the corruption scandals afflicting PSOE: only last June, a former minister in Sánchez’s cabinet was sentenced to twenty-four years in prison for influence-peddling related to substandard Covid-19 face masks. Ever the survivor, Sánchez has seized the moment with a characteristically audacious move. He has framed the election on 29 November as a plebiscite on the housing question, shifting the blame for it onto the right and boldly appealing to the electorate to ‘subdue the elites’ …

title: «12 de Octubre, nada que celebrar»: pueblos originarios marchan contra los desalojos y la extranjerización de la tierra
content:
Marcha del Contrafestejo del 12 de octubre de 2024. Foto: archivo Nicolás Parodi / Página 12


Bajo la consigna “¡Nada que celebrar, muchas luchas que sostener!”, la Organización de Comunidades y Pueblos Originarios (ORCOPO) convocó a una marcha y contrafestejo para este lunes 12 de octubre, a las 18, en Plaza de los Dos Congresos. La jornada de lucha denunciará el avance de los desalojos, la criminalización de las comunidades indígenas, la extranjerización de la tierra, los proyectos extractivistas, la entrega, el saqueo y el despojo, en un escenario de creciente conflictividad territorial luego del reciente fallo de la Corte Suprema. La convocatoria se da en el marco de la confirmación judicial del desalojo de la Lof Inalef, en Río Negro, y una nueva amenaza contra la Lof Melo, en Neuquén. Ambos casos se suman a otros conflictos territoriales que atraviesan comunidades originarias en distintas regiones del país y que, para las organizaciones indígenas, evidencian una ofensiva sobre sus territorios en paralelo con el desmantelamiento de herramientas de protección y la reactivación de la derogación de la Ley de Tierras Rurales. También exigen justicia por Rafael Nahuel y libertad para quienes permanecen detenidos por luchar.

Por ANRed.

title: Çelik: No budget’ for students’ demands, yet 7.4 billion TL transferred to foundations
content:
As universities begin the autumn semester of the 2026–2027 academic year, a student at Istanbul Technical University (ITÜ) was expelled from a dormitory run by the Credit and Dormitories Institution (KYK) on the grounds that they had failed to pass the preparatory year in a single semester. With nowhere to stay, the student was forced to take refuge in the university library for days. They are now trying to continue their education while working to support themselves.


The experience of the ITÜ student is one example of the problems faced by thousands of students who are forced to work to continue their education, only to be labelled academically unsuccessful as a result and deprived of their right to housing.


Being a university student in Turkey is increasingly becoming less an educational experience and more a struggle for survival. The monthly scholarship or student loan of 4,000 TL (some 73 euros) provided to undergraduate students by the Ministry of Youth and Sports is not even enough to cover their basic needs, particularly in the face of rental prices and living costs in major cities.


Students forced working while studying


Rapidly rising rents for private dormitories and apartments in major cities have made KYK dormitories virtually the only housing option for students. Unable to receive sufficient financial support from their families due to the deepening economic crisis, students are forced to work in insecure and harsh conditions to make ends meet. When they cannot devote enough time to their studies as a result, the system labels them “unsuccessful”. This “failure” is then punished by depriving them of one of the most fundamental human rights: the right to housing.


ANF spoke with Senem Çelik of the

We Cannot Afford to Live Movement

, which has been working for days to bring the expulsion of an ITÜ student from a KYK dormitory to public attention, about the housing crisis and poverty experienced by students.


Referring to the mother who appealed for help on Instagram for her son, who had been expelled from his dormitory, saying, 'I don’t want my son to be left on the street. He hadn’t slept for two days, and neither have I,' Senem Çelik described what had happened: “Recently, we heard the desperate plea of a mother who explained that her child had been expelled from the dormitory for having to repeat a year. A fellow student at ITÜ has been trying to get through each day and continue their education since the semester began, sometimes staying in the library and sometimes at friends’ homes. The reason our fellow students have had to continue their education this way is that they have been forced to work while studying, which in turn has meant having to repeat the year.”


Stating that the

We Cannot Afford to Live Movemen

t has been working for years to bring the housing crisis facing young people to public attention and secure concrete gains for students, Senem Çelik said the housing problem could not be explained solely through economic indicators. She pointed out that the way university bureaucracies operate, treating students as secondary concerns, and their proposed solutions, which run counter to the ordinary realities of life, further deepen the injustices students experience.


Çelik said university students face not only housing difficulties and poverty but also declining educational quality, the failure of democratic mechanisms within universities to function, sexism in academia and harassment. She added that these problems cannot be considered separately from the deep poverty and the condition of being “excluded from citizenship” experienced by broad sections of society.


Senem Çelik said: “For example, struggles against the injustices experienced by students affected by earthquakes require us to connect with all citizens whose needs are ignored for the sake of profit and to support their struggles. Campaigns against poor living conditions in student dormitories bring together all students who cannot afford to heat their homes with natural gas or even pay for their meals.”


She added: “Alongside the exclusion of the public from all mechanisms of governance and oversight, students at universities, which should be centres of science and free thought, are increasingly being excluded from all decision-making and oversight mechanisms as universities are privatised and run like companies. Students do not even have a say in matters concerning their own living spaces in the dormitories …

title: Diskussionspapier „Recht auf Wohnen“ – Gemeinsam gegen die Wohnungsnot!
content:
Das Thema Recht auf Wohnen in all seinen vielfältigen Facetten treibt uns im Netzwerk Recht auf Stadt Hamburg schon lange um. Nach 2019 veröffentlichen wir nun hier ein Papier, das den aktuellen Diskussionsstand 2026 im Netzwerk wiedergibt. Es wurde von der Arbeitsgemeinschaft Wohnen ist Menschenrecht entwickelt. Nach Diskussion auf einem Workshop des Netzwerkes am 1. Februar 2026 haben wir es in der AG überarbeitet. Der Text wurde auf dem Netzwerktreffen am 13. September 2026 noch an ein paar Stellen korrigiert und ergänzt.

Wir haben uns für 10 Themenbereiche die aktuelle Lage näher angeschaut und daraus Forderungen entwickelt. Wenn euch bestimmte Aspekte interessieren, findet ihr hier in dem Papier auch über Links direkt dort hin. Das Papier soll gern als eine Art Steinbruch für weitere Diskussionen genutzt werden.

author: Helmut Weiss
title: „Was wir nicht verdienen, zahlen wir nicht“ – eine landesweite Initiative in Spanien organisiert Mietstreik
content:
Dossier


„…

Es ist wahrlich kein Aprilscherz. Am 1. April 2020 treten nun viele Familien, Selbstständige sowie kleine und mittlere Firmen im ganzen spanischen Staat in den Mietenstreik. Mietergewerkschaften, wie sie ausgehend von Katalonien ab 2017 wie das „Sindicat de Llogaters i Llogateres“ gegründet haben, und soziale Organisation rufen zum Streik gegen fehlende Notmaßnahmen der sozialdemokratischen Regierung für die einfache Bevölkerung auf. Die 200 Initiativen schlagen vor, ab April die Miete nicht mehr zu bezahlen. (…) Eigentlich hatten sich die Mietergewerkschaften wegen explodierender Mieten gegründet. Sie forderten bisher vor allem stärkere Mieterrechte und eine Regulierung der explodierenden Mieten, vor denen spanische Gesetze praktisch nicht schützen. Einige der Aktivisten hatten Hoffnungen in die neue Regierung gesetzt, doch sie wurden massiv enttäuscht

…“ – aus dem

Beitrag „Mietenstreik wegen Coronavirus in Spanien“ von Ralf Streck am 01. April 2020 bei telepolis


 über die landesweite Initiative. Siehe dazu die weitere Entwicklung und Hintergründe:


„Ni una Maricarmen más“: Zwangsräumung der 87-jährigen Maricarmen Abascal treibt massive Proteste gegen Wohnungsnot und Mietwucher über Madrid hinaus an 


Die 87-jährige Maricarmen, deren Zwangsräumung die Bewegung in Spanien radikalisiert hat, ist vor der erkämpften Rückkehr in ihre Wohnung erschöpft gestorben 


„

Die 87-Jährige ist am Mittwoch im Krankenhaus Gregorio Marañón in Madrid verstorben, wie die Mietervereinigung in einer Erklärung bestätigte (…) In dieser Erklärung, die auch von ihrer Familie und ihrer Anwältin unterzeichnet wurde, erinnern sie daran, dass sie seit der Zwangsräumung im Krankenhaus lag. „Zwar wurde eine historische Einigung erzielt, die ihr die Rückkehr in ihre Wohnung ermöglicht hätte, doch diese Lösung kam viel zu spät“, bedauern sie. Die Unterzeichner sind der Ansicht, dass die Ereignisse nach ihrer Zwangsräumung – Massendemonstrationen, Zeltlager auf den Plätzen, vorgezogene Wahlen und der Aufruf zu einem Generalstreik – „einen Wendepunkt in der Geschichte dieses Landes“ darstellen, warnen jedoch, dass „der Preis, den wir dafür gezahlt haben, zu hoch war“. Und sie verabschieden sich mit der Bitte, die sie ihnen immer wieder gesagt hat: „Kämpft, kämpft weiter für das, was euch gehört.“


Dank des gesellschaftlichen Drucks stand zum ersten Mal in Spanien eine zwangsgeräumte Person kurz davor, in ihr Zuhause zurückzukehren, nachdem der Eigentümer bereit war, einen neuen Mietvertrag abzuschließen. Dennoch hatten die Zwangsräumung und die vorangegangenen Versuche Maricarmen körperlich stark mitgenommen, sodass sie sich in ihren letzten Lebensjahren nur noch im Rollstuhl fortbewegen konnte und bei den alltäglichen Verrichtungen auf Hilfe angewiesen war. Hinter ihr lagen fast sieben Jahre gerichtlicher Auseinandersetzungen, um in ihrem Zuhause bleiben zu können. In den letzten Monaten hatte sich ihr körperlicher Zustand verschlechtert. Sie hatte an Muskelmasse verloren, hatte Schwierigkeiten beim Essen und sagte, dass sich sogar ihre Stimme verändert habe. „Es hat mich in jeder Hinsicht beeinträchtigt. Ich bin jetzt nicht mehr ich selbst“, erzählte sie zwei Tage, bevor sie ihr Haus verließ

…“ span.

Artikel von Lucía Franco und Beatriz Olaizola vom 7.10.2026 in El Pais online


 (maschinenübersetzt) und auch:


Der Verband der Mieterinnengewerkschaften ruft zu einer Schweigeminute und einem Generalstreik für Maricarmen auf


„

Heute, Freitag, um 12 Uhr mittags an allen Arbeits- und Bildungseinrichtungen im ganzen Land. Der Aufruf des Verbandes der Mieterinnengewerkschaften erfolgt, nachdem sich die PP und Vox am Donnerstag geweigert hatten, in der Madrider Regionalversammlung eine Schweigeminute für Maricarmen einzulegen, mit der Begründung, sie wollten „nicht zu ihrer politischen Instrumentalisierung“ in einer „interessengeführten Kampagne“ beitragen, obwohl gerade die Verstorbene selbst dazu aufgerufen hatte, für die politische Sache gegen Zwangsräumungen und für menschenwürdigen Wohnraum zu kämpfen und sich zu mobilisieren. (…) Deshalb bitten wir dich, alle Arbeitnehmerinnen und Arbeitnehmer sowie die gesamte Gesellschaft, morgen, Freitag, um 12 Uhr mittags an allen Arbeits- und Bildungseinrichtungen des Staates eine Schweigeminute einzulegen. Außerdem bitten wir dich, dich darauf vorzubereiten, dass wir am 11. November einen historischen Generalstreik durchführen. Wir werden nicht aufhören, bis wir alles verändert …

author: Harriet Williamson
title: Child Psychotherapist Forced to Close Practice After Holding Sign at Peaceful Protest
content:
A child psychotherapist was forced to close her private practice after being arrested for holding a paper sign at a Palestine Action protest, Novara Media can reveal.


Alex Payne, a

UKCP-registered

 integrative child psychotherapist of 16 years and accredited member of the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy, had her professional indemnity insurance cancelled following her arrests at two protests opposing the genocide in Gaza and the ban on Palestine Action. 


She was arrested in October 2025 and April this year under section 13 of the Terrorism Act for holding signs that read: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.”


Amnesty International UK has slammed Payne’s case as “chilling”. 


Palestine Action was proscribed as a terror organisation under Keir Starmer’s Labour government in the summer of 2025, making it the first direct action group in British history to be banned in this way. 


Payne was charged under the Terrorism Act after her arrest in October 2025. She has not been convicted, but with this charge hanging over her, she hasn’t been able to secure alternative insurance. Payne told Novara Media: “I cannot practice as a child psychotherapist without insurance, so I’ve had to prematurely end therapeutic work with children and young people although I pose no risk to their wellbeing.


“It’s ironic to me that a protest motivated by frustration at the Starmer government’s weak response to the suffering of children in Gaza should have led to my work with children having to end.” 


Payne had been insured by Markel International since 2022, via insurance broker Everywhen. She told Novara Media that she has never needed to make a claim, and that she had used Everywhen as her broker for her entire career. 


In emails seen by Novara Media, an Everywhen advisor told Payne that Markel International accepted that the “matter does not relate directly to [Alex’s] professional practice” but had decided that: “Taking the overall circumstances into account, including the two arrests and the ongoing legal proceedings, we do not feel this is a risk we can continue to support.”


Markel International and Everywhen both declined to comment. 


Amnesty International UK’s law and human rights director Tom Southerden told Novara Media: “To see a child psychotherapist facing arrest, and then having to close their practice simply for peacefully holding a placard, is a chilling attack on our freedom of speech.” 


On what moved her to take action, Payne said: “There is a huge cognitive dissonance in helplessly watching a live-streamed genocide and working with vulnerable and sometimes quite traumatised child clients. You see the impact of abuse and neglect on children and on the developing brain. 


“And then you’ve got this tiny strip of land, Gaza, where you’ve got generation after generation of traumatised children growing up into traumatised adults. And it’s very hard to see that happening and not do anything.”


She added: “I feel desperately guilty because I was doing good work with clients that I’ve had for a long time and clients who I just started working with – from eight or nine-year-olds to young adults.”


Payne is not the only person to have faced professional consequences after being arrested on terrorism charges for participating in Palestine Action protests.


Rachel, a social worker and 65-year-old grandma of three who chose not to give her last name due to fear of reprisals, took part in a protest against the ban on Palestine Action in September 2025, in London’s Parliament Square. Like Alex Payne, she was arrested under section 13 of the Terrorism Act for holding a sign that read: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.”  


Rachel immediately informed her workplace of her arrest and was suspended from her job at a local authority in the south-east of England for eight weeks. According to correspondence seen by Novara Media, she’s now back at work with a formal written warning. We are not naming Rachel’s employer to avoid further repercussions. 


Rachel said while senior management at work were “wetting themselves because it was the Terrorism Act”, she was well-supported by other colleagues who understood that her decision to take part in the protest was in line with her core values as a social worker.

title: Infinite Jail Glitch: Delhi’s Pay-and-Play Public Amenities Overtaken by Delhi Police to ‘Pay-and-Imprison’ Thousands Amidst SIR Protests
content:
Delhi’s makeshift ‘detention centres’, community spaces like stadiums and public event halls repurposed as mass holding cells for thousands of protesters, are ripped straight out of an Atwoodian dystopia. 


 


by

Mouli Sharma


 


New Delhi, 15 October 2026:

On 13 June 1989, late Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi laid the foundation stone to a public sports facility in Delhi’s Surajmal Vihar, a stone’s throw away from Jhilmil. A decade later, the Delhi Development Authority inaugurated the site as the Yamuna Sports Complex, a government run pay-and-play where you can, say, play badminton on an

outdoor daylight court

 for Rs. 100 a turn or take a ‘daily dip’ in the members’ exclusive swimming pools for Rs. 82.60 per head. 


 


On 10 October 2026, this sports complex, which serves as a public funded self sustaining recreational facility whose primary userbase consists of children and senior citizens, was turned into a hostage centre into which protesting lawyers of the supreme court were packed, after they marched toward the blockaded Jantar Mantar protest site demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar. 


“I managed to get away somehow,” said Adv. Awstika Das, one of the few left behind on the Mandi House Circle after around 70 protesters were “detained” and driven away, forcibly dispersing the small march. “They’ve taken the rest to the Yamuna Sports Complex, there are senior advocates there, too. They’ve been beaten,” she said. 


 


While the lawyers were released shortly afterwards in less than two hours—in stark contrast from the many thousands in Delhi who have been detained day after day in an ongoing cat and mouse game between state and citizen since the start of the SIR protests on 2 October—due to a “special, unprecedented”

intervention

 by the Chief Justice of India, the question remained, why were they taken to the complex in the first place, as opposed to a police station with a notified holding facility or lock-up?


 


“I’m not sure that there is any statutory authority supporting this… this repurposing of public spaces or government offices for detention,” said Advocate Archit Krishna, who specialises in criminal law. Advocate Vertika Mani, a human rights lawyer, similarly expressed skepticism about the legality of such repurposing.


 


“It should be challenged in court,” she said. “There is no legal basis for this.”


 


The Delhi Police Act, 1978, which governs the operations of the force in charge of security operations in the capital, which is now overwhelmingly being described as “under siege” of said forces (‘an undeclared Emergency’), provides a wide array of protections and special powers to the Delhi Police official, distinguishing him from the common man to the degree that an FIR may not be filed against him even if he is accused of commiting a cognisable offence, say murder or rape. Such has been the case with one former ACP Vivek Bhagat, who was accused of molestation by a woman journalist on 3 October 2026, against whom an FIR has still not been filed under these special powers. Instead, he has been promoted, and an FIR has been registered against the woman complainant, NewsDiggy reporter Rosy.


 


Notably, though, even

this

legislation does not empower the police to use public amenities as detention centres or give any authority to detain people within them under any circumstances, qualifying the detentions of 10 October as false imprisonment. Chapter IV, Section 36 of the Act allows for the police to temporarily reserve for themselves and therefore prevent public entry into public spaces or streets, but even this reservation requires for a written public notice to be issued by the Commissioner of Police. 


 


“The Commissioner of Police may, by public notice, temporarily reserve for any public purpose any street or other public place and prohibit persons from entering the area so reserved, except on such conditions as may be specified,” the Act says.


Daulatpur Community Centre turned into a detention centre for protesters


As of 14 October 2026, no such public notice has been given, but at least 7 public facilities in addition to the YSC have been “identified” and “prepared” to be used as makeshift prisons during protests, as reported by various mainstream broadcasters including the Hindustan Times, attributing unnamed “government sources”. Many of them have also revealed themselves after repeated mass detentions, which included the illegal detentions of minors …

Wir haben uns relativ schnell aktiv dagegen entschieden, kurzfristig eine WordPress-Infrastruktur aufzubauen, die eure Blogs aufnehmen kann. Das hat folgende Gründe:


 Unser Ziel ist es eine Struktur aufzubauen, die langfristig agiert. WordPress zu hosten ist aufwändig und anfällig für Angriffe und zu wenige von uns möchten das langfristig tun.


 Wir wollen Alternativen zu WordPress in die Bewegung bringen. Alternativen, die besser zu unseren Werten passen. Auch welche, die das NoBlogs-Backup importieren können.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Self-organisation or governing organisation?
content:
by Alessandro Stella


from

lundimatin

 #537, 12/10/2026


The student movement, which has spread like wildfire across France in the fall of 2026, was entirely the work of the secondary school students themselves. Without anyone behind them, without a party, without a union pulling the strings, they acted entirely on their own, like adults. They forced all the adults, all the authorities responsible for them, to take them into account.


The Rebirth of a Revolutionary Youth


They did so by denouncing the undignified and discriminatory conditions of their schools, by expressing their material and psychological suffering, and by formulating concrete and relevant demands. They did this by talking and discussing amongst themselves, by organising within the school, by creating a clear message on banners and placards, and then by taking action.


The form of action chosen by these rebellious secondary school students was to block the entrances to their school. They erected barricades of garbage cans, wooden pallets, street furniture—anything they could get their hands on. It was essentially a picket line and a mobilisation effort, forcing people to look at what was written on their placards and to discuss it. This form of action was adopted throughout France within a few days and quickly became a major news story. With very limited resources, through word of mouth, from group to group, via affinity networks, and then through social media, it spread; modern-day self-organisation, and it worked.


Faced with this youth revolt, the possibility of which had escaped everyone, including Laurent Nuñez (minister/prefect/head of the intelligence services), the State immediately decided, “as an adult responsible for protecting its children,” not to listen to the voices of the protesting secondary school students, but to bring them back into line and discipline. “We asked to be able to take the Baccalaureate exam, and they sent the riot police after us,” the students responded. With unimaginable brutality, especially towards teenagers, causing lifelong disabilities, injuries, and trauma: beaten, handcuffed, violently thrown into a police van, then into a squalid police station cell. In police custody, at 15 …


The rebellious youth managed to resist, to refuse to submit, and instead to fight back physically and morally, every single day. Day after day, without giving up, driven by an awareness of the injustices they suffered, rage against those who controlled their destinies, and a desire for a better future. “Fuck no future!” These ideas resonated with young teenagers everywhere, in cities and in the countryside, fuelling the collective movement. They spread rapidly because these ideas found fertile ground. With few resources, no big guns, no money, no central, structured organisation. Without leaders, just facilitators, collective experiences, self-organisation, and coordination.


The secondary school student revolt in the fall of 2026, despite the price paid in the flesh, has already achieved several victories. In the immediate aftermath, without even realising it, they had disrupted all political and electoral agendas and forced all the powers that be to look at them, to listen to them, especially when they shouted to finally be heard.


The visual, spatial, and sonic emergence of this secondary school student revolt clearly reveals that the spearhead of the rebels are young people from the French colonial past, living in disadvantaged working-class neighbourhoods on the outskirts of cities, who have endured generations of daily humiliation, contempt, and exclusion. This is undoubtedly a first in the history of student revolts, from 1968 to the present day.


The other defining characteristic of this secondary school student movement is this cry of revolt, this rejection of “infantilism,” namely, the denigration of a person based on their age. This discrimination should be considered among the structural forms of inferiority and oppression in our societies, alongside classism, machismo, racism, and all forms of supremacy, based on the contempt of those who look down on another person.


These young people are rebelling against all the schizophrenic powers that dominate them;  Legal minors, subject to parental authority, without the right to vote, yet old enough to be beaten, injured, detained, or even imprisoned.


Through their struggle, they have shown and demonstrated that they have ample reason to revolt, that they are …

author: Unknown
title: Lahur Şêx Cengî Talabanî sentenced to more than five years in prison
content:
Kurdish politician and former co-chair of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), Lahur Şêx Cengî Talabanî (Lahur Sheikh Jangi Talabani), has been sentenced to five years and three months in prison by a court in Sulaymaniyah. His lawyer confirmed the verdict to the news outlet The New Region on Thursday. Talabanî’s brother Polad was also sentenced to three years and six months in prison. The court handed down a two-year prison sentence to their close associate Rebwar Hamid Haci Gali.


Power struggle within the PUK


The case stems from a long-running power struggle within the PUK, one of the two dominant governing parties in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI). Lahur Şêx Cengî Talabanî led the party alongside Bafel Talabanî until he was removed from power in 2021. The two are cousins, and Bafel Talabanî remains the leader of the PUK. Another cousin, Qubad Talabanî, serves as deputy prime minister of the Kurdistan Region.


Following his removal from the party leadership, Lahur Şêx Cengî Talabanî founded the opposition People’s Front (Bereyî Gel). In August 2025, PUK-affiliated security forces deployed tanks and drones to arrest the politician at his residence in the Lalezar Hotel in Sulaymaniyah. The operation triggered hours of heavy fighting in a residential area of the city. According to official figures, two members of Talabanî’s staff and three members of the PUK security forces were killed. Other reports indicate a higher death toll.


Defense calls for an independent trial


Following the clashes, Lahur Şêx Cengî Talabanî, his brother Polad, and numerous others were arrested. A total of 27 people detained in connection with the fighting remain in prison. The trial had been repeatedly postponed since then.


Talabanî’s defense team had requested that the proceedings be transferred to Hewlêr (Erbil), where they believed a more transparent and fair trial could be held. His lawyers also criticized alleged human rights violations against detained members of his security team.

author: labor4pal
title: Universities fire dozens amid pressure from Zionist billionaires (Electronic Intifada)
content:
Ali Abunimah Rights and Accountability 14 October 2026

Universities in the United States and Canada have fired, suspended and harassed employees for speaking out against Israel’s genocide in Gaza, often using ostensibly neutral disciplinary procedures to conceal politically motivated retaliation.

That is the finding of a new report from the Academic Freedom Initiative, a project of the Middle East Studies Association (MESA).

“Lessons in Repression: Silencing Campus Workers on Palestine Since October 7, 2023” is the first systematic study of retaliation against university employees for their Palestine-related speech and activism in the two countries.

The report draws on a database of 196 incidents recorded through 20 August 2026 and in-depth interviews with 31 targeted employees.

Of those incidents, 76 – nearly 40 percent – resulted in termination, while 59 involved suspension or campus bans.

Both tenured professors and precariously employed instructors and staff have been targeted. Of 134 cases in which racial or ethnic identity was known, nearly two-thirds involved people of color. Some 16.5 percent of those targeted identified as Jewish.

Most retaliation had nothing to do with classroom teaching. More than half the incidents stemmed from other on-campus activities, including protests, while only 11 percent concerned alleged classroom interactions.

Another 16 percent of cases arose from off-campus speech and 12 percent from social media posts, “suggesting that teaching is a relatively less common context provoking punishment.”

Major drivers of the repression include pressure from wealthy pro-Israel donors, government interference and the political loyalties of university administrators and trustees, the report says.

Growing financial dependence of universities on wealthy benefactors, alongside austerity and the widespread use of precariously employed workers, also makes institutions more vulnerable to political pressure.

At the University of Pennsylvania, for example, trustee Cheryl Peisach is married to the treasurer of a family foundation that donated $100,000 to Canary Mission in 2023.

The notorious pro-Israel blacklisting website publishes dossiers attacking students and academics who support Palestinian rights.

US immigration authorities have admitted to using its dossiers to target Palestine activists.

In another case at Penn, a tenured professor faced a vicious online harassment campaign over her support for Palestine, including hundreds of messages containing rape and death threats.

The donor funding her endowed chair withdrew support. According to the professor, a dean told her that donor pressure had led the university to encourage her retirement. She retired in June 2026.

Billionaire Bill Ackman demanded a blacklist of Harvard students who disagreed with his views, while billionaire Leon Cooperman threatened to stop donating to Columbia University following a Palestine solidarity walkout.

Pressure from the Trump administration has reinforced the crackdown.

During the last two months of 2023, the US government opened more federal “anti-Semitism” investigations against universities than in all previous years combined.

Dozens of institutions agreed to government monitoring, including sharing the names of students and employees accused of anti-Semitism, to close investigations.

Harvard provided a notable example of such cowardice. Even as it fought a Trump administration lawsuit falsely portraying Gaza solidarity protests as anti-Jewish terror, the university boasted of its own crackdown on alleged anti-Semitism rather than defend its students’ right to protest Israel’s genocide.

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit in August, finding that the government had failed to plausibly allege any ongoing violation of civil rights law.

Six congressional hearings between December 2023 and July 2025 subjected university leaders to McCarthyite interrogations over alleged failures to combat anti-Semitism.

In Illinois, Northwestern University journalism professor Steven Thrasher was suspended shortly after being singled out during one of these hearings and was later denied tenure and terminated. He is currently suing the university for discrimination and violations of his First Amendment rights.

The repression has also affected Canada, where provincial ministers have publicly accused academic staff and students of anti-Semitism, attacked discussions of Palestine and genocide, and demanded the …

author: Amy Goodman
title: Israeli Forces Raid Palestinian NGOs in the West Bank Ahead of Israeli Elections
content:
The raids come four years after the forced closure of multiple NGOs that Israel designated as “terrorist” organizations.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Israeli forces have raided what they say are the offices of several Palestinian NGOs in the occupied West Bank. Palestinian officials say a child was injured from Israeli gunfire, while others suffered from tear gas inhalation. At least one journalist was reportedly detained in the raids, which come four years after the forced closure of multiple NGOs that the Israeli government designated as “terrorist” organizations.

“This is part of the whole propaganda show that this government is actually implementing just before the Israeli election,” says human rights lawyer Sahar Francis. “They just wanted to cause harassment, and this is the main message: the persecution and the collective punishment for the whole Palestinian community.” Francis was formerly the general director at Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association, one of the organizations that Israel claims to have raided this week despite the fact that it was already forced to close its West Bank offices in 2022.

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

In the latest crackdown on human rights defenders in the occupied West Bank Tuesday, Israeli forces raided what they say are the offices of several Palestinian NGOs, confiscating legal files, court records, valuable equipment. Israeli forces also deployed snipers around the entrances to Ramallah’s Palestine Medical Complex, the largest government medical facility in the occupied West Bank. At least one journalist was reportedly detained. Palestinian officials say a child was injured from Israeli gunfire; others suffered from tear gas inhalation.

For more in these last few minutes, we go to Ramallah, where we’re joined by Sahar Francis, human rights lawyer, previous general director at Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association, which is one of the groups that Israel just raided.

Sahar Francis, welcome back to Democracy Now! We had you on when you were the head of Addameer, which is the prisoner support and human rights group in the West Bank. I was watching overnight when Israel was raiding, because Al Jazeera was showing the raid live. But these offices, in fact, of your group, your previous group, Addameer, and others, the Palestine Women’s Association, were already closed — is that right? — years ago, because the Israeli government classified these organizations as terrorist. So, what were they raiding?

SAHAR FRANCIS: Exactly. Good afternoon, and thanks for inviting me again to join you in this important discussion.

As you just said, these offices actually were raided in 2020. We were, too, forced closure after the decision to designate the six Palestinian organizations as terrorist organizations. They confiscated property and stole files and equipments at that time.

So, what happened yesterday, I would claim that this is part of the whole propaganda show that this government is actually implementing just before the Israeli election, couple of weeks before the Israeli election, to send a very clear message to the whole Palestinian society, and especially to the Palestinian Authority, because the offices they raided is very close to the official governmental offices and other ministries in Ramallah city, that “We are the masters. We decide what we will do. You cannot interfere. You cannot protect nothing to do with your sovereignty in even Ramallah city, that is supposed to be an Area A.”

And what happened yesterday, they were not confiscating property for illegal organization, claiming that this property is used to support terrorism. And I’m sure you all saw in the videos that were presented by the different media, local or international, that they mostly broke and destroyed the files and the equipment, even the windows. The refrigerator in this office that they claimed it belongs for Addameer, they were throwing it from the second floor down to the ground. They just wanted to cause harassment, and this is the main message: the persecution and the collective punishment for the whole Palestinian community. The raid onto the city center Ramallah is not a lonely activity. It happens every day that they raid different villages, different cities. They arrest …

author: Mada Masr
title: Protests at several prisons, detainee ‘banishments’ surround delay to Criminal Procedure Code
content:
A wave of protests has swept through several prisons over the last three weeks, as prisoners who were hopeful that the new Criminal Procedure Code would bring an end to their prolonged remand detention had their hopes dashed at the eleventh hour when the law’s implementation was postponed, according to several lawyers acting in defense of detainees held at different prisons who spoke separately to Mada Masr over the same time period.


The postponement pushed back what many detainees saw as a window of opportunity for authorities to release dozens of them held in remand after the law’s awaited implementation on October 1.


With that window now firmly shut until October 2027, a wave of demonstrations in detention centers has been met by security forces with measures that the lawyers say include the punitive transfer of detainees to prisons farther away from their families, a practice known as “

taghreeb”

 (banishment).


As cries and claims about the demonstrations and the security forces’ response made their way to social media, the Interior Ministry issued repeated denials that protests and abuses are taking place within prisons, most recently in an October 2

statement

. The Public Prosecution, meanwhile, was yet to issue a statement regarding the claims at the time of publishing.


The state’s National Council for Human Rights (NCHR) intends to pay visits to a number of prisons about which it has received complaints, the council’s deputy head, Mohamed Anwar al-Sadat, tells Mada Masr. Sadat adds, however, that the council has received “assurances” from the prosecution and the Interior Ministry that conditions inside prisons are “normal.”


But lawyers and human right defenders, who continue to hear from concerned families and document the incidents, have raised calls for an independent investigation into possible violations against detainees.


***


Among those subjected to “banishment,” is journalist and researcher Ismail al-Eskandarany, according to human rights lawyer Mahienour al-Massry.


Massry received information on October 1 that Eskandarany, whom she represents, and other detainees had been transferred from the 10th of Ramadan Correctional and Rehabilitation Center “violently, resulting in injuries to some detainees,” as per her

telegraph

 to the public prosecutor, in which she demanded the disclosure of Eskandarany’s place of detention.


Massry tells Mada Masr that Eskandarany’s family was able to confirm independently that he had been moved from 10th of Ramadan center’s prison 6 to the Wadi al-Natroun prison in what is known as a “banishment.”


Massry called, in her telegraph to the prosecution, for an urgent investigation into the circumstances of the transfer and any violations or assaults that may have been committed against Eskandarany or other detainees, noting the investigation should include their referral for forensic medical examination or to other relevant medical authorities to document their condition.


Another human rights lawyer representing prisoners in political cases says that some of his defendants, too, had been transferred from the 10th of Ramadan prison to the Gamasa prison against the backdrop of protests, according to information the lawyer received from three of his clients’ families. Demonstrations had taken place at 10th of Ramadan center’s prison 6, with large numbers of prisoners chanting slogans in protest against their detention conditions and refusing to return to their cells after their recreation time, according to the lawyer. Riot police intervened in an attempt to disperse the gatherings and return the prisoners to their cells, after which prison authorities began transferring a number of detainees to other facilities, the lawyer adds, citing accounts from detainees’ families. The lawyer says he was also informed of an incident in which a prisoner was placed in solitary confinement as a disciplinary measure after going on hunger strike.


The human rights lawyer, two other lawyers and a human rights source confirm to Mada Masr that detainees’ families have complained to them of security forces’ mistreatment of prisoners at the same facility following protests in several cells over recent days, including chanting and banging on cell doors, disabling surveillance cameras in several cells and refusing to leave their cells for recreation time. Prison authorities have also conducted extensive searches of cell contents, according to the lawyers.

author: Unknown
title: There’s probably some weird corner of the internet where “marginalized people need to have…
content:
I really, really don’t think “My turbo-principled position is that because marginalized groups are sometimes maligned as sexual predators, marginalized people need to have solidarity with confessed actual sexual predators!” is a good hill to die on for anybody.

Guys who use their privilege to actually do this stuff don’t need any more people standing up for them. They’ve already got mainstream society making excuses and ensuring that their rights are protected in ways that, say, for example, a trans woman accused of having a bit of a bad vibe could never even dream of.

As a person who’s considered guilty even when proven innocent, you aren’t going to reap any benefits from defending someone who’s already treated like he’s innocent despite being proven guilty.

There’s probably some weird corner of the internet where “marginalized people need to have solidarity with confessed actual sexual predators” is an actual opinion that some people have, but I’ve never really encountered that opinion ever.

What I have encountered far far more is

Because this marginalized group is so often maligned as sexual predators, they will sometimes be convicted as sexual predators, therefore our solidarity should include convicted sexual predators, as some are innocent and we can’t tell which ones they are.

Because this marginalized group is so often a victim of abuse and abuse is often cyclical, some will complete the cycle of abuse and will become abusers. Therefor our compassion should include people who have committed abuse because only with support can we break the cycle of abuse.

We should stand in solidarity with all incarcerated people, no matter how terrible their wrongdoings, because prison abolition and transformative justice for all is the only path to a truly free and just society.

And other variations of that, which then get twisted as “so you think we should have solidarity with confessed actual sexual predators?”, when like, that was not the point.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: "Propaganda Show": IDF Raids Palestinian NGOs in the West Bank Ahead of Israeli Elections
content:
Israeli forces have raided what they say are the offices of several Palestinian NGOs in the occupied West Bank. Palestinian officials say a child was injured from Israeli gunfire, while others suffered from tear gas inhalation. At least one journalist was reportedly detained in the raids, which come four years after the forced closure of multiple NGOs that the Israeli government designated as “terrorist” organizations.


“This is part of the whole propaganda show that this government is actually implementing just before the Israeli election,” says human rights lawyer Sahar Francis. “They just wanted to cause harassment, and this is the main message: the persecution and the collective punishment for the whole Palestinian community.” Francis was formerly the general director at Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association, one of the organizations that Israel claims to have raided this week despite the fact that it was already forced to close its West Bank offices in 2022.

author: Reem Aljeally
title: Class, Creativity, and Cultural Production in Africa
content:
Artistic freedom and expression has long been shaped and constrained by many factors, including power, economic hierarchies, and class. In Africa, the right to create and distribute art without censorship has always been a contested terrain. Artists’ realities in the African region are directly influenced by both their geographical and societal positions; class plays a big role in how the art world runs. What does society consider as art?  Who gets to buy, collect, or even witness art?  Who has access to exhibition spaces or international residencies? These questions are not abstract; they define the careers of many artists, including my own.


Since 2011, we have seen youth-led movements harness creativity as a tool for political resistance, from the Arab Spring uprisings to #FeesMustFall in South Africa, #EndSARS in Nigeria, and, most recently, Kenya’s Gen Z protests. In Sudan, where I was born and raised, the December Revolution was marked not only by chants in the streets but also by murals, poems, songs, and performances that transformed the cityscape into a living archive of resistance. Yet, even within such moments of collective creativity, class distinctions determined who could participate, whose voices were amplified, and whose remained unheard.


In this article, I reflect on how class shapes artistic and cultural production in Africa: how it has defined access to creativity, how it limits cultural consumption, and what mechanisms – grassroots, digital, and transnational – have begun to narrow these divides. My reflections are grounded in personal experience as an artist and curator working between Khartoum and Cairo, as the founder of The Muse multi-studios and the Sudan Art Archive, and as a participant in regional and international networks of cultural production.


Social hierarchy and access to creativity


In Khartoum, where I first studied architecture before turning to painting and curation, access to art education was already limited to two art schools at the Sudan University for Science and Technology and the newly founded Art programme at the Al-Nileen University. Access to these institutions was competitive, and while not restricted in principle, in practice it was shaped by social status and community expectations. Families in Sudan often encouraged more “practical” fields like engineering, medicine, or architecture – disciplines seen as more secure.


Many young Sudanese who aspired to become artists may have had their educational background shaped by these community views, yet it has not stopped them from pursuing a career in the field upon completing their studies. Those who came from upper-class families had a better chance of accessing educational institutions abroad, while the majority were funnelled into informal workshops or self-taught practices because institutions were either non-existent or insufficiently resourced.


German curator and researcher Larissa-Diana Fuhrmann observes that the development of art education in Sudan has been deeply influenced by colonial legacies. Institutions such as the College of Fine and Applied Arts in Khartoum (originally established under British colonial rule) implemented curricula modelled on Western art academies. These frameworks introduced formalist, Eurocentric paradigms that continue to shape artistic discourse, pedagogy, and aesthetic hierarchies in the postcolonial context.


Access to these institutions, and to international art education more broadly, has historically been mediated by class intersecting with gender and racial categories. During both the late colonial and early post-independence periods, educational and cultural policies enabled a small elite (predominantly from Khartoum’s middle- and upper-class families) to study abroad. Upon their return, these artists occupied influential positions in Sudan’s cultural institutions and helped define national artistic narratives. As Fuhrmann notes, the stratification becomes evident when examining how some of these artists categorize work produced outside formal institutions or urban centres as “folkloric”, thereby reinforcing classed and spatial distinctions in cultural valuation.


This dynamic illustrates the broader relationship between class, cultural capital, and aesthetic authority. Artists with international training and transnational visibility have historically been more likely to receive institutional recognition and access to resources such as galleries, collectors, and …

author: dev
title: Du backlash écologique au backlash IA
content:
À quand une psychanalyse des nouveaux contes de fées ? Le vent serait-il en train de tourner ? Entre les Docteur Frankenstein de l'IA qui prennent peur de leur créature et les manifestations contre l'implantation de data centers un peu partout aux USA, mais aussi maintenant en France, l' 'IA mania', qui avait débuté comme un cyber-conte de fées, commence à virer au cauchemar.


Les fournaises estivales devenues habituelles (« il ne fait que 30°C… ça va ») entretiennent des torpeurs mentales qui convergent opportunément avec un aveuglement salutaire pour la santé mentale, sacrée cause nationale. Peut-on être assez inconscient pour se féliciter de la douce moiteur de cet été indien sans en voir ni les causes, ni les conséquences à bien trop court terme ? Comme l'a montré une anthropologue, Elise Boutié, à propos des méga-feux en Californie, les victimes de la catastrophe elles-mêmes (du moins les survivants, car il y a eu des morts) restent souvent dans le déni quant à l'origine climatique de ces incendies et les attribuent au simple hasard

 [

1

]

, un peu comme Emmanuel Macron avec son « Qui aurait pu prédire... ? » en 2022. C'est sans doute la même chose avec l'IA. "Qu'est-ce qui réveille ?" se demandait Lacan. Il semble en tout cas facile de continuer à ignorer le vase communicant entre la courbe des investissements dans l'IA et celle des investissements dans la transition écologique, désormais nettement inférieurs

 [

2

]

. On s'alarme du niveau d'endettement, mais quid de ses causes ? Une transition chasse l'autre : il n'y aura pas assez pour le numérique et pour l'environnement. Et il pourrait ne pas y avoir assez pour aucun des deux. Oui, mais : aux USA, 75 projets de

data centers

 ont été annulés rien qu'au premier trimestre, sous la pression des citoyens de toute sorte

 [

3

]

. Républicains comme démocrates,

rednecks

 ou cols blancs se révoltent contre ces gigantesques aspirateurs à eau et à énergie.


Et en France ? On part de loin : le problème, médiatiquement et politiquement construit, ce sont, semble-t-il, les éoliennes, approuvées sur le principe et en théorie, mais en fait très mal tolérées quand elles s'implantent dans le champ d'à côté. L'IA et le numérique, au contraire, c'est virtuel : comme disent les élèves, « mais comment ça peut émettre du CO2, un téléphone ? Où est le pot d'échappement ? » Si l'on ajoute la fable de la prétendue neutralité du nucléaire sur le plan environnemental, et de son coût prétendument faible, le piège se referme. Et pourtant un rapport récent à la Commission Européenne montre que non seulement le coût de l'énergie produite par les nouveaux EPR sera plus de 3,5 fois supérieur à celui des renouvelables, mais aussi que ces EPR2 bénéficient d'aides à l'investissement inédites (et de conditions particulièrement arrangeantes et coûteuses pour le budget de l'État)

 [

4

]

. A l'heure où l'EPR de Flamanville est à nouveau à l'arrêt, à peine un an après sa mise en service complète, il y a de quoi faire réfléchir au prix de l'électricité.


La France cherche à "rester dans la course" : "attirer les investisseurs", c'est-à-dire d'abord les data centers ("Choose France"), cela veut dire offrir aux GAFAM sur un plateau nos ressources en eau, notre électricité pas (trop) chère, en échange de... hum. Pas de transferts technologiques en tout cas. Quant à Mistral, il semble avoir renoncé à la compétition sur les LLM pour faire du business autrement, en contrats avec les Américains (... et avec Total). "Mistral AI veut être présent", dixit, "sur toute la chaîne de valeur, des data centers aux applications chez les entreprises, pour contrer la domination américaine" : c'est justement le contraire qui est en train de se passer. Et la France, sous l'influence de ses start-ups (théoriquement) souveraines a longuement renâclé avant de finir par signer un texte présenté à l'ONU pour renforcer les mesures de sécurité sur l'IA, sans engagement clair cependant.


Faisons confiance à la communication de la "marque France" : les éléments de langage nous livrent le bon message, mais sous forme inversée. Encore du Lacan !

author: groundxero
title: Blackboxes and Such: New Delhi on the Eve of 10 October, and the Seeds of India’s Undeclared Neo-Emergency
content:
The administrative streets of central New Delhi have now become a terrifying labyrinth of surveillance and armed lockdown – except for the VIP residents who live there, and the exotic nightly businesses that entertain them.

Mouli Sharma

 report on New Delhi on the eve of October 10.


 


10 October 2026, New Delhi:

 At the stroke of the midnight hour on Saturday in the administrative district of India’s capital, a quiet terror overtook the once – illusorily – safe expanse.


 


Preparations for the coming morning’s protest call, for people to take the streets all over the capital, not just the “designated” protest site of Jantar Mantar that has now become a designated “detention” site with an indefinite application of the controversial Section 163 (which empowers district and other magistrates to issue ‘special prohibitory orders’ and temporarily suspend constitutional freedoms in a given region during ’emergencies’) that has since expanded to the India Gate region, the Kashmere Gate region, and then through 54 other localities over ten days of continued protests, began early in the morning a day prior.


 


First, the office of the Joint Commissioner of Police (Transport Range) at Jai Singh Road issued an unprecedented order for the indefinite suspension of Metro rail entry and exit ways (as well as a reduction of train frequencies) in an unprecedented 57 stations, due to ostensible (and unspecified) suspicions of “mob movement”.


 


“In view of the proposed protests at Jantar Mantar and other locations in New Delhi District in 10.10.2026 and the likelihood of unruly mob movement towards sensitive locations, frequency of Metro trains passing through the following Metro stations may be reduced and their entry/exit gates may be closed from 9:00 PM on 09.10.2026, continuing on 10.10.2026 till the situation normalises,” said the notice issued to the Managing Director of the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), Vikas Kumar on Friday.


 


A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymlayla Bagchi and Justice V Mohana was hearing the petitions challenging the curbs imposed in Delhi, and observed on the same day that the total shutdown of the services would affect the rights of citizens who are entitled to avail them. But these services nevertheless remained closed from 9PM onwards, at least within the New Delhi region.


 


Next was a network blackout. Internet services were suspended in a 4km radius extending from the Jantar Mantar protest site an hour after the transport lockdown. A “top secret” circular from the office of the Deputy Commissioner of Police Special Cell, Manishi Chandra, instructing private service providers including Airtel, VI, Jio, along with MTNL Delhi to indefinitely suspend internet services in the region began circulation during the late evening of the 9th, and the over 50 kilometre square expanse was consequently turned into a complete blackbox.


 


***


 


Pushing 10 PM outside the barricading of the site nearest to the Kerala Bhawan, while the networks were still on, the police were bashful. The speakers hanging from trees announced that any violations of “the prohibitions under the order” issued under Section 163 of the BNSS would be punishable by law, but when asked what these prohibitions are, or if this order could be produced such that public could indeed heed its prohibitions, officers present at the scene stood clueless.


 


Come dawn, Vikas Meena, Harnit Singh Sudan and Bharat Bhushan pulled a few reporters to the side, reassuring them that no press would be detained or obstructed during the protests, provided that press themselves did not obstruct the detentions of common folk.


 


“We request that you stay far away and do your job,” Meena said. “If we are detaining someone, don’t try to stop us or come close to us or film what is happening. We have no problem with the press, but recently, journalists have started intervening in our processes and asking questions while we conduct our operations, which makes it difficult for us to distinguish them as press.”


 


When pushed on the precise details and prohibitions listed in the magisterial order, though, Meena repeats a familiar refrain: “Where is the order? It must be somewhere. You’ll have to ask the New Delhi DCP. I’m not from the district, so I don’t know.”


 


Ask at the station, though, over a hundred journalists have, but DCP Sachin Sharma has refused to respond in plain terms, and even …
