title: TELE1 çalışanları hakkını alamadı, Halk TV'de belirsizlik sürüyor: Kayyım baskısı gazetecilerin çalışma alanını da daraltıyor
content:
Son iki yılda aralarında Flash Haber, EkoTürk, Habertürk TV, Show TV, Bloomberg HT, HT Spor, Show Türk, Show Max, TELE1 ve Halk TV’nin bulunduğu 10 televizyon kanalına kayyım atandı. Farklı gerekçelerle yürütülen süreçlerde televizyonların yönetimleri Tasarruf Mevduatı Sigorta Fonu’na (TMSF) devredilirken, TELE1 ve Halk TV’ye yönelik müdahaleler, iktidar çizgisi dışında yayın yapan az sayıdaki televizyon kanalının yönetimlerinin değiştirilmesi açısından diğer kayyım süreçlerinden ayrıldı. Bu kanallarda çalışanların ve işten çıkarılanların yaşadıkları ise basın özgürlüğü ile çalışma hakkının aynı süreçte nasıl kesiştiğini ortaya koydu.

TELE1’e 24 Ekim 2025’te kayyım atanmasının ardından kanalın başına getirilen İbrahim Paşalı, 14 Ekim 2026’da Halk TV’ye de kayyım olarak atandı. Yeni Şafak’ta köşe yazarlığı yapan Paşalı, daha önce Flash Haber, Habertürk, Show TV ve Bloomberg HT’nin de aralarında bulunduğu medya kuruluşlarında kayyım olarak görev almıştı.

TELE1’de kayyım atandıktan sonra istifa eden bir gazeteci kayyım atamasının ardından yaşanan süreci anlattı. Kanalın kayyım yönetimine geçtiğinde 140 kişilik bir çalışan kadrosuna sahip olduğunu belirten gazeteci, önce Ankara bürosunun kapatıldığını, kanalın İstanbul’dan yürütüleceğinin söylendiğini, ardından İstanbul bürosunda da işten çıkarmaların devam ettiğini söyledi.

“140 kişilik ekibimizden 130 kişiyi işten attılar” diyen gazeteci, işten çıkarılan bazı arkadaşlarının Koza TV, İlke TV ve son olarak Halk TV’ye geçtiğini anlattı.

Ancak medya sektöründeki kayyım ve baskı süreçleri nedeniyle gazetecilerin çalışabileceği alanların zaten daraldığını belirten gazeteci, Halk TV’ye de kayyım atanmasının ardından bu alanın daha da küçüldüğünü söyledi. TELE1’de kayyım tarafından işten çıkarılanların önemli bölümünün halen işsiz olduğunu belirten gazeteci, bazı çalışanların ücret ve kıdem tazminatlarını da alamadığını söyledi. “Bu insanlar aylardır işsiz, hakları olan ücretleri alamadı, “bu sadece halkın haber alma hürriyetine kayyım atanması değil, bu gazetecilerin çalışamaması sonucu basının da işlevsiz bırakılmasıdır” dedi.

TELE1’de kayyım sonrasında işten çıkarılan başka bir gazeteci ise tazminat ve diğer alacakların ödenmediğini belirterek, işsizliğin sektördeki daralmayla birlikte ağırlaştığını söyledi.

“24 Ekim 2025’te TELE1’e kayyım atanmasının ardından aslında yıllardır süregelen kayyım uygulamasının mağdurları arasına eklendik” diyen gazeteci, bazı çalışanların ayrılmayı, bazılarının ise ekonomik zorluklara rağmen bir süre çalışmayı tercih ettiğini anlattı.

“Sonuç olarak hepimiz işten çıkarıldık. Aradan geçen zamana rağmen ödenmesi gereken, bilgi mesajıyla iletilen tazminatlarımız hala ödenmedi” dedi.

İşini kaybetmenin yarattığı ekonomik sıkıntıya hak edilen alacakların ödenmemesinin de eklendiğini belirten gazeteci, “Bir günde işten çıkarıldık, hala iş bulamayan basın emekçileri var” diye konuştu.

Gazeteci, bugün işini kaybetmenin yalnızca yeni bir iş aramak anlamına gelmediğini belirterek, “Giderek daralan çalışma alanlarında yeniden iş bulmaya çalışmak, geçinebilmek, kira ve faturaları ödemek, geleceğe dair belirsizlikle mücadele etmek anlamına geliyor” dedi.

TELE1’de işten çıkarılan çalışanların bir bölümünün daha sonra Halk TV’ye geçtiğini anlatan TELE1 çalışanının sözleri, Halk TV’de kayyım sonrası oluşan belirsizlikle de kesişiyor.

Halk TV reji ekibinden bir işçi, kayyım atanmasının ardından çalışanlar ve yöneticiler açısından ciddi bir belirsizlik oluştuğunu söyledi. Kayyım yönetimiyle yapılan görüşme sonrasında Halk TV yöneticileri, “Biz onlara yardımcı olmayacağız. Onlar burayı devam ettirmek istiyorlarmış. Kimseye ‘şunu yapın’ demiyoruz, karar sizin” denildiğini aktardı.

Kayyım yönetiminin kanalı sürdürmek istediğini söylediğini belirten işçi, “Buranın mali durumu iyi. Biz burayı döndürmek, devam ettirmek istiyoruz” ifadelerinin kullanıldığını söyledi.

author: Sally Ncube
title: Child marriage laws in Africa need more funding to protect girls
content:
15th October 2026


Child marriage laws in Africa need more funding to protect girls


12 min read


News and Insights


End child marriage


Africa


With global funding to end child marriage falling yearly since 2019, African governments must take action to strengthen budgeting and implementation of child marriage laws.  


By

Sally Ncube,

 Equality Now, and

Fatou Gueye Ndir,

 Senior Regional Engagement and Advocacy Officer, Girls Not Brides


Although numerous African governments have strengthened laws against child marriage, legal protections remain widely underfunded and ineffectively enforced. Many countries have no clearly outlined, dedicated national budget line for ending child marriage. Instead, allocated money is incorporated into broader gender or social protection budgets, where funds are often difficult or impossible for auditors to trace or civil society to access. 


Funding to end child marriage is falling 


The joint report, ‘

International Funding to End Child Marriage: Reviewing a Decade of Investment

,’ by

Girls Not Brides

 and

Girls First Fund

, with input from

Publish What You Fund

, found that funding to end child marriage accounts for only a tiny fraction of Official Development Assistance (ODA), while local frontline organisations working directly with girls and communities receive only a sliver of available budgets.  


Between 2015 and 2023, just 0.025 per cent of all ODA globally was directed to projects whose primary objective was to end child marriage. A further 0.081 per cent went to broader projects in which addressing child marriage was one of several objectives, rather than the primary purpose, and it was not possible to determine how much of this secondary funding was specifically spent on child marriage interventions. 


Investment to end child marriage peaked in 2019. Since then, it has fallen every year, dropping from US$76 million to US$51 million by 2023, and this deterioration accelerated with

2025’s historic decline in global aid

. With several major donors scaling back investment in gender equality, ODA faces mounting pressure.


Over the next five years, more than 70 million girls worldwide are expected to be at risk of child marriage. Yet current levels of international funding dedicated to ending this form of violence against children amount to less than US$1 per girl at risk each year globally. At a time when conflict, climate change, anti-rights movements and shrinking civic space are all exacerbating the dangers girls face, declining investment threatens to further undermine child protection in Africa.


Ending child marriage is also an economic imperative:

girls who marry later stay in school longer, earn more, and raise healthier families

, with gains that impact entire communities. 


Legal loopholes and poor enforcement of laws leave girls vulnerable to child marriage 


Passing laws is only the first step. Governments must back them with dedicated funding, strengthening relevant institutions and duty bearers, for effective enforcement, oversight, and clear accountability. A dedicated budget line is not a bureaucratic technicality; it is the difference between turning legal promises and human rights obligations and commitments to end child marriage on paper into meaningful real-world protection for girls.


Most African Union Member States have ratified the

African Charter on the Rights and Welfare of the Child

, which requires countries to prohibit child marriage. The Charter has established a strong regional legal framework and contributed to many countries enacting laws to prevent child marriage. What is now needed is a concerted effort to improve implementation of existing laws and remove remaining gaps in legal protections. 


According to the African Union’s 2026 report,

Ending Child Marriage in Africa

, 18 countries in Africa have a minimum marriage age of 18 or above, with no exceptions. The continent’s remaining 37 countries do not meet this standard. Some set a minimum age below 18 for one or both sexes, while others have raised the age of marriage to 18 but permit exemptions, such as allowing judicial, parental or other legal authorisation for a child to marry.


The African Committee of Experts on the Rights and Welfare of the Child (ACERWC), in its 2026

Thematic Report on Harmful Practices Affecting Children in Africa

, stated that despite decades of advocacy and progress in strengthening legal frameworks, child marriage …

author: The Canadian Press
title: Supreme Court of Canada to hear appeal of First Nation’s Nootka Island claim
content:
The Supreme Court of Canada will hear a case about a First Nation’s claim to title over a swath of Nootka Island.


The Nuchatlaht First Nation brought a claim for Aboriginal title to about 200 square kilometres of the island, which lies off the west coast of Vancouver Island.


The trial judge found the Nuchatlaht had established title over only portions of the claimed area.


The First Nation challenged the decision in the British Columbia Court of Appeal.


In April, the Court of Appeal found the trial judge used an “arbitrary boundary” to determine title.


A three-judge panel of the Appeal Court said the Nuchatlaht identified territory it exclusively occupied and used for hunting, fishing and gathering activities, and presented other evidence that established its “strong presence on or over the land claimed.”


The post

Supreme Court of Canada to hear appeal of First Nation’s Nootka Island claim

 appeared first on

APTN News

author: Christopher Cartwright
title: As Resistance to Flock Cameras Grows, Another Surveillance Network Is Spreading
content:
Fusus software is being used in at least 324 US communities, with nearly 624,000 cameras connected to a Fusus network.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

More than 28,000 cameras in Atlanta are integrated into a “real-time crime center,” allowing police live access to many of their video streams. In Hawthorne, California, the city surveillance network includes more than 3,700 cameras. And in Seat Pleasant, Maryland — a town of 4,500 — police have access to one integrated camera for every three residents.

These communities are among hundreds in the U.S. that have adopted Fusus, a surveillance platform that allows police to watch live camera networks in their jurisdictions. While local resistance to Flock Safety automated license plate readers has swept the nation — including vandalism of cameras, cities canceling contracts, and a recent national week of action organized by the group DeFlock — the Fusus software has continued to spread.

Owned by Axon, the company behind Tasers and body-worn cameras, Fusus enables police to link security cameras, automated license plate readers, doorbell cameras, police dash cameras, drones, and body-worn cameras to a central hub that can use AI, according to the company’s website. The software’s distinction is its ability to integrate privately owned cameras from individuals, organizations, and businesses, whose participation the company encourages through its voluntary Community Connect program.

A Prism analysis of public information obtained from Axon’s website and the Fusus application programming interfaces (APIs) shows that the software is being used in at least 324 U.S. communities, with nearly 624,000 cameras connected to a Fusus network. These range from rural areas — such as Plaquemines Parish in Louisiana and Artesia, New Mexico — to major cities, including Dallas, Seattle, Miami, and New York City.

Privacy advocates and community organizers say this integrated system rapidly expands the reach of police power. Ed Vogel, a co-founder of Southerners Against Surveillance Systems and Infrastructure, argued that the Fusus business model inherently encourages additional surveillance.

“Anyone who is concerned about Flock safety and license plate readers should be equally concerned with Axon and Fusus,” he said. “Fusus is a tool that invites the police to build out a surveillance apparatus in order to optimize the technology. Because it’s a software that integrates a variety of surveillance tools into it, in order to make the most of it, the police want to and will try to acquire more technology so that they can integrate more tools.”

Data obtained from the APIs include the number of registered, integrated, owned, shared, and subscribed cameras. Registered cameras are those submitted to a police-maintained database. This doesn’t give law enforcement live access to each camera feed, but allows them to create a network map for future investigations. Integrated cameras are those that give police live access, and Axon’s Fusus manual says police can share these video streams with other law enforcement agencies.

Axon did not respond to multiple requests for comment or clarification on the definitions of owned, shared, and subscribed cameras. On its website’s FAQ page, the company says Fusus “promotes ethical policing by improving the accuracy of suspect identification, helping reduce reliance on potentially biased eyewitness accounts.”

In May 2023, the Electronic Frontier Foundation reported that nearly 150 jurisdictions used Fusus. That number has more than doubled since, according to Prism’s analysis of Fusus API data.

Georgia leads the nation in integrated cameras, with more than 275,000. An Axon-run website urging people to register and integrate cameras into the Atlanta police system, called Connect Atlanta, shows that the city has 29,855 integrated cameras, the most of any Fusus network, as of Oct. 15. Sandy Springs, Georgia, has the second-most at 16,415.

The Illinois State Police, the only state agency publicly reporting that it uses Fusus, has integrated more than 4,100 cameras. Three public universities — the University of Illinois, the University of Missouri and the University of Arizona — also use the technology.

author: Sav Jonsa
title: Seeking Justice: Indigenous people in Manitoba most likely to die in police-involved incidents
content:
Jeremy Ettawakapow remembers celebrating with his dad John when the Winnipeg Blue Bombers won the Grey Cup championship in 2019.


But it wasn’t the joyous event one might expect. Instead of cheers and fireworks for his favourite team, Jeremy visited a cemetery to give a gift to his father, who died only a month earlier in an RCMP holding cell.


“I got that championship winning hat, I wrote a little note in there and I left it at his grave site,” Jeremy recalled in a recent interview with the IJF.


“Even though it’s so many years later … It hits me and I still miss him.”


John Ettawakapow is one of about 100 people in Manitoba whose police-involved deaths

did not result in charges

 against officers following investigations by the

Independent Investigation Unit

 of Manitoba (IIU), the police watchdog responsible for probing all serious incidents involving police since 2015.


Of the 59 people whose identities have been made public, an IJF analysis confirms at least 63 per cent were Indigenous. Indigenous people make up about 18 per cent of Manitoba’s population, according to Statistics Canada’s 2021 census.


The IJF’s ongoing investigation into the IIU’s handling of police-involved death investigations found Manitoba police have been charged in the deaths of only two people in the last eleven years, one of whom was a

First Nations person

. The IIU investigations for both concluded in 2017 and the charges eventually led to convictions.


The IJF spoke with people connected to three police-involved deaths of Indigenous people in Manitoba to learn about the IIU investigation process and how they were impacted by the IIU’s decision not to charge officers in these specific cases.


They shared concerns including the IIU allegedly withholding use of force details involving a weapon in one investigation, that immediate family members have to wait years just to learn how their loved ones died, and that mental health supports are not provided to those intimately affected by police-involved deaths throughout the investigation process.


The IJF requested an interview with the IIU but it was declined.


Bronwyn Dobchuk-Land, an associate professor of criminal justice at the University of Winnipeg, said it can leave a lasting impact on surviving family members when officers are absolved of any wrongdoing in the deaths of their loved ones — which has been the case in 98 per cent of police-involved deaths in Manitoba in the last decade-plus.


“So then where are the families left? They are essentially told the death at the hands of the state of your loved ones was acceptable. And that’s devastating,” says Dobchuk-Land.


She said it might be beneficial for families to “stop expecting a sense of resolution from the IIU. Because even when those [investigations finish], they often produce the very opposite of a sense of justice. They produce the sense of like there’s still unanswered questions.”


John Ettawakapow, 54, Moose Lake


John Ettawakapow

 was arrested for public intoxication and lodged in an RCMP detachment in The Pas, a town in northern Manitoba, on the evening of Oct. 5, 2019.


Only an hour later, the 54-year-old man “stopped moving forever” after a sleeping inmate’s leg accidentally rolled on top of his neck and face. However, guards didn’t find him dead until five hours later.


The IIU concluded no charges would be authorized against police personnel or guards after consultation with the Manitoba Prosecution Service, who stated there was “no basis” for criminal charges, according to the IIU’s final report.


The IIU created a

brief timeline

 of events using video surveillance from the cell including when John was placed inside and when he was found dead by a guard. The timeline detailed the leg was on top of John’s neck for approximately 40 minutes before the inmate moved it in his sleep and that John appeared not to move again afterwards.


“That was a very difficult time when I actually got to look at that report,” Jeremy said. “The images I was grasping in my head were hurtful because it did show he did have signs of life there and then it just stopped.”


The majority of information is withheld from the public during an IIU investigation until the final report is released, which took more than two years in John’s case.


But Jeremy wouldn’t learn the specific details of his dad’s death until the 2024 inquest, which examines a fatality’s circumstances to find ways of preventing it from happening in …

author: Dyepeson Martins
title: Chefe da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro esteve no Senado mas não votou na 6×1
content:
Enquanto governistas discursavam a favor do projeto que estabelecia o fim da escala de trabalho 6×1, parlamentares da oposição se reuniam para debater estratégias e discursos da campanha do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) à Presidência da República. A reunião durou mais de três horas e aconteceu no gabinete do líder do PL no Senado Federal e chefe da campanha de Flávio, Rogério Marinho (RN), que não compareceu ao plenário nem participou da votação da proposta —

aprovada na noite de quarta-feira (14), como mostrou a

Agência Pública

.

 Procurado pela reportagem, Marinho não retornou até a publicação. 


Discussão e votação, em primeiro turno, da proposta de emenda à Constituição que acaba com a escala 6×1


Outros dois aliados de Flávio também não votaram: os senadores Sérgio Moro (PL-PR) e Marcio Bittar (PL-AC). O presidente do Congresso Nacional, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), que presidiu a sessão, não votou. Pelas regras do regimento interno do Senado, o presidente não vota. Entretanto, a norma permite que o parlamentar entregue o comando da Casa a outro senador para que este participe da votação. O texto foi aprovado em dois turnos por 75 votos a favor e um voto contrário: o do ex-vice-presidente da República, Hamilton Mourão (Republicanos-RS). 


O senador Hamilton Mourão (Republicanos-RS) foi o único parlamentar a votar contra a PEC que acaba com a escala de trabalho 6×1 no Senado


Rogério Marinho é autor da Proposta de Emenda à Constituição (PEC), apresentada em maio deste ano, que prevê uma jornada por regime de horas trabalhadas — alternativa da oposição à PEC que estabeleceu o fim da escala 6×1. Flávio Bolsonaro e seus aliados sempre se posicionaram contra a redução da jornada de trabalho sem impacto nos salários, por considerarem que isso representaria prejuízos econômicos à indústria. No entanto, diante da campanha governista e da mobilização popular em favor da proposta, Flávio recuou e afirmou que votaria a favor da aprovação do texto. A mudança foi anunciada na terça-feira (13), após ele visitar o pai, o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, que cumpre prisão domiciliar por tentativa de golpe de Estado. 


Flávio Bolsonaro trocou a votação sobre o fim da escala 6×1 no Senado por um ato de campanha em Porto Alegre


O novo discurso foi reforçado durante a reunião no gabinete de Rogério Marinho. Além dele, três correligionários do PL estavam no encontro: os senadores Magno Malta (ES), Carlos Portinho (RJ) e o eleito José Medeiros (MT). Também estavam presentes três congressistas do PP: a senadora e ex-ministra da Agricultura de Jair Bolsonaro, Tereza Cristina (MS); o senador eleito e ex-presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Arthur Lira (AL); e o deputado federal Ricardo Barros (PR), ministro da Saúde na gestão de Michel Temer. 


“A gente não pode deixar a narrativa nas mãos do adversário”, declarou à

Pública

, sob reserva, um dos membros da reunião a respeito da mudança no discurso da campanha a menos de duas semanas para o segundo turno das eleições. “Foi uma decisão do presidente [Flávio] e o Lira também concordou”, completou o parlamentar. 


Questionado pela

Pública

 após sair da reunião, Lira afirmou que não foi ao gabinete para tratar da PEC em votação.


Flávio Bolsonaro votou à distância enquanto participava de um ato político em Porto Alegre, no Rio Grande do Sul. Ele subiu ao palanque ao lado dos governadores eleitos Luciano Zucco (PL-RS) e Sérgio Moro (PL-PR); e dos governadores reeleitos Jorginho Mello (PL-SC) e Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos-SP). Na ocasião, afirmou aos apoiadores que o governo terá que “pagar a conta” do novo modelo de trabalho para compensar empresários que, segundo ele, estariam “quebrados”.


Senado conservador: “não teremos medo de realizar todas as mudanças necessárias”


Aliados de Flávio confirmaram à

Pública

 que a campanha se reuniu, ao longo do último mês, com empresários para discutir as possíveis consequências da implantação da nova jornada de trabalho. A transição de 44 para 40 horas semanais será gradual e começará a valer dois meses após a promulgação da PEC —  função do presidente do Congresso. Durante o primeiro ano da nova regra, a jornada terá um limite de 42 horas. Após esse período, o limite passará a ser oficialmente de 40 horas. 


Diante disso, Flávio sinalizou ao setor empresarial que, caso eleito, pretende aplicar medidas “compensatórias”; entre elas, propostas legislativas que revertam os efeitos do fim da escala 6×1. As ações seriam possíveis …

title: Kurdish Conference: Conditions for Abdullah Öcalan to work freely must be established
content:
The final session was held under the title “Turkey Between the Peace Process and the Crisis of Democratization: Dialogue, the Rule of Law, and the Future of Political Participation.” Dilek Odabaşı moderated the session.


Speakers included DEM Party MP and Imrali Delegation member Pervin Buldan, DEVA Party MP Mehmet Emin Ekmen, Yeni Party MP Okan Konuralp, and Republican People's Party (CHP) MP Oğuz Kaan Salıcı.


The full conference can be watched here


https://left.eu/events/20th-international-conference-the-european-union-turkey-the-middle-east-and-the-kurds/

left.eu


Pervin Buldan: The EU must play its part


Opening the session, Pervin Buldan assessed the current stage of the peace process. “Achieving lasting peace in Turkey would have a positive impact not only on the Middle East but also on Europe,” she said.


Buldan added: “As a result of the human rights violations, torture, and policies of repression that Kurds have endured for half a century, European countries have become closely acquainted with the Kurdish issue and the Kurdish people. Over the years, the Kurdish issue has become a regional and even global concern, closely connected with Europe as well.”


Noting that Kurds make up a significant portion of the diaspora in Europe today, Buldan said: “For this reason, our fundamental expectation is that the European Union, which once actively defended democratic values, should make a positive contribution to the peace process underway in Turkey, support it, and assume the role expected of it.”


“The project of the century”


Buldan said the peace process had reached a historic turning point and emphasized that it was a “project of the century.”


She said: “Particularly in the face of the enormous risks and threats created by the crises and conflicts in the Middle East, the peace process initiated by Mr. Öcalan's February 27 Call for Peace and a Democratic Society, and opened up through the political will demonstrated by Mr. Devlet Bahçeli and Mr. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, has reached a historic turning point. This process has opened the door to a new era for peoples, democracy, universal law, and democratic politics. It would therefore not be wrong to describe the Peace and Democratic Society Process as the project of the century.”


Buldan continued: “A democratic solution to the Kurdish issue is the strongest guarantee of an environment in which everyone can live in peace and security, on the basis of mutual solidarity and fraternity, both in Turkey and throughout the Middle East. Everyone needs to understand this opportunity correctly. When historic opportunities are used wisely, countries can emerge from crises and move toward democracy.”


She added: “Rallying around the Peace and Democratic Society Process, moving forward together, and building peace and democracy through collective effort will be a step that shapes the course of the coming century. This process is not limited to the democratic rights of the Kurdish people. The Kurdish issue concerns the shared future of both Turkey and the Middle East.


It is a process of building a shared democracy, establishing a legal order that prioritizes the rights of all peoples, guaranteeing freedoms through law, strengthening local democracy, and fully opening the channels of democratic political participation in the most inclusive way possible. The peace process is a shared guarantee for Kurds, Turks, Alevis, and all segments of society with different identities and beliefs.”


“Conditions for Öcalan to work freely must be established immediately”


Buldan continued: “First, we expect the National Security Council to adopt a decision urgently so that the framework law can enter into force, the relevant bodies can begin operating, and the process can move forward. We also emphasize that a monitoring committee must be established in Parliament as soon as possible and begin its work. At the same time, I would like to state that we expect Mr. Öcalan to assume the role of coordinator within the Peace and Politicization Council, which is to be established under his leadership.


This process must advance through reciprocal steps. Just as Mr. Öcalan has played a role in the disarmament phase, his serving as coordinator during the political and democratic reconstruction phase would help the council achieve its objectives. In this context, I would also like to emphasize that the conditions necessary for Mr. Öcalan to work freely must be established as soon as …

author: Unknown
title: Compulsory expropriation approved for oil extraction in Amed
content:
Two plots of land in the Kocaköy district of Amed (Diyarbakır) are to be expropriated for oil extraction. The land will be used by the state-owned Turkish Petroleum Corporation (TPAO) for the Çobantepe-5 drilling site and its associated infrastructure. The decision by the General Directorate of Mining and Petroleum Affairs (MAPEG) under Turkey’s Ministry of Energy was published in the Official Gazette.


The expropriation affects two plots of land covering a total area of 23,333.56 square meters. The plot designated as parcel 143/1 covers 12,926.76 square meters, while the second, designated as parcel 152/2, covers another 10,406.80 square meters.


Previous attempts to acquire the land through mutual agreement had failed because, according to the authorities, the landowners had demanded compensation exceeding market value. Court orders authorizing early possession of both plots had already been issued by the Diyarbakır Court of First Instance.


MAPEG justified the expropriation on the grounds of public interest in oil extraction, citing Article 10, Paragraph 2 of Turkish Petroleum Law No. 6491.

author: Ed Wanderley
title: A linha direta de Vorcaro dentro do Grupo Globo: “Quer que peça pra corrigir?”
content:
Um ano antes de se tornar “radioativo”, na tarde de uma quarta-feira de abril de 2024, Daniel Vorcaro recebeu uma oferta de Frederic Kachar, até então CEO da Editora Globo e do Sistema Globo de Rádio: “Quer que a gente o entreviste no Valor?”. A mensagem se referia a Alexandre Afrange, CEO da Veste – antiga Restoque, que detém marcas como Dudalina, John John e Le Lis Blanc –, empresa da qual o banqueiro do Master tinha controle acionário desde 2022. “Não sabia que a Veste tinha esse ceo”, escreveu Kachar, para então oferecer espaço editorial a Vorcaro no jornal de economia do grupo. 


O diálogo faz parte das mensagens interceptadas pela Polícia Federal (PF) a partir do celular de Daniel Vorcaro e apontam que a relação dos dois, nas palavras do próprio banqueiro, em julho do mesmo ano, seria uma “amizade que supera negócios”.

 Os diálogos mostram que o ex-controlador do Banco Master, preso desde março deste ano como principal investigado pela Operação Compliance Zero, tinha acesso direto ao executivo, onde fazia solicitações diretas e reclamava sobre a linha editorial dos jornais do grupo Globo.


O vazamento das mensagens ganhou força nesta quarta-feira (14), momento delicado para a própria Globo. Isso porque no Auditório Ibirapuera, em São Paulo, a Rede Globo promovia um de seus eventos publicitários mais importantes do ano, o Upfront Globo. Na ocasião, os executivos mais influentes do Grupo Globo, a exemplo de Fred Kachar, como é conhecido, se reúnem com vários dos artistas mais famosos do conglomerado junto a representantes do mercado publicitário para detalhar os planos das empresas Globo para o ano seguinte. Talvez por isso, a reação ao vazamento, já conhecido nos bastidores da empresa, não tenha sido mais imediato. Nesta quinta (15), Kachar foi desligado, segundo nota oficial do Grupo.


Nota Grupo Globo


Grupo Globo comunica desligamento de Frederic Kachar e reforça independência editorial de seus veículos

O Grupo Globo comunicou hoje o desligamento do diretor-geral de Mídia Impressa e Rádio, Frederic Kachar. O conteúdo das conversas privadas mantidas com Daniel Vorcaro entre outubro de 2023 e julho de 2025, às quais a empresa teve acesso ontem, revela uma relação inadequada do executivo com um anunciante.


A Editora Globo reforça seu compromisso com a ética e a transparência e reafirma a absoluta independência editorial do jornalismo de seus veículos, premissa essencial de sua atuação. O protagonismo da cobertura crítica, isenta e independente que tem feito do caso Master é a demonstração concreta do compromisso inegociável de seus veículos com os Princípios Editoriais do Grupo Globo.


A empresa reconhece os 29 anos de dedicação de Kachar ao desenvolvimento de seus negócios de mídia e informa que o nome de seu substituto à frente da Editora Globo e do Sistema Globo de Rádio será divulgado em breve.


Comunicação Globo

Rio de Janeiro, 15 de outubro de 2026

Mais informações

https://imprensa.globo.com/


Relação delicada


Vorcaro chegou a solicitar, no dia 12 de outubro de 2024, a capa da revista Vogue Brasil para a então namorada, Martha Graeff, que acabara de lançar a Happy Aging, empresa de suplementos voltada à longevidade feminina, lançada nos Estados Unidos à época. “De presente pra ela”, justificou. 


O pedido não foi plenamente atendido por Kachar, que alegou inviabilidade da agenda de produção da revista. Cinco dias depois, no entanto, as versões online de

Vogue Brasil

,

Marie Claire

 e

Ela

 destacavam Graeff, cujos links foram enviados pelo ex-diretor-geral a Vorcaro: “Depois me diz se faltou algo”. O banqueiro agradeceu: “ficaram ótimas”, disse, antes de fazer a ressalva: “só a Marie Claire deu uma batidinha no final rsrs esses repórteres são uma bênção”, concluiu o banqueiro. Kachar apenas assentiu: “o próximo passo é capa na Ela ou Marie Claire, só precisamos de um fato novo”.

The Trump administration is working to build a case against Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minnesota) with the hopes of ultimately denaturalizing and deporting the progressive Somali American lawmaker, The Wall Street Journal reports.

The alarming, unprecedented effort — denounced as outright fascism by critics — is wide-ranging, encompassing several federal agencies. U.S. officials and other sources familiar with the investigation told the Journal that the effort is focused, in part, on unearthing information about her deceased father, the circumstances surrounding her arrival in the U.S. when she was a child, and her citizenship.

The Justice Department has issued over a dozen subpoenas in relation to the investigation to Omar’s family, including to her sister and other relatives. The New York Times reported this week that federal officials are attempting to establish a case that Omar’s father lied or omitted information on his immigration forms when he came to the U.S. with Omar in 1995.

Other reports also say that the Trump administration is also looking into whether she lied on papers to obtain legal status and citizenship, and specifically on whether she or her father intentionally misstated her birthdate to obtain citizenship as a minor alongside her father when she was naturalized. The Department of Homeland Security looked into similar allegations of immigration fraud under the Biden administration, but did not move forward because of a lack of evidence, the Times reported.

In a drastic escalation on Monday, agents from Homeland Security Investigations conducted a predawn raid on Omar’s house in Washington, D.C. Officers seized her phone, notebooks, personal computers, and passport.

“President Trump would love to eliminate one of the most effective progressive voices in Congress. There is no basis for this,” Omar told the Journal.

Omar was 12 years old when she arrived as a refugee in the U.S. Her family had fled a bloody civil war and a “human rights disaster,” as dubbed by Amnesty International, in Somalia. She became a U.S. citizen at the age of 17, in the year 2000.

Omar has weathered racist and bigoted personal attacks against her by President Donald Trump and other political figures for years. The Trump administration’s latest attacks on the Minnesota representative have been widely condemned by Democrats as a naked attempt to go after a political opponent just weeks before the midterm elections, in which Omar is up for reelection; as well as a tyrannical, fascist act by the increasingly bold and out-of-control Trump administration.

The allegation that Omar was actually 18 when she was naturalized originally gained traction on conservative social media through a viral video posted in 2019. Her congressional office had her birth year changed on official paperwork from 1981 to 1982, which conservative conspiracy theorists framed as suspicious.

However, her office said it was already in the process of getting her biographical information changed through official channels. Further, it is common for people from war-torn and underresourced countries to put an approximate date on immigration paperwork because they have no official record of their births; a 2020 report found only 6 percent of births are registered with the government in Somalia.

After the raid on Monday, Trump once again spewed racist rhetoric against Omar and Somalis.

“She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, where all they do is shoot each other, and she comes into our country and she says, ‘I have a constitutional right,’” Trump said at a rally in Ohio. “She’s telling us about the Constitution, and she comes from one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.”

The crowd chanted “deport” as he incited violence against Somalis. Just last Friday, Trump openly encouraged a race war against Somalis in Minnesota in a post on Truth Social, telling followers to “fight back.”

Omar has stood up against Trump’s attacks. “Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” said Omar on Monday following the raid. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest …

author: Nehaa Bimal
title: Proposed federal lands act amendment could complicate devolution: premier
content:
Ottawa’s tinkering with its Territorial Lands Act could throw a wrench in Nunavut’s devolution work, says Premier John Main.


He was speaking to a

Senate Standing Committee on Indigenous Peoples Oct. 6 during a hearing about mineral rights in the territory.


Nunavut is preparing the legislative framework that will allow the territorial government to take control of a vast majority of its Crown land. To do so, it’s mirroring several federal acts, including the Territorial Lands Act, to finalize devolution, which is set to happen April 1, 2027.


The act governs use of Crown land in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut, including its sale or lease,

 

mining rights and environmental regulations.


But the Territorial Lands Act could change as its being mirrored.


Working its way through Senate hearings is Bill C-31, which proposes amendments the act that would

allow Canada’s federal cabinet, on the recommendation of the northern affairs minister, to cancel or restrict mineral rights on Crown land in Nunavut if it determines doing so is in the national interest.


“The timing of Bill C-31 creates a particular challenge,” said Main in his opening remarks to the committee.


“The Government of  Nunavut cannot mirror federal provisions that have not yet been enacted.”


If Nunavut were to delay its work until the passage of Bill C-31, it would create a “significant risk” to the territory’s ability to ready itself for the April 1 devolution deadline, Main said.


The mirrored legislation in Nunavut, called the Public Lands Act, was tabled in draft form during the spring sitting of Nunavut legislature and is scheduled for formal introduction during the fall sitting, which is scheduled to start on Oct. 22.


Also discussed during the hearing was implications of foreign investment in Nunavut, including the potential sale of the Mary River iron mine on north Baffin Island.


Baffinland Iron Mines Corp.

sought creditor protection

 in May. In June, a

judge approved

 a $660-million loan from Export Development Canada so the Mary River Mine could remain operational through this year’s shipping season.


Nunavut Senator Nancy Karetak-Lindell raised concerns about potential foreign ownership of mining projects and infrastructure, including the Mary River mine, should it be put up for sale as part of the creditor protection process.


“It’s important for us to be open to investment from foreign interest,” Main said in response.


“If we restricted access in terms of mining or industrial development in Nunavut to only to Canadian companies, we would be seen as not a very attractive jurisdiction to invest in.”


That said, Main acknowledged the territory’s lack of infrastructure could leave

 the territory vulnerable to foreign interests.


“If there’s a vacuum there in terms of investment, it could look like an opportunity for foreign actors,”

 Main said.


While the court has approved a sale and investment solicitation process, no buyer has been selected and no sale approved, said Baffinland spokesperson Peter Akman in an email to Nunatsiaq News.


“It would be premature to speculate about potential bidders or transaction terms,” said.


At a Sept. 29 committee meeting on the same topic, Karetak-Lindell questioned the lack of a definition for “national interest” in the proposed changes to the lands act, and the potential for uncertainty this could cause as Nunavut prepares for devolution.


But the amendment won’t affect decision making over the land being transferred to Nunavut under devolution, said 

Georgina Lloyd, assistant deputy minister of northern affairs.


After devolution, the Territorial Lands Act will remain in place for the “small amount of Crown land that will still be under Canada’s jurisdiction,” she said.


Bill C-31 remains under consideration by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance.

author: Mohanad El-Hemrawi
title: Gaza Child Amputees Are Outgrowing Their Prosthetics Amid Israel’s Restrictions
content:
WHO estimates that over 5,000 people in Gaza have lost limbs since October 2023, and one in five of them is a child.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Abdul-Rahman al-Nashash, 11, holds onto the edge of a chair and pushes his left leg into a plastic prosthetic that doesn’t fit him anymore. The bone that was cut two years ago has kept growing inside, and it presses painfully against his skin.

His doctors told him to stop wearing it. He wears it anyway, every morning, pulling the straps tight and rolling his pants down so no one sees the plastic before he takes his first step. He bites his lip when it hurts and holds his shoulders straight so no one can tell he is limping.

“He forces himself to wear it,” his mother said, “just so no one knows he has a disability.”

Before the genocide, al-Nashash played for a local soccer club, and he would chase the ball across a dirt field until the sun went down. He is the eldest son in his family, and he was the one his mother leaned on at home. When she needed water, he was the one who ran to carry the heavy gallon of water, and he never got tired. Now, he is not able.

When he finally takes the prosthetic off, he sits curled up. He is waiting for his third surgery, and his mother said he will need one every year.

As a child grows, the bone in the amputated leg grows too, but the prosthetic doesn’t. At some point it stops fitting, and sometimes the child needs another operation before he can get a new one. In Gaza, that often means starting over with surgery, then rehabilitation, then a new limb if one can be made at all, because Israel restricts the parts and materials needed to make and repair them. Some children in Gaza have outgrown their limbs and are waiting for new ones. Others never received one, because there are none in Gaza that fit them.

Al-Nashash’s family was forced to evacuate from al-Bureij refugee camp in Central Gaza in 2023 and took shelter in UNRWA schools. His father stayed behind. Two days after they left, on October 20, the house was struck, and his father was killed along with several relatives. The three-wheeled motorcycle that had been the family’s only source of income was parked in the storeroom and was destroyed in the same strike.

From there, the family moved from school to school and tent to tent. They spent about three months in Rafah, then moved to schools in Nuseirat. With no money coming in, his mother opened a small stall with her brother-in-law, selling a variety of canned beans.

Around noon on July 16, 2024, her sister asked her to come light a fire and cook, so she left her son to mind the stall in her place. An Israeli airstrike hit the tents in the middle of al-Razi school, a UNRWA shelter in Nuseirat camp, killing 23 people, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. A piece of shrapnel struck his leg directly. His mother said his injured left foot was split in two, the bones of his toes exposed, and she kept screaming that her son had been killed.

At first, she said, she was told doctors hoped to fix the leg with metal plates rather than amputate. At Al-Aqsa Hospital, one doctor told her the leg would have to be amputated, and she asked them to cut off her own leg and give it to him, because he was the one who took care of her. He was then taken by an ambulance to a hospital by the sea in Deir al-Balah where a foreign medical team was working. There they told her nothing more could be done. The amputation needed her consent. She signed, because there was no other choice.

When al-Nashash woke from the anesthesia, he kept staring at himself as if he were losing his mind. It was only after counselors came and he began to see other children like him that he slowly started to adjust.

After the amputation, therapists from local rehabilitation programs came to work with him regularly. But his natural childhood growth worked against his recovery. “My son grows fast,” his mother said. By March 2025, just eight months after he lost his leg, the bone had already grown too long.

They traveled to Jordan, where surgeons cut the bone back and fitted him with his first prosthetic, the one he still wears today. The trip lasted five months. When al-Nashash returned to Gaza, the boy who used to sprint on the soccer field had to start physical therapy from scratch, learning how to balance and walk all over again.

author: Emma Honeybun
title: Public should be asking questions of candidates who are residential school denialists, says MMF vice president
content:
A vice-president at the Manitoba Métis Federation (MMF) says that if any candidates in the upcoming municipal elections in the province are spreading disinformation about residential schools, the public should be asking about it.


“When there’s trauma, people are afraid to stand up and talk about these things,” said Will Goodon, the minister of housing and property with the MMF. “And now, to have deniers basically say that, you’re just in it to get something, is horrible.”


This comes as a response to a forum which took place in Brandon on Oct. 6, when a candidate running for school trustee was the subject of debate for questionable denialist comments which date back years.


Many in the community have close ties to the Brandon Indian Residential School, closed in 1972 and demolished in 2000, including Goodon himself.


He said that what are masked as “concerns” are built on a “foundation of hate and racism,” and having it appear in political debate is harmful.


“That’s one of the most horrible things. You’re re-traumatizing these survivors over and over and over again, every time they see something like this come up,” he said.


Goodon said that his grandfather was taken and held at the school, but escaped alongside his great aunt.


Although Goodon’s grandfather died before he was born, he still felt the effects of what happened. He said this rings true for many families in the area.


“As far as Brandon is concerned, there is that legacy, that history,” he said. “The school was just up on the hill there. And people just didn’t talk much about it … And [now] there’s monuments there, there’s symbolism there.”


He said that while he has experienced racism throughout his own life, he believes the city, located west of Winnipeg, “has done a lot of healing,” which he attributes to education.


“Education on truth and reconciliation, which I have to say, that the city and a lot of the social agencies, they do an incredible job … And I feel there’s still a lot of verbal things, but Brandon is getting better all the time.”


And while denialism is a topic in the election, the trustee in question is still receiving what the school board’s chair told APTN News is “a lot of flak.”


An inconsistent background


Jim McCrae joined the list of 10 candidates running for Brandon School Division — Ward 1 in July 2026.


The retiree is a former Manitoba MLA who held his seat from 1988 to 1999. Prior to that, he was a Brandon city councillor from 1983 to 1986. He was re-elected to council in 2006, and officially resigned in 2013.


His next appearance in city hall wasn’t until 2023, when he registered in opposition to a motion that acknowledged “residential schools as genocide, as well as a review of how the City of Brandon has been acting on the Truth and Reconciliation calls to action.”


According to the minutes from that meeting, McRae “questioned the prevailing discourse around Residential Schools and whether the conditions could be described as genocide. He concluded by requesting that Council consider their decision on the proposed motion and all implications of the matter carefully.”


McCrae has written several guest columns for the

Dorchester Review

 and the

Western Standard

 on that line of question.


In 2022, in a column called

Speaking the Truth About Residential Schools

, he asserted that he is not a denialist, but rather a “truth seeker.


“Truth seekers ask questions about Indian Residential Schools so as to better understand Indigenous history so all Canadians can participate in the healing that is required before we can move forward together,” he explained. “But those who have questioned any part of the official narrative established by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission [TRC], the federal government, and legacy media have been met with either silence or the outrageous accusation that they are engaging in denialism.”


In 2024, in a column published in the

Western Standard

, McCrae condemned the “Aboriginal Industry”, a term coined in 2008 by former University of Lethbridge professor Frances Widdowson’s book,

Disrobing the Aboriginal Industry

, which claims Indigenous self-governance is a method to pay out leadership “while entrenching the misery of most aboriginal people.”


He writes that the “industry lives on the avails of peddling the narrative of murdered Indigenous children,” and is “fundamentally dishonest at root.”

author: Jesse Staniforth
title: Décision de la Cour suprême : équilibre entre les facteurs Gladue et les préoccupations relatives aux femmes autochtones
content:
La Cour suprême du Canada a maintenu une peine réduite imposée à un homme mi’kmaq condamné pour avoir brutalement agressé sa conjointe mi’kmaq en 2021. Cette décision devrait influencer de façon importante l’approche des tribunaux à l’égard des hommes autochtones reconnus coupables de crimes violents contre des femmes autochtones.


Dans

une décision rendue à cinq voix contre quatre

, la Cour a estimé que la peine initiale de cinq ans n’avait pas suffisamment tenu compte, d’une part, des problèmes de santé mentale de l’accusé et, d’autre part, des considérations autochtones; elle a donc confirmé le jugement de la cour d’appel qui avait réduit la peine à trois ans, assortis de deux ans de sursis après la libération, déduction faite de la période déjà purgée en détention provisoire.


L’affaire portait sur deux considérations importantes pour les peuples autochtones dans le système juridique.


L’une d’elles était l’inclusion de lignes directrices dans le Code criminel à la suite de la décision rendue en 1999 dans l’affaire

R. c. Gladue

, qui ordonne aux tribunaux de tenir compte des facteurs systémiques et historiques qui influent sur la « culpabilité morale » d’un délinquant autochtone, et de tenir compte de la détermination de la peine et des sanctions appropriées à la situation particulière d’un délinquant autochtone.


La deuxième considération était l’orientation du Code criminel découlant de l’Enquête nationale sur les femmes et les filles autochtones disparues et assassinées (FFADA), dans le cadre de laquelle un juge doit accorder la priorité aux objectifs de « dénonciation et de dissuasion » dans la détermination de la peine d’une personne ayant commis des abus à l’encontre d’« une personne vulnérable, notamment parce qu’il s’agit d’une femme ou d’une fille autochtone ».


« L’historique législatif de ces dispositions est clair : elles ont été présentées dans le but de lutter contre la violence faite aux femmes et aux filles autochtones et d’autres victimes vulnérables qui ont été négligées pendant trop longtemps », écrit la juge Michelle O’Bonsawin dans la décision majoritaire qui a été soutenue par les juges Andromache Karakatsanis, Sheilah Martin, Nicholas Kasirer et Mary Moreau.


Michelle O’Bonsawin, juge à la Cour suprême. Photo : Mark Blackburn/APTN.


Une opinion dissidente a été rédigée par les juges Malcolm Rowe et Mahmud Jamal, avec l’appui des juges Suzanne Côté et Richard Wagner. Les juges dissidents ont fait valoir que la peine initiale devrait être rétablie, parce que le juge qui détermine la peine a correctement soupesé tous les facteurs pertinents, tandis que la peine réduite de la Cour d’appel « ne reflétait pas la dénonciation, la dissuasion, la vulnérabilité de la victime ou la conclusion du juge de la peine selon laquelle le délinquant représente un danger continu pour la société. »


Pourtant, la décision de la juge O’Bonsawin souligne que les considérations relatives aux délinquants autochtones et aux femmes et filles autochtones victimes de violence ne doivent pas être perçues comme contradictoires.


« Considérer ces dispositions comme contradictoires déforme leurs objectifs », écrit-elle. « La tâche du juge qui détermine la peine est d’imposer une peine proportionnelle et personnalisée qui tient dûment compte des besoins des délinquants autochtones et des victimes autochtones. La réconciliation doit constituer un important principe directeur dans l’application conjointe de ces dispositions. »


Le crime et la condamnation


L’affaire porte sur Harry Arthur Cope, qui a plaidé coupable relativement à une agression commise en 2021 contre sa partenaire occasionnelle, une femme de la Première Nation de Sipekne’katik. Le jugement décrivait l’attaque comme étant « horrible » et « brutale », où « la tête de la victime a été frappée et écrasée contre le trottoir à maintes reprises, ce qui lui a causé des blessures importantes ».


Au moment de l’agression, M. Cope, que la décision décrit comme ayant de « graves problèmes de santé mentale », avait cessé de prendre ses médicaments depuis un peu plus d’un an et avait consommé des drogues illicites.


Le tribunal a ordonné un rapport sur les antécédents autochtones et un cercle de détermination de la peine a examiné l’affaire. Ce cercle a révélé que les membres de la communauté étaient d’avis qu’une nouvelle incarcération n’aiderait pas M. Cope, pour qui ils ont recommandé de recevoir des soins holistiques, y compris un traitement en …

author: David Venn
title: President, community director roles up for grabs in QIA election
content:
The Qikiqtani Inuit Association is looking for its next president.


It’s also looking for community directors in Iqaluit, Igloolik, Kimmirut, Sanirajak, Clyde River, Pond Inlet and Sanikiluaq, said a news release issued Thursday by Markoosie Qaunirq, spokesperson for QIA.


Each position carries a four-year term.


The nomination period for the election runs from Nov. 9 to 13.


Eligible voters must be Inuit, enrolled under the Nunavut Agreement; at least 16 years old; and have resided in the Qikiqtani Region for one year or more, according to the release.


The current QIA president Olayuk Akesuk

won

 the 2022 election over Paul Okalik, with 61.2 per cent of the vote. He had served in the role since the fall of 2021, when he took over from P.J. Akeeagok, who resigned to run for MLA.


Election day is set for Dec. 14.

author: Chris Walker
title: Americans’ Confidence in Food Safety Plummets Amid Summer of Recalls
content:
Experts have expressed deep concern over Trump administration cuts to federal food monitoring systems.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Americans’ confidence in the safety of the food supply has plummeted, as has their belief in federal food safety standards, according to a new poll from Gallup.

When asked about their confidence in the safety of food in grocery stores across the country, only 65 percent of respondents said they are either “very confident” or “somewhat confident.” While that figure represents a majority of respondents, it’s the lowest confidence rating that Gallup has recorded since it began asking the question in 2019, when 81 percent expressed confidence that the food they were buying was safe.

Additionally, the poll found that respondents are skeptical of how well the Trump administration is ensuring the safety of the food supply. According to the poll, only 47 percent of Americans have a “great deal” or “fair amount” of confidence that the federal government is making sure the food supply is safe, while 53 percent say their confidence levels reach the “not much” or “none” levels.

It’s the first time in the poll’s history that the confidence level in the federal government’s ability to keep food safe has dipped below 50 percent.

The lack of confidence in the government’s ability to monitor and keep food safe comes amid a spate of food warnings this past summer, including recalls of jalapeños, berries, beef, alfalfa sprouts, and more items. A record-breaking cyclosporiasis outbreak relating to lettuce sales sickened thousands with intense bouts of diarrhea, including at least two documented deaths.

One week in August this year saw recalls of 12 different food products. That number is four times higher than it was during a similar period last year, and six times higher than it was in 2024.

Some disease researchers have blamed the Trump White House for the increases in foodborne illness outbreaks and recalls, noting that cuts by the administration, stemming mainly from its so-called “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) initiative, have made monitoring difficult and response time slower.

Indeed, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) lost around one-fifth of its staff since President Donald Trump returned to office, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has lost around 25 percent, including most members of a food parasite-tracking team.

Microbiologist and founder of Food Safety Strategy Jennifer McEntire told Stateline earlier this year that there are “valid questions around the timing of the response” from the administration to the cyclosporiasis crisis, including “the time it took for agencies to recognize the outbreak and to start to investigate it.”

Susan Mayne, an adjunct professor at the Yale School of Public Health and former head of the FDA, has also questioned the Trump administration’s cuts to food safety standards.

“We had a national advisory committee, a committee that advised FDA and [the U.S. Department of Agriculture] on how to prevent microbial contamination in food,” Mayne said back in July. “That advisory committee was disbanded. We used to convene meetings with our Mexican counterparts on how we can work together to improve food safety. That entire team was let go.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Jake Johnson
title: “Because of the Price of Oil … We’re Making a Fortune,” Trump Says at Rally
content:
Trump, who has profited massively from his second term in the White House, is a major investor in oil and gas companies.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump attempted to spin high oil prices as a boon for the United States at a rally in Arizona on Wednesday, just hours after new federal data showed that inflation reached its highest level in months in September.

“Because of the price of oil, Texas and Oklahoma and North Dakota and all these places, we’re making a fortune,” Trump declared, referring to states that produce large amounts of crude oil. Those states are home to major fossil fuel companies that have reported windfall profits amid Trump’s illegal war on Iran.

Trump insisted that gas prices — currently at an average of $4.33 per gallon for regular gas and $6.32 for diesel — would tumble once the Iran war ends, but his administration has repeatedly given false timelines for the deadly conflict and has shown no indication that it is willing to reach a lasting diplomatic agreement.

Trump, who has profited massively from his second term in the White House, is a major investor in oil and gas companies. According to one recent analysis, the president’s investments in fossil fuel stocks have boosted his net worth by up to $15.5 million since January.

Working-class Americans, meanwhile, are struggling to make ends meet as high gas prices compound a broader affordability crisis that extends to food, housing, and other necessities. A tracker maintained by the Watson School of International and Public Affairs estimates that American consumers have paid an extra $135 billion combined in fuel costs since the start of the Iran war — roughly $1,030 per household.

Wage growth has not kept up with inflation, which rose to an annualized rate of 3.7% last month.

“Workers are losing the race between wages and prices,” Elise Gould, senior economist at the Economic Policy Institute, wrote on Wednesday. “Nominal wage growth continues to decelerate as workers lose bargaining power at work. Workers simply don’t have the leverage to bid up their wages. Reduced leverage and higher prices translated into falling [year-over-year] real wages for six months in a row.”

“Workers have seen zero progress on affordability compared to January 2025,” Gould added. “Real wages are essentially stagnant as workers’ leverage has declined and prices have risen. It’s no wonder workers feel left behind in the current economy.”

A Harris poll published by The Guardian on Thursday shows that three-quarters of US voters are concerned about a recession, and a “vast majority of Americans agreed that there is an affordability crisis, including 96% of Republicans.”

Truthout is one of only a few platforms for justice-oriented, grassroots journalism. Today, we face an existential threat.

Due to Google’s launch of AI search, we’ve seen a drastic plunge in our site traffic and, as a result, our revenue. We lost 15 percent of our readership overnight. This was a readership we painstakingly built over decades, and it vanished because Google chose corporate greed over a healthy democracy.

We are fundraising right now to meet our basic operating expenses. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference — we appreciate your support.

author: Pauline Ertel
title: Brazil Abolishes Six-Day Workweek Ahead of Presidential Run-Off
content:
Brazil’s senate has approved a constitutional amendment ending the country’s six-day workweek, delivering a key pledge by president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva just days before an election run-off. 


The reform, passed on Wednesday, shortens the working week from 44 hours to a maximum of 40 hours and is set to

improve working conditions

 for more than 37 million people. That includes 16 million who work six-day weeks and are now guaranteed two days of rest each week without a reduction to their wages.


The amendment primarily affects workers in low paid industries such as retail and hospitality, one of the groups from which Lula has

lost suppor

t since defeating far-right incumbent Jair Bolsonaro in the 2022 election. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a failed coup in the wake of his defeat. 


Informal and gig economy workers, including app-based drivers without employment contracts, will not be covered by the new law.


Lula, who will face far-right Flávio Bolsonaro, the jailed former president’s son, for a second round on 25 October,

called the reform

 a “victory for the working class”. 


He

said on X

 the vote was “a historic achievement for millions of workers, who will now have more time to rest, be with their family, take care of themselves and live,” 


The victory may give Lula a much-needed boost; the leftwing incumbent came second behind Bolsonaro in the first round of voting on 4 October and is still trailing him in the polls, albeit by a

small margin

.


Brazilian trade unions and labour federations

welcomed the amendment,

which they said followed months of widespread

 strikes and protests by workers

. Advocates have been calling for the policy for years, but it gained

 more traction in 2023 thanks to a viral TikTok video by

 pharmacy clerk-turned-influencer Rick Azevedo.  


Bolsonaro long opposed the proposal, calling it an “opportunistic” attempt by Lula to appeal to working-class voters. But he reversed course shortly before the 4 October vote,

telling journalists

 that “most Brazilian workers ‌want to ⁠see the end of the six-day workweek.” 


Seventy-five senators, including Bolsonaro allies, voted in favour of the amendment. The only one to vote against it was former vice-president Hamilton Mourão, who worked under Jair Bolsonaro.

author: Gustavo Faleiros
title: Povos da floresta e do mar contra a extrema direita
content:
Quer receber os textos desta coluna em primeira mão no seu e-mail? Assine a newsletter Ligando os pontos, enviada toda quinta-feira. Para receber as próximas edições,

inscreva-se aqui

.


Em 1987, quando o Brasil acabava de sair das sinistras décadas de ditadura militar, surgiu uma união de forças sociais que até então pareciam distantes. Comunidades extrativistas e indígenas da Amazônia, vítimas históricas dos grileiros,

criaram a Aliança dos Povos da Floresta

. O momento não poderia ter sido mais propício pois, deste grupo, que contava com lideranças como Chico Mendes e Ailton Krenak, saíram propostas que influenciaram a nova Constituição, promulgada em 1988.


O impacto político daquele encontro não pode ser esquecido neste momento em que a extrema direita, representada pela candidatura de

Flávio Bolsonaro (PL)

, busca privatizar o patrimônio natural brasileiro. Se na década de 1980 a suposta direita conciliatória cedia terras públicas a empreendimentos agropecuários, hoje a direita quer privatizar as praias e abrir as terras indígenas para a mineração. 


A partir da união de seringueiros e indígenas, a luta dos povos da Amazônia foi projetada para o mundo, levando preocupação aos chefes dos bancos de desenvolvimento internacionais. O Banco Mundial e o Banco Interamericano de Desenvolvimento (BID) estavam liberando empréstimos para a criação de pólos de produção pecuária e financiando a abertura de estradas que cortavam os territórios tradicionais. Chico Mendes, em uma viagem emblemática a Washington, em 1987, conseguiu congelar alguns destes financiamentos e, como sabemos, pagou com a vida por sua coragem.


Mas sua luta sobreviveu: da profusão de ideias e da resistência criada surgiram outras lideranças, entre elas Marina Silva, a mais jovem senadora a ser eleita pelo Acre, na década de 1990, e depois a ministra de Meio Ambiente nas gestões de Lula. Ela levou a política ambiental para o coração do governo e conseguiu, com o apoio dos melhores cientistas e gestores, provar que é possível conter o desmatamento.


No momento em que escrevo estas linhas, saem notícias mostrando que, em

2025, as taxas de derrubadas

 no Brasil atingiram nova baixa histórica. E o melhor, estes resultados já não estão se restringindo à Amazônia. Os dados do Deter, o sistema de alertas de desmatamento do INPE, mostraram

uma redução de 30% em setembro

 no Cerrado. Uma notícia fantástica, uma vez que este é o bioma sob maior pressão, onde a ilegalidade e invasão de terras prosperaram nos últimos anos. 


Um dos alicerces da política de Lula e Marina para barrar a sanha destruidora é exatamente o combate à grilagem de terras e a promoção da regularização fundiária.

Estudos de renomadas organizações não governamentais

 como o Instituto de Pesquisas da Amazônia (IPAM) têm mostrado que, nos últimos anos, com os embargos e a repressão ao desmatamento em propriedades privadas, os criminosos passaram a fazer mais queimadas e derrubadas em unidades de conservação e terras indígenas.


A grilagem de terras e a invasão de territórios indígenas definem muito o que é o Brasil. Nossa história colonial foi brutal contra os povos da floresta e seus efeitos sobre o nosso cotidiano perduram até hoje, como a persistência da violência no campo e as ameaças constantes sofridas por comunidades rurais.

Nesta polarização tremenda que vive o país, temos falado muito do interior e como a cultura do agro tem ajudado a definir os votos. Mas somos um país atlântico, com identidade litorânea e com uma conexão muito forte com as praias. Por isso, enquanto alertamos para o que está ocorrendo na floresta, não podemos deixar de apontar a especulação imobiliária que pode vir a transformar a costa brasileira.


A Proposta de Emenda Constitucional para regularizar a venda dos terrenos da Marinha

gerou enorme polêmica em 2024

. E agora, nesta eleição, voltou ao debate, pois ninguém menos do que Flávio Bolsonaro é o relator da proposta, que ficou conhecida como a PEC da Privatização das Praias. A ideia é permitir a venda de terras que ficam numa faixa que começa a 33 metros dos pontos mais altos de maré e que pertencem historicamente à União. O argumento dos defensores da proposta é de que isso levaria mais investimentos, em forma de condomínios e resorts, ao nosso litoral. Na prática, isso pode se tornar uma forma de fechar acessos e criar praias exclusivas para os donos do dinheiro.


Diante desta ameaça, fiquei imaginando se não seria o momento da Aliança …

author: Unknown
title: Second death sentence for Warisha Moradi
content:
Warisha Moradi, a Kurdish political prisoner and women’s rights activist, has been sentenced to death for a second time by Branch 15 of Tehran’s Revolutionary Court. This time, the charge is of “membership in a rebel group”.


Her lawyers say the court issued the new sentence without completing the investigations requested by the Supreme Court, and simply changed the charge. The Supreme Court had overturned her first death sentence because of incomplete investigations and procedural violations. Her lawyers say there is insufficient evidence to support the charge and will appeal within the 20-day deadline.


Moradi has been in detention since the summer of 2023.

title: Talabani receives Bakırhan, reaffirms PUK’s support for the peace process in Turkey
content:
Bafel Jalal Talabani, President of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK), received Tuncer Bakırhan, Co-Chair of the DEM Party, in Dabashan.


The meeting on Wednesday was attended by Shanaz Ibrahim Ahmed and Dr Yousif Goran, members of the PUK Political Bureau, and Salar Lala Sarhad, Head of the Kurdistani Relations Board. Discussions focused on continuing joint coordination and cooperation and strengthening bilateral relations in pursuit of shared interests and greater regional stability.


The two sides also exchanged views on the peace process in Turkey. Bafel Talabani reaffirmed the PUK’s support for this historic initiative, stating: “We will continue to follow the same policy pursued by President Mam Jalal until this vital and decisive process succeeds. We believe that peace and coexistence enable us to serve our people, whereas war and division bring nothing but destruction. I therefore hope that everyone will turn a new page and work towards lasting peace.”


For his part, Bakırhan thanked Talabani and the PUK for their efforts to advance the peace process, saying: “We highly value your role and appreciate your steps in support of stability and peaceful coexistence in the region.”


Photos: PUKMEDIA

author: Unknown
title: Savary-Borioli: If Turkey wants peace, it must release Öcalan
content:
Swiss politician and emergency physician Dr. Beppe Savary-Borioli believes that a lasting resolution to the Kurdish question is hardly conceivable without Abdullah Öcalan’s freedom and the fundamental democratization of Turkey. Speaking to ANF, the member of the Ticino cantonal parliament expressed serious doubts about the Turkish government’s willingness to secure the current peace process through binding political and legal guarantees. At the same time, he sees Öcalan’s concept of democratic confederalism as offering a perspective that extends beyond the Kurdish question.


Since Öcalan’s February 27, 2025, Call for Peace and Democratic Society, the Kurdish freedom movement has taken far-reaching steps toward ending the armed struggle against Turkey. According to Savary-Borioli, however, the future of this process depends crucially on whether Ankara is prepared to establish the political conditions necessary for a negotiated settlement on equal terms.


https://1649452211.rsc.cdn77.org/20261013215028_2026-10-14-habermerkezi-dr-beppe-savary-isvicreli-siyasetci-baris-icin-ocalan-ozgur-olmali-1.mp4


“If Turkey truly wants peace, it must release Öcalan”


Savary-Borioli described Öcalan’s continued imprisonment as a fundamental contradiction within the peace process. He stated that a government genuinely seeking a political settlement must allow the Kurdish side’s most important negotiating partner to fulfill his role freely.


“The crucial question for me is this: If Turkey truly wants peace, it must release Öcalan. As long as it fails to do so, everything else lacks credibility,” Savary-Borioli stated.


The politician criticized the authoritarian system of government under President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, comparing his approach to power to that of a sultan. By contrast, he described Öcalan as one of the most important figures capable of making a shared, peaceful future possible for the Kurdish and Turkish populations. Savary-Borioli also referred to the experience of South Africa’s peace process, noting that negotiations to end apartheid gained decisive momentum only after Nelson Mandela’s release. He sees a similar prerequisite for Turkey.


“We cannot speak of negotiations on equal terms when one side is represented by a prisoner and the other by a president who behaves like a sultan. That is simply impossible.”


Doubts about the Turkish government’s guarantees


Savary-Borioli considers the Kurdish freedom movement’s strategic decision to end the armed struggle in favor of political and diplomatic means an important step. However, he believes, a unilateral change in strategy cannot guarantee lasting peace. In particular, he doubts that the Turkish government will actually fulfill its obligations toward former PKK members. A state that disregards international legal norms must first demonstrate that its commitments are credible and reliable, he underlines.


In this context, Savary-Borioli recalled the symbolic burning of weapons by the Kurdish freedom movement in July 2025, which he had personally attended. He said the action had demonstrated the movement’s political will but had not prompted any immediate corresponding steps from the state.


“I remain skeptical. Will a state like Turkey, which does not respect international law, actually honor the guarantees it gives to PKK members after they lay down their weapons?” Savary-Borioli asked. He therefore continues to observe current developments with considerable caution. What matters, he stressed, is not political announcements but verifiable changes to the legal and democratic framework.


Democratization as the foundation for coexistence


Savary-Borioli sees the democratization of the Turkish state as another prerequisite for a lasting political settlement. He argued that the political system is heavily centered on the presidency, while parliament has only limited influence over fundamental decisions.


“Under these conditions, any peace agreement would remain politically uncertain, as its implementation would depend on the position of the country’s leadership at any given time. As long as Turkey does not become a genuinely democratic state, it is extremely difficult to imagine real peace between the Kurdish and Turkish peoples,” Savary-Borioli stated.


He explicitly distinguished between the Turkish population and the government or military. He remarked that the people of both societies could and should live together peacefully. However, this would require …

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!
